Solis user guide

This manual describes what Solis can do right now. It grows with every update: a feature appears here when it reaches the main version, not before.

New to game engines? Start with Concepts, then build your first 2D platformer.

The manual is also the user guide: all its pages as one page to read in your browser, with a search, opened by Documentation at the top right of the editor (The user guide).

Search with the box at the top (press / or Ctrl+K), or pick a chapter on the left. Every heading has a link of its own: point at it and click the # beside it to copy where it is.

Next → · Chapter 1Getting started

Getting started#

How to get Solis onto your computer and open it.

When to use it#

The first time, and whenever you want the newest version.

How to use it#

Install it (Windows, recommended): download solis-setup.exe from the newest release on the repository's Releases page and run it. Solis then updates itself whenever a new build is merged. See Installing and updating.

Or download the program on its own:

  1. Open the Solis repository on GitHub and go to the Actions tab.
  2. Click the newest run of Windows EXE.
  3. At the bottom of the page, download solis-windows.
  4. Unzip it anywhere and double-click dist\solis.exe. (The setup folder beside it holds the installer.)

A copy run this way doesn't update itself. Each download stays available for 30 days.

Build it yourself:

  1. Install Rust from rustup.rs↗.
  2. In the solis folder, run cargo run --release -p app. The first build takes a few minutes; later ones are quicker.
  3. For Documentation to open the user guide, put the guide beside your build once: cargo run -p user-guide -- --out target/release/user-guide/index.html. A downloaded or installed copy has it already.

Opening with a model: solis --import ship.glb opens Solis and imports the model straight away (repeat --import for more than one).

Settings#

Solis remembers your panel layout, accent colour, interface scale, camera and viewport controls in your user folder, so each start looks like the last.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Windows warns that the program is from an unknown publisher. Why: the program isn't signed with a paid certificate yet. Fix: choose More info, then Run anyway.
  • Problem: the viewport says "No 3D view" and a reason. Why: Solis couldn't use the graphics card. Fix: update your graphics drivers. The rest of the editor still works.

Related#

  • Interface tour
  • Your first 2D platformer: once Solis is running, start here.
← PreviousWelcomeNext → · Chapter 2Getting started: your first 2D platformer

Getting started: your first 2D platformer#

Build a small platformer from an empty project, step by step: a level of solid ground, a hero who runs and jumps, a camera that follows, and coins to collect. Along the way you learn the editor and your first Lust code.

When to use it#

Start here if you're new to Solis, to Lust, or to making games at all. It takes about an hour, and needs no art skills: the level is drawn in plain colours, and the hero and coins are two tiny pictures you can make in any paint program.

You'll learn:

  • the editor's parts: the Library, the viewport, Properties and the Area panel;
  • entities and components: how everything in a game is built;
  • tile maps for the level, and 2D settings that keep pixel art crisp;
  • writing components in Lust: fields, update, dt, input, and fetching one file from another.

Each step says why as well as what, so you can change things and make the game your own. Where a step uses a feature, it links to that feature's own page if you want more.

How to use it#

1. Make a project and an area#

A project is a folder holding everything your game is made of. An area is one level (or menu, or room) in it.

  1. File › New project (or New project on Recent projects), make an empty folder called Platformer, and choose it.
  2. Save the empty area: Ctrl + S, name it level. Solis suggests the assets/areas folder; that's fine.
  3. Look in pixels: click the Perspective ▾ pill at the top left of the viewport and choose 2D. The view now looks straight at the world as the game will. Hold the right or middle mouse button and drag to slide it; turn the wheel to zoom.

Why 2D? A platformer is seen from the side. In Solis, a 2D game lies flat and is seen from straight above, so across the screen is x and up the screen is y. The project's 2D settings (File › Project settings) say 16 pixels make one metre, so one 16-pixel tile is one metre. Every number in this guide is in metres, so think of a metre as a tile.

2. Build the level from tiles#

A tile map is a grid of cells, each painted with a terrain. Terrains come from a tileset. We need two: sky (empty air) and ground (solid).

  1. Make the tileset: right-click an empty spot in the Library and choose New › Tileset. Solis makes one with three terrains (grass, tilled, water) and opens it in the Tileset tab.
  2. Turn grass into sky: choose grass, and in Properties rename it sky and make its colour light blue. The first terrain fills every new map, which is why the sky goes first.
  3. Turn tilled into ground: rename it ground and make it brown. Leave water as it is.
  4. Make the map: New › Tile map in the Library. It's filled with sky. Click it in the Library and, in Properties, set its Size to 60 across and 17 up: 17 tiles is about one screen high.
  5. Place it: double-click the map in the Library. It appears in the viewport, where you're looking.
  6. Select it in the Area panel. The Map tab opens beside Properties, and the painting tools appear at the bottom of the viewport.
  7. Make ground solid: in the Map tab, under Terrains, right-click ground's swatch and tick Solid. Solid cells are walls and floors: nothing with a body passes into them.
  8. Paint the level: left-click ground's swatch, then paint with the brush (B) or the rectangle (U). Make a floor along the bottom two rows, a wall up both ends (so the hero can't run off), and a few floating platforms two or three tiles above the floor and each other. Leave a gap in the floor somewhere if you like a challenge.
  9. Press Walls at the top of the viewport: green boxes show what's solid. Check the floor and walls have them.

Why tiles? Painting a level is much quicker than placing every block by hand, and Solis merges neighbouring solid cells into a few big walls, so the hero never catches on the seams between tiles.

3. Make the hero and a coin#

Any paint program will do (Aseprite, Paint, Krita, Photoshop).

  1. Draw a 16 × 16 picture for the hero: a simple figure, or just a coloured block with eyes. Make the space around it see-through. Save it as hero.png in the project's assets folder.
  2. Draw an 8 × 8 yellow circle and save it as coin.png beside it.

Both appear in the Library. A picture becomes a sprite when you place it: an entity that shows the picture, standing on the picture's bottom middle.

4. Place the hero and give it a body#

  1. Drag hero.png into the viewport, into the sky just above the floor. An entity called hero appears, with a Sprite component showing the picture.
  2. With it selected, in Properties choose + Component › Collider2D. This gives it a shape for 2D physics, drawn as a green outline.
  3. Set its Shape to Box, Width 12 and Height 16 (in pixels), and Up 8 so the box sits on the hero's feet instead of being cut in half by them.
  4. Tick Character. A character is moved by game code and stops at walls and floors instead of passing through them.

Why a box? A box stands flat on the edge of a platform, which is what a platformer needs. (Top-down games use a circle, which slips round corners.)

If you press Play now, nothing happens yet: the hero has a body, but nothing tells it to move. That's the code's job.

5. Write the hero's code#

Game code in Solis is written in Lust. A component you write in Lust works like Solis's own: you add it to an entity, set its fields in Properties, and its update runs every tick while the game plays (60 times a second).

  1. Right-click in the Library and choose New › Lust code file. The first one is always main.lst, at the top of assets: your game's code starts there. It opens in your code editor (Ledger).
  2. Make a second one the same way. It's called component.lst; right-click it, choose Rename… and call it hero.lst.
  3. Replace everything in hero.lst with this, and save:
-- hero.lst: the player. Runs left and right, falls, and jumps.
fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component Hero {
    has {
        float speed = 6;
        float jumpSpeed = 13;
        float gravity = 35;
        float fall = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Which way the player pushes: -1 is left, 1 is right, 0 is neither.
        float across = Input:axis(Action.Move).x;

        -- On the floor: stop falling, but keep a small push down, so the
        -- floor still stops it next tick and grounded() stays true.
        is grounded()? then {
            fall = -1;
        }
        -- Going up but stopped: it bumped its head, so start coming down.
        is fall > 0 && velocity().y <= 0? then {
            fall = 0;
        }
        -- Gravity: every tick, it falls a little faster.
        fall = fall - gravity * dt;
        -- Jump, but only from the floor.
        is grounded() && Input:pressed(Action.Jump)? then {
            fall = jumpSpeed;
        }

        walk([across * speed * dt, fall * dt, 0]);
    }
}

pass Hero;
end
// hero.rs: the player. Runs left and right, falls, and jumps.
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Hero {
    speed: f64,
    jump_speed: f64,
    gravity: f64,
    fall: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Hero {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();

        // Which way the player pushes: -1 is left, 1 is right, 0 is neither.
        let across = f64::from(cx.host().action("Move").axis.x);
        let grounded = cx.host().grounded(me);

        // On the floor: stop falling, but keep a small push down, so the
        // floor still stops it next tick and grounded() stays true.
        if grounded {
            self.fall = -1.0;
        }
        // Going up but stopped: it bumped its head, so start coming down.
        let rising = cx.host().velocity(me).unwrap_or_default().y;
        if self.fall > 0.0 && rising <= 0.0 {
            self.fall = 0.0;
        }
        // Gravity: every tick, it falls a little faster.
        self.fall -= self.gravity * dt;
        // Jump, but only from the floor.
        if grounded && cx.host().action("Jump").pressed {
            self.fall = self.jump_speed;
        }

        let step = Vec3::new((across * self.speed * dt) as f32, (self.fall * dt) as f32, 0.0);
        cx.host().walk(me, step);
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- hero.lua: the player. Runs left and right, falls, and jumps.
local Hero = component("Hero", {
    { "speed", "float", 6 },
    { "jumpSpeed", "float", 13 },
    { "gravity", "float", 35 },
    { "fall", "float", 0 },
})

function Hero:update(dt)
    -- Which way the player pushes: -1 is left, 1 is right, 0 is neither.
    local across = solis.Input:axis("Move").x
    local grounded = solis.entity.grounded(self.me)

    -- On the floor: stop falling, but keep a small push down, so the
    -- floor still stops it next tick and grounded() stays true.
    if grounded then
        self.fall = -1
    end
    -- Going up but stopped: it bumped its head, so start coming down.
    if self.fall > 0 and solis.entity.velocity(self.me).y <= 0 then
        self.fall = 0
    end
    -- Gravity: every tick, it falls a little faster.
    self.fall = self.fall - self.gravity * dt
    -- Jump, but only from the floor.
    if grounded and solis.Input:pressed("Jump") then
        self.fall = self.jumpSpeed
    end

    solis.entity.walk(self.me, vec3(across * self.speed * dt, self.fall * dt, 0))
end
  1. Open main.lst, replace everything in it with this, and save:
-- main.lst: where the game's code starts. It fetches the other files.
fetch "hero":[Hero];
fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[FollowCamera2D];
end
// main.lst is where Lust code starts; a Rust component needs none (Solis
// is told of it by its RustKind). The ready-made FollowCamera2D is Lust,
// so a game in Rust keeps a main.lst of two lines beside its Rust, to
// bring the camera in:
//
//     fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[FollowCamera2D];
//     end
-- main.lst is where Lust code starts; Lua files need none, since Solis
-- reads every .lua file in assets. The ready-made FollowCamera2D is
-- Lust, so a game in Lua keeps a main.lst of two lines, to bring the
-- camera in:
--
--     fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[FollowCamera2D];
--     end
  1. Solis checks your code a moment after each save. If you made a typing mistake, the Problems panel says where (click it to jump to the line). An empty Problems panel means the code is sound.

What the code says, line by line:

  • Lines starting with -- are comments: notes for people, which Lust skips.
  • fetch brings in names from another file. Input reads the player's controls, and Action holds their names: Action.Move is WASD or the arrow keys (or a gamepad's stick), Action.Jump is Space (or the gamepad's A). Players can change these keys in File › Project settings › Input without touching your code.
  • component Hero is a new kind of component. Everything in has is a field: a value each hero keeps, shown in Properties so you can change it there. fall is how fast the hero is going up (more than 0) or down (less than 0), in metres a second.
  • update(float dt) runs every tick. dt is how long a tick is, in seconds (about 1/60). Multiplying a speed by dt turns "metres a second" into "metres this tick", so the game runs the same speed on every computer.
  • is …? then { … } is Lust's if: the code in the braces runs only when the question is true.
  • grounded() is true when a floor stopped the hero's last move down. velocity() is how fast its last move really went.
  • walk([across, up, 0]) moves the hero this far, this tick, stopping at walls and floors and sliding along them. The three numbers are across, up and height; a 2D game ignores the height.
  • pass Hero; lets other files fetch it, and end ends the file.

Why main.lst fetches hero.lst: Lust reads main.lst first, then each file it fetches, and each file those fetch. A file nothing reaches isn't part of the game. For a big game, main.lst stays short and fetches a few files that each fetch their own; this is how code stays tidy as it grows.

6. Make it play#

  1. Select the hero. In Properties, choose + Component › Hero. Its four fields appear.
  2. Add a camera: Home › Camera. In the 2D view it's a 2D camera, and a dashed frame labelled Game screen shows what it sees.
  3. With the camera selected, + Component › FollowCamera2D. This is a ready-made component from Solis's kit. Set its target to the hero and its bounds to the map's entity, so it follows the hero and never shows past the map's edges.
  4. Save (Ctrl + S) and press Play. Click the Game panel so it gets the keys.
  5. Run with A and D (or the arrows), jump with Space. Press Stop when you're done: everything goes back to how it was before Play.

Make it feel right. While stopped, select the hero and change its fields in Properties, then play again:

  • speed: how fast it runs. 6 is brisk; 4 is a stroll.
  • jumpSpeed and gravity together set the jump. Higher gravity feels snappier and less floaty; a higher jumpSpeed jumps higher. With 13 and 35 it jumps about 2.4 tiles. Try 10 and 20 for a moon jump.

Changing the numbers in Properties changes only this hero. Changing the = 6 in the code changes the starting value of every hero made from now on.

7. Add coins to collect#

  1. Make another code file, rename it coin.lst, and replace everything in it with this:
-- coin.lst: a coin that disappears when the player touches it.
fetch "solis/world":World;

component Coin {
    has {
        entity player = nothing;
        float reach = 0.8;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        is player == nothing? then {
            return;
        }
        -- How far the player is, across and up.
        vec3 gap = player:position() - position();
        is gap.x * gap.x + gap.y * gap.y < reach * reach? then {
            World:say("Got a coin!");
            despawn();
        }
    }
}

pass Coin;
end
// coin.rs: a coin that disappears when the player touches it.
use reflect::EntityId;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Coin {
    player: Option<EntityId>,
    reach: f32,
}

impl RustComponent for Coin {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let Some(player) = self.player else {
            return;
        };
        let me = cx.me();
        // How far the player is, across and up.
        let there = cx.host().position(player).unwrap_or_default();
        let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        let gap = there - here;
        if gap.x * gap.x + gap.y * gap.y < self.reach * self.reach {
            cx.host().say("Got a coin!");
            cx.host().despawn(me);
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- coin.lua: a coin that disappears when the player touches it.
local Coin = component("Coin", {
    { "player", "entity" },
    { "reach", "float", 0.8 },
})

function Coin:update(dt)
    if self.player == nil then
        return
    end
    -- How far the player is, across and up.
    local gap = solis.entity.position(self.player) - solis.entity.position(self.me)
    if gap.x * gap.x + gap.y * gap.y < self.reach * self.reach then
        solis.World:say("Got a coin!")
        solis.entity.despawn(self.me)
    end
end
  1. In main.lst, add a line fetching the coin under the hero's, and save. It now reads:
-- main.lst: where the game's code starts. It fetches the other files.
fetch "hero":[Hero];
fetch "coin":[Coin];
fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[FollowCamera2D];
end
// Nothing to add in Rust: Solis is told of the Coin by its RustKind,
// as of the Hero.
-- Nothing to add in Lua: Solis reads coin.lua by itself, as it reads
-- every .lua file in assets.
  1. Drag coin.png into the viewport, somewhere the hero can reach (on a platform, say). + Component › Coin, and set its player to the hero.
  2. Make more coins: select the coin and press Ctrl + D to duplicate it, then drag the copy somewhere else. Copies keep their Coin and its player.
  3. Play. Touch a coin: it vanishes, and the Console says Got a coin!

What's new here:

  • entity player = nothing; is a field holding another entity: the one you pick in Properties. nothing means none is picked yet, and return stops update early, so a coin without a player does nothing instead of going wrong.
  • player:position() asks another entity where it is; position() on its own asks this one.
  • gap.x * gap.x + gap.y * gap.y < reach * reach checks the distance without a square root (Pythagoras, both sides squared): the player is within reach metres.
  • despawn() removes the coin from the running game. When you Stop, it comes back, since Play never changes your area.

8. Where to go next#

You've built a game and written two components. Some ideas, each with its page:

  • Animate the hero with frames for running and jumping: draw them in Aseprite as tags, then see Sprites from Aseprite, Animating sprites and Animators.
  • Real tile art instead of colours: give the terrains pictures in the Tileset tab (Tilesets and autotiling).
  • A sky and hills that move slower than the ground, for depth: Parallax layers.
  • A coin counter on screen: Game screens and the UI editor.
  • Sounds for jumping and coins: Sounds and Sound events.
  • Send it to a friend: Exporting for playtesting.
  • Learn more Lust: Game code covers events, spawning and more. This guide teaches Lust; the same game can be written in Lua or Rust (see Which language when): the switch above each example shows it in all three.

Settings#

The fields of the two components you wrote:

ComponentFieldWhat it does
HerospeedHow fast it runs, in metres (tiles) a second.
HerojumpSpeedHow fast it leaves the ground when it jumps. Higher jumps higher.
HerogravityHow quickly it falls faster. Higher feels snappier; lower, floatier.
HerofallHow fast it's going up or down right now. The code sets it; leave it at 0.
CoinplayerWho can collect it. Pick the hero.
CoinreachHow close, in metres, the player must come to collect it.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
RunA D, the arrow keys, or a gamepad's left stick
JumpSpace, or a gamepad's A
Slide the 2D viewHold right or middle mouse, drag
Zoom the 2D viewMouse wheel
Paint with the brush or the rectangle (map selected)B, U
DuplicateCtrl+D
SaveCtrl+S

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the hero falls through the floor. Why: the ground terrain isn't solid, or the hero's Collider2D isn't ticked Character. Fix: right-click ground's swatch in the Map tab and tick Solid (press Walls to check), and check the Collider2D.
  • Problem: nothing happens when I press keys. Why: the Game panel doesn't have the keys, or the hero has no Hero component. Fix: click inside the Game panel while playing; check Properties for Hero; check Problems for mistakes in the code.
  • Problem: Hero or Coin isn't in the + Component list. Why: the code has a mistake, or main.lst doesn't fetch the file (a file nothing fetches isn't part of the game). Fix: look in Problems, and check the fetch lines in main.lst.
  • Problem: the Game panel shows only sky. Why: the camera isn't following, or is looking somewhere else. Fix: check the camera's FollowCamera2D target is the hero.
  • Problem: the hero sometimes won't jump. Why: it only jumps from the floor, and you pressed Space while it was still in the air. Fix: that's how it's meant to work; for a more forgiving jump, see the idea below.
  • Problem: the hero's feet sink into the floor or float above it. Why: the box isn't lined up with the picture. Fix: set the Collider2D's Up to half its Height.
  • Idea: many platformers let you jump a moment after running off a ledge ("coyote time"). Try it yourself: keep a field counting the time since the hero was last grounded, and allow a jump while it's under 0.1 seconds.

Related#

  • Concepts: the words used here.
  • Walls and walking in 2D: solid terrains, Collider2D and walk.
  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view and Characters and cameras (FollowCamera2D).
  • Game code and Input.
  • Your first game: the turret sample: a 3D example, in all three languages.

Installing and updating#

Install Solis once, and File › Updates tells you about every new build from GitHub.

When to use it#

The first time you get Solis, and any time you want to know which build you have or get the newest one now. After installing, you don't need to do anything: new builds arrive by themselves.

If you'd rather not install anything, you can still download the program on its own (see Getting started). That copy doesn't update itself.

How to use it#

Install it (once):

  1. Open the Solis repository on GitHub and click Releases on the right (or go to github.com/Rhyslos/solis/releases).
  2. Under the newest release (Solis build and a number), download solis-setup.exe.
  3. Run it. If Windows says it protected your PC, click More info, then Run anyway. (Solis isn't signed with a paid certificate yet, so Windows doesn't know the publisher.)
  4. Accept the licence.
  5. Choose where to install it, or keep the suggested folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Solis, in your own user folder). Any folder your Windows account can write to works, on any drive. It never asks for an administrator, so only your Windows account gets Solis.
  6. Choose whether you want a desktop shortcut, click Install, leave Open Solis ticked and click Finish.

Solis is now in the Start menu (with its logo, a glowing swirl round a dark centre), and in Windows' Settings > Apps where you can uninstall it. If you ticked the box, there's a desktop shortcut too.

How updates work:

  1. When Solis starts, it asks GitHub in the background whether there's a newer build, and opens Recent projects straight away: nothing waits for the answer, and offline nothing happens.
  2. If there's a newer build, the status bar says so at its right: Build 58 is out (click it), and Updates in the File column gets a New mark. File › Updates has a card across its top about it.
  3. Choose, on that card:
    • Download: the card says Downloading build 58… while Solis checks the download's SHA-256 against the one GitHub published (and throws it away if they differ). Then it says the build is downloaded: Restart to update closes Solis (asking about unsaved work first), installs it and opens the new build; or keep working, and it installs when you close Solis.
    • What the build brings is beside it, on the same page.
    • Not now: the card goes until Solis starts again.
  4. A copy you didn't install with the setup file (a downloaded solis.exe, run from its zip) never updates itself: it downloads nothing and installs nothing. Updating it would put a second, installed copy somewhere else on the computer and leave the one you run as old as before. So it only tells you: there's no Download; the Console says Build 58 of Solis is out, but this copy wasn't installed with the installer, Updates in the File column still gets its New mark, and the Updates page offers Open the releases page in place of Download. Get solis-setup.exe there and run it once, or download the newer zip.

Check now: File › Updates › Check now (or press Space and type Check for updates). If there's a newer build, the same window asks, even about a build you skipped. Update now then downloads it while you keep working, and Restart to update appears in the tab bar at the top, just left of the project's name: click it (Solis asks about unsaved work first), or keep working and the update installs when you close Solis. In a copy you didn't install, the window's button is Open the download page instead. The line under Check for updates says how it went: Up to date (build 57), Build 58 is available, Downloading build 58…, Build 58 is out: install it to update by itself (a copy you didn't install), or what went wrong.

The Updates page: File › Updates puts the same steps in one place: the build you have, the newest build and what it brings, Check now, Download (or Open the releases page, in a copy you didn't install) and Restart to update. A New mark beside Updates says a newer build is out.

Which build do I have? File › About shows the version and build number, as does the window's title.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Check for updates when starting (press Space and type it)On (the usual): Solis asks GitHub for a newer build each time it starts, and File › Updates and the status bar say so when there is one. The same switch is on Preferences › General and on the Updates page. Off: nothing is asked of GitHub unless you choose Check for updates. Remembered between starts.
Skip this version (in the update window from File › Updates › Check now)Stops Solis mentioning that one build. A newer build is shown again; Check for updates always shows what's newest.

Shortcuts#

None: updating has no keys.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: File › Project settings says Built from source: no updates beside Engine version. Why: you built Solis yourself with Cargo, so it has no build number to compare. Fix: install it with the setup file to get updates, or update your own copy with git pull.
  • Problem: the Console says a newer build is out, but this copy wasn't installed with the installer, and there's no Update now. Why: you're running a downloaded solis.exe (from a zip). Solis only updates a copy its installer put there, so this one is never downloaded for or changed. Fix: install with solis-setup.exe once (the Updates page's Open the releases page goes there); from then on it updates.
  • Problem: Couldn't check: couldn't reach GitHub. Why: the computer is offline, or something blocks GitHub. Fix: nothing to do; it tries again later. Your work isn't affected.
  • Problem: GitHub asked to wait before checking again. Why: GitHub limits how often one computer may ask (60 times an hour). Fix: wait an hour.
  • Problem: Couldn't check for updates: the download stopped: the response body is larger than request limit. Why: the first builds, published on 25 and 26 October 2026, had a mistake that refused every finished download. Fix: download the newest solis-setup.exe from the Releases page and run it once; it updates itself from then on.
  • Problem: a download didn't match its checksum. Why: it was damaged or cut short on the way. Fix: it was thrown away; Solis downloads it again next time.
  • What Solis sends: only the request itself, naming the program and its version (GitHub asks every program to). Nothing about you or your projects.
  • Problem: the installer says it can't be installed in the folder you chose. Why: your account can't write there without an administrator (Program Files, say), and Solis must be able to replace itself when it updates. Fix: choose a folder of your own.
  • Moving Solis to another folder: uninstall it (Settings > Apps), then run the setup file again and choose the new folder. Updates always go to the folder you installed in.
  • What's in the installed folder: the program, its licence (LICENSE, MIT), THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt (the open-source libraries built into Solis, with their licences) and the fonts' licences in licenses.
  • Your projects and settings are kept through every update: they live in your project folders and your user folder, not where Solis is installed.

Related#

  • Getting started
  • Concepts: builds, releases, installers and SHA-256

Concepts#

The ideas this manual uses, in plain words. Other pages link here the first time they use a term.

The editor and the engine#

  • Engine: the program a game runs on. It draws the picture, plays the sound, runs the physics and the game's own code. When a game ships, the engine goes with it.
  • Editor: the window you build a game in. Games ship without it. In Solis the engine is written in Rust; game code can be written in Lust, Rust or Lua; see Game code.

The window#

  • Panel: one area of the editor with one job, such as the Viewport or the Console. Each lives in a fixed place: a document in an editor group, or a column of a shelf tab.
  • Editor group: the top part of the middle of the window: a strip of document tabs (the area, the running game, an animator) over the one in front. A tab can show two groups side by side, with a line between them you can drag. See Interface tour.
  • Document: what an editor group shows, with a tab of its own: the area, the Game, an animator, a tileset, a screen. A document that is a file has a × that closes it.
  • Docking: in some programs, dragging panels to any place you like. Solis doesn't do that: each tab's screen is laid out as its design draws it, and you size its parts instead (every border between them drags). Home's three lists can sit in one of four panel layouts. A document's tab can be dragged to a half of the middle, or onto another group's tabs, to split or join groups.
  • Page: a screen that is one sheet of settings or words rather than panels: a File page, the Build tab's Export for playtesting, an unfinished screen's card.
  • Dialog card: a question that stops your work until you answer it, as a card over the dimmed window: unsaved changes, a file changed on disk, keeping what you changed while playing. The main answer is in the accent colour at the right; one that sets your work aside stands at the left.
  • Layout: how a tab's screen is sized: the shelf tab in front, whether the shelf is folded, the size of every border you dragged (the shelf's height, the split between groups, the side columns, the Assets strip, the shelf's columns), and any document dragged to a group of its own. Each tab remembers its own, for each panel layout; a double-click on a border puts that one back, and Reset layout (in the search, and in File › Preferences) puts the whole tab back as it started.
  • Panel layout: where Home's three lists (the Area tree, Properties and Assets) sit, chosen in File › Preferences › Appearance: as tall columns beside the area, with Assets as a strip under it (Area left, Assets bottom, the standard), stacked on the left (Area and Assets on the left), stacked on the right (Area left, Assets right), or side by side on the shelf (The shelf (as designed)). See Interface tour.
  • Border: the thin line between two parts of the window (two columns, a column and the area, the shelf and what's above it, two editor groups). Point at one and the pointer becomes a two-headed arrow: drag to give one side more room, double-click to put it back.
  • Tab bar: the dark strip along the top of the window: the logo, the tabs (File, Home, Library and so on), the search box, the open project and area, and the chevron that collapses the ribbon. See Interface tour.
  • Workspace: what one tab of the tab bar shows for one kind of work: Home for building areas, Library for files, Animate for sprites, UI for game screens, Audio for the mixer, Debug for testing the game, Build for exporting it. Each has its own editor groups and shelf, and remembers its own layout. See Interface tour.
  • Accent colour: the one colour the editor uses to mark what's chosen or in front: the front tab's underline, the chosen tool, the selected row. Everything else is a neutral grey, so the accent is easy to spot. Blue unless you pick another of the five in Settings. Colours that mean something keep their own: Play (Stop, while the game runs) is the one light button, and errors are red.
  • Interface scale: how large the whole editor is drawn, as a percentage, set in Settings. At 150% every button, word and gap is half as large again. It's for screens whose pixels are too small to read at 100%; it doesn't change your game.
  • Density: how much room the editor's controls take, set in Settings: Compact, Default or Comfortable. It changes the height of buttons and fields, not the size of text.
  • Unfinished part: a place in the editor for a feature that isn't built yet. Solis's interface follows one design, which has room for things that come in later updates; each is shown where it will be, in grey with a small hollow square, and does nothing but say so. One setting hides them all. Other programs call such a thing a placeholder. See Unfinished parts.
  • Ribbon: the band of buttons under the tabs along the top: each tab (Home, Library, Animate and so on) shows its own buttons there, gathered into named groups, with the Play group at its right end. It took the place of the menus. See Interface tour.
  • Contextual tab: a tab of the tab bar that is there only while something it works on is open or selected, after the tab it belongs to: Home tools · Tile map while a tile map is selected, Library tools · Tileset while a tileset is open, Library tools · Picture while a picture's crops are, Library tools · Model while the model viewer (not built yet) is in front. Its small capitals say which tab it belongs to. Its ribbon holds the tools for that one thing, so they are out of the way the rest of the time. See Painting tiles, Tilesets and Atlas Crop.
  • File page: what the File tab shows in place of the ribbon and the editor: a column of items down the left (Recent projects, New project, Open…, Project settings, Preferences, Learn, Updates, About, Exit) and the page chosen beside it. Solis starts on File › Recent projects. Esc or Back to editor leaves it. See Projects and Settings.
  • Placing: Home with its Place shelf tab in front: the ribbon in its building form and the files that can be placed in the Assets list, ready to drag into the area. See Projects and the Library.
  • Shelf: the wide band along the bottom of the window, under the editor groups, with tabs of its own on its bar: on Home, Place, the Console, Problems and, in the shelf panel layout, Entity (the Area tree, Properties and the Assets column side by side). Drag its grip or its top edge to size it; Ctrl + Space folds it to its bar and back. See Interface tour.
  • Pill: a small see-through button floating over the viewport, such as Perspective ▾ or the frame time. Pills keep the picture as large as it can be. See Moving around the viewport.
  • Card: a lifted box holding a few settings that belong together, such as one component in Properties. Cards sit side by side as many as fit.
  • Status bar: the thin strip along the very bottom: whether the code is clean, the problems' counts, what's going on, and the version. See Interface tour.

The 3D view#

  • Viewport: the panel that shows the 3D world as the editor's camera sees it.
  • Z is up. Solis measures height along Z. The ground is the flat X and Y directions.
  • Axes: the three directions in 3D. Solis colours them the same everywhere: X red, Y green, Z blue. The red and green lines across the ground are the X and Y axes; they cross at the origin (the point 0, 0, 0).
  • Metres: one unit in Solis is one metre. The grid's small squares are 1 metre across.
  • Grid: lines on the ground to judge size and distance by. Brighter lines mark every 10 and 100 metres. The grid fades out with distance so it doesn't clutter the horizon.
  • Flat view (orthographic): a view from straight above, the front or the side, where things keep their size however far away they are, so edges and heights line up exactly. The usual view, where far things look smaller, is perspective. See Moving around the viewport.
  • View: one picture in the viewport, with its own camera. The viewport can show one, two or four at once.
  • Fly camera: the way you move around the viewport: you steer the camera like a drone. See Moving around the viewport.

The area#

  • Area: everything in one place of your game (a level, a menu, a room), made of entities. Other engines call this a scene. Each area is saved as one .solarea text file; see Saving areas. See Entities and components.
  • Entity: one thing in an area: a model, a light, the sky. On its own it's only a name; its components make it something.
  • Component: one part of what an entity is, with settings. A Transform says where it is; a Light makes it shine; a Model draws an imported model. Mixing components makes different things, the way one Lego brick goes into many builds.
  • Transform: an entity's position, rotation and scale.
  • Assembly: a group of entities saved once and placed many times; each placed copy follows the assembly but can have its own changes. Other engines call it a prefab. See Assemblies.
  • Unpack: turning a copy of an assembly, or an imported model, into separate ordinary entities.
  • Parent and child: an entity can belong to another, like a lamp to the room model it came with. A child moves with its parent, and deleting the parent deletes its children. A child's position is measured from its parent, so moving the parent carries it along.
  • Brush: a shape made in the editor itself (a box, a ramp, stairs), kept in the area and solid in the game, for blocking out a level before (or instead of) making models. See Brushes.
  • Brush list: the list of shapes a brush can start as (Box, Ramp, Cylinder, Stairs, Arch, Sphere, Wedge), opened with B over the view or Home's Shape button. See Brushes.
  • Drawing out: making a brush with the mouse: drag its footprint (the shape's outline on the ground, its two sides), then move the mouse up for its height and click. See Brushes.
  • Mesh: a shape made of points joined into flat faces, each face's sides being its edges. Models and brushes are meshes; a brush's faces can have any number of corners, and are cut into triangles to draw.
  • Point, edge, face: the parts of a mesh. A point (a corner, also called a vertex) is one spot; an edge is the straight side between two points, where two faces meet; a face is one flat side, its edges all the way round. Editing a brush's insides moves these. A face is bent when its corners aren't all on one flat plane: allowed, and cut into triangles to draw. See Brushes.
  • Editing a brush's insides: working on a brush's points, edges or faces instead of the whole brush, started with Tab. See Brushes.
  • Block-out: a first, rough version of a level made of simple shapes, to try how it plays before anything is modelled.
  • Instance: one copy of a mesh drawn somewhere. A mesh used many times (a crate in a hundred places) is stored once and drawn as many instances, which is much faster than storing a hundred crates.

Projects#

  • Lust data file: a Lust file that only holds values, read by Solis without running anything. Everything Solis makes (tile maps, tilesets, and the rest as they move over) is one, named for what it holds: farm.tilemap.lst. See Backups and upgrades.
  • Project: a folder holding one game: its assets, settings and areas. See Projects and the Library.
  • Recent projects: the File page Solis starts on, listing your projects as cards, where you open, pin and tidy them, and start from a template. It was once called the launcher. See Projects.
  • Build: one numbered version of Solis, made from the code at one moment (build 57, then 58). Installed copies update from one build to the next; each project remembers the build that last opened it.
  • Asset: a file the game uses: a model, a picture, a sound, an assembly, code.
  • Sidecar: the small .solmeta text file beside each asset holding its ID, so renaming the file breaks nothing. Commit it with the asset.
  • Library: the panel showing the project's files, folder by folder, with thumbnails; drag from it to place things.
  • Thumbnail: a small picture of a file, so you can see what a model or picture is without opening it.
  • Recycle Bin: where deleted files wait until you empty it; deleting in the Library sends files there, so nothing is lost by accident.
  • Cache: files Solis makes to work faster (models it has already read). Safe to delete: they're made again.
  • Hot reload: a changed file shows in Solis straight away, without restarting.
  • Format version: a number at the top of each file Solis saves, saying how it's laid out. When an update changes the layout, the number goes up and the update brings an upgrader, so older files keep opening. Before Solis saves an older file in the new layout, it keeps a copy in .solis/backups/. See Backups and upgrades.

Models#

  • Model: a 3D object made in a modelling program (Blender, Aventail): its shape, and how its surface looks. See Importing models.
  • glTF: the standard file format for game models, in two forms: .glb (everything in one file) and .gltf (a text file, with its data and textures in files beside it).
  • Mesh: a model's shape, made of triangles.
  • Triangle: the smallest piece of a 3D shape. Graphics cards draw everything as triangles; a game character has a few thousand to tens of thousands.
  • Level of detail (LOD): a simpler version of a mesh, with fewer triangles, drawn when a copy is so small on screen that the difference can't be seen. Solis makes them on import, or uses a model's own (named _LOD1 and so on). See Levels of detail.
  • Material: how a surface looks: its colour, how shiny, how see-through.
  • Texture: an image wrapped around a model, giving it detail (paint, wood grain, panels).
  • Metallic and roughness: the two numbers that decide how a surface shines. Metal reflects its surroundings; rough surfaces spread their shine out until it disappears.
  • Normal texture: a texture that stores small bumps and grooves as directions, so a flat surface catches the light as if it were carved. It looks light blue, because "facing straight out" is stored as blue.
  • Look: how models are shaded in the viewport: standard, stylized (cel-shaded) or unlit. See Looks.

Light#

  • Sun: light from very far away, arriving in parallel from one direction everywhere, like daylight. One per area. See Lights and shadows.
  • Lamp: a light in the area. A point light shines every way from one spot, like a bare bulb; a spotlight shines a cone, like a torch or a stage light.
  • Watts (W): how strong a lamp is, in the same units as Blender, so numbers carry over. The sun's strength is in watts per square metre (W/m²).
  • Range: how far a lamp reaches. Real light fades on forever, getting weaker with distance; a range makes it stop sooner, which games use to keep many lamps cheap.
  • Shadow: where something blocks a light. Solis draws the sun's shadows with a shadow map: the area drawn once more from the sun's side, so each point can be checked for whether it sees the sun.
  • Sky light (ambient light): the soft light that comes from the whole sky rather than from the sun, so shadows are never black.
  • HDR (high dynamic range): working out light brighter than a screen's white, as the real world is: a sunlit wall can be many times brighter than a shaded one.
  • Exposure: how bright the picture is made, in stops (EV) as on a camera: +1 doubles the brightness, -1 halves it.
  • Tone mapping: squeezing HDR light into what a screen can show, so bright highlights roll off softly instead of turning flat white. Solis uses AgX, as Blender does, unless you choose otherwise.
  • Fog: distant things fading into a colour, as in haze or mist. It gives a sense of distance and depth.

Tools#

  • Tool: what a click in the viewport does: Select, Move, Rotate, Scale or Transform, chosen in the toolbox (the column down the viewport's left edge) or by key. See Selecting and moving things.
  • Selection: the entities you're working on. Selected things are outlined in the accent colour in the viewport and highlighted in the Area panel; Properties shows one of them.
  • Gizmo: the coloured arrows, rings and boxes drawn on the selection, which you drag to move, turn or resize it. Each handle works along one axis, in its colour.
  • Pivot: the point a selection turns and grows around: the middle of the selected entities.
  • Snapping: making moves, turns and sizes jump in steps (to the grid lines, 15° at a time, 10% at a time) so things line up exactly.
  • Hidden and locked: ways to keep things out of your way while you work: a hidden entity isn't drawn in the editor, and a locked one can't be clicked in the viewport. The game still has them both.
  • Axis lock: stopping drags from changing one axis, such as Z, so a drag slides along the floor without lifting.
  • World and object axes: the world's X, Y and Z are the same everywhere; an object's own axes turn with it. The gizmo can follow either.
  • Console: the panel where the editor reports what it's doing, and where you can type commands. See The Console.
  • Command: a short instruction typed in the Console's command line, such as select Crate or set Transform.position 0 0 2. Commands do the same things as the menus, so each change can be undone.
  • Problem: a mistake in the area that Solis can't fix by itself, such as a model whose file is gone. The Problems panel lists them. See Problems.

Playing#

  • Game UI: what a game draws over its picture: health bars, money, menus, an inventory. Each piece is pinned (anchored) to a corner, an edge or the middle of the screen, so it stays there on any screen shape. A screen's scale rule says how big it gets on a bigger screen: grow with the screen (the same share of it), keep its size (the same pixels) or whole steps (pixel art, scaled ×2, ×3, ×4 so every pixel stays square).
  • Screen (game UI): one of a game's screens (the HUD, a pause menu), written as a Lust file in the ui folder and shown by a Screen component. It reads the game's values after every tick and never changes the game. See Game screens.
  • Piece (of a screen): one thing in a screen's view: a column, a text, a button, an image. Pieces hold others (a column holds its rows) and line up one after another, so moving one moves it between its neighbours.
  • Tie (of a screen's piece): a piece showing one of the game's values: words, a bar's fill, how see-through it is, read again after every tick. The UI editor writes it as ordinary Lust (health.hp.text()). More.
  • Player setting: a choice the player makes for themselves, not part of the game: text size, UI size, fullscreen, the window's size. The game's own menu offers them through Screens: and Window: calls; they're not in save games or recordings. More.
  • Playtest build: a folder holding your game and a program named after it, for someone else to play without the editor. It runs the game's code as Play does, so it's made in seconds; a finished release comes later. More.
  • Focus (of a screen's buttons): the button the keys or a gamepad are on, shown with a blue ring. The arrow keys or the stick move it to the nearest button that way, and Space, Enter or A chooses it. See Game screens.
  • Canvas (UI editor): where a screen is drawn on the editor's UI tab to pick its pieces and change them. Each change rewrites only the letters it must in the screen's Lust file. See The UI editor.
  • Play mode: running the area as a game inside the editor. Press Play to start and Stop to finish. Stop puts the area back as it was, then asks whether to keep the changes you made yourself meanwhile; what the game did (entities it spawned or removed, values it changed) is never kept. See Play mode.
  • Game: what players see and do. In the editor it's shown in the Game panel, through the game's camera, without the editor's grid and markers.
  • Camera: an entity the game looks through. The game uses the first camera in the area. Its field of view is how wide it sees.
  • World: the game's own copy of the area while it runs, kept in a form a game can run over quickly. It's made when you press Play and thrown away on Stop.
  • Drawing between ticks (interpolation): showing everything part way between where it was at the last tick and where it is now, so a screen faster than the game's 60 ticks a second shows smooth movement. See Play mode.
  • Frame: one picture on screen. Games aim for 60 frames a second (fps), which leaves about 16.7 milliseconds (thousandths of a second) for each; 30 fps still feels playable. See The Profiler.
  • Frame-time graph and timeline: the Profiler's two pictures of frames: a bar for each of the last 240 frames, and, for the one picked, its parts laid end to end along a ruler of milliseconds. See The Profiler.
  • CPU and GPU: the computer's processor, which runs game code and the editor, and its graphics card, which draws. They work at the same time; the slower one sets the frame rate.
  • Culling: leaving out what the camera can't see before drawing. Each copy of a model is checked against the view (a ball around it is enough), so a huge area costs only what's in view. Things just out of view are still drawn into the sun's shadow map when their shadow can fall into it.

Game code#

  • Game code: the part of a game written as code: its rules, and what things do on their own. See Game code.
  • Lust: a programming language made for games like Solis's, which reads like plain English. Solis checks it and runs it. Lust can also become Rust, which runs fastest, for the finished game.
  • Native method: a method Lust knows the name and values of, but whose work is done by the engine, such as moveTo or World:say. The engine's are listed in the solis folder Solis writes into each project.
  • Mistake (in code): something the checker finds before the code runs, such as a misspelt name or text where a number should be. Solis lists each one with its file, line and column (how far along the line).
  • Projectile: something small and fast a game fires in its thousands (a laser, a bullet), which isn't an entity: Solis moves it every tick until its time is up, and draws all of them in one go. Game code fires one with fire. See Game code.
  • Game-wide object: one thing for the whole game rather than an entity (a clock, the money, the weather), written as a Lust object. Solis runs its update once a tick before any component, and keeps it in save games; components read it but only its own update changes it. See Game code.
  • Spawn: game code making an entity while the game runs (a copy of an assembly); despawn takes one away. See Game code.
  • Benchmark: a ready-made test of how much a computer can play at once. Solis's is two fleets of ships firing lasers: see The benchmark.
  • Tick: one step of the running game. Solis runs 60 a second, whatever the frame rate, and game code's update runs once each tick, so the game behaves the same on a fast or slow computer. During a tick, game code sees the world as it was when the tick started (plus its own changes), so it can run on every core at once and still come out the same.
  • Random number: a number game code gets by chance, such as a die roll (World:randomInt(1, 6)). Solis makes them from a seed: the same seed gives the same numbers in the same order, so a play can be repeated exactly. Each Play has a new seed unless you choose one (seed in the Console).
  • Tween: a value gliding to a new one over a set time (a door swinging open over half a second), written in Lust as tween open to 1 over 0.5;. Solis moves every tween a step each tick, before the components' updates. The way it speeds up and slows down is its ease ([ease OutCubic]). See Game code.
  • Event: a message one component sends to an entity, such as "you were hit, for 2.5". Each of that entity's components that cares reacts to it. Events let components work together without knowing about each other, even when they're written in different languages.

Simulation#

  • Physics: making things move like real objects without writing how: they fall, collide, stack and get pushed. See Physics.
  • Rigid body: what makes an entity move by physics. Dynamic ones are moved by physics, kinematic ones only by game code (pushing dynamic ones aside), and fixed ones never move.
  • Collider: the shape physics bumps into (a box, sphere or capsule), which can be simpler than what's drawn. A collider on its own makes a floor or wall that never moves. A Solid brush is its own collider, its shape exactly as drawn.
  • Impulse (push): a sudden push, like a kick. The same push moves a light thing more than a heavy one.
  • Ray: an invisible line from a point in a direction, asking "what's the first thing along here?". Games use them to see whether a character stands on the ground, or what a gun points at.
  • Determinism: a game coming out exactly the same every time it's given the same inputs, on any computer. Solis keeps to it (decimals rounded the same way, everything done in a fixed order), so a recording replays exactly, and players online can keep their games in step by sending only their inputs.
  • Action: something the player does, by name (Move, Jump), which game code asks about instead of keys. Its bindings are the keys, mouse buttons and gamepad buttons that set it off; rebinding changes them. See Input.
  • Character controller: what moves a player's character: it walks, climbs steps and slopes, slides along walls instead of sticking, and stands on moving platforms. It isn't pushed around by physics like a crate; it moves itself, and pushes physics things out of its way. Solis's is the CharacterBody component plus the ready-made CharacterController. See Characters and cameras.
  • Ready-made components: components Solis writes into every project's solis/kit/ folder, in Lust (the character controller and the cameras): use them as they are, or read and copy them to make your own.
  • Combination: a key pressed while holding Ctrl, Alt or Shift, bound as one input (Alt+Left).
  • Axis: an action that gives numbers instead of on or off: a stick, or four keys, giving which way and how far.
  • Recording: every tick's input from a play, kept so the play can be run again exactly, checking it comes out the same. See Input.
  • Save game: the whole game at a moment, kept in a file: every entity, every component's values, physics, the clock and the random numbers. Loading it carries on exactly as the game would have. See Save games.
  • Checksum: one number made from everything in the game at a moment. Two plays that agree on it at the same tick are in the same state; when they don't, something differs. checksum in the Console shows it.

Sound#

  • Sound card: the part of a computer that turns sound into what speakers and headsets play. Most computers have one built in; a USB headset brings its own. With none, Solis keeps working and plays nothing.
  • WAV and Ogg: the two kinds of sound file Solis reads. WAV keeps every sample as it is (big files, right for short effects from a sound editor); Ogg (Ogg Vorbis) is squeezed to about a tenth of the size with little to hear, right for music and anything long.
  • Sample rate: how many times a second a sound is measured, such as 44,100 (CD quality) or 48,000. Higher keeps finer detail, in a bigger file.
  • Channels: how many separate sounds a file holds side by side: one (mono) or two (stereo, left and right).
  • Sound event: what a game plays, such as "footstep": a few recordings and how to vary them each time. See Sound events.
  • Take: one recording of a sound, as in a recording studio. A footstep event might hold five takes of a foot on gravel.
  • Decibel (dB): how loudness is measured. Every 6 dB is about twice (or half) as loud, and 0 dB means as recorded.
  • Semitone (st): one step on a piano keyboard. 12 semitones is an octave: twice the pitch. Playing a sound faster raises its pitch.
  • Bus: a group of sounds turned up or down together, like a channel on a mixing desk: music, effects, voices, ambience and the interface each have one. Buses sit inside other buses, all inside Master. See The Mixer.
  • Fader: a bus's volume control, the slider on its strip in the Mixer.
  • Strip: one bus in the mixer, a narrow column with its name, fader, meter, M and S, like a channel on a mixing desk. Master's strip is last.
  • Meter: a bar showing how loud a bus is right now: grey, topping out in amber when it's loud. A thin line over it holds its loudest moment for a second (its peak); a click on the meter drops it.
  • Ducking: turning one bus down automatically while another plays: music under speech.
  • Reverb: the echo a space adds to every sound in it: short in a small room, long in a cave. See Reverb zones.
  • Listener: where the game hears from: a Listener component on a camera or character, or with none the camera. See Listeners and who hears what.
  • Voice: one sound playing. A game can have thousands of sounds wanting to play; only so many voices are heard at once, the most important first.
  • Resting (virtual) sound: a looping sound that isn't heard right now, so it isn't mixed, but keeps its place in time, so it carries on where it would be when it's heard again.
  • Mute and solo: mute silences a bus; solo plays only the soloed buses, to hear one part on its own.
  • Streaming: playing a long sound a piece at a time as it's read from its file, instead of reading all of it first, so a long piece of music doesn't fill the memory. Solis streams sounds longer than ten minutes.

2D#

  • Atlas crop: a named part of a picture (one item from a sheet of them), cut out in the Atlas Crop tab and kept in a file beside the picture, which never changes. Game code names one Picture.Sprites.Tools.Axe. See Atlas Crop.
  • 2D in Solis: flat things lying on the ground, seen from straight above by a camera with no perspective. They're in the same world as 3D, so light, sound, physics, saving and game code work on them too. Height (Z) says what's drawn over what. See 2D: the pixel-perfect view.
  • Pixel art: pictures drawn one pixel at a time, at a small size, meant to be shown scaled up with every pixel kept square and sharp.
  • Base resolution: the size a 2D game is drawn at before it's scaled up to the screen, such as 480 × 270. Smaller shows chunkier pixels and less of the world.
  • Pixels per unit: how many of the game's pixels make one metre of the world. With 16, a 16-pixel tile is one metre.
  • Pixel-perfect: every pixel of the game shown as the same whole number of screen pixels, never blurred or uneven. Solis draws the game at its base resolution and scales it up in whole steps (×2, ×3, ×4…).
  • Whole steps: scaling by a whole number. When the screen isn't a whole number of times the base resolution, the rest is black bars; Fill scales a little further instead, smoothing only the edge of each pixel.
  • 2D camera: a camera whose View is 2D: it looks straight down at the game's base resolution, follows its entity's place, and never turns.
  • Tile: one square of a 2D world's grid, usually 16 pixels; tile maps are built from them.
  • Sprite: a flat picture in a 2D world, such as a character or a crop: one frame of a sprite sheet, lying on the ground at its entity. See Sprites from Aseprite.
  • Sprite sheet: a picture holding a sprite's frames, from one Aseprite file. Solis reads .aseprite files as they are; nothing needs exporting.
  • Frame: one picture of a sprite sheet. Showing frames one after another animates it.
  • Tag: in Aseprite, a named run of frames (walk, swing) with a direction (forward, reverse, ping-pong) and repeats: a clip to play.
  • Slice: in Aseprite, a named rectangle on the picture (feet, hand), used for where a sprite stands, where a held tool goes, or what can be hit.
  • Pivot: the point a sprite stands on: it sits on its entity's place, so the sprite turns and flips round it. Usually between the feet.
  • Atlas: one big picture with many frames packed into it, so the graphics card draws a sheet's sprites all at once instead of one at a time.
  • Clip: a run of a sprite sheet's frames played as an animation (walk, hoe), each frame shown for its own time, forward, backward or ping-pong (there and back), over and over or a number of times. Aseprite's tags are clips; you can make more in Solis. See Animating sprites.
  • Clips file: a .solframes file beside an Aseprite file, holding what Solis adds to its clips (speed, events) and clips made in Solis. Open it to edit its clips in the Clips and Frames tabs.
  • Animator: a .solanim file that chooses which clip a sprite plays, from states, transitions and parameters, edited in the Animator tab; an Animator component puts one on an entity. See Animators.
  • State: one thing an animated sprite can be doing (Idle, Walk), drawn as a box: it plays a clip, or a clip for each facing direction.
  • Transition: an arrow from one state to another (or from Any state), taken when all its conditions hold.
  • Parameter: a value an animator's transitions look at: a number, a switch (on or off), a trigger (fired for one tick) or a direction (which way it faces).
  • Graph editor: the canvas of boxes and arrows the Animator tab draws on; materials and effects will use the same one, with the same controls.
  • Frame event: a name on a frame of a clip (footstep). When the clip reaches the frame, a sound event of that name plays and game code hears CueReached, with the event as Cue.Footstep.
  • Tile map: a grid of cells laid out in a 2D world, saved as a .tilemap.lst file and placed by an entity's Tile Map component. Each cell holds a terrain on each layer, and values. See Tile maps.
  • Tileset: a .tileset.lst file listing the terrains a tile map's cells can be. Every map that uses it draws its terrains the same way.
  • Terrain: what a cell is (grass, tilled, water), with a name, a colour and the one character a map file writes for it (its code, such as . for grass).
  • Layer (tile map): one of a map's stacked grids, such as Ground, Decoration and Above. A layer is drawn under sprites (the ground they walk on) or over them (roofs they walk behind).
  • Cell value: something every cell of a map has besides its terrain: a number (growth), a switch (watered) or a choice (crop: wheat or corn). The game changes them as it plays, and saves keep them.
  • Chunk: a 32 × 32 block of a map's cells. A map is saved and checked chunk by chunk, so a change to one cell touches only its chunk.
  • Autotiling: picking each cell's tile of art from its neighbours, so edges and corners come out right without choosing tiles by hand. See Tilesets and autotiling.
  • Copy (stamp): cells of a map copied with the tile painter's eyedropper, to paint with: flipped, turned, and repeated like a pattern. See Painting tiles.
  • Exact tile: a cell that shows one tile of its tileset as it is, chosen by hand, instead of the one autotiling would pick. Art only: the game reads the cell's terrain. See Painting tiles.
  • Kind (terrain): how a terrain's tiles are picked: plain (one tile), 16-tile, 47-tile, edges (fences, roads) or its own rules.
  • Slot: one situation a terrain's art has a tile for, such as "tilled to the north and east only". Each kind has its own slots; a slot with no tile shows pink.
  • Dual grid: drawing art half a cell off the cells, so each tile sits where four cells meet and is chosen by which of them are the terrain. 16-tile terrains use it: 15 drawings cover every edge and corner.
  • Variation: another tile for the same slot, picked by weight so a field doesn't look repeated. Each cell always gets the same one.
  • Template: a picture with every slot of a kind laid out at your tile size, to draw your tiles over.
  • Solid (terrain): a terrain nothing with a 2D collider can walk into, such as a fence or water. Your game chooses which terrains are solid, in the Map tab. See Walls and walking in 2D.
  • Walls (2D): what 2D physics makes of a map's solid cells: neighbouring cells merged into a few rectangles, so sliding along a fence never catches on the seams between tiles. The viewport's Walls switch shows them.
  • Collider2D: a built-in component giving an entity a shape on the ground for 2D physics, in pixels: a circle or a box. Solid and still, or a character that game code walks and that slides along what's in its way.
  • Parallax: things far away seem to move less than things close by when you move. A parallax layer is a sprite with a Parallax component: it moves with the camera at its own speed (its scroll: 0 stays put, 1 moves with the world), drawn behind everything or in front, so a flat 2D level feels deep. See Parallax layers.
  • Top-down movement: walking across a map seen from above, in 8 directions (with diagonals) or 4. The kit's TopDownController does it, never faster diagonally than straight.

Getting Solis#

  • Build: one version of the program, made by GitHub each time a change is merged into the main version. Each build has a build number that goes up by one or more each time, so a bigger number is newer. File › About shows yours. See Installing and updating.
  • Release: a build published on GitHub's Releases page for anyone to download. Solis publishes every build as a release called build- and its number.
  • Installer: a program that puts another program on your computer properly: in its own folder, in the Start menu, and in Windows' list of apps so you can uninstall it. Solis's is solis-setup.exe.
  • Splash screen: the picture a program shows while it starts: Solis's logo, name and version, and what it's doing ("Starting…").
  • Manual and user guide: the manual is the set of pages explaining every part of Solis (these pages, in the docs/manual folder of the code). The user guide is the same pages made into one page for your web browser, with a search and a contents list, which comes with every build and opens from Documentation in the tab bar. One is made from the other, so they always agree. See The user guide.
  • Default browser: the web browser Windows opens links in, set in Windows' own settings. The user guide opens in it unless you choose another in File › Preferences.
  • SHA-256: a 64-character fingerprint of a file's contents. Change one byte and it's completely different, so comparing fingerprints shows a download arrived whole and unchanged.
← Previous · Chapter 3Installing and updatingNext → · Chapter 5The user guide

The user guide#

The whole manual as one page in your web browser, with a search, opened by Documentation at the top right of the editor.

When to use it#

Whenever you want to know how something works, or what a key does. The guide is this manual: every page of it is a chapter there, so what you read in the guide and what you read here are always the same words. It describes the copy of Solis it came with, and every update brings the guide that matches it.

The guide is a single file on your computer, in the user-guide folder beside the program. It opens without an internet connection, and nothing in it is fetched from anywhere.

How to use it#

  1. Click Documentation at the right end of the tab bar, beside the project's name. It is always there: on every tab, on the File pages, and before any project is open.
  2. The guide opens in your browser (which one is a setting; see below), at the welcome. File › Learn and File › About open it too, and a component's ? in Properties opens the chapter about that component.
  3. Find what you're after:
    • Search: press / or Ctrl+K (or click the box at the top) and type. Every part of the guide holding all the words you typed is listed, with the words around them; Up and Down choose, Enter goes there and marks the words on the page, Esc clears the search.
    • Contents: the list on the left has every chapter, numbered and in groups. The chapter you're reading opens out to show its sections, and the one you're in is lit. Above the list, how much of the guide you've read so far.
    • Where you are: the top bar names the chapter and section you're reading.
  4. To keep or share a place, point at a heading and click the # beside it: the link to that heading is copied.
  5. Top (bottom right) goes back to the start. The button at the top right switches between Auto (as your computer is set), Light and Dark; your browser remembers the choice.

On a narrow window the contents fold away behind the button at the top left, and the line saying where you are opens them too.

The guide is made from the manual's pages each time Solis is built, so it can never say something the manual doesn't. If you find a mistake in it, it's a mistake in the manual: the page to fix is the chapter's own page in docs/manual.

Settings#

In File › Preferences › General, under Help:

SettingWhat it does
Open the guide inWhich program shows the guide. Default browser (the standard) is the one Windows opens web pages in. Below it are the browsers Windows lists as installed on this computer, and A program you choose… asks for any program file. If the browser chosen isn't there any more, the guide opens in the default browser and the status bar says so.

Shortcuts#

The editor has no key for the guide: Documentation is a click. Inside the guide:

ActionShortcut
Search the guide/ or Ctrl+K
Choose a resultUp, Down
Go to the result chosenEnter, or click it
Clear the search, or close the contents on a narrow windowEsc

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: clicking Documentation only says "The user guide isn't beside this build". Why: this copy of Solis was built on your own computer, not installed: the guide is made and put beside the program when a build is published. Fix: the Console gives the line to make it, cargo run -p user-guide -- --out <the program's folder>/user-guide/index.html. The same page, as it is in the repository, is in docs/user-guide/index.html.
  • Problem: the guide opened in a different browser from the one chosen. Why: the browser chosen was uninstalled or moved, so the default browser opened it instead (the status bar said so). Fix: choose again in File › Preferences › General › Open the guide in.
  • Problem: the theme choice or the place you were reading is forgotten. Why: some browsers don't let a page opened from a file remember anything. Fix: nothing is lost: the guide follows your computer's light or dark setting instead.

Related#

  • Settings: the other Preferences.
  • Keyboard shortcuts: every key in one place.
  • Concepts: the manual and the user guide.

Interface tour#

What's where in the editor, and how to rearrange it.

When to use it#

When finding your way around, or making the layout suit your screen.

How to use it#

This page follows what you see, in the order you meet it: Recent projects, the File page Solis starts on, then the editor from its tab bar down to its status bar. All of it is drawn in one look: dark neutral greys, lighter the nearer a surface is to you, with one accent colour for what's chosen. The accent, and how large the editor is drawn, are yours to choose in File › Preferences (Settings).

Recent projects is what Solis always starts on, in its full window: the File tab's first page. Your projects are cards (pinned ones first, with Search projects, Sort by, Open… ▾ and New project); double-click one and the editor opens with it. Under them, Start from a template: an empty project or one of the four examples. Why start there? Solis doesn't open the last project by itself, so you always choose what to work on. Until a project is open the other tabs are dimmed; Esc, or Carry on without a project, opens the editor with none. See Projects.

The tab bar is the dark strip along the very top. From left to right:

  • The logo, in a small light tile.
  • The tabs: File, Home, Library, Shading, Animate, UI, VFX, Audio, Debug and Build. Each is one kind of work, and a click on one changes the ribbon under it and what the editor shows (see The tabs below). The tab in front is lit, with a line of the accent colour under it. Shading and VFX are grey with a small hollow square after their names: those screens aren't built yet (Unfinished parts).
  • A tab that comes with a file (a contextual tab): while a tileset, a picture's crops or a selected tile map is open, a tab such as LIBRARY TOOLS · Tileset stands right after the tab it belongs to, with a ribbon of that file's own tools. Click it to bring that file to the front; it goes when the file closes. A tileset and a picture's crops fill their tab (with ‹ Back to Library at the right of the document's tab); a tile map's tab is Home with the Map shelf tab in front.
  • Search or run a command, in the middle: one search for everything (see below). Its right end shows its key, Space.
  • The project and the area, as in Harbour / docks, with an amber dot after the area's name while it has unsaved changes. Before a project is open it says No project open.
  • Documentation opens the user guide, this manual as one page in your browser, with a search. It is there on every tab, the File pages too, project or not.
  • The chevron at the far right collapses the ribbon (see below).

The ribbon is the band under the tab bar: the things you do on the tab in front, as buttons you can see instead of menus you have to open. Why a ribbon? Everything for the job at hand is on screen at once, each with its name under it, and nothing is hidden two menus deep. It is made of groups, each with its name underneath:

  • A large button is an icon over a word. Point at one and it says what it does, its shortcut if it has one, and, when it is greyed, why it can't be used right now.
  • A small row is a line of words: a switch has a box that is filled while it is on (Grid · 1 in Snapping), and a row with a small arrow opens a list (More).
  • A button that makes one of several kinds has a small arrow at the end of its name: click the button for the usual kind (Light makes a point light), or click the arrow, or right-click the button, for the list (a spotlight).
  • Grey controls with a small hollow square aren't built yet: they show where things will be (Unfinished parts), and one setting hides them all.

The Play group is at the ribbon's right end on every tab: Play is the one light button on screen. While the game runs it becomes Stop, with Pause and Step beside it; nothing else in the editor changes colour. See Play mode.

When the window is narrow the ribbon doesn't wrap: it scrolls sideways. Turn the mouse wheel while pointing at it.

To give the ribbon's room to the editor, click the chevron at the tab bar's right end, or double-click a tab: only the tabs stay. Click a tab then and the ribbon drops down over the editor until you choose something on it or move the pointer below it. The chevron, or another double-click, brings the ribbon back for good.

The tabs, one per job:

  • Home is for building areas: the area big in the middle with the toolbox down its left edge, and its entities (the Area list), their Properties and your files (Assets) round it, where the panel layout puts them (see Home's panel layouts below). Its ribbon: Edit (Undo and Redo, each named for the step it acts on when you point at it; see Undo and redo), Create (Empty, Model, Sprite, Light, Camera, Shape (the brush list; its key, B, is written beside it), Tile map, and More for a reverb zone or an assembly from the selection), Snapping (Grid, Angle and Scale; click the value after "·" for the steps, see Selecting and moving), and Project (Save saves the area; Build opens Export for playtesting). With the Place shelf tab in front the ribbon takes its build form for placing.
  • Library is the project's files (Projects and the Library). Its ribbon: Add (Import, Create, Folder), View (List, Show folders), Filter (Type) and Use (Place).
  • Animate is for animating sprites: a clips file's frames and clips, or an animator's graph and preview, each with a ribbon of its own (Animating sprites, Animators). With neither open it shows the Sequencer's page, not built yet.
  • UI draws game screens on the Canvas, with the drawing tools down its left edge; double-click a screen's file in the Library and Solis switches to UI with it open (The UI editor).
  • Audio is the mixer: a strip per bus with Master last, the bus you pick beside it with its ducking, and the project's sound events on the shelf. Its ribbon: Bus (a new bus), Add rule, Remove, Clear solo, Mute the game and Heard at once.
  • Debug is for testing the game: the Profiler fills the middle (the frames as bars, the frame you click as a timeline, and Statistics), with the Game as a tab beside it, and the Console in front on the shelf. Its ribbon has CPU and GPU for the Profiler and the Session group: Load save (Save games), Play and record inputs and Replay a recording… (Input).
  • Build is Export for playtesting as a page: the game's name, the area it starts in, the folder and the window, with Export, and the Console on the shelf. Its ribbon has Export and Open folder (the last export's folder); the full export beside them isn't built yet.
  • Shading and VFX, and the model viewer (a model's right-click in the Library, Open in the model viewer), are screens that aren't built yet: their ribbon and shelf tabs are shown greyed, round one page saying what will be there and when (Unfinished parts).

Each tab remembers its own shelf tab, the shelf's height, the split between its groups and every border you dragged, separately.

File is different: it is a page in place of the ribbon and the editor, with a column of items down its left side. Back to editor (or Esc) returns to the tab you came from.

ItemWhat it does

New project, Open…Make a project in a folder, or open one (Projects and the Library).
Save allSaves the open area. Every other file saves as you change it.
Project settingsThis project's settings: General, 2D, Input (the game's actions and their keys, see Input) and Build (Settings).
PreferencesThe editor's own settings, such as its accent colour (Settings).
PluginsNot built yet.
