UpdatesThe build you have, the newest one, and Check now (Installing and updating).
AboutThe program's name, version and build, its licences, and the user guide.

One search for everything: press Space (with nothing being typed) or click Search or run a command in the tab bar. Type part of a name and the list finds:

  • everything the editor can do (Save area, Add point light, Play…), each with where it lives and its shortcut beside it when it has one, so you pick up the keys as you go. Going to a tab, collapsing the ribbon, folding the shelf and hiding unfinished parts are there too;
  • every file in the project, which opens it as a double-click in the Library would. A file you place rather than open (a model, an assembly, a sprite sheet, a tile map or a picture) is picked in the Library instead, with its folder open, ready to drag in;
  • every entity in the area, which selects it and points the camera at it;
  • a panel by its name, which comes to the front.

Up and Down choose, Enter does it, Esc closes. Why? You don't have to remember which tab something is on: type what you want. Things without a button on the ribbon are found here too, wherever else they are: New area and Open area… (the + after the area's tab), Save area as… (a right-click on the area's tab), Duplicate, Delete, Rename, Select all and Select nothing (a right-click in the Area list), Reset layout (File › Preferences), Documentation ↗ (the tab bar) and Add the sample area (File › Learn), Check for updates (File › Updates), and showing or hiding the viewport's corner controls (its Show ▾ pill). Things that can't be done right now (Pause while editing, Delete with nothing selected) aren't listed. In the Frames tab, Space still plays and stops the clip, so point somewhere else first.

The middle of the window is the same on every tab: one or two editor groups on top, the shelf under them, the status bar along the bottom; on Home, the Area list, Properties and Assets sit where the panel layout puts them. Why the same everywhere? Each tab of the tab bar is one kind of work, and its screen keeps your things in the same places: what you're working on big in the middle, the tools and lists for it round it. Panels don't move between places; every tab remembers how you sized it.

Home's panel layouts. Home has three lists you use all the time: the Area tree, Properties and Assets. Where they sit is a setting, File › Preferences › Appearance › Panel layout, and it changes at once, so try each:

Panel layoutWhere the lists are
Area left, Assets bottom (the standard)The Area list a tall column at the left of the area, Properties a tall column at the right, Assets a wide strip under the area.
Area and Assets on the leftThe Area list over Assets in one column at the left; Properties at the right.
Area left, Assets rightThe Area list at the left; Properties over Assets at the right.
The shelf (as designed)All three side by side on the shelf's Entity tab, under the area, as the design first drew them.

Why choose? Tall columns show many more entities and files at once, and Properties gets room for its cards; the shelf layout gives the area the whole width. In the first three the shelf keeps its other tabs (Place, Console, Problems, Map while a tile map is selected) and still folds with Ctrl + Space, which gives the columns the whole height. Placing is the same in every layout: click Place on the shelf's bar. In the side layouts its tab holds how placed things land (Placement), and the Assets list, wherever it is, shows what can be placed, with its chips and search. When the window is too narrow for the columns, the area gets narrower first (down to 240 points), then the right column, then the left one (down to 180 each); narrower still, the lists go back on the shelf until the window is wide enough again.

  • Editor groups hold documents: the area, the running game, an animator, a tileset, the mixer. Each group has a strip of tabs along its top (the one in front is lighter, with a thin accent line on top); click one to bring it to the front. A tab for a file has a × that closes the file; nothing asks whether to save, because those files save as you change them. When a tab shows two groups side by side, drag the thin line between them to give one more room; when the window is too narrow for both, they sit one above the other.
  • Drag a document's tab onto the left or right half of the middle and it gets a group of its own there, the rest beside it; drag it onto another group's tabs and the two groups join. Esc while dragging puts it back. Each tab keeps what you did while Solis runs.
  • The area's tab carries a +: New area and Open area…. Right-click the tab for Save, Save as…, Close others and Show in the Library. (Close is there but greyed: one area is open at a time, so open or make another in its place.)
  • The shelf has its own tabs along its bar. Click one to show it; its contents sit side by side as columns, each with a header. Drag the grip at the bar's left (or the bar's top edge) up or down to make the shelf taller or shorter, and press Ctrl + Space to fold it down to its bar and back, even while you're typing. At the bar's right are tools for the tab in front: the Console's level filters, search, Clear and Copy while the Console is there.
  • Every border drags. Point at the thin line between two parts (two columns, a column and the area, the Assets strip and the area, two lists stacked in a column, two shelf columns, two groups) and the pointer becomes a two-headed arrow: drag to give one side more room. Double-click a border to put it back to its standard size. Each part has a least size, so nothing can be dragged away. When the window narrows, the shelf's columns give way too: first the one that takes what's left, then the others from the right; narrower still, they sit under each other.
  • What each tab remembers: the shelf tab in front, whether the shelf is folded, and every border you dragged (the shelf's height, the split between its groups, the columns), separately for each panel layout, also after closing Solis. Reset layout puts the tab you're on back as it started, in every layout.

Point at a row for its eye (hide) and lock; right-click it for Rename, Duplicate, Delete, Add…, Create assembly and Select all or nothing.

Below, each component is a card with its settings, side by side as many as fit; a card's ? opens its chapter of the user guide and its ⋯ (or a right-click on the card) copies, pastes, resets or removes it. Opening the file brings its tab to the front.

Questions that stop your work (unsaved changes, a file changed on disk, keeping what you changed while playing) are a card over the dimmed window: the answer that sets your work aside at the left, the main one in the accent colour at the right.

The status bar along the bottom says what's happening, so you don't have to go looking:

  • On the left, a green dot and Ready while the game's code is clean (Solis checks it when the project opens and each time you save a code file; hover to see when it last did), or, in red, how many mistakes it has.
  • Beside it, the branch and its changes (not built yet), then the problems as two coloured counts: red for mistakes in the game's code, amber for problems in the area. Click them to open the Problems tab.
  • On the right: while the brush list is open or a brush is being drawn out, what's going on (Choosing a shape brush: Ramp) in place of the next two; Playing or Paused while the game runs; Saved, Unsaved changes or Not saved yet for the open area (Saving areas); the area's name, whether the viewport shows it in 2D or 3D, and for 2D the game's size in pixels (farm · 2D · 480 × 270, from File › Project settings); what moves snap to and which way the gizmo points (Snap 0.25 · World, or Snap off); then Solis's version, and Restart to update once an update has downloaded. For three seconds after you click a part that isn't built yet, the words before the version say so instead (Unfinished parts).

From an older build: panels used to be dragged anywhere and the Library could be a drawer. Neither is so now, and an arrangement you made before isn't carried over: every tab starts as the design draws it, and the Console says so once.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a panel has disappeared. Why: it lives on another tab, on a shelf tab not in front, or the shelf is folded. Fix: press Space and type its name: choosing it brings its tab and shelf tab to the front. Ctrl + Space unfolds the shelf.
  • Problem: a menu from an older build is gone (File, Edit, Entity, Help). Why: the tabs and the ribbon took the menu bar's place. Fix: press Space and type what you want: the list says where it lives now.
  • Problem: the panels are where an older build didn't have them. Why: the middle of the window is the design's now, and panels don't move. Fix: see the table above for where each one lives; Space and its name finds it.
  • Problem: Properties is cramped. Why: its column is narrow, or (in the shelf layout) it shares Home's shelf with the Area tree and Assets. Fix: drag the border at its edge (or the shelf's grip) for more room, it's remembered; or choose another Panel layout in File › Preferences.
  • Problem: Home's lists jumped onto the shelf. Why: the window is too narrow for the columns beside the area. Fix: widen the window: they go back by themselves.
  • Problem: a border won't go further. Why: each part keeps a least size, and the area keeps room. Fix: make the part beside it smaller first, or double-click the border to start again.
  • Problem: two of a tab's documents are side by side, or one group holds them all. Why: a tab was dragged. Fix: drag it back, or Reset layout.

Settings#

Preferences, the editor's own settings, and Project settings, the open project's: two File pages, each with sub-tabs and one search.

When to use it#

When you want to change how the editor itself looks or behaves (its accent colour, how large it's drawn, what the viewport shows, where Home's lists sit, putting the shelf back as it started, or hiding the parts that aren't built yet), or a setting that belongs to the whole project, such as its 2D resolution, its game's controls or how it is exported.

  • Preferences are yours, kept on this computer. They aren't saved in the area or the project.
  • Project settings are saved in the open project's folder, in small text files Git can merge, so they travel with it to other computers and other people. They need a project open.

Neither is an undo step. Every change applies at once: there is no Save or Apply button.

How to use it#

  1. Click the File tab, then Preferences or Project settings in its column. Or press Space and type Preferences.
  2. Pick a sub-tab under the heading: Preferences has General, Appearance, Viewport and Shortcuts; Project settings has General, 2D, Input and Build. The faint sub-tabs with a small square (Source control, Physics, Platforms and others) are unfinished parts.
  3. Each setting is a row, with its name and a line about it on the left and its control on the right: a switch, a row of choices side by side, a drop-down list, colour swatches, a number or a button. They work from the keyboard too: Tab moves from one to the next (a thin ring in the accent colour shows where you are), Space or Enter presses or flips it, and the arrow keys move along the swatches and the choices, or step through a drop-down list without opening it.
  4. Can't find something? Type in the search at the top right: it looks through every sub-tab of the page, at the settings' names and their lines, and shows the matches together.
  5. On Preferences, Reset to defaults (in the column at the right) puts the sub-tab's settings back as they were at first. On Project settings, a setting changed from its standard has a dot before its name and Reset after it; the heading counts them ("2 changed from defaults"), and a card at the right lists each, from what to what.
  6. Back to editor (or Esc) leaves the page.

Preferences#

SettingWhat it does
General › Look for updates when Solis startsAsks GitHub for a newer build at each start, in the background. Off, nothing is asked until you choose Check now on File › Updates.
General › Show hintsThe Hints card, last under Properties, says what's selected and what you can do with it. Its Turn hints off does the same as this switch.
General › Open the guide inWhich program shows the user guide when you click Documentation: Default browser (the standard), a browser Windows lists as installed on this computer, or A program you choose…. A browser that's gone falls back to the default, and the status bar says so.
General › Hide unfinished partsSome places in the editor are for features that come in later updates. They are shown faint with a small hollow square, and do nothing yet. Switch this on to hide every one of them, so only what works is on screen. The card beside it shows what one looks like. See Unfinished parts.
Appearance › Accent colourThe colour that marks what's chosen and selected: the chosen tool, the front tab, the selected row. Five colours: Blue (the standard), Grey, Orange, Teal and Purple. Colours that mean something keep their own: Play is the one light button on screen, and warnings and errors are amber and red. The small picture at the right shows the editor in the colour chosen.
Appearance › Interface scaleHow large everything is drawn: 100% to 200%. Raise it when text is too small, common on a laptop or a very sharp (4K) screen. Everything grows together, and thin lines stay crisp. It doesn't change your game.

A number you drag is saved once, when you let go.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: everything in the editor is tiny. Why: on a very sharp screen each pixel is small. Fix: raise Appearance › Interface scale.
  • Problem: a setting is faint, has a small square after its name, and its switch won't move. Why: it's an unfinished part. Fix: rest the pointer on it to read what it will do; switch on General › Hide unfinished parts if you'd rather not see it.
  • Problem: Project settings says Open a project first. Why: its settings belong to a project, and none is open. Fix: open or make one (File › Recent projects).
  • Problem: the Console says pixels.solpix had a mistake. Why: the file was edited by hand and can't be read. Fix: the standard 2D settings are used meanwhile; change anything on the 2D tab and the file is written again, with the damaged one kept beside it as pixels.solpix.bak.
  • Problem: the shelf is so tall (or folded) that what you want isn't in sight. Why: its height and fold are remembered per tab. Fix: Ctrl + Space unfolds it; double-click its grip, or Reset layout, puts it back.
  • Problem: after an update, Home's Area list and Properties are columns beside the area, not on the shelf. Why: that is the new standard panel layout. Fix: choose The shelf (as designed) under Appearance › Panel layout to have them back on the shelf.
  • Problem: I can't find the Settings window, or File › Input. Why: they became these pages. Fix: Preferences and Project settings are in the File column; Input is a sub-tab of Project settings.

Unfinished parts#

Parts of the editor that aren't built yet are shown in grey with a small square mark, and one setting hides them all.

When to use it#

Solis's interface is being rebuilt to one design, and that design is larger than what Solis can do today: it has places for things that come in later updates, such as materials, effects and a built-in code view. Rather than leave holes, the editor shows each of those places where it will be, marked so you can tell it apart from what works. This is called an unfinished part.

Read this page when you see a grey control with a small hollow square beside it and wonder why a click does nothing, or when you'd rather not see any of them.

Why show them at all? So the editor's layout stays the same as it grows: what you learn now is where things will still be, and you can see what's coming and roughly when. If you'd rather work with only what works today, hide them: nothing you can use disappears with them.

They are on the ribbon, the shelf, the File pages (templates on Recent projects, sub-tabs and rows of Preferences and Project settings, Input's Contexts and Fires on), Build's full export, Audio's effects, the Profiler's thread lanes, and whole screens: Shading, VFX and the model viewer (a model's right-click in the Library, Open in the model viewer), each in its own place. File › Preferences › General has a small card showing what one looks like.

How to use it#

  1. Recognise one. An unfinished part has three signs, always together:
    • its words are a quieter grey than a working control's, and its icon fainter still;
    • a small hollow square sits at its top right corner (on a button) or just after its words (on a tab, a row or a setting);
    • it doesn't light up when the pointer is over it.
  2. Find out what it will be. Rest the pointer on it. A note says its name, what it will do in one sentence, and which step of the roadmap↗ builds it, for example: Not built yet: Code editor split. Shows game code next to the viewport when a code file is open. Not planned yet. "Not planned yet" means the design has a place for it but no step of the roadmap builds it so far.
  3. Clicking it does nothing, on purpose. The right-hand end of the status bar says so for three seconds (Code editor split isn't built yet (not planned yet)), and that's all: no window opens and nothing changes.
  4. Hide them all: open File › Preferences, and on General switch on Hide unfinished parts. Or press Space and type hide unfinished. Every unfinished part goes, and what's left closes up, so there are no gaps where they were.
  5. A whole screen that isn't built (Shading, VFX, the model viewer) is its ribbon and its shelf's tabs, all marked, round one card in the middle saying what it will be and when. The card's Hide unfinished parts link hides them all. With them hidden, Shading and VFX leave the tab bar and a model's menu has no way into the viewer.
  6. Show them again: switch it off in the same place, or press Space and type show unfinished.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
General › Hide unfinished partsOff (the standard): unfinished parts are shown, marked. On: none is shown anywhere, and the things around them close up. It's remembered next time you start. Reset to defaults on General turns it off again. See Settings.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Hide or show unfinished partsSpace, then type unfinished and press Enter

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: I clicked a button and nothing happened. Why: if it's grey with a small hollow square, it's an unfinished part: it marks where a feature will be. Fix: rest the pointer on it to read what it will do and when. For what can be done today, the manual's list of pages covers everything that works.
  • Problem: is a grey control broken, or switched off? Why: neither is the same as unfinished. A control that works but can't be used right now (Add the sample area on Learn with no project open, say) is faded and has no square mark; resting the pointer on it says what to do first. An unfinished part always has the mark. Fix: look for the square.
  • Problem: something I saw before is gone. Why: Hide unfinished parts may be on: it hides only what never worked. Fix: switch it off on File › Preferences to see the marked places again.
  • Problem: I can't find an unfinished part with the search. Why: the search (Space) lists only what can be done. Fix: nothing to do: when a part is built, it joins the search.

Related#

  • Settings: the Appearance page and its other settings.
  • Interface tour: the editor's tabs, groups, shelf and bars.
  • Concepts: unfinished part, ribbon, shelf, accent colour.
← Previous · Chapter 7SettingsNext → · Chapter 9Moving around the viewport

Moving around the viewport#

Fly the camera through the 3D world, split the viewport into several views (flat ones too), and use the toolbox and the pills floating over each view.

When to use it#

Whenever you want to look at the world from somewhere else. Solis has one camera style, the fly camera: you steer it like a drone, as in Unreal Engine.

How to use it#

Looking and flying:

  1. Point at the viewport and hold the right mouse button. The pointer disappears.
  2. Move the mouse to look around.
  3. While still holding the button, use the keys:
    • W forward, S back, A left, D right (forward follows where you look, so looking down and pressing W flies down);
    • E straight up, Q straight down;
    • Shift to go three times faster while held.
  4. Let go of the right button. The pointer comes back where it was.

Without holding the right button:

  • Mouse wheel: moves forward or back in steps.
  • Hold the middle button (the wheel) and drag: slides the view sideways and up or down. The ground under the pointer moves with it.

Several views (the view's pill, Perspective ▾, under Views): One view, Two side by side, Two, one above the other, or Four views. Each view has its own camera and its own look; with four, they start as Perspective, Top, Front and Right, the classic way to line things up exactly.

  • Click in a view (or turn the wheel over it) to use it: it gets a thin coloured outline, the frame time and the axis locks. F, the ribbon's Create buttons, and anything else that goes "where the camera looks" use that view.
  • Selecting, the gizmos, and dragging things in from the Library work in every view.
  • Maximise (in each view's own Perspective ▾ list, while there are several) shows that view alone, filling the viewport; All views brings the others back.
  • Solis remembers the layout and every view's camera next time.

Flat views (concepts): the Perspective ▾ pill at the top left of each view chooses what it shows: Perspective, Top, Front or Right. A flat view shows things at their true size whatever their distance, with the grid standing in the view's own plane, so lining up edges and heights is exact.

  • Hold the right or middle button and drag to slide the view.
  • Turn the wheel to zoom in or out, towards the pointer.
  • Flat views don't fly: switch back to Perspective for that.
  • Flat views have no fog, so faraway parts are as clear as near ones.
  • A camera or spotlight added from a flat view (and Move here) goes just in front of where the view looks from, as if it were a camera above or beside the area looking in.

These are the flat-view controls Unreal Engine uses.

The 2D view (the last in the Perspective ▾ list): a flat view from above like Top, measured in your game's pixels, for 2D games (2D). It slides the same way, but the wheel zooms in whole steps (100%, 200%, 300%…) and every pixel of the game lands on whole screen pixels, so pixel art looks as it will in the game. The grid is the project's tile size, a dashed frame shows what each 2D camera sees, and the pills at the bottom right are Lock X Y, Snap: Whole pixels ▾ (moves land on whole pixels, tiles, or anywhere), the grid and Zoom ▾. Moves go across the ground only (X and Y).

The toolbox runs down the viewport's left edge: Select (Q), Move (W), Rotate (R), Scale (S) and Transform (T); while a tile map is selected its painting tools follow them; then four tools that aren't built yet, marked as unfinished parts. See Selecting and moving things. There is one toolbox however many views there are. When the shelf is dragged tall, the toolbox scrolls with the mouse wheel.

The pills float over each view, so the picture stays as large as it can be:

  • Top left, on every view: the view (Perspective ▾: its kind, and how many views), the look (Standard ▾, how models are shaded; see Looks) and Show ▾: what the viewport shows (the frame time, the axis locks and camera speed, the toolbox) and Preview animation.
  • Top right, on the view in use: the time each frame takes and the frames per second. Point at it to see how many entities and triangles there are. When nothing moves it says Idle: Solis then draws only when something changes, so your computer isn't kept busy (and a laptop stays cool and quiet). Fly the camera or press Play to see the frame rate.
  • Bottom right, on the view in use: Lock X Y Z (the axis locks), World ▾ or Object ▾ (which way the gizmo points) and the camera's speed. See Selecting and moving things.

Snapping (Grid, Angle, Scale) is on the ribbon, in Home's Snapping group.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Camera speed (1 to 8)How fast W, A, S, D, Q and E move: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 metres a second. Change it by turning the mouse wheel while holding the right button. 4 (8 metres a second) is a good start; use 6 to 8 to cross a big map. Shown in the Camera box.

The camera's position, direction and speed are remembered next time.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Look aroundHold right mouse, move the mouse
FlyHold right mouse + W A S D
Down, upHold right mouse + Q, E
Faster for a momentHold Shift while flying
Change speedHold right mouse + mouse wheel
Forward, back in stepsMouse wheel
SlideHold middle mouse, drag
Slide a flat viewHold right or middle mouse, drag
Zoom a flat viewMouse wheel (towards the pointer)
Use a viewClick in it

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pressing W picked the Move tool instead of flying. Why: the right mouse button wasn't held. The tool keys work only when it isn't. Fix: hold the right button first, then press W.
  • Problem: you're lost. Fix: fly up with E, look down, and find where the red and green lines cross: that's the origin.
  • Problem: holding the right button doesn't fly. Why: the view is a flat one (Top, Front or Right). Fix: drag to slide it, or switch it to Perspective.
  • Problem: the right button didn't fly while you were drawing a selection box or dragging a gizmo. Why: with the left button held on one of those, a right click cancels it (see Selecting and moving things). Fix: let go of both buttons, then hold the right one.
  • Problem: F or Add entity went to the wrong view. Why: they follow the view in use, the one with the outline. Fix: click in the view you want first.
  • Problem: flying feels too slow or too fast. Fix: change the speed with the wheel while holding the right button.

Related#

  • Keyboard shortcuts
  • Concepts: Z up, axes, metres, grid.
← Previous · Chapter 8Unfinished partsNext → · Chapter 10Entities and components

Entities and components#

Everything in an area is an entity, and what it does comes from its components.

When to use it#

Every area in Solis is built the same way, so once you know this you can understand any of them (concepts):

  • An entity is one thing: the sun, a lamp, an imported model, the sky. On its own it is only a name.
  • Components make it something. A Transform gives it a place in the world, a Light makes it shine, a Model draws an imported model, an Environment sets the sky and fog, a Camera is what the game looks through (Play mode), and a RigidBody and a Collider make it take part in physics.

A lamp is just an entity with a Transform and a Light. Give a model a Light (+ Component › Light) and it shines like a lamp too. Your game's own code adds components of its own (Game code), shown the same way.

How to use it#

See what something is made of

  1. Click it in the Area panel, or in the viewport (Selecting and moving things).
  2. Properties shows its Name and each of its components in a card of its own, Transform first, with their settings. Point at a setting's name to see what it does.
  3. Each card's ? opens this manual's page about that component. A component from your game code shows the file it's written in instead, with Open in Ledger ↗ to open that file in the program you write code in. A component written in Lua says Show in folder ↗ and shows its file in its folder for you to open from your editor. Why? Solis only ever opens pictures, text and Lust in another program: a downloaded project's .lua file, opened by a program on your computer that runs Lua, would run outside Solis's sandbox (see Projects and the Library).

What's been changed: a small dot in the accent colour before a setting's name means it isn't the component's standard value (what it starts with). Beside the setting, ↺ and the standard value (↺ 1000) put it back, as one step Ctrl + Z undoes. Why? So you can see at a glance what you've tuned, and undo an experiment without remembering the old number. Places, turns and picked files aren't marked: they start empty and are meant to be set. (A component that came set up for a job, such as the Sun's Light, shows dots on what makes it a sun.)

Shared files: a file several entities use, such as a model or sprite sheet, says shared by 3 beside it. Changing the file itself (in Aseprite, say) changes all of them, so this tells you before you do.

Add an entity

  • Home › Empty adds an empty one (only a Transform) at the point the camera looks at. Light beside it adds a point light, and its small arrow lists the spotlight (lights); Camera, Sprite and Tile map are there too; importing a model adds an entity for it.

Add or remove a component

  • Click + Component at the top right of Properties, type part of a name to narrow the list, and pick one (or press Enter for the first): a Light turns any entity into a lamp, a Model shows a model, and so on. It starts with its usual settings. The list is in two groups: Built in (Solis's own) and Game code (the ready-made kit's and your own); point at one to see what it does.
  • A setting that points at another entity (a camera's target, say) shows that entity's name. Click it for a list of the area's entities, with a box to find one by name, and None to point at nothing.
  • A card's ⋯ (or a right-click anywhere on the card) has Remove, which takes the component off. Game code's own components appear in the same list.

Select several

  • Click one to select just it. Ctrl + click adds one to the selection, or takes it out. Shift + click selects every row from the one you picked first to this one.
  • With one selected, Properties shows it. With several selected, Properties shows the components they all have. A setting that differs between them shows —; change it and every one of them gets the new value, as one step Ctrl + Z undoes. Change one number of a position or rotation (say Z), and only that number changes on each, so they keep their own X and Y.

Find, fold, hide and lock in the Area column

  • Search (the magnifier in the Area column's header): a field opens under the header; type part of a name to list only the entities called that, with what they belong to. Esc empties and closes it.
  • ▾ / ▸ before an entity with children folds them away or shows them again. The header's fold button folds everything; its ⋯ has Unfold everything, Fold everything, Show everything hidden and Unlock everything. Selecting something in the viewport unfolds the way to it, so you can see it in the list.
  • Point at a row to see its two switches on the right: the eye hides the entity in the editor (it isn't drawn, and nor is anything under it), and the padlock locks it, so clicks in the viewport pass through it to what's behind (handy for a floor you keep clicking by mistake). The switches stay showing while they're on. Show everything hidden and Unlock everything, on the Area column header's ⋯, turn them all off.
  • Hiding and locking are only how you see the area while you work: they aren't saved in the area, aren't undo steps, and don't change the game.

Copy settings from one entity to another

  • A card's ⋯ has Copy values, Paste values and Reset to defaults. Copy a Light from one lamp and paste it onto another to make them match; pasting onto an entity without that component adds it.
  • The ⋯ beside the entity's name has Copy components, which copies all of them at once, and Paste components, which gives them to everything selected.

Rename, move, copy or delete

  • Click its name at the top of Properties and type, press F2, or double-click it in the Area column (or choose Rename in its right-click menu) to rename it (Enter to keep, Esc to cancel).
  • Change Position under Transform, or choose Move here in the ⋯ beside its name to bring it to where the camera looks.
  • Ctrl + D duplicates the selection, with everything under each one, and selects the copies.
  • Unpack (in the ⋯ beside a model's name, or beside a placed assembly's note) splits it into separate entities.
  • Delete (the key, the ⋯ beside its name in Properties, or Delete in a row's right-click menu in the Area column) removes the selection and everything under it.
  • Right-click a row in the Area column for its menu, close to hand: Rename, Duplicate, Delete; Add entity, point light, spotlight or camera; Create assembly from selection; Select all and Select nothing. The row right-clicked is selected first, so the menu acts on it. These are the same things the Home tab's ribbon and the search do.
  • F points the camera at the selection.

Parents and children (concepts): drag an entity in the Area panel onto another to put it under that one; it then moves, turns and is deleted with its parent. Drag it onto the empty space below the list to make it stand alone again. It stays exactly where it is in the world either way: only its numbers change, because a child's Position is measured from its parent. Lights brought in with a model start under it. Dragging one of several selected entities moves them all.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Add to or take from the selectionCtrl+click
Select a rangeShift+click
RenameF2, or double-click (Enter keeps the name, Esc leaves it)
Select everythingCtrl+A
Select nothingEsc
DuplicateCtrl+D
DeleteDelete
Point the camera at the selectionF
Put under anotherdrag onto it in the Area panel
Make it stand alonedrag onto empty space in the Area panel

Settings#

The Transform every placed entity has:

SettingWhat it does
PositionWhere it is, in metres along X, Y and Z (Z is up). A child's position is measured from its parent.
RotationHow it's turned, in degrees: X tilts it forward and back, Y tilts it sideways, Z turns it round like a weathervane.
ScaleHow big it is: 1 is its own size, 2 twice as big along that axis.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Properties says Missing component. Why: the area uses a component Solis doesn't know, such as one from game code that isn't there. Fix: nothing is lost: its values are kept as they are. Click Remove if you don't need it.
  • Problem: my entities are gone after closing Solis. Why: the area wasn't saved. Fix: save with Ctrl + S (Saving areas); Solis asks before closing with unsaved changes.
  • Problem: I dragged an entity onto another and nothing happened. Why: an entity can't go under itself or its own children (that would make a loop).
  • Problem: something is missing from the viewport. Why: it (or something it belongs to) is hidden with the eye in the Area panel. Fix: Show everything hidden, in the Area column's ⋯ menu.
  • Problem: clicking something in the viewport selects what's behind it. Why: it's locked (the padlock). Fix: click its padlock, or Unlock everything in the Area column's ⋯ menu.
  • Every change here can be undone with Ctrl + Z (Undo and redo).

Related#

  • Lights and shadows
  • Sky, fog and exposure
  • Importing models
  • Concepts: entity, component, transform, parent
← Previous · Chapter 9Moving around the viewportNext → · Chapter 11Selecting and moving things

Selecting and moving things#

Click things in the viewport to select them, then move, turn and resize them with the gizmos.

When to use it#

Whenever you build an area: picking a model to change it, arranging crates, turning a lamp to face a wall, making a rock bigger. Clicking in the viewport is the quickest way to pick something you can see; the Area panel is better for things you can't see (an entity with no model, or one hidden behind another).

How to use it#

Selecting:

  1. Click a model or a lamp's marker in the viewport. It's outlined in the accent colour, and the Area panel and Properties show it.
  2. Ctrl + click adds another one to the selection, or takes it out if it's already selected.
  3. Drag on empty space to draw a box: everything you can see inside it is selected. Hold Ctrl while dragging to add to what's selected. To give up on a box before letting go, press Esc or click the right mouse button: the selection stays as it was.
  4. Esc selects nothing; Ctrl + A selects everything in the area.

Clicking on empty sky or ground selects nothing.

Copies of assemblies are selected whole the first time: clicking any part of a placed lamp post selects the whole lamp post. Click again on a part to select just that part. This stops you from pulling a copy apart by accident. See Assemblies.

Moving, turning and resizing:

  1. Select something.
  2. Choose a tool with its key or its button in the toolbox, the column down the viewport's left edge: Move (W), Rotate (R), Scale (S), or Transform (T), which shows all three. Select (Q) shows no gizmo, so clicks only select.
  3. A gizmo appears on the selection. Drag one of its handles:
    • Move: drag an arrow to move along that axis, a square to move in that flat plane (the blue-sided square slides along the ground), or the dot in the middle to move across the screen.
    • Rotate: drag a ring to turn around that axis (the blue ring turns like a record on a turntable), or the outer ring to turn around the line you're looking along.
    • Scale: drag a box at the end of a line to stretch along that axis, a square to grow two axes together, or the dot in the middle to grow evenly (right or up grows, left or down shrinks).
  4. While you drag, a note by the mouse says how far or how much ("X +1.50 m", "+15.0°", "× 1.30").
  5. Let go. The whole drag is one undo step: Ctrl + Z puts it back.

To give up on a drag before letting go, press Esc or click the right mouse button: everything goes back to where it was, and nothing is added to undo.

While the left button is held on a box or a gizmo, the right button only cancels: it doesn't start flying the camera, in any kind of view. Let go of both, and it flies again.

When several things are selected, the gizmo sits in the middle of them and they move together. Something inside another selected entity (a lamp inside a selected room) moves with it, not twice.

Settings#

The axis locks and the axes are the pills at the viewport's bottom right; snapping is the ribbon's Snapping group on the Home tab. Solis remembers them on this computer, and the status bar says what moves snap to ("Snap 0.25 · World").

SettingWhat it does
Lock X Y ZLock an axis: drags leave it alone, and its handles disappear. The letter is lit in the accent colour while locked; click it or press its key again to free it. Example: lock Z, then drag the middle dot to slide something around without lifting it off the floor.
World ▾ / Object ▾Which way the gizmo's arrows point: along the world's axes (X, Y and Z of the whole area), or along the selected entity's own axes (useful for a turned object, to slide it along its own length).
Grid · 1Snapping for moving: ticked, moves land on the grid lines, so things line up. Click the number (or right-click the row) to choose the step: 1, 0.5, 0.25 or 0.1 m. With object axes, moves go in steps of that size instead.
Angle · 15°Snapping for turning: ticked, turns go in steps. Click the number (or right-click) to choose 5°, 15°, 45° or 90°.
Scale · 10%Snapping for resizing: ticked, sizes change in steps of 10%.
The camera pillThe camera's speed step (see Moving around the viewport).

Hold Ctrl while dragging to flip snapping for that one drag: on if it's off, off if it's on. Hold Shift to drag ten times more finely, for small adjustments.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
SelectClick
Add to or take from the selectionCtrl + click
Select with a boxDrag on empty space (Ctrl + drag adds)
Select nothingEsc
Select everythingCtrl + A
Select, Move, Rotate, Scale, TransformQ, W, R, S, T
Snapping on or off for one dragHold Ctrl while dragging
Ten times finerHold Shift while dragging
Cancel a box or a gizmo dragEsc, or right click
Lock or free an axisX, Y, Z
World or object axesL

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: no gizmo appears. Why: the Select tool (Q) is chosen, nothing is selected, or what's selected has no position (the area's Environment, for example). Fix: press W, R, S or T, and select something with a Transform.
  • Problem: an arrow or ring is missing. Why: its axis is locked (its letter is lit in the Lock pill), or the arrow points almost straight at you, so it's too short to grab. Fix: free the axis, or move the camera a little.
  • Problem: clicking a part of a placed assembly selects the whole thing. Why: copies are selected whole first. Fix: click the part again.
  • Problem: a turned box stretches oddly when scaled. Why: stretching a turned object along the world's axes would skew it, which a Transform can't hold, so Solis keeps the nearest shape without a skew. Fix: press L for object axes, so it stretches along its own sides.
  • Tip: you can't select something hidden behind another model by clicking; select it in the Area panel instead.

Related#

  • Entities and components: the Area panel and Properties
  • Undo and redo
  • Moving around the viewport
  • Keyboard shortcuts
  • Concepts: gizmo, snapping, selection
← Previous · Chapter 10Entities and componentsNext → · Chapter 12Undo and redo

Undo and redo#

Take back any change to the area, and bring it back again.

When to use it#

Whenever a change didn't turn out as you hoped: a light dragged too bright, an entity deleted by mistake, a model imported into the wrong area. Every change to the area can be undone, so it's safe to experiment.

How to use it#

  1. Press Ctrl + Z (or choose Home › Undo) to take back the last change. Point at the button and it names the step, such as Undo Change Light.strength.
  2. Press again to go further back.
  3. Press Ctrl + Y or Ctrl + Shift + Z (or Home › Redo) to bring a change back.

Undo also selects what the change was about, so you can see what came back.

What counts as one step:

  • A whole drag of a number is one step, however long you drag. Dragging back to where you started leaves no step at all.
  • Typing a name is one step until you click somewhere else.
  • An import is one step, with the lights that came with the model.

Tabs with their own undo: the Clips and Frames tabs, the Animator, the Tileset tab and the Map tab each keep their own steps: Ctrl + Z with the pointer over the tab undoes there. A tileset's steps belong to its file, not to the tab: they are kept while the project is open, whether the change was made in the Tileset tab, in the tileset's Properties (clicked in the Library) or by ticking Solid in the Map tab, and Ctrl + Z over the Tileset tab, or over Properties while it shows the tileset, undoes the last of them. While a tile painting tool is in use, Ctrl + Z undoes the last stroke (each stroke, from pressing the button to letting go, is one step). In these tabs, and in the Atlas Crop tab, a whole drag of a number or of a colour in its picker is one step too: the field shows the value as you drag, and the change is made, and the file saved, once, when you let go. A typed number counts when you press Enter or click somewhere else.

What isn't undone: selecting things, moving the camera, and the editor's own settings (panels, look, accent colour). They aren't part of the area.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
UndoCtrl+Z
RedoCtrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Ctrl + Z changed the text I was typing instead of the area. Why: while you type in a field, Ctrl + Z undoes the typing first. Fix: click outside the field, then press Ctrl + Z.
  • Problem: I undid something, made a new change, and now Redo is greyed out. Why: a new change starts a new path; what you undid can't come back after that, as in most programs.
  • Problem: a change I made in a tab was taken back, and the Console says Couldn't save … It's shown as the file has it, without your change. Why: tile maps, tilesets, clips files, animators and atlases are saved the moment you change them, and this time the file couldn't be written (the disk is full, another program has the file open, or its folder is gone). Solis never shows as saved a change that isn't in the file, so it shows the file as it is, and keeps your change as an undo step. Fix: put right what the Console says went wrong, then press Ctrl + Z with the pointer over the tab the message names: your change comes back and is saved again.
  • Solis keeps the most recent changes, up to about 64 MB of them; the oldest are forgotten first. That's thousands of ordinary changes.

Related#

  • Entities and components
  • Keyboard shortcuts
← Previous · Chapter 11Selecting and moving thingsNext → · Chapter 13Saving areas

Saving areas#

Save an area as a file, open it again, and share it through Git without merge trouble.

When to use it#

Save whenever you've built something you want to keep. An area (a level, a menu, a room) is one file ending in .solarea, kept in your project (Solis suggests its assets/areas folder).

The file is plain text, written so that two people changing different things in the same area can merge their work in Git without conflicts. It's also safe to read and edit by hand.

How to use it#

  1. Save: press Ctrl + S (or Home › Save). The first time, choose a name and a folder.
  2. Save as: Ctrl + Shift + S saves a copy under a new name and carries on with that one.
  3. Open: Ctrl + O (or Open area… (press Space and type it, or Ctrl + O)). The models it uses are read from the project, from the cache, so it opens quickly.
  4. New: Ctrl + N starts a fresh area with a sun and an environment.

The tab bar at the top shows the project and the area's name, with an amber dot after it while it has changes that aren't saved (the window's title shows a • too). Solis asks before anything would lose them: a new or another area, another project (the example projects of File › Learn too), or closing. Save, Don't save or Cancel.

Changed on disk: if the file changes while it's open (a Git pull, or an edit in a text editor), Solis loads the new version as one step you can undo with Ctrl + Z. If you have unsaved changes too, it asks: Keep mine or Load the file.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
New areaCtrl+N
Open areaCtrl+O
Save areaCtrl+S
Save area asCtrl+Shift+S

What the file looks like#

-- An area. Safe to edit by hand: one block per entity, one line per field.
area version 3;

entity 2B8D4NE6TV0HC {
    name = "Sun";
    order = "a0";
    Light.kind = "Sun";
    Light.strength = 3.0;
    Transform.rotation = [0.25881904, 0.0, 0.0, 0.9659258];
}
  • One block per entity, sorted by its ID (13 letters and digits that never change), never by the tree or by when it was made, so renaming or moving an entity never moves its block.
  • One line per setting: Component.setting = value;. Text is in quotes, lists in [ ], and -- starts a comment.
  • A child names its parent with parent = "…";.
  • A copy of an assembly is one block naming its assembly. Each part you changed in that copy has a short block of its own, named after the copy and the part (copy/part), holding only what you changed. If you moved the part, its parent line names what it's under now, or is parent = ""; when you moved it out to the top level.
  • Models are named by their asset ID, with the file's path in a comment for people to read; the comment is rewritten on every save and never read.
  • Components Solis doesn't know (from game code that isn't there) are kept exactly as written.
  • A brush's shape is three long lists of numbers, written twelve to a line so no line grows too long: Brush.points (x, y and z of each point, in metres), Brush.faces (for each face, how many corners it has, then which points, counting from 0) and Brush.materials (each face's material, 0 for the plain one). Each brush may hold at most 65,536 points and 65,536 faces, and a face at most 256 corners.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: "line 12: …" when opening. Why: the file has a mistake, perhaps from a hand edit or a bad merge. Fix: the message says the line and what's wrong; fix it in a text editor. Solis never opens half a file.
  • Problem: "it was saved by a newer version". Why: someone saved it with a newer Solis, which may write things this one can't read. Fix: update Solis.
  • Problem: the Console says an area "was saved by an older version". Why: the file's first line says which version of the layout it's in, and this Solis writes a newer one (version 3; version 2 can say that a part of a copy was moved out to the top level, and version 3 holds brushes). Nothing is lost: it opens as it always did. Fix: nothing. When you save, the old file is first copied into the project's .solis/backups folder.
  • Problem: Git reports a conflict in an area file. Why: two people added entities in the same spot, or changed lines right next to each other in the same component (both rare). Fix: open the file in a text editor and keep both blocks, or the line you want; Solis's own merge tool, which isn't built yet, will do this for you.
  • Problem: "Not saved: … already exists". Why: the name typed in the Save window had no .solarea, and a file with that name and .solarea is already there; the window only asked about replacing the name as typed. Fix: choose Save as again and pick the existing file to replace it, or type another name.
  • Problem: "Stop playing first" when saving. Why: the game is running, and saving now would save its changes, which Stop undoes. Fix: press Stop, then save. A Save window opened before Play finishes after Stop.
  • Renaming or moving the open area in the Library is safe: Solis saves to its new name from then on. If it's deleted, the next save asks where to put it.
  • Saves are written to the disk in full before they replace the old file, so a crash or power cut leaves either the old file or the new one, never half of one.
  • Numbers are written as briefly as possible but always read back exactly, so saving without changes doesn't change the file.

Related#

  • Projects and the Library
  • Undo and redo
  • Entities and components
  • Concepts: area, entity, component
← Previous · Chapter 12Undo and redoNext → · Chapter 14Assemblies

Assemblies#

Build something once (a lamp post, a market stall, a whole street) and place copies of it everywhere. Change the original and every copy follows.

When to use it#

Use an assembly for anything that appears more than once: props, buildings, groups of enemies, even whole districts (assemblies can hold other assemblies). Each copy can still have its own changes: one lamp brighter, one stall without its awning. Those changes are kept when the assembly changes.

Other engines call this a prefab. An imported model works the same way: placing it makes one entity, and Unpack splits it into its parts when you need them.

How to use it#

Make one

  1. Build it in an area: a parent entity with everything under it (drag entities onto the parent in the Area panel).
  2. Select the parent and choose Home › More › Assembly from selection.
  3. It's saved in your project's assets/assemblies folder, appears in the Library, and what you selected becomes the first copy of it.

Place copies: double-click the assembly in the Library (or click its +). The copy goes where the camera looks.

Change one copy: select any part of it and change it as usual. Settings that differ from the assembly show in bold, with two small buttons:

  • ↺ puts that setting back to the assembly's value;
  • ↑ makes it the assembly's value, for every copy (Apply).

Move a part of one copy: drag it in the Area panel, under another entity or onto empty space to bring it out to the top level. It keeps its place in the world and is still part of its copy: the move is one of that copy's own changes, saved with the area, and the part still follows the assembly in everything else. From then on it belongs where you put it: deleting the part it used to be under leaves it alone, and deleting what you moved it under takes it along, as with any entity. If you delete the whole copy, a part you moved out of it stays, as an ordinary entity that no longer follows the assembly (undo puts both back).

Change every copy: use ↑, or open the .solassembly file and edit it (in Solis or a text editor). Every copy updates, and each keeps its own bold changes.

Unpack: select a copy's top entity and click Unpack in Properties. It becomes ordinary entities that no longer follow the assembly. For a model, Unpack splits it into one entity per part of the file (as in Blender's outliner), so each part can be moved, hidden or given components on its own.

Settings#

What you seeWhat it means
A copy of …This entity is the top of a placed assembly.
Part of …This entity is inside a placed assembly.
Bold settingThis copy's own change.
This part is gone from …The assembly no longer has this part, but this copy had changes to it. They're kept in case it comes back; Remove if you don't need them.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: "assemblies place each other in a loop". Why: assembly A contains B, which contains A. Fix: remove one of the copies from the other.
  • Problem: "placed more than 16 deep". Why: assemblies inside assemblies, 17 levels down. Fix: unpack some of the middle levels.
  • Problem: I undid Create assembly and the file is still in the Library. Why: undo changes the area, not files; delete the .solassembly file in Explorer if you don't want it.
  • An area file stores each copy as one block naming its assembly, plus only the settings that differ, so copies keep files small and Git merges them easily.
  • A model's parts keep their links through a new export from Blender, as long as the parts keep their names.

Related#

  • Entities and components
  • Saving areas
  • Projects and the Library
  • Concepts: assembly, copy
← Previous · Chapter 13Saving areasNext → · Chapter 15Brushes

Brushes#

Shapes made in the editor itself: a box, a ramp, stairs, drawn out on the ground, reshaped point by point, edge by edge and face by face, saved in the area and solid in the game.

When to use it#

For blocking out a level: the floors, walls, ramps, steps and platforms you walk on while you work out how a place plays. A brush is a shape made of flat faces, kept in the area itself, so there's no model to make in another program first: you can try a layout, play it, change it and play it again in minutes. Once the layout is right, brushes can stay (simple, clean shapes suit many art styles) or be replaced by models made elsewhere.

Use an imported model instead for anything detailed or curved, such as a character, a tree or a statue: a brush is made of flat faces.

How to use it#

A brush is made in two parts: you choose its shape from the brush list, then draw it out in the view: first its footprint on the ground, then its height.

Choosing a shape

  1. Rest the pointer over the 3D view (or the 2D view) and press B. The brush list opens beside the pointer: Box, Ramp, Cylinder, Stairs, Arch, Sphere and Wedge, each with a small picture.
  2. Press B again to move the highlight down the list, as many times as you need: after Wedge it comes back to Box. The status bar says which one is highlighted ("Choosing a shape brush: Ramp").
  3. Press Space to take the highlighted shape, or click any row. Esc, or a click anywhere else, closes the list without taking one.

The Shape button on Home, in the Create group (its key, B, is written small beside it), opens the same list. It stays lit while the list is open and while you draw.

Drawing it out

  1. Press the left mouse button on the ground where one corner of the brush should be, and drag to the opposite corner. This is the brush's footprint: its size shows in metres beside two of its edges, and in the steps at the top of the view ("1 Footprint · 4 × 3 m").
  2. Let go. Now move the mouse up (without pressing anything): the brush rises from the footprint, and an arrow shows its height in metres.
  3. Click to keep it. The brush is added to the Area list, named after its shape (Box_01, then Box_02; Ramp_01 for the first ramp) with its shape's picture and name beside it, and picked, so its gizmo and Properties are ready.

Corners and heights land on the grid, in the step set in the ribbon's Grid (Grid · 0.5: half a metre), so brushes line up with each other; drawing out snaps whether or not Grid is ticked. Hold Ctrl while dragging or pulling up to draw freely, off the grid. Esc or a right-click gives the brush up at any point, leaving nothing behind. Ctrl+Z takes a brush you kept away again in one step, like any change (Undo).

A drag that starts on top of a brush draws the new one on top of it, at that height: that's how you stack a platform on a block, or a step on a floor. Anywhere else it starts on the ground grid.

The Ramp and the Stairs climb along the longer side of the footprint, starting low where your drag started. Stairs get a step for every 25 cm of height; a Cylinder and a Sphere have 16 sides, and an Arch's curve 12 pieces.

In the 2D view (and the flat Front and Right views), the footprint is drawn flat in the view itself and there is no height step: letting go makes the brush, one grid step deep. The status bar and Hints say so.

What you see while drawing: the steps along the top of the view (the shape, 1 Footprint, 2 Height, the one in hand outlined), the keys for that step along the bottom, the sizes beside the brush, and what's happening in the status bar ("Drawing a Box: height 1.75 m · Click to keep · Esc to give up"). The Hints card in Properties (Interface tour) says how it works too.

Once made, a brush moves, turns and resizes with the gizmos like any entity (Selecting and moving), and its Transform's scale stretches it. Press Play: characters stand on it and bump into it, because it is Solid.

A brush is drawn flat: every face is one shade, so its edges look crisp, as a block-out should. Picked, a brush is outlined along its own edges.

Editing its insides

A brush is made of points, edges and faces. Editing its insides lets you move those parts, not just the whole brush: pull one face of a box out to make it longer, lift one corner of a floor into a slope, turn the top of a pillar.

  1. Pick one brush (click it, or click it in the Area list) and press Tab. The ribbon becomes Home tools · Brush, the other entities fade so the brush stands out, its edges are drawn in white, and the top of the view and the status bar say "Editing Box_03 · Faces · nothing picked".
  2. Choose what clicks pick: 1 points (corners), 2 edges (where two faces meet) or 3 faces (the flat sides). The same three are the first buttons on the ribbon. Editing starts in faces mode; points show as dots, and each face as a dot at its middle. Switching keeps what you picked: the points of a picked face, or the edges and faces made wholly of picked points.
  3. Pick parts as you pick entities: a click picks the part under the pointer (it lights up before you click), Ctrl + click adds a part or takes it away, a drag on empty space picks everything inside the box (through the brush, its far side too), and a click on empty space picks nothing. Clicks reach only this brush: the others can't be picked while you edit.
  4. Use the Move, Rotate or Scale tool (W, R, S) as for entities. The gizmo sits in the middle of what's picked; drag it. Snapping follows Grid and Angle on the ribbon, and Ctrl turns it off for one drag. World or Local (the pill at the bottom right, or L) chooses the world's axes or the brush's own.
  5. Press Tab again, or Done, to stop. The ribbon goes back to Home.

Each drag is one undo step (Ctrl+Z). Parts shared by what you picked move together, so the brush never comes apart at a seam: moving a face moves its edges and corners, and the faces beside it stretch to follow.

A change that would break the brush is refused. If a move, turn or stretch would fold a face over itself (turn it inside out), flatten a face to nothing (two corners on one spot), or push the brush through itself, the brush snaps back when you let go and the status bar says why ("Put back: it would fold a face over itself"). A face that ends up bent (its corners no longer on one flat plane, after lifting one corner) is fine: it is cut into triangles to draw and to be solid.

Undo while editing steps back through the brush's changes as usual; undoing past the moment you pressed Tab (the brush's own making, say) ends editing. Picking something else in the Area list ends editing too and picks that instead. Delete and Backspace do nothing while you edit (they never delete the whole brush): deleting parts comes with the next update, and the status bar says so. Extrude, Inset, Split, Delete and Material are on the ribbon already, marked as not finished yet.

In the 2D view you edit the same way, moving parts across the view's plane.

Settings#

The Brush card in Properties:

SettingWhat it does
Made asThe shape the brush was made from. Choosing another makes the brush again as that shape, filling the same box it filled (a 4 × 2 × 1 m box becomes a 4 × 2 × 1 m cylinder), in one undo step. If you had edited its insides, those edits are replaced by the fresh shape, and the status bar says so: Ctrl+Z brings them back.
SizeThe brush's box, in metres (X across, Y deep, Z up), in its own space. Typing a size stretches the brush about its middle, as one undo step; a stretch that would break the brush is refused. Each side is kept between 1 cm and 10 km.
MaterialNot finished yet: brush materials come with a later update. Every face is drawn in the plain material.
SolidOn: the game's characters and bodies collide with it, as with a floor or a wall. Off: it's only drawn, and things pass through it (a light shaft, a hint of where something goes). A brush never falls: it stays where it's placed. Also on the ribbon while editing.
Points, Edges, FacesHow many the brush has, in three boxes; while its insides are edited, the box of the mode in use is outlined, and the line under them says what's picked ("Picked: 1 face · Faces mode").

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Open the brush list (pointer over the 3D or 2D view)B
Move down the list (it wraps round)B
Take the highlighted shapeSpace, or click its row
Close the listEsc, or click elsewhere
Draw the footprintDrag on the ground
Draw freely, off the gridHold Ctrl while dragging or pulling up
Keep the brushMove the mouse up, then click
Give it upEsc, or right-click
Start or stop editing the picked brush's insidesTab
Pick points, edges or faces (while editing)1, 2, 3
Pick a part; add or take one away; pick with a boxClick; Ctrl + click; drag on empty space
Pick every part of the mode; pick nothing (while editing)Ctrl+A; Esc

With a tile map picked, B is the tile map's Brush instead (Painting tiles); the Shape button still opens the list.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Tab does nothing. Why: editing needs exactly one brush picked, and the game stopped. Fix: click one brush (not a lamp or a model), or stop the game.
  • Problem: a drag snapped back when let go. Why: it would have broken the brush; the status bar said how. Fix: move less far, or move the faces beside it too (pick them with Ctrl + click), so nothing folds over.
  • Problem: clicking another entity while editing doesn't pick it. Why: while editing, clicks reach only the brush being edited. Fix: press Tab to stop, or pick the other entity in the Area list.
  • Problem: Delete doesn't delete the brush. Why: while editing, Delete is kept for deleting parts, which comes with the next update. Fix: press Tab to stop editing, then Delete.
  • Problem: pressing B paints tiles instead of opening the list. Why: a tile map is picked, and B is its Brush. Fix: pick something else (or nothing, Esc), or use the Shape button.
  • Problem: "Nothing made: the footprint had no size". Why: you clicked without dragging. Fix: press and drag to the opposite corner before letting go.
  • Problem: "Nothing made: the brush had no height". Why: you clicked before moving the mouse up. Fix: after letting go of the footprint, move the mouse up until the height shows, then click.
  • Problem: a brush stands in mid-air. Why: the drag started on top of another brush, so it was drawn at that height. Fix: move it down with the gizmo, or undo and start the drag on the ground.
  • Problem: a character falls through a brush. Why: its Solid is off. Fix: tick Solid.
  • Problem: a brush gives a body or a collider of its own as well. Why: a Collider component on the same entity is used instead of the brush's shape. Fix: take the Collider off to collide with the brush's own faces.
  • Problem: a brush from a damaged file shows nothing, and the Problems list names it. Why: its points or faces couldn't be read (the problem says which: a face naming a point that isn't there, say, or more than a brush may hold, 65,536 points or faces). Fix: the file's text is kept as it was, so it can be put right by hand; or choose its Made as again, which makes it again as that shape at its standard size; or delete it and draw it again.

Related#

  • Entities and components: a brush is an entity with a Brush component.
  • Physics: colliders and bodies, which a Solid brush works with.
  • Saving areas: how a brush is written in the area's file.
  • Keyboard shortcuts: every key in one place.
  • Selecting and moving things: the gizmos, snapping and world or local axes, which editing a brush's insides uses too.
  • Concepts: brush, footprint, mesh, point, edge, face.
← Previous · Chapter 14AssembliesNext → · Chapter 16Play mode

Play mode#

Run the area as a game inside the editor, try things, and press Stop: keep what you changed, or get everything back exactly as it was.

When to use it#

Whenever you want to see the area the way a player will: through the game's camera, with no grid, gizmos or markers. The game's own code runs too: every component written in Lust runs its update 60 times a second. You can move things, delete things and experiment freely while playing: when you press Stop, Solis lists what you changed and asks whether to Keep it or Undo all, so nothing is lost by accident and nothing sticks that you didn't mean.

How to use it#

Add a camera first (once per area)

  1. Move the viewport to look the way the game should look.
  2. On the Home tab, click Camera in the ribbon's Create group. A camera appears exactly where you're looking from, facing the same way, and is selected. In the viewport it's drawn as a small wire pyramid pointing the way it looks; click it to select it.
  3. Move and turn it like anything else (W, R). Its Field of view in Properties sets how wide it sees.

The game looks through the first camera in the Area panel's list. With no camera, the Game panel shows the editor's own view and says so.

Play, pause and stop (the Play group, at the right end of the ribbon on every tab)

  1. Press Play (▶), the one light button in the editor. A Game tab appears beside the area's tab on Home and comes to the front, showing the game (on the Debug tab the Game is a tab beside the Profiler, which stays in front: click the Game's tab to watch it there). Play itself becomes Stop (■), still the one light button, and Pause and Step appear beside it. Nothing else changes colour: the editor is the same editor while the game runs, and the button that would start the game is the button that ends it. (Earlier builds tinted the whole window blue while playing and amber while paused; the design the editor now follows doesn't.)

  2. Work as usual: the Area panel, Properties, the viewport and its gizmos all still work. Changes show in the game straight away. For game code's components, Properties shows their values as they are right now (a counter counting, a camera's yaw turning), and a value you set there reaches the game: the running component takes exactly what you set, whatever the game had made of it. That holds when you set the value it started with, too: a turret that has fired down to 7 has 12 again when you type 12, or click the ↺ 12 beside the field. Its other values stay as the game has them. When you press Stop, every value the game changed goes back as it was before Play; a value you set yourself is one of your changes, which Stop asks about (step 6). Click the area's tab beside Game to move things with the gizmos in the viewport; click Game to go back. On Stop the Game tab goes from Home, and the area's tab is in front again.

  3. Press Pause (❚❚) to stop the game's clock; the button stays lit while the game is paused (game code can pause itself too, for a pause menu: the corner then says Game speed 0, and the game still runs its code, see Game screens); press Pause again to carry on. The Game panel's corner shows Playing or Paused and how long the game has run.

  4. While paused, press Step (▶❙, beside Pause; faint until the game is paused) to run exactly one tick: game code runs once, everything moves on by a sixtieth of a second, and the game stays paused. It's the way to watch something that happens too fast to see, one step at a time.

  5. Press Stop (■). The game is thrown away and the area comes back exactly as it was when you pressed Play: every entity and setting, the undo history (Ctrl + Z carries on from where you were) and the selection.

  6. If you changed the area while playing, a question lists what you did (Add Point light 1, Move Crate…):

    • Keep makes your changes again on the area as it was before Play, and each can still be undone with Ctrl + Z.
    • Undo all leaves the area as it was before Play.

    Why ask? Other engines quietly throw away everything changed while playing, and people lose work that way. Solis asks instead. The question waits for an answer; until then, Play and the editor's keys wait too. So does anything that would leave the area: quitting, closing the window, a new or another area, and another project go ahead only once you've answered, so your changes can't slip away unasked. If you close the editor's window to go back to Recent projects while the game plays, the question is asked there.

Only your own edits are kept, never what the game did. After Keep, the area is exactly the area as it was when you pressed Play, plus the changes in the list. Entities the game spawned are gone, entities it removed are back, and every value and place it changed is as it was. That holds after loading a save game while playing too: your edits are made on your area, not on the save's. Solis can tell the two apart because each edit of yours is an undo step and nothing the game does is one. What that means when the two meet:

  • A value you set that the game also changes (a counter, where a cart stands) is kept as you set it, not as the game left it.
  • A value you set back to what it was before Play (the turret's 12 again) is in the list too, since you did set it. Keep and Undo all then end the same way for it: the area holds that value either way.
  • A change to something the game made (renaming a bullet it spawned) can't be kept, because that entity goes with the game. It's left out of the list, and the Console says which changes those were. When one change touched your entities and the game's together (a crate and a bullet deleted in one go), your entities' share of it is kept.
  • A change to an entity the game removed afterwards is kept: Stop brings the entity back, and Keep makes your change to it.
  • An entity you deleted stays deleted, whatever the game would have done with it.
  • Undoing, while playing, a change made before Play is a change too: the list says Undid a change made before Play, and Keep leaves it undone (Ctrl + Y makes it again).
  • A change you made while playing and undid again with Ctrl + Z is simply gone: after Stop, Ctrl + Y can't bring it back.

An edit while the game runs changes only what you edit. The field you set takes your value at once, even if the game had changed it. Everything else on that entity stays as the game has it: the screen it shows, a sound game code switched off, the clip its sprite plays and which way it's flipped, its animator, its tile map, where it stands and how it moves. So you can tune a lamp on the entity that shows the health bar without the health bar vanishing, and adding or deleting another entity doesn't put anything back either.

You can also type play, pause, step and stop in the Console.

Playing with the keys, mouse and gamepad: click the Game panel to give the game the mouse and keys (the pointer disappears, and the editor's own keys are off); press Esc to give them back. A gamepad works whenever the game plays. The Debug tab's Session group also records a play's input and plays it back exactly (Play and record inputs and Replay a recording…, see Input), and its Load save plays from a save game.

Smooth on any screen: the game itself always runs 60 ticks a second, so it plays the same on every computer. A screen can show more frames than that (120 or 144 a second): between two ticks, the Game panel draws everything part way from where it was at the last tick to where it is now, so movement looks smooth instead of stepping. What you see is up to a sixtieth of a second behind the game, which no one can notice. While paused, it shows exactly where things are.

What waits until you stop: saving, opening another area or project, new areas, and making or changing assemblies. If you try, the Console says Stop playing first: saving now would save the game's changes, which Stop is about to undo. Quitting or closing Solis while playing stops the game first. If you changed the area while it played, Keep or Undo all is asked before anything closes; then Solis asks about unsaved changes as usual (after Keep, the changes you kept are unsaved, so it asks about them).

Changes from outside while playing: if an assembly's file changes (a Git pull, or Notepad), the game shows it at once, and its copies are updated again after Stop. That isn't one of your changes, so Stop doesn't ask about it, and the area you Keep has the updated copies too. If the area's own file changes on disk, Solis waits until Stop, and until you've answered Keep or Undo all, to offer it.

Renaming, moving or deleting the area's file while playing (in the Library) holds after Stop: the area keeps its new name and place, whether you Keep your changes or not, and Ctrl + S saves it there. If you deleted the file, the area counts as unsaved after Stop, and saving asks where to put it. That's the one thing Stop doesn't put back, because the file really did move.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Camera > ViewPerspective, as the eye sees, or 2D: flat, straight down, drawn pixel-perfect at the project's base resolution (2D).
Camera > Field of viewHow wide the camera sees, top to bottom, in degrees. 50° looks like a normal photo; 90° sees much more but stretches the edges. A 2D camera doesn't use it.
Camera > NearThe nearest it sees. Raise it if far surfaces flicker.
Camera > FarThe farthest it sees; anything beyond isn't drawn.

Shortcuts#

Play, Pause, Step and Stop are buttons only, so a stray key never starts or stops the game. They are in the search too (press Space and type the name), and in the Console: play, pause, step, stop.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: I changed something while playing and it went back when I pressed Stop. Why: you chose Undo all when Stop asked. Fix: Undo all can't be taken back; next time choose Keep. A value the game changed (not you) always goes back: copy the component's values with ⋯ > Copy values before Stop, and paste them after.
  • Problem: I chose Keep, but one change I made while playing isn't there. Why: it was a change to something the game made (an entity it spawned, or one a loaded save held), and those go with the game; the Console named it when you pressed Stop. Fix: make the change where the entity comes from: the assembly game code spawns, or an entity of the area itself.
  • Problem: the Game panel shows the editor's view. Why: the area has no camera. Fix: on the Home tab, Create › Camera.
  • Problem: new entities appear in the Area panel while playing. Why: game code made them (World:spawn, see Game code). Fix: nothing: they go when you press Stop.
  • Problem: pressing keys while playing changes the area (W picks the move tool). Why: the editor has the keys. Fix: click the Game panel to give them to the game; Esc gives them back.
  • Problem: I can't tell whether the game is running. Why: the window no longer changes colour while it plays. Fix: look at the ribbon's right end: Stop is there instead of Play while the game runs, and Pause is lit while it is paused. The status bar says Playing or Paused too, and the Game tab is in front.
  • Problem: Step is greyed out. Why: it runs one tick of a paused game. Fix: press Pause first.
  • Problem: the game shows the wrong camera. Why: it uses the first one in the Area panel's list. Fix: delete the cameras you don't need, or take their Camera component off (Remove Camera, in the ⋯ on its card in Properties).
  • Problem: the picture in the Game panel looks different from the viewport. Why: the game always uses the standard look; the viewport's look is only for editing. Hidden entities (the eye in the Area panel) show in the game, because hiding is only for the editor.

Related#

  • Interface tour
  • The Console
  • Entities and components
  • Concepts: play mode, game, camera
← Previous · Chapter 15BrushesNext → · Chapter 17Projects

Projects#

File › Recent projects, where Solis starts: every project you've worked on as a card, the templates to start a new one from, and beside it Learn, Updates and About.

When to use it#

Solis always starts here, in its own full window: the File tab's Recent projects page. You pick the project to work on, and the editor opens on it. Solis never reopens the last project by itself, so you always choose; the projects you opened most recently come first, so it's one double-click.

Until a project is open, the other tabs along the top are dimmed and the top right says No project open. They still work: clicking one, or Carry on without a project at the top of the File column (or Esc), opens the editor with nothing open, which is handy for looking at a model on its own. The editor opens on the tab you left in front last time.

Closing the editor's window brings you back to this page, with the project still open behind it (Back to editor returns to it). Closing the window while a File page is in front quits Solis, asking about unsaved work first. The page is also there at any time from File › Recent projects.

Use it to:

  • open a project you've worked on before, without hunting for its folder;
  • keep the projects you're working on now at the front (pin them);
  • see, before opening a project, which build of Solis last opened it: useful after an update, or when a project comes from someone with a newer copy;
  • tidy the list: a project you've finished with, or one whose folder has gone, can be removed from it, and one you moved can be found again;
  • rename a project, make a copy of it to try something risky, or open its folder in Explorer;
  • find projects already on your computer (copied from a USB stick, cloned from Git) without opening each one;
  • start something new: an empty project, or one of the four examples to learn from.

How to use it#

  1. Each project is a card: a large letter where its picture will be (pictures are an unfinished part), its name, its folder, when you last opened it, and the build that last opened it. Pinned projects come first.
