  2. Double-click a card to open it, or click it once and press Enter (Enter in Search projects opens it too, while the search still shows it; with no card picked, Enter there opens nothing). The arrow keys walk from card to card: left and right along a row, up and down between rows. With unsaved changes in the open area, Solis asks first.
  3. The pin at the right of a project's name keeps it at the front; click it again to unpin.
  4. Right-click a card for its menu:
    • Open.
    • Pin (or Unpin).
    • Show in Explorer: opens the project's folder.
    • Rename…: changes the project's name (in the title bar and on its card). Its folder keeps its name, so nothing that points at the folder breaks. Type the new name and press Enter; Esc leaves it as it was.
    • Make a copy…: choose an empty folder, and the whole project is copied there, named "… copy". Handy before trying something you may want to undo. The import cache is left out (the copy makes its own when it opens), and so are links to elsewhere on the computer. A big project takes a while: a note under the heading says when it's done, and the copy joins the list.
    • Remove from list: only forgets the project here. Its folder and files stay exactly where they are, and Open… brings it back.
  5. Search projects narrows the cards as you type, by name or folder. Every word you type must appear somewhere, in any order. Click it to type: when Solis starts, the keys are the cards' (the arrows walk them, Esc carries on into the editor).
  6. Sort by orders the cards by when each was last opened, or by name. Pinned projects always come first.
  7. New project makes a folder into a new project. Open… ▾ has Open a project folder… (one that isn't in the list yet) and Scan a folder for projects…, which looks through a folder you choose, and the folders inside it (four levels down), and adds every project it finds, without opening them. It doesn't look inside projects or hidden folders.
  8. Start from a template, under the cards: Blank project is the same as New project; Playground, Turret sample, UI sample and Benchmark each make one of Solis's examples as a new project, in a folder you choose. The faint tiles after them (First-person, Top-down, Platformer, and All templates) are unfinished parts: templates to come. The four examples can be made from the command line too, for a script: solis --sample playground "C:\Games\Try" makes the playground in that empty folder and opens it (the others are game, ui and benchmark).

Learn, Updates and About#

The File column has three more pages:

  • Learn: the four examples again, each with a sentence about it and Make it in a folder…; Your first hour, five steps for someone new; Open the user guide (this manual, as one page in your browser: The user guide); and Add the sample area, which adds a small ready-made area to the open project to look around in.
  • Updates: when a newer build of Solis is out, Updates has a New mark in the File column, the status bar says Build N is out (click it to come here), and a card across the top of the page says what it is, with Not now and Download (it downloads while you work), then Restart to update (Solis asks about unsaved work, closes, installs it and opens again). In a copy you didn't install with the setup file, the step is Open the releases page instead. Under the card: the build you have, the newest build with Check now, the Look for updates when Solis starts switch, the releases page and the list of every change. Beside them, what the new build brings, from its release on GitHub. See Installing and updating.
  • About: the program's name, version and build, what it is, Open LICENSE (its licence), Open the notices (the libraries and fonts built into it, each with its licence), and the way to Updates and the user guide.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
PinKeeps a project at the front, whatever the order. Use it for the projects you're working on now.
Sort byLast opened (the most recent first; projects whose time isn't known come last) or Name (A to Z).
Look for updates when Solis starts (Updates)Asks GitHub for a newer build at each start, in the background. Off, nothing is asked until you press Check now. The same switch is on Preferences › General.

The build each project was last opened with#

Every copy of Solis installed from GitHub has a build number (build 57, then 58, and so on). When a project opens, Solis writes its build number into the project's project.solis file, so its card can tell you about it before you open the project:

MarkMeaning
build 57 · this oneLast opened with the build you're using. Nothing to think about.
build 52 · older (amber)Last opened with an older build. It opens as usual; any of its files laid out the old way are upgraded when saved, with a backup first (Backups and upgrades).
build 60 · newer (amber)Last opened with a newer build than yours. Update Solis first (Installing and updating): parts made with the newer build may not open in yours.
—Not known: the project hasn't been opened since builds were noted, or only by a copy built from source.

A copy built from source has no build number of its own: it shows each project's build without comparing.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Open the project pickedEnter, or double-click
Walk the cards← → ↑ ↓
A card's menuRight-click it
Back to the editor (or carry on without a project)Esc
In Rename…: keep the new name, or leave it as it wasEnter, Esc

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a card says Folder not found and its letter is a ?. Why: the folder was moved, renamed or deleted, or it's on a drive that isn't plugged in. Fix: plug the drive in and come back to Recent projects (it looks each time). If you moved the folder, click Locate… and choose where it is now: the project keeps its pin. Otherwise click Remove.
  • Problem: a card says project.solis is gone from its folder. Why: the folder is there, but the file that makes it a project isn't. Fix: if the project is in Git, get the file back from there; otherwise Remove it.
  • Problem: project.solis shows as changed in Git after opening a project. Why: Solis noted its build number in it (saved_by). Fix: commit it with your other changes: it tells your teammates which build last opened the project.
  • Problem: Make a copy… says the folder isn't empty. Why: a copy never goes over other files. Fix: make a new, empty folder for it (the folder window has a New folder button).
  • Problem: Scan a folder for projects… says it stopped early. Why: it looks through at most 20,000 folders, so choosing a whole drive can't keep it busy for long. Fix: choose the folder your projects are in, such as Documents.
  • Problem: the arrow keys move the search's caret instead of walking the cards. Why: the search has the keys while you type in it. Fix: click a card first; the arrows walk from there.

Related#

  • Projects and the Library: what a project is and what's in it.
  • Settings: Preferences and Project settings, the File column's other pages.
  • Installing and updating: getting a newer build.
  • Backups and upgrades: what happens to a project made with an older build.
  • Concepts: project, build, File page.
← Previous · Chapter 16Play modeNext → · Chapter 18Projects and the Library

Projects and the Library#

A project is a folder holding your game's files: models, pictures, areas and code. The Library shows what's in it, with pictures of each model, and is where you place things from.

When to use it#

Make a project as soon as you start something you want to keep. Without one, Solis works as a viewer: models you import are shown but not kept. With one:

  • models you import are copied into the project's assets folder, so the project has everything it needs, on any computer;
  • each asset gets an ID that never changes, so renaming or moving a file (in Solis, in Explorer, or through Git) breaks nothing;
  • when you save a model again in Blender or Aventail, Solis notices and shows the new version straight away;
  • the Library shows every file, folder by folder, with a thumbnail of each model and picture and the waveform of each sound, ready to drag into the area (or, for a sound, to listen to: see Sounds).

How to use it#

Make a project

  1. File › New project and choose an empty folder (make one in the window if you need to). The project is named after the folder.
  2. Solis makes project.solis, an assets folder, and a hidden .solis folder for its cache. If you use Git, it also adds .gitignore and .gitattributes files set up for games.

Open a project: File › Open… and choose the project's folder, or pick it from File › Recent projects (Projects). Solis doesn't open the last project again when it starts: it always starts on Recent projects, so you choose what to work on, and the projects you opened most recently are at the top of its list (after any you pinned), one double-click away.

Opening another project starts afresh. Everything of the project you leave goes with it: its area, the files open in tabs (Clips, Frames, Animator, Map, Tileset, Atlas Crop, the UI canvas) and their undo steps, components' values you copied, and a seed chosen in the Console. Nothing of one project can then be saved into another by mistake, which matters most with a copy of a project, whose files have the same names. What's yours stays as it is: the layout, the cameras, the theme and the Console's messages.

Add models: Library › Import, or drop a .glb or .gltf file onto the window: it's copied into the project's assets and placed in the area. You can also put files straight into the assets folder (or a folder inside it) from Explorer: they appear in the Library within a moment.

Find your way around the Library

  • The Library tab's ribbon holds what you do with files: Add (Import with its list, Create for anything New makes, Folder), View (List for a list in place of tiles, Show folders for the folder tree), Filter (Type: All ▾: one group of kinds at a time) and Use (Place: puts the picked file where the camera looks, and brings Home to the front). Tags, Missing references, Source control and Show in area are unfinished parts.
  • With Show folders on, the folder tree is on the left: click a folder to see what's in it. The line above the files (Harbour › props) shows where you are; click a part of it to go back up.
  • The folder's files are tiles that fill the width: each a square for its picture, then its name, and a coloured dot and word saying what kind of file it is. The colours are the design's: models cyan, assemblies blue, pictures and sprite sheets coral, clips and animators purple, sounds amber, tilesets and tile maps green; sound events, code files and areas keep the colours they had, and text files are one light blue. The picked tile is tinted with the accent and outlined inside. The shelf bar's right end counts the folder's items and how many are picked.
  • Search the project, beside the chips, finds files by name in every folder.
  • The chips (All, Models, Sprites, Maps, Sounds, Code, each with its kind's dot) show only one kind of file, so a busy folder is easy to scan. All shows everything, your code files included (the Code shelf tab, on the Library tab, lists only code).

Where the Library is

  • On Home, the Assets list is the Library's open folder as tiles, with Import last, so you can drag files from it straight into the area (or double-click one to place it where the camera looks). Where it sits depends on the panel layout chosen in File › Preferences: a wide strip under the area (the standard), under the Area list at the left, under Properties at the right, or a column of the shelf's Entity tab. The Place shelf tab (Home's first) is for placing: see below. The folder is the Library tab's: open another folder there and Assets follows. Drag the border at its edge for a bigger list, and press Ctrl + Space to fold the shelf away when you want the viewport bigger. (Older builds had a Library drawer with Pin and Unpin; the shelf takes its place.)
  • The Library tab of the tab bar shows it filling the window, with the file picked shown on the shelf's Details tab and the code files on its Code tab.
  • Point at a file to see its full path and what you can do with it.

Place a model or assembly

  • Drag it from the Library into the viewport: it goes on whatever surface is under the mouse when you let go (a table, the floor), or on the ground. In a flat Front or Right view, dropped on empty space, it goes exactly where you point, at that height. It's selected, ready to move.
  • Drag it onto an entity in the Area panel: it goes under that entity, at its place.
  • Or double-click it in Home's Assets list to place it where the camera looks. In the Library tab a double-click only picks a file that would be placed (so a stray double-click never drops something in the area); use Place on the ribbon, or drag it.

Placing, with the Place shelf tab Bringing Home's Place shelf tab to the front is placing: the ribbon shows its building form (Place, Snapping, Paint and Transform, which holds the five tools while the toolbox is put away), the shelf shows Placement (how placed things land; in the shelf panel layout with the Area tree and the files beside it), and the Assets list shows only the files that can be placed, wherever it is (Favourites and Recent are unfinished; All, Models, Sprites, Maps, and Find something to place, which looks in every folder). While you drag a file over the viewport, a square in the accent shows where it will land, a label says what it is and where ("crate", "x 2.75 y -13.25 · grid"), and a strip at the bottom says how. With the ribbon's Grid on and Align to: Grid, it lands on the grid's step; Free never snaps, and holding Ctrl as you drop doesn't snap that once. Choosing another shelf tab (Entity, or the Console in the other layouts) leaves placing.

Open things: double-click an area to open it (Solis asks first if yours has unsaved changes). Double-click a picture to open it in its own program (your picture editor, say); to put it in the world as a sprite, drag it into the viewport instead. Any other file, one Solis doesn't know, opens its folder instead of the file itself, and its name is shown in full with its ending: a file called brick.png.exe is a program pretending to be a picture, and opening it would run it. Projects you download or are sent can hold anything, so Solis never runs what's in them.

Make new things: right-click anywhere in the Library (empty space, a folder or a file) and choose New, or use Create on the Library ribbon. Everything is made in the folder shown (or the one you right-clicked):

  • Lust code file: your game's code. The first one is main.lst, at the top of the assets, because game code starts there; later ones are component.lst, ready to fetch from main.lst. Each starts with a component and opens in the program your computer uses for .lst files (Ledger, once it's installed). See Game code.
  • Folder: "New folder".
  • Area: an empty level, saved there and opened (Solis asks first if yours has unsaved changes). See Saving areas.
  • Tile map, Tileset, Animator and Sound event: see Tile maps, Tilesets and autotiling, Animators and Sound events.

Text files (.md and .txt notes, and data in .json, .csv, .toml and .ron) show in the Library in one light blue. Click one and Properties shows it, read only: a Markdown file's headings, lists, quotes, code and bold as they read, the others as plain text (up to 512 KB and the first 3,000 lines). Open in its program (or a double-click) opens it in the program your computer uses for that kind of file, such as Ledger for Markdown, to edit it there; Properties shows the change as soon as you save. They're under the Code chip too.

Import on the Library ribbon brings in a model. It's greyed until a project is open, since the model is copied into it.

Organise files (right-click a file or folder):

  • Rename…: type a new name. The file's ID file goes with it, so nothing using it breaks. Changing only capitals works too. Renaming the open area is fine: Solis saves to the new name. A name must work on every computer: at most 100 characters, none of < > : " / \ | ? *, and not a name Windows keeps for a device (CON, NUL, COM1 …); the Console says why if it isn't.
  • Move: drag a file onto a folder in the tree.
  • New: makes something new in that folder (see below).
  • Open or Place (a sprite's clips file and a picture offer both): Open does what a double-click on that file does, and Place puts it in the area. Place is greyed on a file Solis hasn't given its ID yet, such as one copied in a moment ago: try again shortly.
  • Show in Explorer opens the folder in your system's file browser.
  • With the pointer over the Library or the Assets column, F2 renames and Delete deletes the file picked there (anywhere else they act on the selected entity).
  • Delete moves the file (or folder) to the Recycle Bin, with its ID file, so you can get it back. Anything in the area still using it keeps showing it until Solis restarts.

A .gltf model reads the files beside it, so it can't be moved to another folder on its own: move its whole folder instead. Renaming it in place is fine.

The Code tab beside the Library lists the project's code files (Lust .lst, Lua and Rust), with a search box. Double-click a Lust file to open it in the program Windows has for .lst files: make that a text or code editor (right-click a .lst file in Explorer > Open with > Choose another app), never a program that runs Lust, since a downloaded project's code should only run inside Solis's sandbox. A Lua file shows its folder instead (some computers have a program that runs .lua files rather than editing them), so open it from there in your editor. Solis checks your Lust whenever you save; see Game code. The solis folder holds files Solis writes, describing the engine to your code.

Change a model: export it again over the same file in Blender. Everything using it shows the new version a moment later. If the new file is broken, the old version stays, and the Console says why.

Settings#

File or folderWhat it is
project.solisMarks the folder as a project and holds its name.
assets/Everything you made or brought in. Watched for changes.
<file>.solmetaA small text file beside each asset holding its ID. Commit it with the asset, and move or rename them together (Solis copes if you forget, as long as the content didn't change).
.solis/Solis's own folder. cache/ holds models it has already read, so they open quickly; it keeps within 4 GB, deleting the models used least lately, and is safe to delete (it's rebuilt). backups/ holds copies of files saved by an older Solis, kept before they were upgraded (Backups and upgrades). Never committed.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the Console says a sidecar couldn't be read. Why: the .solmeta file was damaged, perhaps by a bad Git merge. Fix: fix it in a text editor, or delete it to give the model a new ID (anything using the old ID will then say the model is missing).
  • Problem: the Console says a model "is a copy, so it got a new ID". Why: a file was copied together with its .solmeta; two files can't share an ID. The original (whose .solmeta is older) keeps its ID, so nothing using it changes. Nothing is wrong.
  • Problem: a model I saved into the assets folder from Blender takes a couple of seconds to show in the Library. Why: Solis waits two seconds before giving a new file its ID, because Git writes a file and its .solmeta one after the other: a look in between would give the file a new ID and lose the one it has on other computers. Fix: nothing; models brought in with Import model show at once.
  • Problem: I renamed a model in Explorer and changed it before Solis was open, and it lost its ID. Why: Solis finds a renamed file by its content; with the content changed too, it can't tell. Fix: rename and change in separate steps, or rename the .solmeta along with it.
  • Problem: models placed before opening a project disappeared. Why: opening a project starts a new area. Fix: Solis asks to save first; save the area inside the project to keep it.
  • Imported models open much faster the second time: the cache remembers them, even after a rename.
  • Problem: a file shows an icon instead of a thumbnail. Why: thumbnails are made for models and pictures only, a few at a time, and a damaged file gets none. Fix: wait a moment; for a damaged file, the Console says what's wrong when you place it.
  • Problem: Solis says there's already a file with that name. Why: renaming and moving never replace another file. Fix: choose another name, or delete the other file first.

Related#

  • Importing models
  • Entities and components
  • Concepts: project, asset, sidecar, cache
← Previous · Chapter 17ProjectsNext → · Chapter 19Backups and upgrades

Backups and upgrades#

Files saved by an older Solis keep opening, and a copy of each is kept before Solis changes it.

When to use it#

You don't need to do anything: it works by itself. This page explains what happens when you open a project after updating Solis, so the messages in the Console make sense.

Each kind of file Solis saves (areas, assemblies, sound events, the Mixer's buses, input actions, recordings, save games, the project file and sidecars) has a format version: a number at its top saying how it's laid out. When an update changes how a kind of file is laid out, its number goes up, and the update brings an upgrader that turns the old layout into the new one.

How it works#

  1. Opening an older file: Solis upgrades it as it reads it, in memory. The file itself isn't changed. For an area, an assembly you open, the input actions and the Mixer, the Console says so: "input.solinput was saved by an older version (format 1), so it's been upgraded to format 2 as it was read…".

  2. Saving it: before the file is written in the new layout, Solis:

    1. checks that the new file reads back exactly as what's being saved;
    2. copies the old file to the project's .solis/backups/ folder, into a folder named by the date and time (such as .solis/backups/2026-10-28 09-15-02/input.solinput), keeping its place in the project;
    3. writes the new file, and checks it on disk.

    This happens for areas, assemblies, sound events, the input actions and the Mixer, the files you change in the editor, and for save games: a save made by an older Solis is copied before a new save replaces it in its slot (the saves folder isn't in Git, so the copy is the only one). If any step fails, the old file stays exactly as it was and the Console says why. When it works, the Console says where the copy went.

  3. Files moving to Lust (what Solis makes is Lust): the files Solis makes are becoming ordinary Lust files you can read and check in Ledger, each named for what it holds, such as farm.tilemap.lst and ground.tileset.lst. When you open a project, each older one (farm.soltilemap, ground.soltileset) is moved at once: Solis writes the Lust file beside it, checks it reads back the same, moves the small .solmeta file with it (so everything that uses it still finds it), and puts the older file in .solis/backups/. The Console says how many moved. One that can't move (it's damaged, or a file already has the new name) stays as it is and still works, and the Console says why. Why: Lust is the language you write your game in, so every file of your project reads the same way, and Ledger can open them all.

  4. After that the file is in the new layout, so later saves don't make more copies. Your project's Git history is the undo for ordinary changes.

A file saved by a newer Solis than yours isn't opened at all: the Console says to update. Solis never changes a file it doesn't fully understand: input actions or a Mixer from a newer Solis aren't saved over (the Console says to update), and a save game from a newer Solis is copied to the backups before a new save replaces it in its slot.

Settings#

There are none. Old backups are tidied away by themselves:

RuleWhat it means
Older than 90 daysRemoved the next time a backup is made.
More than 1 GB in allThe oldest are removed until they fit, but never one less than a week old (a save game's backup may be its only copy).
The newest, and the one just madeAlways kept, however old or big.

Tips and common problems#

  • A file you save from inside .solis/backups/ (to look at an old one) is saved as it is, with no backup of its own: Solis never tidies away a backup you're working in.
  • Problem: you want the old file back. Why: an upgrade changed something you didn't expect. Fix: copy the file from .solis/backups/<date and time>/ back over the new one, or use Git to go back. To open it in its old layout, use the Solis build that saved it (the last ten are kept on the Releases page; see Installing and updating).
  • Problem: the backups are gone. Why: .solis/ is also Solis's cache; deleting the whole folder deletes the backups with it. Fix: nothing is lost while the project is in Git: its history has every committed version. Deleting .solis/cache alone keeps them.
  • Problem: the Console says "this … file was saved by a newer version". Why: someone saved it with a newer Solis. Fix: update Solis (File › Updates › Check now).
  • The backups folder isn't committed to Git (new projects' .gitignore leaves out .solis/), so each computer keeps its own.

Related#

  • Saving areas: how areas are saved, and why they merge in Git.
  • Installing and updating: how updates arrive.
  • Concepts: format version, cache, sidecar.
← Previous · Chapter 18Projects and the LibraryNext → · Chapter 20Checking a project before updating

Checking a project before updating#

Opens a project without the editor, reads every file, checks the game's code and plays back recordings, and says whether anything changed.

When to use it#

Before you update Solis on a project that matters (your own game), or in a workflow that tries each new build on it before you do. It answers one question: does this build still open my project and play my game the same? If the answer is no, don't update yet: the report says what changed.

The samples Solis makes (the turret sample, the benchmark and the playground) are checked this way by Solis's own tests on every change, so a build that breaks them never ships.

How to use it#

  1. Keep a few recordings as checks. Play your game while recording its input (Debug › Play and record inputs, see Input), then press Stop. The recording is saved in the project's recordings folder. Move the ones you want checked into recordings/checks/. A good check is a minute of ordinary play: walking, using things, saving.

  2. Run the check from a command prompt, with the build you're about to use:

    solis --check-project "C:\Games\My farm"

  3. Read the report. It's printed, and kept in the project as .solis/check-report.txt (on Windows, Solis has no window to print to, so open that file). Each line says ok, note (fine, but worth knowing: an older file that was upgraded as it's read) or FAIL. The last line says whether the project checks out.

The check opens the project the way the editor does (with its input actions, 2D settings and Mixer), so it also writes the engine's description files (assets/solis/) and any missing sidecars, as opening it in the editor would. It never changes your areas, code or other files.

What it checks#

StepWhat fails
FilesAny area, assembly, sound event, Mixer, input actions, 2D settings, tile map, tileset, Atlas Crop file, animator, clips file, recording, save game, sidecar or project file that this build can't read. An older one that's upgraded as it's read is a note, not a failure.
Game codeAny mistake in the game's Lust or Lua. A call to a name that was renamed is a note.
RecordingsEach recording in recordings/checks/ is played back in the area it was recorded in, with the project's sprite sheets, tilesets and tile maps read as the editor reads them (so a 2D game's walls are there). If the game comes out differently from the same input on any tick, it fails, with the tick. It also fails, saying so, if the area isn't as it was when recorded (record it again), or if it was made before recordings said their area. Saves the game makes while it plays back are kept by the check, never written into your project.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a recording fails that used to pass, and you changed the area or the code since. Why: the check compares the game with what it did when recorded; your change makes it play differently, which is what it's for. Fix: record the check again after your change.
  • Problem: a recording fails with only a Solis update in between. Why: the new build plays your game differently. Fix: keep using the build you had (the last ten are on the Releases page; see Installing and updating) and report it, with the recording.
  • Problem: "its area isn't as it was when this was recorded". Why: the area was changed and saved since, or the recording was made with unsaved changes (the check reads the saved area; Solis warns when you start recording with unsaved changes). Fix: save the area, then record the check again.
  • Problem: the check takes a couple of seconds longer after you've just made a file. Why: a new file gets its sidecar (the small file beside it holding its ID) once it has been still for two seconds, so a file Git is still writing isn't given a wrong ID. The check waits for it, so the file is checked with its ID in the same run. Fix: nothing: it's on purpose.
  • Problem: "it doesn't say which area it was recorded in". Why: recordings made before this version didn't name their area. Fix: record it again.

Related#

  • Input: recording and replaying play.
  • Backups and upgrades: what happens to older files.
  • Installing and updating.
← Previous · Chapter 19Backups and upgradesNext → · Chapter 21Importing models

Importing models#

Bring a 3D model from Blender, Aventail or any other program into the viewport.

When to use it#

Whenever you want to see a model in Solis. Solis reads glTF files (concepts), the standard format for game models: Blender, Aventail and most 3D programs export it.

An imported model becomes an entity in the area, where its file puts it. With a project open, the file is copied into the project and saving the area keeps the model in it. Without one, Solis works as a viewer: the model is shown but not kept.

How to use it#

From the menu:

  1. Choose Library › Import.
  2. Pick a .glb or .gltf file and press Open.

By dragging: drag a .glb or .gltf file from your file explorer onto the Solis window. While you drag, the window shows where it will go; let go anywhere.

Then:

  • The model is read in the background, so the editor keeps running while it loads. The Console says Importing…, then Imported with the model's triangle count and size in metres.
  • The camera moves to show the whole model, and picks a camera speed that suits its size.
  • With a project open, the file is first copied into the project's assets folder (with the .bin and images a .gltf reads), so the project keeps it; it then also appears in the Library.
  • The model appears in the Area panel as one entity, however many parts the file has (they keep their places inside it). Unpack in Properties splits it into one entity per part when you need them (Assemblies). A mesh used many times in the file is stored once, with its triangle count. The × at the end of its row deletes it from the area. Select it to see its Transform and Model in Properties.

Exporting from Blender: File › Export › glTF 2.0, choose glTF Binary (.glb), and keep +Y Up ticked (the standard). Solis turns glTF's "Y is up" into its own "Z is up" for you, so the model stands upright.

Exporting from Aventail: export as glTF (Aventail's manual, "Export and import", explains how). Kits exported from Aventail import the same way.

Settings#

What Solis readsNotes
MeshesPlaced where the file puts them. Triangles only: points and lines are left out, with a warning in the Console.
MaterialColour, metal, roughness, normal, occlusion and glow, with their textures (PNG or JPEG, inside the .glb or as files beside a .gltf). See Looks.
See-through partsCut-out (leaves, fences) and blended (glass).
Double-sided surfacesDrawn from both sides when the file says so; otherwise the back of a surface is hidden.
UnitsMetres, as glTF uses. The Console shows the model's size, so you can spot one exported 100 times too big.
Levels of detailMade for each mesh as it's imported, or taken from objects named _LOD1 and so on. See Levels of detail.

Limits: files up to 1 GB, models up to 30 million triangles, and textures up to 16,384 pixels across. Textures bigger than your graphics card holds are scaled down to fit.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the model is lying on its back or facing the wrong way. Why: it was exported with a different "up" setting. Fix: in Blender, keep +Y Up ticked when exporting glTF.
  • Problem: the model is tiny or enormous. Why: it was made in other units (centimetres, inches). Fix: check the size in the Console; scale it in your modelling program, or set the export's scale.
  • Problem: the Console says a texture was left out. Why: the image file isn't next to the .gltf, or it isn't PNG or JPEG (Solis goes by how the file begins, not its name: another kind of picture renamed to .png is still left out). Fix: export as glTF Binary (.glb), which keeps everything in one file.
  • Problem: "Couldn't import … the file is damaged". Why: the file is incomplete or broken. Fix: export it again.
  • Problem: "the part … is placed or scaled past what numbers can hold", or "a corner of the part … lands further away than numbers can hold". Why: something in the file sits or reaches further away than a computer's numbers go (more than a billion billion billion billion metres), so there's nowhere to draw it. Only a broken file or a wildly wrong scale does this. Fix: in your modelling program, check the scale and place of the part the message names, and export again.
  • Problem: the model looks flat and grey-blue in the shadows. Why: where the sun doesn't reach, only the sky's soft light does. Fix: move the sun or add lamps; see Lights and shadows.
  • Problem: "it needs a glTF extension Solis doesn't read yet". Why: the file was saved with compression (Draco or meshopt, common from Sketchfab or gltfpack). Fix: export it again without compression; in Blender, untick Compression in the glTF export.
  • Very large models are split into pieces the graphics card can hold; you won't see the seams, but the Area panel's triangle count stays the same.
  • Lights in the file: lamps exported from Blender (point lights and spotlights) come in with the model as entities under it in the Area panel, and are deleted with it; a sun in the file sets the area's sun. Turn on Punctual Lights under Include in Blender's glTF export to export them.
  • Want to see how it should look? Add the sample area (press Space and type it) brings in a model made for checking the looks. With a project open, it's added to the project's assets as Sample area.glb, like any import, so areas using it open again.

Related#

  • Levels of detail
  • Moving around the viewport
  • Concepts: models, meshes, triangles, materials, textures, glTF.
← Previous · Chapter 20Checking a project before updatingNext → · Chapter 22Sounds

Sounds#

Put WAV and Ogg sound files in your project, see their waveforms in the Library, and listen to them before you use them.

When to use it#

  • To bring sounds into a project: footsteps, doors, music, birdsong. Solis reads two kinds of sound file: WAV, which keeps every sample as it is (right for short effects straight from a sound editor), and Ogg Vorbis, about a tenth of the size (right for music and anything long). Most sound programs save both; if yours makes MP3 or FLAC, save as Ogg instead.
  • To check a sound before using it: listen to it, and see how long it is, whether it's mono or stereo, and its sample rate.

Sounds are played through sound events: an event holds one or more sound files (takes) and how to vary them. Game code plays them in the game (Game code: Sounds), an AudioSource on an entity plays one from a place in the level (Sounds that keep playing), and the Mixer balances them all.

How to use it#

  1. Add a sound: copy a .wav or .ogg file into the project's assets folder, or a folder inside it, from Explorer. It appears in the Library within a moment, with a teal stripe and a picture of its waveform: how loud it is from start to end.
  2. Listen to it: point at its tile and click the ▶ in its corner. Click ■ to stop. Only you hear it: what you hear in the Library is never affected by the game's own volumes.
  3. See what it holds: click its tile. Properties shows a larger waveform with a line where it's playing, Play and Stop, and its details (below). Pick something in the area again and Properties shows that instead.

Right-click a sound for Play, Show in Explorer, Rename… and Delete, as with any file.

Settings#

Properties shows these about a sound (they come from the file, so change them in your sound program):

DetailWhat it means
LengthHow long it plays: milliseconds, seconds, or minutes and seconds.
ChannelsMono is one sound; stereo is two, left and right. A file with more (surround sound) is mixed down to one.
Sample rateHow many times a second the sound was measured. 44,100 Hz and 48,000 Hz are usual; 8,000 Hz to 192,000 Hz are read.
FormatWAV or Ogg Vorbis.
KeptFrom memory for sounds up to ten minutes long (at the highest quality, 192 kHz, up to about a minute and a half), ready to play at once. Longer ones are streamed: played from their file a piece at a time, so a long piece of music doesn't fill the memory.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the Console says "No sound: couldn't open the sound card". Why: Solis found no sound card it could use: none plugged in, or another program holding it. Fix: plug in speakers or a headset; Solis tries again every 30 seconds and says "Sound is on." when it finds one. Everything else works meanwhile, and ▶ says there's nothing to play on.
  • Problem: a sound's tile shows a speaker instead of a waveform, and Properties says Solis couldn't read it. Why: the file is damaged, isn't really WAV or Ogg Vorbis, or is outside what's read (more than 256 MB, more than 8 channels, or a sample rate outside 8,000 to 192,000 Hz). Solis checks every sound file carefully, so a broken one is refused instead of crashing. Fix: save it again from your sound program, as WAV or Ogg Vorbis.
  • Problem: an MP3 or FLAC file shows as a plain file. Why: Solis reads WAV and Ogg Vorbis only, so every library it uses can stay free for any game to use. Fix: save it as Ogg Vorbis (for music) or WAV (for short effects).
  • Double-clicking a sound shows it in its folder rather than opening another program, as for other files Solis doesn't edit itself.

Related#

  • Projects and the Library
  • The Console
  • Concepts: Sound
← Previous · Chapter 21Importing modelsNext → · Chapter 23Sound events

Sound events#

A sound event is what your game plays, such as "footstep": a few recordings (takes) and how much to vary them, so the same sound never sounds copied.

When to use it#

  • For anything heard more than once: footsteps, gunshots, doors, coins. A real footstep never sounds exactly the same twice; playing one recording over and over sounds mechanical very quickly. An event picks a different take each time, and changes its pitch and volume a little.
  • To set how a sound is heard in one place: how loud, whether it comes from a place in the world or is heard the same everywhere, how far it carries, and which bus it belongs to. Game code plays the event by name (Game code: Sounds), so changing the event changes every place that plays it.
  • A single sound you only ever play once, such as one piece of music, still works best as an event with one take: the event holds its settings.

How to use it#

  1. Make one: in the Library, New › Sound event (right-click in the Library, or + New). It's made in the folder shown, called "New sound event", and shown in Details (Properties). Rename it like any file (right-click › Rename…), say to footstep.
  2. Add takes: drag sound files from the Library onto the event's tile, or into the Takes list in Properties. Five to eight takes of a footstep is plenty. The tile shows how many it has (×5).
  3. Listen: press Play in Properties, or point at the event's tile and click its ▶. Each press picks a different take, pitch and volume, never the same take twice in a row, and the line under Play says what it picked. Press it a few times to hear the variety.
  4. Every event in one place: the Audio tab's Sound events shelf tab lists every sound event in the project, with its bus, volume, where it's heard and how many takes; click one to change and play it beside the list, as in the Library's Details.
  5. Change how it sounds: edit the settings below in Properties. Each change is saved to the event's .solsound file as soon as you let go of the mouse. To take a take out, click the × at the end of its row (the sound file itself stays in the project).

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
VolumeHow loud, in decibels (dB): 0 is as recorded, −6 about half as loud, +6 about twice. The second number is how much each play may be louder or quieter: 1 to 3 dB is subtle and natural.
PitchHow high or low, in semitones (st): 12 is an octave up. The second number is how much each play may differ: 0.5 to 2 st keeps footsteps fresh without sounding odd.
BusWhich bus it plays through (Music, Effects, Voice, Ambience, UI, or one of your own), so its fader, ducking and a game's options turn it up or down with the others.
LoopPlays again from the start when it ends: an engine hum, a siren, music. Played by game code, it goes on until stopSounds stops it or the game stops, so play it on an entity (playSoundOn) to be able to stop it. An AudioSource always loops, whatever this says.
PlacementIn the world: it comes from a place, quieter far away and from its direction (a footstep, a door). It plays as one channel (mono), mixed down from stereo if need be, so it can come from one side. Everywhere: heard the same wherever you are, as recorded, in stereo if the file is (music, the interface). Each take in the list says whether its file is mono or stereo.
Full until, Silent pastFor sounds in the world: full volume up to the first distance, silent past the second, in metres. A footstep might be 2 m and 30 m; an explosion 10 m and 300 m.
FadeHow it gets quieter between the two distances. Realistic drops quickly at first, as sound does outdoors; Even drops steadily; None stays full until the far distance.
At onceThe most plays of this event heard at the same time; more are skipped. 8 is a good start; a machine gun might want 4. When game code asks for one event many times in one tick (a volley of a hundred shots), up to 3 copies play, a little louder, instead of a hundred.
Heard byWho hears it: Everyone, Only who caused it (the listener on the entity that played it), or Groups (listeners in one of its groups). See Listeners and who hears what.
PriorityWhen more sounds want to play than the project's Heard at once (in the Mixer), High ones are heard first, then the loudest where you are; Low ones go first.

Sounds that keep playing#

An engine's hum, a campfire, a radio: add an AudioSource to the entity (Properties › + Component › AudioSource), and type the sound event's name in Sound event, its file in assets without .solsound (sfx/engine). It plays over and over while the game runs, following the entity, from Play (or when game code makes the entity) until the entity goes. Playing switches it off and on, and game code does the same with setSoundPlaying (Game code: Sounds). Volume makes it louder or quieter on top of the event's own.

Thousands of them are fine: only the most important are heard at once (the Mixer's Heard at once), and the rest rest. A resting one isn't mixed at all, but it keeps its place in the sound: walk up to a campfire that was resting and it carries on where it would have been, not from the start. A save game keeps whether each was on or off.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Play says "it has no takes yet". Why: the event has no sound files in it. Fix: drag sound files onto it from the Library.
  • Problem: a take shows as an ID with "(missing)". Why: that sound file was deleted, or its .solmeta file was lost, so the event can't find it. Plays skip it. Fix: click its × and drag the file in again.
  • Problem: Properties says Solis couldn't read the event. Why: the .solsound file was edited by hand and has a mistake, which the message points to by line. Fix: correct that line in a text editor, or delete the file and make the event again.
  • A .solsound file is plain text, one setting per line, so Git shows exactly what changed and merges two people's changes cleanly. A value out of range (a volume of 99, say) is brought into range when read, and a note in Properties says so.
  • Pressing Play in the editor plays on its own, so you hear the event even while the game's sound is turned down.

Related#

  • Sounds
  • Projects and the Library
  • Concepts: Sound
← Previous · Chapter 22SoundsNext → · Chapter 24The Mixer

The Mixer#

The Audio tab: the project's buses as strips side by side, each with a fader, a meter, mute and solo, the bus picked with its ducking rules, and the project's sound events.

When to use it#

When you want to balance a game's sound as a whole rather than one sound event at a time: the music a little quieter, every effect a little louder, voices always clear. Each sound event plays through a bus, and a bus's fader turns all of its sounds up or down together, like a channel on a mixing desk. To change how one sound is heard (its volume, how far it carries), change its event instead.

How to use it#

  1. Click Audio in the tab bar. The mixer fills the left of the middle (its tab is the project's mixer file, mixer.solmix): a strip per bus, side by side, with Master last at the right. Beside it is the Bus group, showing the bus you picked (Master until you pick one).
  2. Each strip, top to bottom: the bus's name and where it goes ("Bus → Master"; Master's is "Output"), an Insert and a Pan that aren't built yet (Unfinished parts), the fader on its scale of dB beside the meter, the fader's value, and M (mute) and S (solo). Master has M only: every other bus is inside it, so its fader turns everything up or down.
  3. Drag a fader up or down. Hold Shift while dragging for a fine move. Double-click it to put it back to 0 dB. The change is heard at once and saved in the project when you let go. To type a number, use Volume in the Bus group.
  4. Press Play: the meters show how loud each bus is as the game plays, grey, topping out in amber when loud. A thin white line over each meter holds its loudest moment for a second; click the meter to drop the line back to the level now. If Master's meter keeps reaching amber, turn something down.
  5. Click a strip's name to pick it: its strip is outlined in the accent colour and the Bus group shows its Name, the bus it's Inside, its Volume, and its ducking rules as cards. The switch at the group's top right turns it to the bus's Effects, which aren't built yet.
  6. Bus on the ribbon makes a new bus inside the one picked (or inside Master): "Footsteps" inside Effects, say, so footsteps can be balanced on their own. Then pick it as the Bus of the sound events that belong to it. Remove (or Remove bus in the Bus group) removes the bus picked; Master is shown after, with nothing picked, so a second click removes nothing.

Ducking turns one bus down while another plays, so speech is always heard over the music without turning the music down by hand. A new project already has one rule: while Voice plays, Music goes down 8 dB, taking 0.2 s to go down and 1 s to come back after the last voice ends. Each rule is a card, Quieter while Voice plays; Add rule on the ribbon (or + Add a ducking rule) adds one to the bus picked. While a rule is working, the ducked bus's strip says so in amber ("ducked -8"), its card says Right now, and the shelf bar says who is ducking whom.

Heard at once, on the ribbon, is how many sounds play at the same time: 64 to start with, from 16 to 256 (its list). When more want to play (a big battle), the most important are heard: by their event's Priority, then the loudest where you are. Sounds too far away aren't counted at all. More voices sound fuller and cost a little more time each frame (the Profiler's Sound part shows it).

Mute and solo are for listening while you work, and aren't saved: M silences a bus (its strip goes faint), S plays only the soloed buses (and the buses they're inside), so you can hear one part of the game on its own. Clear solo on the ribbon hears every bus again. Mute the game on the ribbon, or the speaker in the Game tab's top right corner, mutes everything.

The sound events are on the shelf's Sound events tab: every event in the project as a row (its bus, volume, where it's heard and how many takes), and the one you click beside them, to change and play (Sound events).

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
NameWhat sound events call the bus. Renaming it renames it everywhere in the Mixer (buses inside it, ducking rules); sound events that named the old name play through Master until you pick the new one. Master keeps its name.
InsideThe bus it's inside: its sounds go through that bus's fader too. A bus can't be inside itself or a bus inside it, and buses nest up to 8 deep.
VolumeThe fader, from -60 dB (silent) to +12 dB; type or drag the number in the Bus group. 0 dB plays the sounds as they are; -6 dB is about half as loud.
Quieter whileThe bus whose sounds turn this one down (a bus inside it counts too).
ByHow much quieter, down to -60 dB. -6 to -10 dB is usual for music under speech.
Fade downHow long going quieter takes, in seconds. Short (0.1 to 0.3 s) so the first word is clear.
Fade backHow long coming back takes after the last of those sounds ends. Longer (0.5 to 2 s), so the music doesn't jump back between sentences.

A bus can have up to 8 ducking rules (Add a ducking rule, and the card's × to remove one), and a project up to 64 buses. Remove bus moves the buses inside it up to its parent. Adding, removing or moving a bus while the game plays rebuilds the mix: sounds already playing once stop (sounds that keep playing start again at once), so do it while stopped if you're listening closely.

From game code, Audio:setVolume(Bus.Music, volume) sets a bus for the rest of the play to a share of its fader, from 0 (silent) to 1 (as set in the Mixer): what an options menu's sliders call. See Game code: Sounds.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Move a fader finelyHold Shift while dragging it
Put a fader back to 0 dBDouble-click it
Drop a meter's peak line to the level nowClick the meter

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a sound event isn't affected by its bus's fader. Why: its Bus names a bus that isn't there any more (renamed or removed), so it plays through Master. Fix: pick the bus again on the event (Audio's Sound events tab, or its Details in the Library).
  • Problem: some sounds don't play in a busy moment. Why: more sounds wanted to play than Heard at once allows, and they ranked lowest. Fix: raise their event's Priority, or raise Heard at once.
  • Problem: the meters don't move. Why: they show the game's sounds while it plays; the Library's ▶ and a sound event's Play don't go through the buses. Fix: press Play.
  • Problem: everything is silent. Why: a bus is soloed (only soloed buses are heard), Master is muted, or the game is muted. Fix: Clear solo, click the lit M, or turn off Mute the game.
  • Problem: the Console says the mixer file had a mistake. Why: mixer.solmix was edited by hand and can't be read, so the standard buses are used. Fix: fix the line it names, or change anything in the Mixer: that writes the file again and keeps the old one as mixer.solmix.bak. Changes made to the file by hand are read when the project is opened.

Related#

  • Sound events: each event's Bus.
  • Game code: Sounds: Audio:setVolume.
  • Concepts: bus, ducking, decibel.
← Previous · Chapter 23Sound eventsNext → · Chapter 25Reverb zones

Reverb zones#

Places where sounds echo: walk into a cave and every footstep rings.

When to use it#

Any time a place should sound like a place: a cave, a hall, a tunnel, a small room, a sewer. Reverb is the echo a space adds to every sound in it, and it's one of the strongest cues of where you are: the same footstep sounds tight in a cupboard and huge in a cathedral. A reverb zone adds it while the game's camera (the listener) is inside, so the sound changes as you walk in and out, without touching any sound event.

How to use it#

  1. Add an entity where the space is (Home › Empty), and move it to the middle of the space.
  2. In Properties, + Component › ReverbZone.
  3. Pick its Shape: a Box for rooms, halls and tunnels (set its Size along X, Y and Z), or a Ball for caves and domes (set its Radius). With the entity selected, the zone is outlined in the viewport in teal, so you can see what it covers. It grows, turns and moves with its entity.
  4. Pick what it Sounds like, and its Strength.
  5. Press Play and move the camera in and out: sounds placed in the world (Audio:playAt, an entity's playSound, AudioSources) echo inside, and the echo fades in across the Soft edge as you go in.

Only sounds placed In the world get the echo; music and the interface, heard the same everywhere, don't. Echoes follow their bus: turn a bus down or mute it in the Mixer and its echoes go with it.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
ShapeBox or Ball.
SizeA box's size along X, Y and Z, in metres. A hall might be 30 × 20 × 10.
RadiusA ball's radius, in metres.
Soft edgeHow far in from the edge the echo is full, in metres: walking in, it fades in over this distance, so there's no sudden switch. 2 m suits a doorway; 0 switches at the edge.
Sounds likeSmall room: short and close. Hall: long and smooth. Cave: long and dark. Sewer: hard and ringing. Outdoors: a little air, for a valley or a courtyard.
StrengthHow strong the echo is: 1 full, 0.5 half, 0 none.

Overlapping zones: where zones overlap, the smaller wins: a cupboard inside a hall sounds like the cupboard, and stepping out of it blends into the hall. Up to 4 zones are heard at once.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: no echo inside the zone. Why: the sound plays Everywhere (only sounds In the world echo), its bus is muted or turned down, or the camera isn't in the zone (the listener is the game's camera, not the player). Fix: check the sound event's Placement, the Mixer, and where the camera is with the zone selected.
  • Problem: the echo switches on suddenly. Why: the Soft edge is 0 or very small. Fix: 1 to 3 m.
  • Problem: everything sounds washed out. Why: the zone's too strong for the place, or a big zone covers more than it should. Fix: lower its Strength, or make it smaller.

Related#

  • Sound events: Placement, In the world.
  • The Mixer: buses, which echoes follow.
  • Concepts: reverb.
← Previous · Chapter 24The MixerNext → · Chapter 26Listeners and who hears what

Listeners and who hears what#

Where the game hears from, and which sounds each listener hears.

When to use it#

Most games need none of this: with no Listener, the game hears through its camera, and every sound is heard. Use it when that isn't enough:

  • The ears should be somewhere else than the camera: a top-down game that should hear from the character on the ground, not the camera high above. Put a Listener on the character.
  • Some sounds are only for one player: your own footsteps in first person, a click in your own menu, your own team's radio. A sound event's Heard by says who hears it.

Who hears what never changes the game: it only decides what's played on this computer, so a recording replays the same, and a multiplayer game (later, with netcode) sends no sound over the network.

How to use it#

  1. Select the camera or the character the game should hear from, and + Component › Listener in Properties.
  2. Leave Hears now on. If a level has several listeners (a player and a spectator camera), this computer hears through the first with Hears now on.
  3. Give it Groups if some sounds are for groups: names with commas between, such as Team Red, Radio.
  4. In a sound event's Properties, set Heard by:
    • Everyone (the start): every listener hears it.
    • Only who caused it: only the listener on the entity whose code played it, or on what that entity is part of (a character and the camera inside it count as one). An AudioSource is caused by its own entity.
    • Groups: only a listener in one of the event's Groups.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Listener > Hears nowWhether it's the one hearing. The first with this on hears; with none on, the camera does.
Listener > GroupsThe groups it's in, with commas between. Sounds heard by Groups reach it if they share one.
Sound event > Heard byEveryone, Only who caused it, or Groups, as above.
Sound event > GroupsThe groups that hear it, with commas between (when Heard by is Groups).

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a sound heard by Groups is never heard. Why: no listener hears now that's in one of its groups; the camera on its own is in no group. Fix: add a Listener with that group to the camera or character.
  • Problem: a sound heard by Only who caused it is never heard. Why: it's played by code on an entity that isn't the listener's, nor inside it, nor what it's inside. Fix: play it from the player's own entity, or a child of it.
  • Problem: sounds come from the wrong place. Why: the listener is on a different entity than you expect (the first with Hears now on). Fix: turn Hears now off on the others.

Related#

  • Sound events
  • Game code: Sounds
  • Concepts: listener.
← Previous · Chapter 25Reverb zonesNext → · Chapter 27Levels of detail: simpler models far away

Levels of detail: simpler models far away#

Far from the camera, Solis draws simpler versions of your models, so thousands of them cost far less without looking any different.

When to use it#

You don't have to do anything: every model you import gets levels of detail (LODs) on its own. A ship a few pixels tall on screen doesn't need its 20,000 triangles; drawing 2,000 of them instead lets a battle of thousands of ships keep its frame rate.

Make your own when the automatic ones don't suit a model: a character whose face should stay recognisable, a building whose outline matters, or a low-poly model that can't be simplified (Solis leaves those in full).

How it works#

  1. When you import a model, Solis makes up to three simpler versions of each of its meshes: about a half, a quarter and an eighth of the triangles. It does this once, and keeps them with the imported model, so later imports and Play are just as quick.
  2. While drawing, Solis works out how tall each copy of the model is on screen. It draws the simplest version that differs from the full one by less than a pixel, so you shouldn't be able to see the switch.
  3. A copy near the point where it would switch keeps the version it had until it's clearly past that point, so it doesn't flicker between two.

To see it at work, open the Profiler while looking out over many copies: its last line says how many are drawn in full and at each level. Properties shows a model's triangles, then its simpler levels after "far away": Ship · 20,000 tris · far away 10,000 → 5,000 → 2,500.

Making your own#

  1. In your modelling program, make the simpler version of the object as a separate object, in the same place.
  2. Name it after the full one with _LOD1 on the end: for an object called Ship, name it Ship_LOD1. Make even simpler ones Ship_LOD2, Ship_LOD3 and Ship_LOD4 if you like. Upper or lower case both work, and the full one may also be called Ship_LOD0.
  3. Export the model as glTF with both objects, and import it (or save over the file Solis already has).

Solis then uses your versions for that object instead of making its own, and doesn't draw them as parts of their own. In Blender, the names are the ones in the Outliner. If an object has several meshes (several materials), they're matched in order.

Your own levels are used from about a quarter of the screen tall (level 1), each next level at about half that size.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a model pops between versions as the camera moves. Why: the simpler version differs more than Solis's estimate says, often with your own levels, which don't say how much they differ. Fix: make the level closer to the full model, or tell us which model it is.
  • Problem: the Console says Ship_LOD1 looks like a level of detail, but there's no part called Ship. Why: the full object has another name (ship, Ship.001). Fix: rename one so the names match exactly, apart from _LOD1. Until then it's drawn as a part of its own.
  • Problem: a model has no simpler levels in Properties. Why: it has fewer than 64 triangles in each mesh (already cheap), or its shape couldn't be simplified without changing it too much. Fix: nothing; it's drawn in full.
  • Problem: the first import of a very detailed model takes longer. Why: making the levels takes time, about a second for a few million triangles. It's done once; meshes with more than 4 million triangles are left in full.

Related#

  • Importing models
  • The Profiler
  • Concepts: mesh, triangle, level of detail
← Previous · Chapter 26Listeners and who hears whatNext → · Chapter 28Looks: standard, stylized and unlit

Looks: standard, stylized and unlit#

Choose how models are shaded: realistic, cel-shaded with outlines, or plain colours.

When to use it#

  • Standard shows a model as most engines and Substance Painter would: shiny metal, rough plastic, bumps from its normal texture. Use it to check a model's materials.
  • Stylized is a cartoon or "cel-shaded" look, like many stylized games: light in a few flat bands, crisp highlights and dark outlines. It's the look Solis is built for.
  • Unlit shows colours and textures exactly as painted, with no light at all. Use it to check a texture.

The look applies to every model in the view at once: a material can't have a look of its own yet.

How to use it#

  1. At the top left of the viewport, click the look's pill (it shows the look in use, such as Standard ▾).
  2. Choose Standard, Stylized or Unlit. The menu stays open, so you can compare.
  3. For the stylized look, choose how many Bands of light (2, 3 or 4), and whether to draw Outlines.
  4. Click anywhere else to close the menu. Solis remembers your choice.

To try the looks without a model of your own, choose Add the sample area (press Space and type it): a checker cube, a row of plastic spheres from glossy to rough, a row of metal ones, and a wall with grooves and a glowing stripe.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Bands of lightHow many steps the stylized light goes in, from shadow to full light. 2 is bold and graphic; 4 is softer. 3 is a good start.
OutlinesDark edges around models in the stylized look, about 1.5 points wide.

What the standard look reads from a model's material:

Material settingWhat it does
Colour and colour textureThe surface's colour.
Metallic0 for paint, plastic and wood; 1 for bare metal, which reflects its surroundings tinted by its colour.
Roughness0 mirror-smooth with a tiny sharp highlight; 1 chalky with no shine.
Normal textureSmall bumps and grooves that catch the light, without extra triangles.
Occlusion textureDarkens creases and corners.
Glow (emissive)Light the surface gives off itself: screens, lamps, engines. It glows in every look.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: metal looks dark or dull. Why: metal shows what it reflects, and for now it reflects only the sky's soft light and the highlights of the sun and lamps. Fix: add a lamp near it (Lights and shadows), or switch to the daylight sky (Sky, fog and exposure), which metal reflects.
  • Problem: white surfaces look light grey rather than pure white. Why: the AgX tone mapping, as in Blender, keeps room above white for brighter light. Fix: raise the exposure, or choose Standard tone mapping (Sky, fog and exposure).
  • Problem: no outline on part of a model. Why: outlines are drawn only on solid, one-sided surfaces; see-through and double-sided ones are left without.
  • Problem: everything looks the same in Unlit. Why: that's the point: no light, just colour.

Related#

  • Importing models
  • Concepts: material, texture, metallic, roughness, normal texture.
← Previous · Chapter 27Levels of detail: simpler models far awayNext → · Chapter 29Lights and shadows: the sun, point lights and spotlights

Lights and shadows: the sun, point lights and spotlights#

Light your models with a sun that casts shadows, and with lamps you place yourself or bring in from Blender.

When to use it#

Light decides how a model reads: which side is bright, where its shadows fall, what mood the area has. Use it to check how a model looks in daylight, under a warm lamp, or in a dark room lit by one torch.

  • The sun (concepts) lights everything from one direction, like daylight, and casts shadows. A new area has one.
  • A point light shines every way from one spot, like a bare bulb or a candle.
  • A spotlight shines a cone, like a torch, a car headlight or a stage light.

Everything also gets soft sky light, so shadows are never pitch black.

Every light is an entity with a Light component; where it is and which way it points come from its Transform. Lights are saved with the area.

How to use it#

Change the sun

  1. In the Area panel, click Sun.
  2. In Properties, under Transform, drag the first Rotation number (X) to tilt the sun: 0° shines straight down (noon), 90° skims the horizon (sunrise), so a bigger tilt gives longer shadows. Drag the third number (Z) to turn it around the sky.
  3. Under Light, click the Colour swatch for a warmer or cooler light, and drag Strength to brighten or dim it. Untick Shadows to turn them off.

Add a lamp

  1. Fly the camera to where the light should be (Moving around the viewport).
  2. Choose Home › Light to place a bulb 2 m above the point the camera looks at, or Home › Light's small arrow, then Spotlight to place a spotlight at the camera, shining where the camera looks (like holding a torch).
  3. The lamp appears as a small cross in its colour (a spotlight also has a line the way it shines). It's listed in the Area panel and selected, with its settings in Properties.
  4. To move it, fly somewhere else and choose Move here in the ⋯ beside its name in Properties. Delete, in the same menu, removes it.

Bring lamps from Blender: export with Punctual Lights ticked (under Include in Blender's glTF export), then import the model. Its lamps come in as entities under the model in the Area panel, and are deleted with it. A sun in the file sets the area's sun.

Settings#

Transform (every light has one):

SettingWhat it does
PositionWhere the light is, in metres (X, Y, Z). Drag a number to move it. A sun's position doesn't matter: it's infinitely far away.
RotationWhich way it shines, in degrees. With all three at 0 a light shines straight down. X tilts it (90° is level with the ground), Z turns it round. Point lights shine every way, so their rotation doesn't matter.
ScaleNot used by lights.

Light:

SettingWhat it does
KindSun, Point or Spot.
ColourThe light's colour. Slightly warm white is daylight; orange is evening.
StrengthPoint lights and spotlights: in watts, as in Blender, so numbers carry over: 1000 W lights a room, 100 W is a small lamp close by. The sun: in watts per square metre; 3 is the editor's clear day, 0 turns it off for a night area lit by lamps.
Range0: the light fades on forever, getting weaker with distance, as real light does. More: it stops at this many metres. Games use ranges to keep many lamps cheap.
Cone (spotlights)How wide the light reaches, in degrees from the middle of the cone, from 1° to 89°.
Soft edge (spotlights)How gradually the light fades at the cone's edge: 0° for a hard circle, more for a soft one, up to 89°. A soft edge wider than the cone fades the whole cone.
ShadowsWhether it casts shadows. For now only the sun does.
Only at nightOn from dusk to dawn, by the Environment's day and night: a street lamp, a lantern. With day and night off, it's always on.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a lamp lights through a wall. Why: for now only the sun casts shadows; lamps don't. Shadows from lamps come with the lighting choices of decision 0008↗.
  • Problem: a lamp seems to have no effect. Why: it may be too weak for its distance: light gets four times weaker each time the distance doubles. Fix: raise its strength, or move it closer.
  • Problem: everything is washed out near a lamp. Why: the lamp is very strong for its distance. Fix: lower its strength, or the exposure under Environment.
  • Problem: in a 2D game, a lamp lights nothing on the sprites. Why: a lamp lights the ground beneath it, so it must be above the sprites: one level with them, or under an "over" tile layer, lights nothing. Fix: raise it 1 to 2 m above the sprites (and see Light sprites).
  • Problem: a street lamp is off at night. Why: Only at night follows the Environment's Day and night: it's on while the day's colour is darker than half the brightest one. Fix: check the night colours are darker than the day's, and that Day and night is ticked.
  • Problem: lamps far from the camera stop lighting. Why: up to 16 lamps light the view at once, the ones nearest the camera.
  • Problem: things far from the camera have no shadows. Why: the sun's shadows reach 200 m from the camera. The shadow map covers only what the view shows within that distance, so its detail goes where you're looking, however big the area. Fix: move closer; at that distance, shadows are too small to see anyway.
  • Problem: shadows look blurry. Why: the shadow map covers everything in view up to 200 m away, so looking out over a wide area spreads its pixels further. Fix: look from closer, or from higher up so less ground is in view.
  • Problem: a spotlight's cone isn't the number written in the area file. Why: an area file is text, so a number can be typed into it by hand or left there by a merge. A light only works with a cone from 1° to 89°, a soft edge from 0° to 89°, and a strength and range that aren't below 0, so a number outside that is read as the nearest one that works (a cone of -5 shines as 1°). Fix: set the number you meant in Properties.
  • Problem: I deleted the sun and everything went dark. Why: the sun was the only light. Fix: undo (Ctrl + Z), or add an entity and give it a Light (+ Component › Light) with Kind set to Sun.

Related#

  • Looks: both the standard and stylized looks are lit; the unlit look ignores light.
  • Sky, fog and exposure: a daylight sky that follows the sun, and how bright the picture is.
  • Importing models
  • Entities and components: how lights, models and the environment are built.
  • Concepts: sun, lamp, watts, range, shadow, sky light
← Previous · Chapter 28Looks: standard, stylized and unlitNext → · Chapter 30Sky, fog and exposure

Sky, fog and exposure#

Choose what's behind your models, add fog for distance, and set how bright the picture is.

When to use it#

  • Sky: the editor backdrop is a calm grey that keeps your attention on the model; it's the default for working. The daylight sky shows your model outdoors: blue at noon, orange at sunset, dark at night, always matching the sun. Its light also colours the shadows, so a sunset gives warm light and cool shadows.
  • Fog makes distant things fade into the sky, as haze or mist does. It gives large areas a sense of depth, and is a classic way to hide where a level ends.
  • Exposure and tone mapping decide how bright light is shown on your screen (concepts). Solis works out light brighter than white, as the real world is, and squeezes it onto the screen the way Blender does. Raise the exposure for a darker area, lower it if things look washed out.

How to use it#

  1. In the Area panel, click Environment.
  2. In Properties, choose the Sky: Backdrop or Daylight.
  3. For fog, tick Fog, then set Half hidden at: the distance at which half of a thing disappears into the fog.
  4. Adjust Exposure and choose the Tone mapping.

Day and night (for a game with a clock: a farm, a town):

  1. Tick Day and night. Set how long A day lasts (in minutes of play: 24 is an hour of the day a minute) and the hour it Starts at.
  2. Colours shows the day as a strip, from midnight to midnight. Each colour has an hour: the world is tinted by them, smoothly from one to the next. Click a colour to change it, drag its hour between its neighbours (or type 19:30 to put it anywhere), + Add a colour for another (it goes in the longest stretch of the day), and Remove to take one out.
  3. Tick Preview time and drag it to see the area at any hour in the viewport: a dusk tint, the street lamps on. The preview isn't saved, and the game always starts at Starts at.

The time of day runs with the game's time, so a paused game's day stands still, and save games keep it. Changing A day lasts or Starts at while playing moves the clock to the hour that setting gives, so the hour jumps. Game code reads it and sets it (Game code): World:timeOfDay() gives the hour (19.5 is half past seven), and World:setTimeOfDay(6) after a night's sleep moves the day on to six in the morning.

Light sprites lights a 2D game's sprites and tile maps with the day's colour and the lamps: a lamp shines on the ground beneath it, in a pool that's brightest right under it. The light is worked out for each of the game's own (big) pixels, so it stays crisp. Light steps draws the lamps' pools in bands (3 is a good stylized look; 0 is smooth); the day's colour isn't banded, so a dark night stays dark rather than black. New areas have Light sprites on; areas made before it have it off, so they look as they did. With no lamps and day and night off, a lit sprite looks exactly as drawn.

These settings belong to the area (the Environment is an entity like any other), so they're saved with it; a new area starts with the usual ones. With the daylight sky, try selecting Sun and dragging its Rotation X from 30° up to 90° and beyond to watch the day turn to sunset and night.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
SkyBackdrop: the calm grey you work against, with a neutral soft light. Daylight: a sky that follows the sun, with the sun's disc and a glow around it.
Sky strength (daylight)How bright the sky and its light in the shadows are. 1 is natural; lower gives darker, more dramatic shadows.
FogTurns fog on.
Half hidden atIn metres. At this distance half of a thing is hidden; at twice the distance, three quarters. 50 m is thick mist, 500 m light haze.
Fog matches skyTakes the horizon's colour, so things fade into the sky. Untick it to use Fog colour, such as green for a swamp.
Fog colourThe fog's own colour, when it doesn't match the sky.
ExposureIn stops (EV), as on a camera: +1 is twice as bright, -1 half. 0 is a good start.
Tone mappingAgX (default, as in Blender): bright light rolls off softly towards white, with natural colours. ACES: the film look many games use, with more contrast and colour. Standard: no mapping; anything brighter than white is cut off.
Day and nightThe day's colours tint the world as the game's time of day runs: the sun, the sky and its light in 3D, and lit sprites in 2D. The daylight sky's own sunset colours are for later.
A day lastsHow long a whole day lasts, in minutes of play.
Starts atThe hour the game starts at (8 is eight in the morning).
ColoursThe day's colours at their hours (up to 8). A lamp with Only at night is on while the tint is darker than half the brightest colour: from dusk to dawn, whatever the colours.
Preview timeShows the area at another hour in the viewport. The editor's alone: never saved.
Light spritesSprites and tile maps are lit by the day's colour and by lamps.
Light steps0 for smooth light from lamps on sprites; 2 to 8 for bands of light (1 counts as 2).

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: white surfaces look light grey. Why: AgX keeps room above white for brighter light, as in Blender. Fix: raise the exposure a little, or choose Standard.
  • Problem: the daylight sky is black. Why: the sun is below the horizon (night), or its strength is 0. Fix: lower the sun's Rotation X below 90°, or raise its Strength.
  • Problem: everything disappears into the fog. Why: the half-hidden distance is short compared with the area. Fix: raise it.
  • Problem: the unlit look ignores exposure. Why: unlit shows colours exactly as painted, by design.
  • Problem: at night my sprites are too dark to see. Why: the night colour is dark on purpose, and lit sprites take it. Fix: make the night colour lighter (a deep blue rather than near black), or add lamps.
  • Problem: a lamp lights nothing on my sprites. Why: Light sprites is off (an area made before it), the lamp is too weak or too high, or it's level with the sprites or below them: a lamp lights the ground beneath it, so one at the sprites' own height lights nothing. Fix: tick Light sprites, and raise the lamp above the sprites; a lamp of 100 to 300 W, 1 to 2 m up, makes a good pool.
  • Problem: the colours jump instead of changing smoothly. Why: two colours sit close together in the day. Fix: move them apart, or take one out.
  • The grid and the editor backdrop are never changed by exposure or tone mapping, so the editor stays easy on the eyes whatever the area looks like.

Related#

  • Lights and shadows: the sun, which the daylight sky follows, and lamps that shine only at night.
  • Sprites: what Light sprites lights.
  • Looks
  • Concepts: HDR, exposure, tone mapping, fog
← Previous · Chapter 29Lights and shadows: the sun, point lights and spotlightsNext → · Chapter 31Game code

Game code#

Your game's own rules (how a turret aims, when a door opens) are written as code, as components you put on entities. Solis checks the code as you save, shows its fields in Properties, and runs it when you press Play.

When to use it#

Whenever your game needs to do something: react to the player, count score, move things on its own. Areas and assemblies say what's in the world; game code says what happens in it.

Solis games can be written in three languages:

  • Lust, made for Solis's kind of games and the one this manual teaches first;
  • Lua, if you know it from Roblox or modding;
  • Rust, the language Solis itself is written in.

Not sure which? Which language when compares them, with numbers.

Right now: Lust and Lua components work: they appear in Properties, run in play mode, talk to each other through events, and take new code while the game runs. Rust components can join them, but for now only in a Solis built from source.

How to use it#

  1. Open a project. Solis puts a solis folder in its assets. Everything in it is written by Solis for your code to read, and written again whenever the project opens, so changes you make there don't last:

    • a Lust file for each part of the engine (world.lst, entity.lst, input.lst and so on). They describe what your code can ask of the engine, such as World:say (write in the Console) or moveTo (put an entity somewhere). What the engine offers lists every call and the file it's in.
    • project.lst, which holds your project's own names, such as its assemblies, written again whenever you add or rename one.
