    • folders: kit holds the ready-made components, animators and maps hold a file for each animator and tile map you make, and data says what the Lust files Solis makes (tile maps, tilesets and the like) hold.

    Why files? Lust checks every call you write against them before the game runs, so a misspelt call is a mistake you see at once, not a surprise while playing.

  2. Right-click in the Library and choose New › Lust code file. The first one is main.lst, at the top of the assets folder: your game's code starts there. Lust reads main.lst first, and every other code file is fetched from it, or from a file it fetches. The file opens in your code editor for Lust (Ledger), with a component to start from. You can also make the file by hand in any text editor.

  3. Write a component. An entity's own abilities, such as position() and moveTo(place), need no get: they're on every entity. The engine's other parts are objects you fetch, such as fetch "solis/world":World; for World:say(…). The switch above the code shows the same component in Rust and in Lua (a Lua file is any .lua file in assets, made in any text editor):

    component Spinner {
    has {
        float speed = 2;
    }
}

pass Spinner;
end
    use reflect::{ComponentData, Value};
use script::RustComponent;

pub struct Spinner {
    speed: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Spinner {
    // Its fields, for Properties and saves.
    fn values(&self) -> ComponentData {
        let mut data = ComponentData::default();
        data.set("speed", Value::Float(self.speed));
        data
    }

    fn set(&mut self, data: &ComponentData) {
        if let Some(speed) = data.get("speed").and_then(Value::as_f64) {
            self.speed = speed;
        }
    }
}
    local Spinner = component("Spinner", {
    { "speed", "float", 2 },
})

  4. Save. Solis checks the code within a moment. Mistakes appear in the Problems panel, such as "main.lst, line 6:15: speed is a float, but this is text". The Console says how many there are. Notes go to the Console too, as warnings: things that aren't mistakes, so the code still runs, but worth changing (writing me where Lust now says this). Each is said once, until the notes change.

  5. Click a mistake to open its file in your code editor, fix it and save. It disappears from Problems by itself.

Components#

A component written in Lust works like Solis's own: put it on an entity, set its fields in Properties, and it does its job when the game runs. This one moves its entity along, a little every tick:

component Mover {
    has {
        float speed = 2;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        vec3 ahead = [1, 0, 0];
        moveTo(position() + ahead * speed * dt);
    }
}

pass Mover;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use reflect::{ComponentData, ComponentSchema, FieldInfo, FieldKind, Value};
use script::{Context, RustComponent, RustKind};

pub struct Mover {
    speed: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Mover {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let ahead = Vec3::new(1.0, 0.0, 0.0);
        let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        cx.host().move_to(me, here + ahead * (self.speed * dt) as f32);
    }

    // Its fields, for Properties and saves.
    fn values(&self) -> ComponentData {
        let mut data = ComponentData::default();
        data.set("speed", Value::Float(self.speed));
        data
    }

    fn set(&mut self, data: &ComponentData) {
        if let Some(speed) = data.get("speed").and_then(Value::as_f64) {
            self.speed = speed;
        }
    }
}

// How Solis makes one: its name, its fields and their starting values.
pub fn mover() -> RustKind {
    RustKind {
        schema: ComponentSchema {
            name: "Mover".into(),
            help: "Moves its entity along x.".into(),
            fields: vec![FieldInfo::new("speed", "Speed", FieldKind::Float, Value::Float(2.0))],
        },
        make: |data| {
            let mut mover = Mover { speed: 2.0 };
            mover.set(data);
            Box::new(mover)
        },
    }
}
-- mover.lua: any .lua file in assets.
local Mover = component("Mover", {
    { "speed", "float", 2 },
})

function Mover:update(dt)
    local ahead = vec3(1, 0, 0)
    local here = solis.entity.position(self.me)
    solis.entity.moveTo(self.me, here + ahead * self.speed * dt)
end

In Lua, component takes the name and the fields in order, each as { name, kind, starting value } (a state also lists its options: { "mode", "state", "Single", { "Single", "Burst" } }). The fields are self.speed and so on, the entity is self.me, the engine's methods are under solis., and vec3(x, y, z) makes a vector (a Luau vector, the same kind of value a Lust vec3 is) you can add, take away and scale, with v.x reading a part. A Lua component works the same way as a Lust one from here on, and both can be in the same game.

In Rust, a component is a type that implements script::RustComponent: update and handle (for events) are the ones you write, cx.me() is the entity, and cx.host() reaches the engine with the same calls in snake case (position, move_to). values and set hand its fields to Properties and save games, and a RustKind tells Solis its name, its fields and how to make one. Those parts always have this shape, so the other Rust examples in this manual leave them out. Solis can't build a game's own Rust yet (that comes with the full export); until then the turret sample's Rust component is built into Solis to show how it works.

  1. Save the file. When the code has no mistakes, Mover appears in Properties' + Component list.
  2. Select an entity and add Mover. Its has fields show in Properties with their starting values (speed as Speed), and are saved in the area like any other component's.
  3. Press Play. Every tick (60 times a second), Solis runs each component's update, with dt, how long a tick is in seconds. this is the entity the component is on (older code says me, which still works: the Console shows a note saying to write this). The Game panel shows the entity moving.
  4. Change Speed in Properties while it plays: the running Mover takes the new speed at once, and keeps everything else it has (here, where it is). While the game plays, Properties shows a game code component's values as they are right now, not the ones it started with: a turret that has fired shows the ammo it has left. Why? So you can watch what your code is doing without writing anything to the Console. A value you set there is taken by the running component as you set it, even when it's the value it started with: type the turret's full ammo and it has full ammo again. (With several entities selected, it shows the values they started with.)
  5. Press Stop. Everything the game changed is back as it was before Play. The Speed you changed yourself is a change to the area, so Solis lists it and asks: Keep it, or Undo all (see Play mode).

What a field can hold: bool, int, float, string, a state (shown as a choice of its options), vec3, vec2, rotation, colour and entity (another entity, or nothing).

  • vec2 is two numbers, for 2D: a place on a tile map, a direction to walk (vec2 speed = [2, -1];). Properties shows its X and Y.
  • colour is red, green and blue from 0 to 1, and how solid it is (colour tint = orange5;, colour shadow = [0, 0, 0, 0.5];). Properties shows a colour picker; picking a colour keeps how see-through it was. Why it matters: a field of either kind is saved in the area and in save games, and a loaded game carries on with it exactly as it was.
  • In Lua they're tables: { "speed", "vec2", { x = 2, y = -1 } } and { "tint", "colour", { r = 1, g = 0.5, b = 0 } } (a, how solid, is 1 when left out). In Rust they're FieldKind::Vec2 and FieldKind::Color (a colour's fourth number is there only when it isn't solid).

Order: each tick runs entities in the order of their IDs, and an entity's components in the order of their names, so a game runs the same way every time.

What game code sees during a tick: the world as it was when the tick started, plus its own changes. Solis runs game code on every core of your processor at once, so components can't see each other's moves while they happen. Instead:

  • position(), rotation(), name() and World:find read the world as it was at the start of the tick. A component that moves its own entity sees the new place at once; another component sees it next tick.
  • moveTo, turnTo, face and World:say are kept, and happen when every update is done, in the order above. If two components move the same entity, the last one in that order wins.
  • Events are delivered after that, a round at a time; each round sees the world as the round before left it.

So a game runs the same way on a computer with 2 cores or 32. Most code never notices: a unit chasing another simply aims at where the other was a sixtieth of a second ago. Code that needs to see a move straight away should move things from one component, or tell the other with an event.

When something goes wrong while it runs, such as dividing by zero, that component stops and the Console says which one, on which entity, and where in the Lust: "Divider on Splitter stopped: main.lst, line 8: …". The rest of the game keeps going. A component that runs for more than a tenth of a second without stopping (a loop that never ends) is stopped the same way, so it can't freeze Solis.

When code changes too much at once: a loop that calls moveTo, World:fire, World:spawn or World:say hundreds of thousands of times in one tick has the changes past 200,000 left out (for each core), and the Console says so once. It's nearly always a loop that never ends.

When the whole tick is too slow: if the game's code takes more than a quarter of a second in one tick on any one core (many slow components, say), the rest of that tick waits and the game pauses, with a message in the Console saying why. None of the components is to blame on its own, so none stops; make the slow ones faster, then press Pause or Play to carry on. Without this, the game would try to catch up and the editor would hardly respond.

What game code says goes to the Console a line at a time. A very long line is cut short, and past 200 lines in one tick the rest are counted ("Game code said 800 more lines just now"), so a component that talks too much can't drown the Console or fill the computer's memory.

Changing code while the game runs#

Keep the game playing, change your Lust, and save. In about a third of a second the running game has the new code, and nothing starts over:

  • Every running component keeps its values, field by field, by name: a turret keeps the ammo it has left, a mover stays where it got to. Only update and the on reactions are new.
  • A field whose kind changed (an int that's now a float), or a new field, takes its starting value. The Console says which: "Gun's ammo is float now, not int, so it starts at 10."
  • A removed field is dropped; a removed component stops.
  • A component new in the code starts on every entity that has it.
  • A component that stopped after a failure runs again, since its code changed.
  • A mistake in the new code leaves the game running the last code that worked, and the mistake shows in Problems. Fix it and save again.

The Console says what changed each time: "The running game took the new code (Gun changed; Radar new); components keep their values."

Events#

Components tell each other things with events: a gun tells a target it was hit, the target's health tells its entity it died. An event says what it carries. A component reacts to it with on, and anything sends it to an entity with send:

fetch "solis/world":World;

event Hit(entity by, float damage);
event Died();

component Health {
    has {
        float hp = 10;
    }

    on Hit(entity by, float damage) {
        is hp > 0? then {
            hp = hp - damage;
            is hp <= 0? then {
                send Died() to this;
            }
        }
    }

    on Died() {
        World:say("down!");
    }
}

component Gun {
    has {
        entity target = nothing;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        send Hit(this, 2.5) to target;
    }
}

pass Health, Gun;
end
use reflect::{EntityId, Value};
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

// The events are declared in Lust, as in the Lust example: what they
// carry is checked against it.
pub struct Health {
    hp: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Health {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        match event.name.as_str() {
            // Hit carries who hit it, then the damage.
            "Hit" => {
                let damage = event.values.get(1).and_then(Value::as_f64).unwrap_or(0.0);
                if self.hp > 0.0 {
                    self.hp -= damage;
                    if self.hp <= 0.0 {
                        let me = cx.me();
                        cx.send(Some(me), "Died", Vec::new());
                    }
                }
                true
            }
            "Died" => {
                cx.host().say("down!");
                true
            }
            _ => false,
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}

pub struct Gun {
    target: Option<EntityId>,
}

impl RustComponent for Gun {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.send(self.target, "Hit", vec![Value::Entity(Some(me)), Value::Float(2.5)]);
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
-- The events are declared in Lust, as in the Lust example: what they
-- carry is checked against it.
local Health = component("Health", {
    { "hp", "float", 10 },
})

function Health:on_Hit(by, damage)
    if self.hp > 0 then
        self.hp = self.hp - damage
        if self.hp <= 0 then
            solis.send(self.me, "Died")
        end
    end
end

function Health:on_Died()
    solis.World:say("down!")
end

local Gun = component("Gun", {
    { "target", "entity" },
})

function Gun:update(dt)
    solis.send(self.target, "Hit", self.me, 2.5)
end
  • When they arrive: after every component's update in the tick (and after the moves those made), in the order they were sent (by the sending entity's ID, then component name). On the entity, each component with an on for it reacts, in the order of the components' names. An event sent while reacting to another (Hit sends Died) arrives later in the same tick.
  • To something you just spawned: an event sent to an entity spawned in the same tick (entity shot = World:spawn(…); send Launch(dir) to shot;) arrives at the start of the next tick's events, once its components exist. Its first update runs just before, so set it moving in the on, not in update's first run.
  • An event to nothing goes nowhere, so a gun with no target is harmless.
  • An event sent while starting goes nowhere too. The lines outside components run before anything plays, and a field's starting value is worked out as its component is made (int id = register();, where register has a send in it): nothing is running yet to take the event. Send from update or an on.
  • Lust checks that every send carries what the event says, so a misspelt event or a missing value is a mistake in Problems before anything runs.
  • Components that keep sending to each other forever are stopped after 10,000 events in one tick, with a message in the Console (once, until the code changes), so the game can't freeze. At most 10,000 events can wait at once, holding at most 16 MB of text: past that, the send itself fails, so the Console points at the component sending too much.
  • A component whose reaction keeps failing (an on that divides by zero, every time) is said once in the Console; it keeps running, and its later failures with events aren't said again until the code changes.

In Lua, solis.send(to, "Hit", by, 2.5) sends an event, and a function called on_ and the event's name reacts to it. When the Lust declares the event, what Lua sends is checked against what it carries: a wrong value means the event isn't sent, and the Console names the Lua component that sent it. Lua can also send events no Lust declares; their numbers arrive as floats (Lua has one kind of number, so 2 and 2.5 arrive alike).

A Lua component's fields can't be called me (the entity it's on), update, or anything starting with on_ or __: those are its methods, and Lua's own.

Each Lua file has globals of its own. A helper a file makes global (function helper() … end) is seen by that file only, and no file can change Lua's own libraries (string, table, math) or solis, component and vec3: trying to is a mistake. That way one file can't break another, or the Lust. To share code between Lua files, put it in a component's events, or in Lust.

What Lua game code can't do. Game code is sandboxed, so a game you download can't harm your computer: it has no require, no files, and no way out of its time and memory limits. It has no loadstring, getfenv or setfenv either: those reach past a file's own globals, into another file's or Solis's own, and calling one is a mistake ("attempt to call a nil value"). table.move moves at most a million items at once (a bigger one couldn't be stopped in time), and collectgarbage only tells you how much memory is used (collectgarbage("count")).

In Rust, handle takes each event by name, with what it carries in event.values, in the order the Lust declares, and returns whether it reacted; cx.send(to, "Hit", values) sends one. Like Lua's, a Rust send is checked against what the Lust declares: one that doesn't fit isn't sent (send returns false), and the Console says why, naming the component.

Other code files can sit in any folder in assets. Fetch them by their path from assets, such as fetch "weapons/gun":Gun; for assets/weapons/gun.lst. The Library's Code tab lists them all.

Projectiles#

Lasers, bolts and tracer rounds come in their thousands, so they aren't entities: they're projectiles, which Solis moves itself, every tick, on every core.

fetch "solis/world":World;

component Turret {
    has {
        int cooldown = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        cooldown = cooldown - 1;
        is cooldown <= 0? then {
            World:fire(position(), [0, 1, 0], 60, 2, [4, 0.3, 0.2]);
            cooldown = 30;
        }
    }
}

pass Turret;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent, Shot};

pub struct Turret {
    cooldown: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Turret {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        self.cooldown -= 1;
        if self.cooldown <= 0 {
            let me = cx.me();
            let from = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
            cx.host().fire(Shot {
                from,
                direction: Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0),
                speed: 60.0,
                life: 2.0,
                colour: [4.0, 0.3, 0.2],
            });
            self.cooldown = 30;
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
local Turret = component("Turret", {
    { "cooldown", "int", 0 },
})

function Turret:update(dt)
    self.cooldown = self.cooldown - 1
    if self.cooldown <= 0 then
        local from = solis.entity.position(self.me)
        solis.World:fire(from, vec3(0, 1, 0), 60, 2, vec3(4, 0.3, 0.2))
        self.cooldown = 30
    end
end

fire takes where it starts, which way it flies (any length), its speed in metres a second, how long it lives in seconds, and its colour as red, green and blue. Above 1 glows brighter: [4, 0.3, 0.2] is a hot red laser.

  • It flies in a straight line and disappears when its time is up. It doesn't hit anything: lasers are kept out of physics so a million can fly. To see what a shot would hit, look along its line with castRay.
  • It's drawn in the Game panel as a glowing streak, as long as it flies in two frames. Streaks add their light where they cross.
  • Up to 1,000,000 can fly at once. Past that, new shots aren't fired until some run out, and the Console says so once.
  • Like a move, a shot lands after every update in the tick is done (what game code sees), so it starts flying next tick.

Making and removing entities#

Game code can make copies of assemblies while it plays, and take entities away:

fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/project":Assembly;

component Hangar {
    has {
        int made = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        is made < 10? then {
            entity ship = World:spawn(Assembly.Ships.Fighter, [made * 5, 0, 10]);
            made = made + 1;
        }
    }
}

pass Hangar;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Hangar {
    made: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Hangar {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        if self.made < 10 {
            // The assembly by its file in assets, without .solassembly.
            let place = Vec3::new(self.made as f32 * 5.0, 0.0, 10.0);
            let _ship = cx.host().spawn("ships/fighter", place);
            self.made += 1;
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
local Hangar = component("Hangar", {
    { "made", "int", 0 },
})

function Hangar:update(dt)
    if self.made < 10 then
        -- The assembly's name as text: Assembly.Ships.Fighter is "Ships.Fighter".
        local ship = solis.World:spawn("Ships.Fighter", vec3(self.made * 5, 0, 10))
        self.made = self.made + 1
    end
end
  • Which assembly: one of the project's, named from its file with folders as options inside options: ships/fighter.solassembly is Assembly.Ships.Fighter (each part's first letter a capital). Solis writes the names into solis/project.lst whenever you add, rename or remove an assembly, so a misspelt or deleted one is a mistake before the game runs, listing the real ones. A file whose name can't be a Lust name (it starts with a digit, has a dash or space, is all capitals, or is one of Lust's own objects like time) is left out, and the Console says which. Assembly.None is there when the project has none, and makes nothing.
  • When: like a move, it happens after every update in the tick (what game code sees). World:spawn gives back the new entity at once, so you can keep it. It joins the game at the end of the tick, after the tick's moves: its components start then and run from the next tick, even when a slow frame runs several ticks at once. A despawn lands at the same moment, in the order they were asked for, so spawning something and taking it out in one tick leaves nothing behind. New copies go at the end of the area's tree, in the order they were spawned.
  • Where it shows: copies game code makes appear in the Area panel while playing, and are gone when you press Stop, like everything else the game did. They aren't undo steps, which is how Solis tells them from your own edits: Stop offers to keep only yours (Play mode), so a change you make to one of these copies goes with it.
  • At most 10,000 copies are made in one tick, and an area holds at most a million entities; past that, the Console says so and the rest aren't made.
  • When a copy can't be made: World:spawn still gives back an entity, but nothing appears, and the Console says why in a warning: Game code spawned "squad", but it places an assembly (…) that isn't in the project, so nothing was made. The reasons are those of assemblies themselves: the assembly places another whose file is missing or can't be read, assemblies place each other in a loop (the message names them in order), they're placed more than 16 deep, or a copy would be more than a million entities. Each assembly's reason is said once each time you press Play, however many times the code asks, so a spawn in update doesn't fill the Console. Fix the assembly and press Play again.
  • despawn() is how a component takes its own entity away, and target:despawn() takes another. It ends at the end of the tick.

Random numbers#

Dice, loot, where an enemy wanders next: random() gives a number from 0 up to 1, randomRange(low, high) one between two numbers, and randomInt(low, high) a whole number, both ends included.

fetch "solis/world":World;

component Die {
    method update(float dt) {
        World:say("rolled " + World:randomInt(1, 6).text());
    }
}

pass Die;
end
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Die;

impl RustComponent for Die {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        // random() is from 0 up to 1: six sides make 1 to 6.
        let roll = (cx.host().random() * 6.0).floor() as i64 + 1;
        cx.host().say(&format!("rolled {roll}"));
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
local Die = component("Die", {})

function Die:update(dt)
    solis.World:say("rolled " .. solis.World:randomInt(1, 6))
end

Solis makes them from the game's seed (random numbers), so the same seed gives the same numbers, on any computer and any number of cores. Each Play has a new seed; type seed in the Console to see it, and seed 42 to start every Play from 42, so you can watch the same game again. setSeed(n) starts the numbers again from n at the end of the tick. Lua's own math.random and math.randomseed follow the same seed. Lust's own Random (Random[1, 6], Random:chance, an array's pick and shuffle) doesn't yet: its first roll starts it from the computer's clock, and with it the game's seed, so the same game can't be played again. Use World:random and the rest above. The numbers carry on while the game is paused with World:setGameSpeed(0): every tick still rolls new ones, so a pause menu can shuffle or roll like any other code.

Tweens#

A door that swings open over half a second, a health bar that slides down, a light that fades: a tween glides a field to a new value over time, so you don't write the in-between steps yourself.

fetch "solis/world":World;

component Door {
    has {
        float open = 0;
    }

    on Opened() {
        tween open to 1 over 0.5 [ease OutCubic] {
            World:say("the door is open");
        }
    }
}

event Opened();
pass Door;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

// Tweens are Lust's own. In Rust, move the field a step in update:
// here a steady glide from 0 to 1 over half a second.
pub struct Door {
    open: f64,
    opening: bool,
}

impl RustComponent for Door {
    fn handle(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Opened" {
            return false;
        }
        self.opening = true;
        true
    }

    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        if self.opening {
            self.open = (self.open + dt / 0.5).min(1.0);
            if self.open >= 1.0 {
                self.opening = false;
                cx.host().say("the door is open");
            }
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
-- Tweens are Lust's own. In Lua, move the field a step in update:
-- here a steady glide from 0 to 1 over half a second.
local Door = component("Door", {
    { "open", "float", 0 },
    { "opening", "bool", false },
})

function Door:on_Opened()
    self.opening = true
end

function Door:update(dt)
    if self.opening then
        self.open = math.min(1, self.open + dt / 0.5)
        if self.open >= 1 then
            self.opening = false
            solis.World:say("the door is open")
        end
    end
end
  • What it moves: a field of the component (or a variable at the top of the file) that's an int, float, vec2, vec3, colour or rotation. [ease OutCubic] picks how it speeds up and slows down (any of the Ease curves; leave it out for a steady glide), and the { } after it, if any, runs once when it gets there.
  • When: each tick, tweens move after the game-wide objects and before any component's update. So an update sees this tick's value, and what a done block changes is there for the same tick's updates. A tween started in an update first moves on the next tick. Starting another tween on the same field replaces the first, whose { } never runs.
  • New code while playing stops the tweens the old code started, where they are, without their { }.
  • A game-wide object's fields can't be tweened: an object changes only in its own update (below), so the tween stops with a message saying so. Glide the field in the object's update instead, with Maths:moveTowards(hour, 18, dt) or lerp.
  • When a tween fails (its { } divides by zero, say), the Console says where, once, until the code changes. Tweens started after it wait until it has run its time, so fix it first.

Tweens are Lust's own. In Lua or Rust, move the field a step in update, as the switch above shows; for an ease, bend the step with a curve of your own.

Game-wide objects#

Some things belong to the whole game, not to any one entity: the time of day, the player's money, the weather. Write one as a Lust object and pass it, and Solis runs it for you (game-wide object):

object Clock {
    has {
        int day = 1;
        float hour = 6;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        hour += dt / 60;
        is hour >= 24? then {
            hour -= 24;
            day += 1;
        }
    }

    method bool isNight() {
        return hour < 6 || hour >= 20;
    }
}

component StreetLamp {
    has {
        bool lit = false;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        lit = Clock:isNight();
    }
}

pass Clock, StreetLamp;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

// Game-wide objects are Lust's own: Rust and Lua components can't read
// them yet. Keep the clock in Lust, as in the Lust example, and have a
// Lust component tell the lamps with an event when night falls.
pub struct StreetLamp {
    lit: bool,
}

impl RustComponent for StreetLamp {
    fn handle(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        match event.name.as_str() {
            "NightFell" => self.lit = true,
            "DayBroke" => self.lit = false,
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
-- Game-wide objects are Lust's own: Lua and Rust components can't read
-- them yet. Keep the clock in Lust, as in the Lust example, and have a
-- Lust component tell the lamps with an event when night falls.
local StreetLamp = component("StreetLamp", {
    { "lit", "bool", false },
})

function StreetLamp:on_NightFell()
    self.lit = true
end

function StreetLamp:on_DayBroke()
    self.lit = false
end
  • Ticked first: each passed object's update(float dt) runs once a tick, objects in order of their names, before any entity's components. So every lamp sees the same hour, the one the clock has just moved to.
  • Read anywhere, changed only in its own update. Components read an object's fields and call its methods (Clock.hour, Clock:isNight()). Changing one of its fields anywhere else (Clock.hour = 12; in a component) stops that component, with a message pointing at the line: "Clock.hour can't be changed here: an object changes only in its own update". An object's update may change other objects too. Why: Solis runs game code on every core of the computer at once, each core with its own copy of the code. Objects run on the first, and their fields are copied to the others before the components run; if a component on one core could change the clock, the others would never know.
  • Kept in save games: a save keeps every object's fields, and loading gives them back (Save games). New code while the game runs keeps them too, field by field, by name, like a component's.
  • Which fields: the kinds a component's fields can be (bool, int, float, string, a state, vec3, vec2, rotation, colour, entity) are copied and kept. A list, a map or a thing in an object isn't saved yet, and each core keeps its own copy, so the Console says so when you press Play. Keep what every part of the game must see in plain fields.
  • An object that fails in its update stops, and the Console says where, like a component; it runs again when the code changes. Components can still read it.
  • Lust only: objects are written in Lust. Lua and Rust components can't read them yet.
  • An object that isn't passed is its file's own helper, and Solis leaves it alone.

Saving and loading#

Saves:saveTo("quick") saves the whole game and Saves:loadFrom("quick") puts it back exactly as it was: see Save games. (save and load on their own are Lust's own words, for its files.)

Sounds#

Game code plays sound events by the project's names for them: Solis writes each event into solis/project.lst as state Sound, folders as options inside options, so assets/sfx/footstep.solsound is Sound.Sfx.Footstep. A misspelt or deleted event is a mistake before the game runs. Fetch Audio from solis/sound and Sound from solis/project:

fetch "solis/sound":Audio;
fetch "solis/project":Sound;

component Walker {
    has {
        int steps = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        steps = steps + 1;
        is steps % 30 == 0? then {
            Audio:playAt(Sound.Sfx.Footstep, position());
        }
    }
}

pass Walker;
end
use script::{Context, RustComponent, SoundAt};

pub struct Walker {
    steps: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Walker {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        self.steps += 1;
        if self.steps % 30 == 0 {
            // The sound event by its file in assets, without .solsound.
            let me = cx.me();
            let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
            cx.host().play_sound("sfx/footstep", SoundAt::Place(here));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's, under Components.
}
local Walker = component("Walker", {
    { "steps", "int", 0 },
})

function Walker:update(dt)
    self.steps = self.steps + 1
    if self.steps % 30 == 0 then
        -- The sound event's name as text: Sound.Sfx.Footstep is "Sfx.Footstep".
        solis.Audio:playAt("Sfx.Footstep", solis.entity.position(self.me))
    end
end
  • Audio:play(Sound.Music.Theme) plays it the same everywhere: music, the interface.
  • Audio:playAt(Sound.Sfx.Footstep, place) plays it at a place in the world: quieter far from the camera, and from its direction (for an event whose Placement is In the world).
  • playSound(Sound.Sfx.Engine) plays it on the component's entity and follows it as it moves: an engine, a voice (target:playSound(…) on another). stopSounds() stops them, with a short fade, even ones asked for earlier in the same tick; it doesn't stop the entity's AudioSource (use setSoundPlaying for that).
  • setSoundPlaying(playing) turns the entity's AudioSource (a sound that keeps playing: an engine, a campfire) on or off.
  • Audio:setVolume(Bus.Music, volume) sets a bus for the rest of the play (the buses are the Mixer's, as state Bus in solis/project.lst; the UI bus is Bus.Ui, since Lust names aren't all capitals), from 0 (silent) to 1 (as set in the Mixer): what an options menu's volume sliders call. Stop puts the Mixer's back.

In Lua they're solis.Audio:playAt("Sfx.Footstep", solis.entity.position(self.me)) and so on (the option's name as text; "sfx/footstep" works too). In Rust, through the component's host: cx.host().play_sound("sfx/footstep", SoundAt::Place(place)), and cx.host().set_bus_volume("Music", 0.5).

Sound never changes the game. None of these gives anything back, so code can't ask "is it still playing?": a game plays exactly the same with sound on, off, or with no sound card, and a recording replays the same. Each play picks its take from the game's seed and the tick, so the same game even sounds the same each time. Like a move, a sound lands at the end of the tick.

  • The camera is what hears (or a Listener), and the entity whose code plays a sound is who caused it, for a sound event heard by Only who caused it: a sound to its right comes from the right. Pausing the game pauses its sounds, Play carries them on, and Stop fades them out. A Step plays that tick's sounds.
  • A sound placed past its event's Silent past distance isn't started at all.
  • Up to 256 sounds can be asked for in one tick (more are left out, and the Console says so once), and up to 256 play at once.
  • If the computer stalls for a moment, only the last few ticks' sounds play, so a hitch doesn't play a pile of footsteps at once.

Input#

Game code reads the player's controls as named actions, never keys: Input:axis(Action.Move), Input:pressed(Action.Jump), Input:held(Action.Sprint), with Input from solis/input and Action from solis/project. See Input, which also covers gamepads, rebinding and recording a play.

Physics#

Things that fall, collide and get pushed have a RigidBody and a Collider: see Physics. Game code pushes them (push), reads and sets how fast they move (velocity, setVelocity), and looks along lines with Physics:castRay, which gives back a RayHit. Characters with a CharacterBody are moved with walk and asked grounded: see Characters and cameras, which also has the ready-made character controller and cameras in solis/kit/.

What the engine offers#

InMethodWhat it does
solis/worldWorld:say(string words)Writes words in the Console.
solis/worldfloat World:time()How long the game has been running, in seconds.
solis/worldentity World:find(string name)The first entity with this name, in the Area panel's order, or nothing.
solis/worldWorld:fire(vec3 from, vec3 direction, float speed, float life, vec3 colour)Fires a projectile (see Projectiles, below).
solis/worldentity World:spawn(Assembly which, vec3 place)Makes a copy of one of the project's assemblies at a place (see Making and removing entities, below).
solis/worldfloat World:frameTime()How long the last frame took, in seconds of real time (1/60 at 60 frames a second).
solis/worldfloat World:random()A random number from 0 up to 1 (see Random numbers, above).
solis/worldfloat World:randomRange(float low, float high)A random number from low up to high.
solis/worldint World:randomInt(int low, int high)A random whole number from low to high, both included.
solis/worldWorld:setGameSpeed(float speed)Runs the game at a speed, from the end of the tick: 0 pauses it (time, physics, projectiles and sprites stop and dt is 0, but components still run, so a pause menu works), 1 as usual, up to 4.
solis/worldWorld:gameSpeed()How fast the game runs, as the tick started.
solis/screensScreens:setTextSize(float size), Screens:textSize()The player's text size on every screen, 0.5 to 3 (1 as designed), from the end of the tick (Game screens).
solis/screensScreens:setUiSize(float size), Screens:uiSize()The player's UI size: every screen bigger or smaller, 0.5 to 2.
solis/windowWindow:setFullscreen(bool on), Window:fullscreen()Whether the game fills the screen (Alt+Enter switches it too).
solis/windowWindow:setResolution(int width, int height), Window:resolution(), Window:useNextResolution()The window's size in pixels, and the next usual one, for a menu.
solis/windowWindow:quit()Closes the game at the end of the tick, for a menu's Quit button. While playing in the editor, play stops (Exporting for playtesting). In Lua solis.Window:quit(); in Rust quit.
solis/worldfloat World:timeOfDay(), World:setTimeOfDay(float hour)The game's hour, 0 up to 24, from the Environment's Day and night; setting it moves the day on from there, at the end of the tick (Sky, fog and exposure). In Lua solis.World:timeOfDay(); in Rust time_of_day.
solis/worldWorld:setSeed(int seed)Starts the random numbers again from a seed, at the end of the tick.
solis/worldSaves:saveTo(string slot)Saves the whole game in a slot, at the end of the tick (Save games).
solis/worldSaves:loadFrom(string slot)Loads the game saved in a slot, at the end of the tick.
solis/projectstate AssemblyThe project's assemblies, folders as options inside options (Assembly.Ships.Fighter).
solis/soundAudio:play(Sound event)Plays a sound event the same everywhere (see Sounds, above).
solis/soundAudio:playAt(Sound event, vec3 place)Plays a sound event at a place in the world.
solis/soundAudio:setVolume(Bus bus, float volume)Sets a bus's volume for the rest of the play, 0 to 1.
any entityplaySound(Sound event)Plays a sound event on the entity, following it.
any entitystopSounds()Stops the sounds on the entity, with a short fade.
any entitysetSoundPlaying(bool playing)Turns the entity's AudioSource on or off.
solis/projectstate Sound, state BusThe project's sound events (Sound.Sfx.Footstep) and the Mixer's buses (Bus.Music).
any entityanimate(Clip clip)Plays a clip on the entity's Sprite; already playing or finished it, it carries on as it is (Animating sprites).
any entityanimateFromStart(Clip clip)Plays a clip from its beginning, whatever it was doing.
any entitystopAnimation()Stops the entity's Sprite where it is in its clip.
any entitysetFlip(bool across, bool down)Mirrors the entity's Sprite: across faces it the other way, down turns it upside down.
solis/animationevent CueReached(Cue cue)Sent when a sprite's clip reaches a frame with an event (bring it in with fetch "solis/animation":CueReached;).
solis/animationevent ClipFinished(Clip clip)Sent when a sprite's clip has played all its times.
solis/projectstate Clip, state CueThe sprites' clips, under their sheets (Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Walk), and their frame events (Cue.Footstep).
any entityshowScreen(Screen which)Shows one of the game's screens on the entity, at the end of the tick (Game screens).
any entityhideScreen(Screen which)Hides it, if the entity shows it.
any entityscreenShown(Screen which)Whether the entity shows that screen, as the tick started.
solis/projectstate ScreenThe game's screens, by their files in ui/ (Screen.PauseMenu for ui/pauseMenu.lst).
solis/animators/<file>class <File>Animator, state <File>StateEach animator's own file: anim:setMoving(true), anim:current() (Animators).
solis/maps/<file>class <File>Map, its layers, terrains and choices as statesEach tile map's own file: farm:setWatered(x, y, true), farm:terrain(FarmLayer.Ground, x, y) (Tile maps).
solis/inputbool Input:held(Action action)Whether an action is held this tick (Input).
solis/inputbool Input:pressed(Action action)True once, the tick an action went down.
solis/inputbool Input:released(Action action)True once, the tick it came up.
solis/inputvec3 Input:axis(Action action)An axis action's x and y.
solis/inputstring Input:binding(Action action)The key that sets an action off, for "Press F".
solis/inputInput:rebind(Action action, string input)Binds a new input to an action, from the next tick.
solis/projectstate ActionThe project's input actions (Action.Jump), from File › Project settings › Input.
solis/physicsRayHit Physics:castRay(vec3 from, vec3 direction, float reach)What a line meets first: found, distance, entity and normal (Physics).
any entityvec3 position()Where the entity is in the world, in metres.
any entitymoveTo(vec3 place)Puts the entity at a place in the world.
any entityrotation rotation()Which way the entity faces.
any entityturnTo(rotation facing)Turns the entity to face this way.
any entityface(vec3 direction)Turns the entity, upright, to face along a direction (its forward is +Y): face(target:position() - position()) faces a place.
any entitystring name()The entity's name.
any entitydespawn()Takes the entity, and everything under it, out of the game.
any entitypush(vec3 impulse)Gives its body a push (Physics).
any entityvec3 velocity()How fast and which way its body moves, metres a second; for a 2D character, how fast its last tick's move went.
any entitysetVelocity(vec3 velocity)Sets how fast and which way its body moves.

any entitybool grounded()Whether a character stood on something after its last move (3D or 2D).
solis/entityrotation facingAlong(vec3 direction)The upright rotation facing along a direction, for working out a turn without making it.

An entity's abilities are called bare for the component's own entity (moveTo(place)) and with : on any other (target:moveTo(place)). In Lua they're solis.entity.moveTo(target, place), and the objects' solis.World:say(words).

Calls that changed. Solis's calls now follow one shape (methods on things, the project's names as states), so some older ones are written differently. Old code is a mistake that says the new way: "positionOf is now written target:position() (inside a component, position() for its own entity)".

BeforeNow
positionOf(e), moveTo(e, p)e:position(), e:moveTo(p) (bare for the component's own entity)
rotationOf(e), turnTo(e, r), nameOf(e), despawn(e)e:rotation(), e:turnTo(r), e:name(), e:despawn()
turnTo(this, facingAlong(d))face(d)
say, time, frameTime, find, fire, random, randomRange, randomInt, setSeedthe same names on World: World:say(words)
spawn("ships/fighter", p)World:spawn(Assembly.Ships.Fighter, p)
saveGame(slot), loadGame(slot)Saves:saveTo(slot), Saves:loadFrom(slot)
held("Jump"), pressed, released, axis("Move")Input:held(Action.Jump) and so on, with fetch "solis/input":Input; and fetch "solis/project":Action;
bindingOf("Jump"), rebind("Jump", key)Input:binding(Action.Jump), Input:rebind(Action.Jump, key)
push(e, f), velocityOf(e), setVelocity(e, v)e:push(f), e:velocity(), e:setVelocity(v)
moveCharacter(e, w), onGround(e)e:walk(w), e:grounded()
playSound("sfx/x"), playSoundAt("sfx/x", p)Audio:play(Sound.Sfx.X), Audio:playAt(Sound.Sfx.X, p)
playSoundOn("sfx/x", e), stopSoundsOn(e), setSoundPlaying(e, b)e:playSound(Sound.Sfx.X), e:stopSounds(), e:setSoundPlaying(b)
setBusVolume("Music", v)Audio:setVolume(Bus.Music, v)
playClip(e, "walk"), replayClip, stopClip(e)e:animate(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Walk), e:animateFromStart(…), e:stopAnimation()
on AnimationCue(string name), on ClipFinished(string clip)on CueReached(Cue cue), on ClipFinished(Clip clip)
castRay(…), castRayHit(…), castRayNormal(…)one call: RayHit hit = Physics:castRay(…); then hit.distance, hit.entity, hit.normal
Lua solis.positionOf(e), solis.say(w), solis.held("Jump")solis.entity.position(e), solis.World:say(w), solis.Input:held("Jump")

When an update renames something. What game code can call doesn't change by accident: Solis's own checks stop any update that changes it without saying so. When a name does change on purpose, the old name keeps working for a few phases, so your game still runs the day you update. Each place your code uses the old name shows in the Problems panel as a warning, with its file and line, the new name, and when the old one stops working. Change the call to the new name before then.

Safe to open#

Game code runs inside a sandbox: it can reach the game through the engine's methods, and nothing else. It can't read or write files, start programs or reach the network, it has 64 MB of memory, and code that runs too long is stopped. Lua's require isn't there either (it would read files from anywhere on the computer). So a project you download or are sent can't harm your computer through its code, and Solis never runs the other files in it (see Projects and the Library).

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Problems says "there's already something called Health". Why: two components, classes, objects, nodes or schemas have the same name (often a copied one not yet renamed), perhaps in two files; the message says where the other is. Fix: rename one.
  • Problem: Problems says checking the code took more than 30 seconds and was given up on. Why: something in the code is more than the checker can handle; it shouldn't happen. A check can't be stopped once it has started, so that one keeps running in the background (and keeps one processor core busy) until it ends by itself, which it may never do. Fix: undo your last change, then restart Solis so the code can be checked again, and please report it with the code that caused it.
  • Problem: Problems says "the code wasn't checked: the check that started … never finished, and is still running". Why: an earlier check was given up on (the problem above) and is still running. Solis doesn't start another beside it, or every save would leave one more running and slow the computer down further. The message says what that check was checking: the same code as now, or the code before the files it names changed (the trouble is in that older code). Fix: restart Solis to check the code straight away. If you'd rather wait, the code is checked by itself as soon as the old check ends.
  • Problem: Problems says the game's code starts at main.lst and there isn't one. Why: there are .lst files of your own, but none is called main.lst in the assets folder itself. (The files Solis writes into its own folder don't count: a game written only in Lua needs no main.lst.) Fix: make assets/main.lst, and fetch your other files from it.
  • Problem: changes I made to solis/world.lst (or solis/kit/…) disappeared. Why: Solis writes the solis files again when the project opens, so they always match the engine. Fix: put your own code in your own files, outside solis/: anything in that folder counts as the engine's, never as your game's code. To change a ready-made component, copy its file outside solis/ and rename the component.
  • Problem: my component isn't in + Component. Why: the code has a mistake (see Problems), or its Lust file isn't fetched from main.lst (directly, or through a file main.lst fetches). Lua files are all read, wherever they are in assets. Fix: fix the mistake, or fetch the file.
  • Problem: "solis.entity.moveTo isn't something the engine offers" in Lua. Why: the name is misspelt, or the method was used outside update or an on_ function, when the game isn't running. Fix: check the name against the table above.
  • Problem: the Console says a call "wants text for words, and was given nothing (nil)" in Lua. Why: one of the values given to the call isn't the kind it takes. Nothing (nil) usually means a value is missing, a variable's name is misspelt (a name Lua doesn't know is nil), or the call is written with a dot where it needs a colon: solis.World.say("hello") for solis.World:say("hello"). Fix: the message names the call, the value and the line; check that value there.
  • Problem: the Console says "this calls something of Solis's that was kept from earlier" in Lua. Why: a call was put in a variable, as local say = solis.World.say at the top of a file does. Solis lends its calls to game code only while that code runs, so the one kept stops working as soon as the file has loaded. Fix: write the call out where it's used (solis.World:say("hello")), or keep the object and call through it: local World = solis.World, then World:say("hello").
  • Problem: a component is called the same as one of Solis's (Light) or a Rust one, or a Lust and a Lua component share a name. Why: two components can't share a name. The one in your code doesn't run (Solis's own, or the Rust one, does). Fix: rename yours; Problems says where it is.
  • Problem: I saved new code while playing, and the Console says the running game couldn't take it. Why: the code's start failed with the game's world (it ran fine with no world while checking). Fix: fix the line it points at; the game keeps the last code meanwhile.
  • Problem: Problems says something is nested too deeply. Why: more than 150 levels of brackets, blocks or operators inside each other (a + b + c … counts each +) is more than Lust takes. Fix: split it up with variables or methods.
  • Problem: Problems says the code stopped while starting. Why: Solis runs the code's own start (the lines outside components, and each field's starting value) to read its components, before anything plays and with no world: World:find finds nothing then. A start that fails or takes more than a second is a mistake. Fix: fix the line Problems points at.
  • Problem: the Console says a code file was left out. Why: each code file can be at most 1 MB, and all of them together 16 MB. Files that aren't text are left out too. Fix: split a huge file into smaller ones.
  • Problem: a component reads another entity's place and gets where it was before this tick's move. Why: during a tick, game code sees the world as it was when the tick started (see Components, above), so every core sees the same world. Fix: usually nothing: it catches up next tick. If it must be at once, do both in one component, or send an event (events see the moves made before them).
  • Commit the solis folder with your game, so lust check works on other computers too.

Which language when#

Lust, Lua and Rust can all write game code, and they work together on one entity. This page says which to use for what, with Solis's own measurements.

When to use it#

When you're starting a component and wondering which language to write it in, or when the Profiler says game code takes much of a frame.

The short answer#

  • Lust for most of your game: it's made for Solis, Problems checks it as you type, and it's fast enough for almost everything. Start here.
  • Lua for logic you already know how to write in Lua, or code copied from elsewhere: deciding things, reacting to events, menus, quests. It's fine anywhere the work is small per tick.
  • Rust for the heaviest per-tick work on many entities (crowds, simulations), once it's clear that's where the time goes. For now, Rust components need a Solis built from source.

All three can sit on the same entity and send each other events (see Game code), so you can start a component in Lust and move just the slow part later.

The numbers#

The same work, written once in each language: 2,000 entities each doing a running sum of 40 sines every tick. Milliseconds for one tick of all 2,000 (a frame at 60 frames a second has about 16 ms in all), from Solis's scale check:

RustLustLua
40 steps of number work each0.362.76.0
400 steps each (ten times as much)4.32736

What that means:

  • Rust is about 7 times quicker than Lust at number work, and Lust about twice as quick as Lua when the work is light.
  • Most of Lua's time is reaching its own fields (self.value), which Solis checks every time. A Lua component that keeps its sums in local variables and writes its fields once at the end runs closer to Lust.
  • All three give exactly the same answer, to the last bit, so a game plays the same whichever you choose, and recordings replay the same.

Solis tried making Lust and Lua faster with Luau's "native code". Lust's heavy work got about a third quicker but Lua's got slower, so it's off for now (the report↗).

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: game code takes most of a frame. Why: many entities do a lot each tick. Fix: see which component it is, then: do the work every few ticks instead of every tick; keep sums in local variables; or move that component to Lust (from Lua) or Rust (from Lust).
  • Problem: "is Lua bad, then?" Why: no: 2,000 Lua components doing light work each tick take about 6 ms, which fits easily in a frame. Fix: nothing, unless the Profiler says otherwise.

Related#

  • Game code: writing components in all three languages.
  • The Profiler: where each frame's time goes.
  • Concepts: game code, components.

Physics#

Make things fall, collide, stack and get pushed, the same way on every computer.

When to use it#

Whenever something in your game should move like a real object without you writing how: a crate that tips off a ledge, a ball that bounces, a door that swings shut and knocks things out of the way, or a floor and walls that characters and objects can't pass through.

Not everything needs it. Projectiles (lasers, bullets) fly in straight lines without physics, which is why a million of them are cheap. And a unit that only slides across a map is simpler to move yourself with moveTo.

Solis's physics is strict: the same game, with the same inputs, comes out exactly the same on every computer, to the last decimal (determinism). Recordings play back the same anywhere, and online strategy games can keep every player's game in step. It costs physics a little speed, which you won't notice at the sizes Solis aims for.

How to use it#

A floor

  1. Select the entity that should be the floor (an imported model, or an empty one from Home › Empty, placed where the floor goes).
  2. In Properties, choose + Component › Collider. A green outline shows its shape in the viewport while it's selected.
  3. Set its Shape and Size to cover the floor. A box 20 × 20 × 1 m is a good start; its middle sits at the entity, so lower the entity half a metre to put the top at its feet, or set Centre to 0 0 -0.5.

An entity with a collider and nothing else never moves: floors, walls, rocks.

Quicker still: a Solid brush (B over the view, or Create › Shape, then drawn out on the ground) is a floor or wall with no collider to add. Its own faces are what physics bumps into, exactly as drawn, and it never falls, even with a RigidBody (a Kinematic one still moves it as game code says, as a platform). A Collider on the same entity is used instead of its faces.

A crate that falls

  1. Select the crate and add a Collider sized like it (a 1 m crate: Box, size 1 1 1).
  2. Add a RigidBody too. Its Kind is Dynamic: physics moves it.
  3. Press Play. The crate falls onto the floor and settles. Press Stop and it's back where it was.

Moving things yourself

  • A Kinematic body is moved only by your game code (moveTo, turnTo), and pushes dynamic things out of its way without being pushed back: lifts, moving platforms, doors. A character standing on one is carried along.
  • For 2D games, use a Collider2D instead, with solid terrains for walls: see Walls and walking in 2D.
  • A player's character is better with a CharacterBody, which climbs steps, slides along walls and walks up slopes: see Characters and cameras.
  • A Fixed body never moves, like a collider on its own.
  • You can still moveTo a dynamic body to put it somewhere new (say, back on its shelf); physics carries on from there.

From game code, a body's abilities are on its entity (ball:push(force), or push(force) for the component's own), and rays are asked of Physics (in Lua, solis.entity.push(e, force) and solis.Physics:castRay(from, direction, reach), whose answer is a table with the same four fields; in Rust, cx.host().push(e, force) and cx.host().cast_ray(from, direction, reach), which gives back the hit or nothing):

fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/physics":[Physics, RayHit];

component Kicker {
    has {
        int kicked = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        entity ball = World:find("Ball");
        is kicked == 0? then {
            ball:push([5, 0, 2]);
            kicked = 1;
        }
        -- Is anything below, within 2 metres?
        RayHit below = Physics:castRay(position(), [0, 0, -1], 2);
        is below.found? then {
            World:say(below.entity:name() + " is below me");
        }
    }
}

pass Kicker;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Kicker {
    kicked: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Kicker {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        if self.kicked == 0 {
            if let Some(ball) = cx.host().find("Ball") {
                cx.host().push(ball, Vec3::new(5.0, 0.0, 2.0));
            }
            self.kicked = 1;
        }
        // Is anything below, within 2 metres?
        let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        if let Some(below) = cx.host().cast_ray(here, Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, -1.0), 2.0) {
            let name = cx.host().name(below.entity).unwrap_or_default();
            cx.host().say(&format!("{name} is below me"));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Kicker = component("Kicker", {
    { "kicked", "int", 0 },
})

function Kicker:update(dt)
    local ball = solis.World:find("Ball")
    if self.kicked == 0 then
        solis.entity.push(ball, vec3(5, 0, 2))
        self.kicked = 1
    end
    -- Is anything below, within 2 metres?
    local below = solis.Physics:castRay(solis.entity.position(self.me), vec3(0, 0, -1), 2)
    if below.found then
        solis.World:say(solis.entity.name(below.entity) .. " is below me")
    end
end
MethodWhat it does
push(vec3 impulse)A push, like a kick: a heavy body moves less than a light one. [5, 0, 0] gives a 1 kg crate 5 m/s along X.
vec3 velocity()How fast and which way it's moving, metres a second.
setVelocity(vec3 velocity)Makes it move this fast, this way, whatever its weight.
RayHit Physics:castRay(vec3 from, vec3 direction, float reach)Looks along a line and gives back what it met, all at once: hit.found (whether anything was within reach), hit.distance (how far, or -1), hit.entity (whose collider, or nothing) and hit.normal (which way its surface faces: [0, 0, 1] for a floor).

Why one call for a ray? Each question a ray answers is worked out at once, so asking for the distance, the entity and the surface separately looked three times; RayHit keeps them together.

Like moves, pushes and velocities land when every update in the tick is done, then physics moves everything on once (what game code sees). A ray sees the world as the tick started. A ray that starts inside a collider (your own character's, say) passes out of it and finds what's beyond.

Settings#

RigidBody

SettingWhat it does
KindDynamic: moved by physics. Kinematic: moved by game code, pushing dynamic things. Fixed: never moves.
MassHow heavy, in kilograms. 0 works it out from the collider's size: a kilogram for each cubic metre (a 1 m box weighs 1 kg). Give real things their real weight: a crate 20 kg, a person 75 kg.
DampingHow quickly it slows down by itself, like air resistance. 0 never; 1 or 2 feels like moving through water.
Turn dampingHow quickly it stops spinning by itself.
GravityHow much gravity pulls it: 1 as normal, 0 floats, below 0 rises.
Stays uprightIt never tips over or spins: for characters and things that should stand.
FastChecked between ticks too, so it can't pass through thin walls when it moves fast (thrown things). Costs a little more.

Collider

SettingWhat it does
ShapeBox, Sphere, or Capsule (a cylinder with rounded ends, standing up: the usual shape for a character).
SizeA box's size along X, Y and Z, in metres.
RadiusA sphere's or capsule's radius.
HeightA capsule's height, end to end.
CentreWhere the shape's middle is, from the entity's origin. Raise a character's capsule by half its height so its feet are at the origin.
FrictionHow much it grips: 0 ice, 0.5 most things, 1 rubber.
BouncinessHow much it bounces back: 0 not at all, 1 keeps all its speed.

Shapes grow with the entity's Scale.

CharacterBody is described in Characters and cameras. It takes the place of a RigidBody and Collider on the same entity, and doesn't grow with Scale.

Shortcuts#

Physics adds no keys. In the Console, seed and checksum help check that two plays come out the same.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: my crate falls through the floor. Why: the floor has no Collider, or it's smaller than it looks (check the green outline with the floor selected). Fix: add a Collider to the floor and size it.
  • Problem: something small and fast passes through a thin wall. Why: between two ticks it went from one side to the other. Fix: tick Fast on its RigidBody, or make the wall thicker.
  • Problem: a dynamic body doesn't move when I push it. Why: it's heavy for the push (a push of 5 moves a 1 kg box at 5 m/s, but a 100 kg one at only 0.05 m/s), it's resting on something with high friction, or it's Kinematic or Fixed. Fix: push harder, or make it Dynamic.
  • Problem: my character tips over. Why: physics turns it when it bumps into things. Fix: give it a CharacterBody instead of a RigidBody (Characters and cameras), or tick Stays upright.
  • Problem: a collider under another entity (a lift's floor) and the lift moves. Why: everything with physics under something that game code or an edit moves goes with it, at the next physics step: colliders, kinematic and dynamic bodies, characters (a crate in a group you move comes along). What's under a body physics moves goes too, except dynamic bodies, which physics moves itself. Fix: nothing to do. But don't put a collider under a dynamic body: it follows, but the body bumps into it. Give the body its collider directly.
  • Problem: the Console says the game has the most physics bodies it can. Why: at most 100,000 entities take part in physics at once. Fix: use fewer bodies; things that never move can share one big collider.
  • Problem: the game paused, saying physics took too long. Why: one tick of physics took more than a quarter of a second. Fix: fewer bodies, or simpler shapes.

Related#

  • Game code
  • Play mode
  • Entities and components
  • Characters and cameras
  • Concepts: physics, rigid body, collider, determinism
