Input#

Your game's controls as named actions: Move, Look, Jump, Sprint, Interact, the cameras' Pan, Turn, Zoom and Drag, the menus' MenuMove, MenuChoose, MenuBack and Pause, and any you add, from the keyboard, mouse or a gamepad, and rebindable.

When to use it#

Whenever the player controls something. Game code never asks "is W down?"; it asks "is the player moving?" (Input:axis(Action.Move)) or "did they press Jump?" (Input:pressed(Action.Jump)). Which keys and buttons mean Jump is set in one place, File › Project settings › Input, so:

  • a gamepad works without extra code (the A button is bound to Jump too);
  • players can change the keys (rebinding) without changing your game;
  • a play's input can be recorded and played back exactly, which is how you check the game always comes out the same.

How to use it#

Playing with the keys and mouse

  1. Press Play.
  2. Click the Game panel. The game now has the mouse and keys: the pointer disappears (moving the mouse turns, instead of moving a pointer), and the editor's own keys (W for the move tool, Delete, Ctrl + Z…) are off, so they can't change your area by accident while you play.
  3. Press Esc to give the mouse and keys back to the editor. Stop does too.

A connected gamepad works whenever the game is playing; it has nothing of the editor's to clash with. Solis uses the first one connected, Xbox layout.

The ready-made actions

ActionKeyboard and mouseGamepadWhat game code gets
MoveW A S D, or the arrow keysleft stickwhich way to go: x across (right +1), y forward (+1)
Lookmouseright stickhow far to turn this tick, in degrees
JumpSpaceAheld, pressed, released
SprintShiftleft stick clickheld, pressed, released
InteractFXheld, pressed, released
Panarrow keysleft stickwhich way to move the RTS camera
TurnAlt + left and right arrowsright stickwhich way to turn the RTS camera
Zoommouse wheel, Page Up and Page Downright and left triggershow far to zoom this tick, in steps (a wheel notch is one)
Dragmiddle mouse buttonheld while dragging the map
MenuMovearrow keysd-pad, left stickmoves the focus between a screen's buttons
MenuChooseEnter, SpaceAchooses the button with the focus
MenuBackBackspaceBheld, pressed, released (your code decides what "back" does)
PausePStartheld, pressed, released (your code opens its pause menu)

While a screen with buttons is shown, only the four menu actions reach game code: Jump on Space doesn't also jump while Space chooses a button. A project whose input actions file is from before them still gets them while playing.

Changing them: File › Project settings › Input

  1. The table lists every action: its name, whether it's a Button or an Axis, its keyboard and mouse inputs as keys, and its gamepad's. All devices, Keyboard & mouse and Gamepad over the table show one kind or both; Find action or key narrows the rows.
  2. Click an action's row to pick it: its card at the right lists its bindings, each with the device it's on. Click a binding to pick it, then Backspace clears it; its × does the same.
  3. + Add binding (on an axis: + Up, + Down, + Left, + Right), then press the key, mouse button or gamepad button to bind. Esc calls it off; while it waits, Backspace is a key you can bind like any other. Hold Ctrl, Alt or Shift while pressing a key to bind the combination, such as Alt+Left; turn the mouse wheel to bind a notch up or down.
  4. An axis (like Move) has Up, Down, Left and Right keys, and whole-axis inputs (a stick, the mouse's movement, or the mouse wheel), ticked under Whole axis. One that goes with the mouse or the wheel has a Mouse speed and a Stick and key speed. Button and Axis at the top of the card change which it is; Remove the action takes it away.
  5. Add action ▾: type a name and choose Add button or Add axis (letters, digits and _, starting with a capital: OpenMap, Fire_2, so game code can name it Action.OpenMap).
  6. Add the ready-made actions it's missing appears in projects made before the cameras: it adds the ones it lacks (Pan, Turn, Zoom and Drag; MenuMove, MenuChoose, MenuBack and Pause) and changes nothing else. Restore the ready-made actions puts all the ready-made ones back as they were, leaving your own.

Clashes. The ready-made actions share some keys on purpose: the arrows are Move, Pan and MenuMove, and Space is Jump and MenuChoose. When an action of your own shares a key with another, both are marked with ⚠ and the key in amber, and a line under the table says which: both fire on one press. Contexts, Fires on, Buffer, the stick's dead zone and Invert look Y are unfinished parts.

Combinations. A key on its own doesn't count while you hold modifiers that some action binds with it. With Turn on Alt+Left and Pan on Left, holding Alt and pressing the left arrow turns, and doesn't pan as well. The up arrow (with no Alt+Up bound) still pans while Alt is held.

Changes are saved straight away, and a game that's playing takes them at once (any rebinding game code did in this play gives way to them). A speed you drag shows its number as you go and counts when you let go of the mouse, and a typed one when you press Enter or click somewhere else: the change is saved, and reaches a playing game, then. They're kept in the project's input.solinput, a small text file beside project.solis that Git can merge.

In game code, the actions are names Lust checks: Solis writes them into solis/project.lst as state Action whenever you change them here, so Action.Jmp is a mistake before the game runs, listing the real actions. Fetch Input and Action, and ask Input. In Lua the action's name is text (solis.Input:held("Jump")), and in Rust the host gives an action's whole state at once (cx.host().action("Jump"), with held, pressed, released and axis):

fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component Walker {
    has {
        float speed = 4;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        vec3 way = Input:axis(Action.Move);
        vec3 step = [way.x, way.y, 0];
        moveTo(position() + step * speed * dt);
        is Input:pressed(Action.Jump)? then {
            moveTo(position() + [0, 0, 1]);
        }
    }
}

pass Walker;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Walker {
    speed: f32,
}

impl RustComponent for Walker {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let way = cx.host().action("Move").axis;
        let step = Vec3::new(way.x, way.y, 0.0);
        let here = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        cx.host().move_to(me, here + step * self.speed * dt as f32);
        if cx.host().action("Jump").pressed {
            cx.host().move_to(me, here + Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Walker = component("Walker", {
    { "speed", "float", 4 },
})

function Walker:update(dt)
    local way = solis.Input:axis("Move")
    local step = vec3(way.x, way.y, 0)
    solis.entity.moveTo(self.me, solis.entity.position(self.me) + step * self.speed * dt)
    if solis.Input:pressed("Jump") then
        solis.entity.moveTo(self.me, solis.entity.position(self.me) + vec3(0, 0, 1))
    end
end
MethodWhat it gives
bool Input:held(Action action)Whether it's held down this tick (an axis: not at rest).
bool Input:pressed(Action action)True once, the tick it went down. A tap between two ticks still counts.
bool Input:released(Action action)True once, the tick it came up.
vec3 Input:axis(Action action)An axis's two numbers as x and y (z is 0).
string Input:binding(Action action)The key that sets it off, such as F, for showing "Press F" to the player.
Input:rebind(Action action, string input)Binds a new input ("E", "Mouse Right", "Pad Y") in place of its others of the same kind, from the next tick: what a controls menu does. Lasts while the game plays.

Input is read once per tick, so every component, on every core, sees the same input for that tick.

Recording and playing back (the Play menu)

  1. With a project open, choose Debug › Play and record inputs. Play as usual.
  2. Press Stop. The recording is saved in the project's recordings folder (the Console says its name).
  3. Choose Debug › Replay a recording… and pick it. (While it replays, the game's Saves:saveTo makes its save as the recorded play did, but doesn't write over your saves.) Solis plays from the start with the same seed and every tick's recorded input, checking the game is exactly the same tick by tick (checksums). At the end it pauses and says whether it matched, or by which tick it stopped matching (the world is compared every tick, game code's own values once a second).

A replay that stops matching means the game came out differently from the same input: the area or code changed since recording, or something in the game isn't deterministic. That's how you find it the tick it starts.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Mouse speedFor an axis that goes with the mouse: how far a pixel of movement (or a notch of the wheel) goes. For Look, 0.15 degrees suits most mice; raise it for a faster turn. For Zoom it's 1: a notch is one step.
Stick and key speedHow far a stick or key held all the way goes in a second. For Look, 180 is half a turn a second; for Zoom, 8 steps.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Give the game the mouse and keysClick the Game panel while playing
Give them back to the editorEsc
Give up binding an input (after + Add binding)Esc
Clear the picked bindingBackspace
Pick an actionClick its row

While the game has them, every key is the game's: the editor's shortcuts are off.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: my character doesn't move when I press W. Why: the editor has the keys. Fix: click the Game panel first; its corner says when the game has the mouse and keys.
  • Problem: pressing W while playing picked the move tool. Why: the same: the game didn't have the keys. Fix: click the Game panel.
  • Problem: Input:pressed(Action.Jump) is never true. Why: the action has no inputs. Fix: check File › Project settings › Input.
  • Problem: the Console says an input action "can't be named in game code". Why: game code names actions as Lust names, which start with a capital and hold letters, digits and _ (OpenMap, Fire_2), and aren't all capitals. Fix: rename it in File › Project settings › Input.
  • Problem: Esc does nothing in my game. Why: in the editor, Esc gives the mouse and keys back, so a game can't use it there. Fix: give the action another key as well, to try it in the editor (the ready-made Pause is on P). In an exported game every key is the game's, Esc included.
  • Problem: the Console says the input actions couldn't be read. Why: input.solinput was changed by hand and has a mistake. Fix: the Console says what; fix it, or change any action in the window, which writes it again.
  • Problem: the Console says the input actions file had a mistake and was kept as input.solinput.bak. Why: the file couldn't be read, so the ready-made actions were used; changing anything in the window writes the file again, so Solis kept yours first. Fix: copy what you need from the .bak file, then delete it.
  • Problem: recording paused, saying it reached the most Solis keeps. Why: a recording is at most an hour, or 64 MB. Fix: Stop saves what was recorded; record shorter plays.
  • Problem: a replay stops matching at once. Why: the area or the code changed since it was recorded, or it was recorded with an earlier Solis, whose checks were worked out differently. Fix: record again.

Related#

  • Game code
  • Play mode
  • Physics
  • Characters and cameras
  • Concepts: action, binding, recording
← Previous · Chapter 33PhysicsNext → · Chapter 35Game screens: a HUD and menus in Lust

Game screens: a HUD and menus in Lust#

A screen (the HUD, a pause menu, a shop) is a Lust file that says what's on it, drawn over the game while it plays and reading the game's values as it goes.

When to use it#

Use a screen for anything the player reads on top of the game: the day and time, money, an energy or health bar, an ammo count. A screen only shows the game; it can't change it, so it can never make the game play differently on another computer or in a replay.

A screen can also have buttons (a pause menu's Resume, a shop's Buy). A button doesn't change the game either: it sends an event, and game code decides what happens, in the next tick. That keeps a menu as fair as the keys: what was clicked is kept in a recording like a key press, and plays back the same.

A menu can be used with the keys or a controller too: the arrow keys (or the d-pad) move a ring between its buttons, and Enter (or A) chooses.

This page writes screens by hand in Lust. The UI editor draws them on a canvas instead, and edits the same files, so you can go back and forth.

How to use it#

  1. Make the file. In the Library, make a folder called ui inside your assets, and a Lust file in it named after the screen: ui/hud.lst is the screen Hud. Its name starts with a letter and holds only letters and numbers.

  2. Write the screen. The file holds an assembly with the screen's name and a view, and passes it. The view uses Lust's own pieces (the same ones as Lust's windows):

    fetch "main":Clock;

assembly Hud {
    has {
        int coins = 3;
    }

    view [width 1920, height 1080] {
        stack [width fill, height fill, bottom, left, pad 48] {
            column [gap 8] {
                text "Day " + Clock.day.text() + ", " + Clock.hour.text() + ":00" [size 32, bold, white];
                progress Clock.energy [to 100, width 300, height 20, green];
            }
        }
    }
}

pass Hud;
end
    // A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Hud", true);
    -- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Hud")
    • [width 1920, height 1080] is the size you design at. On other screens everything grows or shrinks with the screen's height, and a wider screen (ultrawide) gets more room at the sides.
    • To pin something to a corner, put it in a stack as big as the screen (width fill, height fill) and say where: bottom, top, left, right, center, middle, with pad for the distance from the edge.

  3. Show it. Add a Screen component to an entity (the player, or a "Game" entity), and pick Hud in its Screen field. Shown turns it on and off; Order decides which of several screens is on top.

  4. Press Play. The screen is drawn over the Game panel, and changes with the game: after every tick it reads the game's values again.

What a screen can read:

  • the game's game-wide objects (Clock.hour, Money.amount);

  • its own fields (coins above): the screen's memory;

  • the entity it's shown for (the one whose Screen component shows it): Ui:entity(), and a copy of any of that entity's Lust components, with a reading method named after the component: Ui:entity():health() gives its Health. Fetch Ui from solis/screen and the component from its file:

    fetch "solis/screen":Ui;
fetch "main":Health;

assembly DroneHealth {
    view {
        Health health = Ui:entity():health();
        text "Drone " + health.hp.text() + " / 20" [size 26, bold, white];
        progress health.hp [to 20, width 360, height 18, red5];
    }
}

pass DroneHealth;
end
    // A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "DroneHealth", true);
    -- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "DroneHealth")

    The copy is the component as the last tick left it: its methods work (health:fraction()), and changing it changes nothing in the game. The turret sample (Make the sample game… (press Space and type it, or use File › Learn)) has this health bar over its drone.

    Lua and Rust components, and Solis's own (Transform, Sprite, Camera, AudioSource and the rest) are read the same way. Solis describes each one to screens as a Lust component of its fields, so fetch it from solis/screen instead of from a file of yours:

    fetch "solis/screen":[Ui, Transform, Sparks];

assembly Where {
    view {
        Transform t = Ui:entity():transform();
        Sparks s = Ui:entity():sparks();
        text "x " + t.position.x.text() + ", sparks " + s.shown.text() [white];
    }
}

pass Where;
end
    // A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Where", true);
    -- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Where")

    Their fields are copies, as Lust components' are; they have no methods. A field Lust can't hold (a model or other asset, or one named like one of Lust's own words) is left out.

Buttons. A button has its words and, in { }, what a click does: usually send an event to the entity the screen is shown for. Declare the event in game code, fetch it in the screen, and handle it in a component on that entity:

-- ui/pauseMenu.lst
fetch "solis/screen":Ui;
fetch "main":[Resumed, Quit];

assembly PauseMenu {
    view {
        stack [width fill, height fill, center, middle] {
            column [gap 12, background gray9, pad 32, round 12] {
                text "Paused" [size 40, bold, white];
                button "Resume" [width 240, blue] { send Resumed() to Ui:entity(); }
                button "Quit" [width 240, hover:[background red7]] { send Quit() to Ui:entity(); }
            }
        }
    }
}

pass PauseMenu;
end
// A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "PauseMenu", true);
-- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
-- main.lst
fetch "solis/project":Screen;

event Resumed();
event Quit();

component Pauser {
    on Resumed() {
        hideScreen(Screen.PauseMenu);
    }
}

pass Pauser, Resumed, Quit;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

// The events are declared in Lust (main.lst), where the screen fetches
// them from.
pub struct Pauser;

impl RustComponent for Pauser {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Resumed" {
            return false;
        }
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.host().show_screen(me, "PauseMenu", false);
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The events are declared in Lust (main.lst), where the screen fetches
-- them from.
local Pauser = component("Pauser", {})

function Pauser:on_Resumed()
    solis.entity.hideScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
end
  • A button is drawn light grey with rounded corners; a colour word (blue, green, red5) colours it, and its words turn white or dark to stay readable. disabled greys it out and stops clicks.
  • Under the pointer it darkens a little, or takes the styles in its hover:[…].
  • The { } may also change the screen's own fields (a tab picked, say). It can't change the game: send an event for that.
  • What a button sends reaches the game at the start of the next tick, before the components' updates.

Showing and hiding screens from game code. Every entity can show one screen at a time. Its calls take the screen by name, from solis/project.lst (fetch Screen from "solis/project"):

CallWhat it does
showScreen(Screen.PauseMenu)Shows that screen on the entity's Screen component, at the end of the tick. An entity without one is given one.
hideScreen(Screen.PauseMenu)Hides it, at the end of the tick, if the entity shows that screen.
screenShown(Screen.PauseMenu)Whether the entity shows that screen, as the tick started.

In Lua they're solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu"), solis.entity.hideScreen(…) and solis.entity.screenShown(…) (the screen's name as text), and a button's event arrives in on_Resumed. In Rust, through the component's host: cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "PauseMenu", true) (false hides it) and cx.host().screen_shown(cx.me(), "PauseMenu").

Use another entity (a "Menus" entity) for a second screen shown at the same time. Which screens are open is part of the game: it's in save games and recordings.

The mouse while a screen has buttons. While a screen with buttons is shown, the pointer stays visible over the Game panel, even after you click the game to give it the keys, so you can click the buttons. A click on a button goes to the button, not to the game; a click anywhere else gives the game the mouse and keys as usual. When the last screen with buttons goes, the pointer is held by the game again.

With the keys or a controller. Once the game has the keys, MenuMove (the arrow keys, the d-pad or the left stick) moves the focus to the nearest button that way, shown with a blue ring; held down, it moves on again every tenth of a second. MenuChoose (Enter, Space or A) chooses the button with the focus, just as a click would. A menu's first button has the focus to start with, so Down moves to the second. The focus is on the topmost screen with buttons, and moving the mouse over a button moves the focus there (the ring hides until the keys are used again).

While a screen with buttons is shown, the game's own actions wait: only MenuMove, MenuChoose, MenuBack (Backspace, B) and Pause (P, Start) reach game code, so Space choosing a button doesn't also jump. Use MenuBack and Pause in game code to close a menu or open the pause menu: is Input:pressed(Action.Pause)? then { showScreen(Screen.PauseMenu); }. They're ordinary input actions, rebindable in File › Project settings › Input.

A pause menu. World:setGameSpeed(0) stops the game while game code keeps running: game time, physics, projectiles and sprites stand still and every dt is 0, but components' updates, events and the screens go on, so a menu can be used. World:setGameSpeed(1) carries on (anything between 0 and 4 runs slower or faster). The Game panel's corner says Game speed 0 meanwhile, and the speed is kept in save games. The turret sample has one: press P (or Start) while it plays.

fetch "solis/world":World;
fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":[Action, Screen];

event Resumed();

component Pauser {
    method update(float dt) {
        is Input:pressed(Action.Pause)? then {
            showScreen(Screen.PauseMenu);
            World:setGameSpeed(0);
        }
    }

    on Resumed() {
        hideScreen(Screen.PauseMenu);
        World:setGameSpeed(1);
    }
}

pass Pauser, Resumed;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Pauser;

impl RustComponent for Pauser {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        if cx.host().action("Pause").pressed {
            let me = cx.me();
            cx.host().show_screen(me, "PauseMenu", true);
            cx.host().set_game_speed(0.0);
        }
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Resumed" {
            return false;
        }
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.host().show_screen(me, "PauseMenu", false);
        cx.host().set_game_speed(1.0);
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Pauser = component("Pauser", {})

function Pauser:update(dt)
    if solis.Input:pressed("Pause") then
        solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
        solis.World:setGameSpeed(0)
    end
end

function Pauser:on_Resumed()
    solis.entity.hideScreen(self.me, "PauseMenu")
    solis.World:setGameSpeed(1)
end

Text size and UI size for players. Some players need bigger text, and a game played from a sofa needs a bigger HUD. Two player settings grow every screen: text size (Screens:setTextSize(1.5): every text half as big again, from 0.5 to 3; the columns and rows round it make room, and long lines wrap) and UI size (Screens:setUiSize(1.25): the whole screen bigger, from 0.5 to 2). A pause menu usually offers them. They're the player's, not the game's: they're not in save games or recordings, a loaded game keeps the player's, and they're kept from one play to the next. So only let them change what's shown and offered, never the game itself (how hard it is, say): a recording played back with other settings would go differently. Screens read them too (text "Text " + Screens:textSize().text();), but only game code changes them, so a menu's button sends an event and the entity's code does it:

fetch "solis/screens":Screens;
fetch "solis/window":Window;

event BiggerText();
event Fullscreen();
event NextResolution();

component Pauser {
    on BiggerText() {
        float size = Screens:textSize() + 0.25;
        is size > 2? then {
            size = 1;
        }
        Screens:setTextSize(size);
    }
    on Fullscreen() {
        Window:setFullscreen(not Window:fullscreen());
    }
    on NextResolution() {
        Window:useNextResolution();
    }
}

pass Pauser, BiggerText, Fullscreen, NextResolution;
end
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Pauser;

impl RustComponent for Pauser {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        match event.name.as_str() {
            "BiggerText" => {
                let mut size = cx.host().text_size() + 0.25;
                if size > 2.0 {
                    size = 1.0;
                }
                cx.host().set_text_size(size);
            }
            "Fullscreen" => {
                let on = cx.host().fullscreen();
                cx.host().set_fullscreen(!on);
            }
            "NextResolution" => cx.host().use_next_resolution(),
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Pauser = component("Pauser", {})

function Pauser:on_BiggerText()
    local size = solis.Screens:textSize() + 0.25
    if size > 2 then
        size = 1
    end
    solis.Screens:setTextSize(size)
end

function Pauser:on_Fullscreen()
    solis.Window:setFullscreen(not solis.Window:fullscreen())
end

function Pauser:on_NextResolution()
    solis.Window:useNextResolution()
end

The window. Window:setFullscreen(true) fills the screen, and Window:setResolution(1920, 1080) (or Window:useNextResolution(), for a menu's Resolution button) sizes the window; Window:fullscreen() and Window:resolution() read them. Alt+Enter switches fullscreen in any game, as players expect. Window:quit() closes the game, for a menu's Quit button. While you play in the editor, the game stays in the Game panel: the Console says what the exported game would do, the settings are kept so the menu shows them, and Quit stops play. In an exported game they're real: the window changes, the game closes, and the settings are kept in the player's own folder.

A screen's look. On the Screen component, Glow puts a soft light round everything on the screen, in each piece's own colour; Outline puts a line just outside everything, in Outline colour; and Pixel size draws the whole screen in blocks that many pixels big, for a pixel-art look that matches a 2D game's. They're on the component, not in the file, so the same screen can glow on one entity and not on another. For a single piece, Lust's own shadow (box [shadow, red]) draws a soft glow in its colour.

Drawing it instead of writing it. Double-click a screen's file in the Library to open it on the UI editor's canvas: pick pieces, drag them, size them and change their look, and Solis writes the Lust for you, changing only what it must.

Pictures. image shows a picture from your assets, named by its place inside them: image "sprites/coin.png";. To show one part of a sprite sheet, cut it out with Atlas Crop and add # and the crop's name: image "sprites/tools.png#Axe";. A crop is better than a picture of its own for icons: the artist keeps drawing on one sheet, and every crop follows.

assembly Hotbar {
    view {
        stack [width fill, height fill, bottom, center, pad 24] {
            row [gap 8, background gray9, pad 8, round 8] {
                image "sprites/tools.png#Axe" [width 64];
                image "sprites/tools.png#Hoe" [width 64];
                image "sprites/tools.png#Can" [width 64, opacity 0.4];
            }
        }
    }
}

pass Hotbar;
end
// A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
// files in ui/ are Lust only. A Rust component shows and hides it
// through its host:
//
//     cx.host().show_screen(cx.me(), "Hotbar", true);
-- A screen is written in Lust, whatever language the game is in: the
-- files in ui/ are Lust only. A Lua component shows and hides it:
--
--     solis.entity.showScreen(self.me, "Hotbar")
  • A picture is as big as it is unless you give it a width or a height; give one and the other follows, keeping its shape. Give both and it fits inside that box, in the middle; add cover to fill the box instead, cutting off what reaches past it.
  • round rounds its corners, and opacity fades it.
  • Shown bigger than it is, a picture's pixels stay sharp squares, as pixel art wants; shown smaller, it's smoothed so it doesn't flicker.
  • The name can be worked out as the game runs (image item.icon;): that picture is read the first time it's shown.
  • A name written out in the screen's code that names no picture, or no crop of it, is listed in Problems with its line before you press Play. A missing picture shows as a grey box with its name.

What a screen can use: column, row, stack, space, text, button, image, progress bars, and canvas with box, circle and line placed by x and y (anything reaching past the canvas's edges is cut off there, so a needle or a bar can't spill out of its dial). Styles: pad (and padX, padTop…), gap, width and height (a number, or fill), grow, size, bold, the alignment words, colour words (white, red5, gray9, #ff8800), background, round, border, opacity and, for pictures, cover. Other pieces are laid out but not drawn yet.

Settings#

The Screen component:

SettingWhat it does
ScreenWhich screen: a file in assets/ui, by its name (ui/hud.lst is Hud).
ShownWhether it's on screen. Game code shows and hides screens with showScreen and hideScreen.
OrderWhich screen is on top when several are shown: higher is on top.
GlowA soft light round everything on the screen, in each piece's own colour, this many pixels out (on its design size). 0 for none.
OutlineA line just outside everything on the screen, this thick. 0 for none.
Outline colourThe outline's colour.
Pixel sizeDraws the whole screen in blocks this many pixels big (1 is smooth).

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Problems says "each file in ui/ passes the assembly named after it". Why: Solis finds a screen by its file's name. Fix: the file ui/hud.lst holds assembly Hud { … } and ends with pass Hud;.
  • Problem: the Console says "The screen Hud stopped: … can't be changed here". Why: a screen only reads the game; it tried to change one of the game's objects. Fix: change the game in game code, and let the screen show the result. A screen may change its own fields.
  • Problem: the screen stopped, and the Game panel still shows the last picture. Why: something in its view failed (the Console names the file and line), so its last good picture stays. Fix: fix the line; the screen runs again when the code is saved.
  • Problem: the Console says the screen's view "holds too much text" or "has too many styles". Why: after a view runs, Solis copies its pieces out of your code, and one view may hold 10,000 pieces, 200 thousand styles and 4 MB of text in all (a piece's words, or one style's such as a tip, are cut at 16 KB), so that no screen can slow the game to a crawl or fill the memory. Pieces past the 10,000th are left out; past the other two the view isn't shown, and its last picture stays. Fix: show less at once: a page of a long list rather than all of it, and shorter texts.
  • Problem: the Console says "this entity has no Health, so health() has nothing to give". Why: the entity whose Screen shows the screen has no such component. Fix: put the Screen component on the entity that has it, or add the component.
  • Problem: the Console says "Screens can't read the component Position: entities already have a position()". Why: a reading method is named after its component, and this name is an engine call on entities already. Fix: give the component another name.
  • Problem: game code says there's no file solis/screen.lst. Why: only screens can fetch it: game code reads other entities through its own calls. Fix: fetch it only in files in the ui folder.
  • Problem: clicking a button does nothing in the game. Why: the event goes to the entity the screen is shown for (Ui:entity()), and only its components' on blocks hear it. Fix: put the component that handles it on the entity with the Screen, and check the event's name and values match its on line.
  • Problem: Screen.PauseMenu is "not an option". Why: a screen's name comes from its file, first letter made a capital: ui/pauseMenu.lst is PauseMenu. Names in all capitals (HUD) can't be Lust names. Fix: rename the file, or use the name the Problems panel suggests.
  • Problem: the Console says a screen "sent events the game couldn't take". Why: at most 64 events wait for each tick, and an event from a screen carries plain values (no assets, texts of at most 4,096 letters). Fix: send fewer, smaller events.
  • Problem: Problems says "there's no picture sprites/x.png in the project". Why: image names a picture by its place inside your assets, with / between folders and its ending (.png). Fix: check the path in the Library: right-click the picture to see where it is.
  • Problem: Problems says a picture "has no crop called Axe". Why: the part after # is the name of a crop made in Atlas Crop, and capitals don't matter but spelling does. Fix: open the picture's Atlas Crop tab and name a crop that, or use one of the names Problems lists.
  • Problem: a picture "can't be shown on a screen: there's no room left". Why: all the screens' pictures share one sheet of 2048 × 2048 pixels on the graphics card. Fix: use smaller pictures, or crops of one sprite sheet instead of whole big pictures.
  • Problem: the Console says "a screen can't change the player's settings". Why: screens only read the game, settings included. Fix: have the button send an event, and call Screens:setTextSize in the entity's code.
  • Problem: with a big text size, words reach past a box. Why: a piece with a set width or height stays that size, so its text has no room to grow. Fix: leave the size out (it then fits what's in it), or use minWidth; check on the canvas with Text 150% and 200%.
  • Problem: text is dark and hard to read over the game. Why: like Lust's windows, text is dark unless told otherwise. Fix: give it a colour word: white.

Related#

  • Game code: game-wide objects, which screens read.
  • Play mode: the Game panel, where screens are drawn, and recordings.
  • The UI sample: a HUD and a pause menu with the player's settings, start to finish.
  • Concepts: game UI, screen.
← Previous · Chapter 34InputNext → · Chapter 36The UI editor: drawing a screen on the canvas

The UI editor: drawing a screen on the canvas#

Opens a screen on a canvas, so you can pick its pieces, move them, size them and change how they look, while Solis rewrites its Lust file for you.

When to use it#

A screen (a HUD, a pause menu) is a Lust file in your project's ui/ folder. You can always write it by hand, but placing and styling pieces is quicker when you can see them: drag a button above another, stretch a panel, try another colour, and see each change at once.

The canvas never takes your file away from you. It changes only the letters it has to (the gap 14 becomes gap 20, and nothing else moves), so comments, spacing and code you wrote by hand stay exactly as they were. You can keep the file open in a code editor beside Solis: a change saved there shows on the canvas within a second.

How to use it#

  1. In the Library, open the ui folder and double-click a screen's file (pauseMenu). Solis switches to the UI tab and draws the screen on the Canvas.
  2. Pick a piece: click it on the canvas, or its row in Elements, on the shelf under the canvas. Shift-click (Ctrl-click in Elements) picks more; drag a box round pieces on an empty part of the canvas to pick everything inside it.
  3. Change it in Properties, beside Elements on the shelf's Screen tab: its words, its width and height, how what's inside it lines up, its padding, colour, corners and opacity. Every change is saved straight away, and Ctrl+Z over the canvas undoes it.
  4. Move it: drag it on the canvas to another place among its neighbours, or into another column or row; a blue line shows where it will land. A piece inside a canvas goes exactly where you drag it instead: an outline follows the pointer, and the piece is moved there when you let go (one Ctrl+Z puts it back). In Elements, drag its row above or below another row, or onto the middle of a column's row to put it inside.
  5. Size it: pick one piece and drag the small square on its right edge, bottom edge or corner.
  6. Check the screen on other screen sizes with the size list in the UI tab's ribbon (Full HD, 4K, ultrawide, a phone), and with players' bigger text with its Text list (150% and 200%). The dashed line is the safe area: keep text and buttons inside it, since some TVs cut the edges off.
  7. Open as code (the ribbon's Code group) opens the file in your code editor, for anything the canvas doesn't edit.
  8. Close the screen: the × on the Canvas tab closes it. Nothing is lost: every change was saved as you made it. Double-click the file in the Library to open it again.

Drawing new pieces#

The toolbox down the canvas's left edge holds the tools, as the viewport's toolbox does on Home: Select (picking and moving, as above), Box, Ellipse, Line, Pen, Text, Image and Button. Keys 1 to 7 pick them while the pointer is over the canvas, and E opens them all in a ring at the pointer, so your hand never leaves the canvas. The hint along the canvas's foot names these keys.

  • Box, Ellipse, Line: drag where it goes. Inside a canvas piece the shape is placed where you drew it (its x and y); anywhere else it gets a small canvas of its own, just big enough, among the pieces where you started the drag. (Shapes only exist inside a canvas in Lust, so a lone box is a canvas holding one.)
  • Pen: click each corner, then press Enter or double-click to finish. Each corner-to-corner part becomes a line. Curves wait for Lust to have paths.
  • Text, Button: click where it goes. In a column or a row it goes between the pieces where you click (a blue line shows where), so the column stays tidy.
  • Image: choose the picture in the Pictures column of the Screen shelf tab first (a click there takes the Image tool too), then click.

The new piece is picked at once, so Properties is ready to change it. Esc goes back to Select (or, with the Pen, forgets the corners so far).

Tying a piece to the game#

A screen is only useful when it shows the game: the player's health, the coins. Under Tied to the game in Properties, Tie to… lists the components of the entity the screen is shown for (its own Lust components, and Solis's own such as Transform), and the fields that fit:

  • Words (text and buttons): shows the field as words, health.hp.text().
  • Value (progress bars and sliders): progress health.hp.
  • Fill across, Fill up (anything with a set width or height): a bar that's as wide as it is now when the field is at its most. Pick the field, then what it is out of: another field holding the most, or its starting value (health starts full): width 300 * health.hp / health.maxHp, or / 20.
  • Opacity: fades it with a number field.

Solis writes the Lust for you: it reads the component once at the top of the view (Health health = Ui:entity():health();) and fetches it from its file, then uses it. It's ordinary Lust, so you can change it as code later.

Preview values (top of the canvas) lets you try other numbers for what the screen reads, with a slider each: drag health down to see the bar empty. They're never saved; Back to the starting values forgets them.

What a button does#

A button's When clicked in Properties has a Sends list: the events your game's code declares (event Pause();). Pick one and the button sends it to the screen's entity (Solis fetches it at the top of the screen's file for you), whose code reacts with on Pause() { … }. This is the safe way for a screen to change the game: screens never change it themselves (why). A button whose { } does more than send one event shows its code instead.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
WordsThe text on a text or a button. Text worked out by code ("Score " + score.text()) shows as code and is changed in the file.
Width, Heightset a size in the screen's pixels (on a 1920 × 1080 design), fill the room it has, or auto: as big as what's in it.
AlignWhere what's inside it sits: a 3 × 3 grid, from top left to bottom right. On a column or a row this places its pieces; on text, the words.
PaddingRoom inside its edge, all round.
GapRoom between the pieces inside a column or a row.
X, YWhere a piece sits inside a canvas. Dragging it on the canvas changes these, by as many of the screen's pixels as you dragged it, whatever the zoom.
ColourA button's or shape's colour, text's colour, or a column's background, from Lust's colour words (blue, gray9, red5).
CornersHow round its corners are, in pixels.
Opacity1 is solid, 0 is invisible.
Text size, BoldFor text and buttons.
HoverA look while the pointer is over it. + Add a hover look dims it a little; edit it in All its settings.
DisabledGreyed, and clicks do nothing.
Tie to…Shows a field of one of the entity's components in this piece: its words, its value, how full it is, or its opacity.
SendsFor a button: the event sent to the screen's entity when it's clicked, from the game's events.
When clickedWhat a button does, as written in its { }, when it's more than one event: change it as code.
Preview valuesOther numbers to try on the canvas for what the screen reads. Never saved.
All its settingsEverything in the piece's [ ], as written. Type anything Lust has (nowrap, spread, minWidth 200); press Enter to keep it. If it doesn't read, it isn't changed.
Text 100% / 150% / 200%Previews the screen with players' bigger text (Screens:setTextSize), to check nothing spills out.
Safe areaShows the guide 5% in from each edge.
SnapSizes snap to whole pixels and to other pieces' edges.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Select, Box, Ellipse, Line, Pen, Text, Image1 to 7 (pointer over the canvas)
All the tools in a ring at the pointerE
Back to Select (Pen: forget the corners)Esc
Finish the Pen's lineEnter or double-click
Pick more (canvas)Shift+click
Pick more (Elements)Shift+click or Ctrl+click
Delete what's pickedDelete (over the canvas or Elements), or Backspace (over the canvas)
Copy what's picked, just after itselfCtrl+D
Pick nothingEsc, or click an empty part of the canvas
Undo, redoCtrl+Z, Ctrl+Y (over the canvas or Elements)
ZoomMouse wheel
Move the viewMiddle mouse button drag
Fit the canvasDouble-click an empty part, or click the zoom button

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a piece has a yellow code badge and can't be picked. Why: code made it: a loop or an is …? then in the view. The canvas draws it from the screen's starting values, but its letters are code. Fix: Open as code and change it there.
  • Problem: the canvas says it "can't follow" the file. Why: the file has a mistake the canvas can't read past, such as a [ never closed. Fix: Problems says where; fix it as code, and the canvas follows again.
  • Problem: "Updating…" shows after a piece was moved, added or deleted. Why: the canvas waits for the game's code to be checked again, which takes a moment. Fix: nothing: it goes in about a second.
  • Problem: a bar or a number shows as empty. Why: the canvas draws the screen for an entity whose values are all their starting ones (health 0, say). Fix: try other numbers with Preview values, or press Play to see it with the game's real values in the Game panel.
  • Problem: Tie to… says to give the entity a component. Why: the game's code has no components a screen can read yet, or has a mistake. Fix: write a component (component Health { has { float hp = 20; } }), check Problems is empty, and try again.
  • Problem: Sends has nothing to pick. Why: the game's code declares no events yet, so there's nothing a button could send. Fix: declare one in your game code (event Pause();, and pass it), and check Problems is empty.
  • Problem: the canvas says The screen's view stopped: … in place of the screen. Why: the screen's own code stopped with an error as its view ran (the message says what and where), so there's nothing to draw. The canvas tries a screen once each time the game's code changes, not over and over. Fix: put the line right as code and save: the canvas draws the screen again by itself.
  • Problem: dragging a piece doesn't move it where expected. Why: in a column or a row, pieces go one after another: a piece moves between its neighbours, not to any spot. Fix: to place pieces freely, put them in a canvas and drag them there.

Related#

  • Game screens: what a screen's Lust file holds, and how the game shows it.
  • Atlas Crop: pictures cut from a sheet, for image pieces.
  • Concepts: screen, canvas, tie.

The UI sample: a HUD and a pause menu, start to finish#

A small game whose screens show everything game UI can do: a HUD that follows the game, a health bar, and a pause menu offering the player's settings, each drawn on the UI editor's canvas.

When to use it#

Open it when you're about to give your own game a HUD or a menu: it's the shortest working example of each part, and every file is meant to be read and changed. The turret sample is the place to start for game code itself; this one is about screens.

How to use it#

  1. Make the UI sample… (press Space and type it, or use File › Learn) (or UI sample among Recent projects' templates), and choose an empty folder. The project opens on its area.
  2. Press Play, then click the Game panel so the game has the keys.
    • Space (or a gamepad's A) fires the turret at the drone. The HUD in the bottom left counts the ammo and the hits, with a yellow bar that empties as you fire; the drone's health bar at the top follows its health.
    • P (or Start) pauses: the game stops and the pause menu shows. Move with the arrow keys or the stick, choose with Space, Enter or A, or click.
  3. Try the menu:
    • Text size makes every screen's text a quarter bigger each time (back to 100% after 200%). The menu's buttons grow to fit it (they're at least 360 wide, minWidth 360, rather than exactly).
    • Fullscreen and Resolution say in the Console what the exported game would do; in the editor the game stays in the Game panel.
    • Resume carries on, and Quit closes the game (Window:quit()): while you play in the editor, play stops; in an exported game, the game closes.
  4. Press Stop, open the Library's ui folder and double-click hud: it opens on the canvas. Pick a piece and change it in Properties, or try Preview values to see the ammo bar empty.

How its parts fit together:

FileWhat it does
main.lstThe game code: the Turret (fires on Jump, reloads), the drone's Health, and the Pauser, which opens the menu and changes the player's settings when the menu's buttons say so.
ui/hud.lstThe HUD, shown by the Turret's Screen component. It reads the turret's ammo and hits (Ui:entity():turret()); the bar is a box whose width is 300 * ammo / maxAmmo, and while the turret reloads it stays empty, with shadow for a glow. The Screen component's Glow gives the whole HUD a soft light.
ui/droneHealth.lstThe drone's health bar, shown by the Drone's Screen component, reading its Health.
ui/pauseMenu.lstThe menu. It reads the settings (Screens:textSize(), Window:fullscreen(), Window:resolution()) to show them, and each button sends an event to the Game entity (send BiggerText() to Ui:entity();), since screens never change the game themselves.
ui.solareaThe area: the camera, the turret, the drone and the Game entity with the Pauser.

Why the buttons send events instead of changing the settings themselves: a screen only reads the game. That keeps every change in game code, where recordings and replays see it, so the sample plays back the same from a recording, menu and all.

Settings#

The sample has no settings of its own. The Screen components on the Turret and the Drone have the screen's look (Game screens): try Pixel size 4 on the Turret's for a pixel-art HUD.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
FireSpace, or the gamepad's A
Pause, and backP or Start (Backspace or B too)
Move in the menu, chooseArrow keys or the stick; Space, Enter or A
Switch fullscreenAlt+Enter

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pressing Space does nothing. Why: the editor still has the keys. Fix: click the Game panel first; Esc gives the keys back.
  • Problem: Fullscreen doesn't fill the screen. Why: while playing in the editor, the game stays in the Game panel. Fix: it's the exported game that changes its window; the Console says what it would do.
  • Problem: after a big text size, the HUD's words reach past its panel. Why: a piece given a fixed width keeps it. Fix: leave sizes out where text grows, and check with Text 150% and 200% on the canvas.

Related#

  • Game screens: what a screen's file holds, the player's settings, and screens' looks.
  • The UI editor: drawing and changing screens on the canvas.
  • Your first game: the turret sample, for game code in all three languages.
  • Concepts: screen, tie, player setting, focus.

2D: the pixel-perfect view#

Make a 2D game whose pixel art stays crisp: the game is drawn small, at its own resolution, and scaled up to the screen in whole steps, and the editor's 2D view shows the world in pixels.

When to use it#

For a 2D game, especially one in pixel art: a farming game, a platformer, a top-down adventure. Pixel art is drawn one pixel at a time, and it only looks right when every one of its pixels becomes the same number of screen pixels. Draw it straight at the screen's size and pixels end up different widths, edges blur when the camera moves by less than a pixel, and sprites shimmer as you walk. Solis avoids all three by drawing the game small, at its base resolution, then scaling the finished picture up.

2D in Solis lives in the same world as 3D: flat things lie on the ground, seen from straight above, so lights, the sun, sound, saving and game code all work on them as they do in 3D. A project can mix both, with a 3D camera in one area and a 2D camera in another.

This page covers the groundwork: setting a project up for 2D, looking at it in pixels and playing it through a 2D camera. What you put in that world has pages of its own: sprites from Aseprite, animating them, tile maps for the ground, and walls and walking.

How to use it#

  1. Set the project's 2D settings: File › Project settings › 2D. The standard ones suit most pixel-art games: 480 × 270, 16 pixels to a metre and 16-pixel tiles. They're saved in the project (pixels.solpix), so everyone working on it shares them.
  2. Look in pixels: in the viewport, the Perspective ▾ pill at the top left, then 2D. The view looks straight down at the ground. The grid is the tile size, and the corner shows the zoom. Beside the pointer, a small readout says where it is in the game's pixels (x 192 · y 64 px, with y counting down the picture as in pixel-art programs) and, with a tile map selected, the cell under it (cell 12, 4), so you can place things exactly without counting grid lines.
    • Hold the right or middle button and drag to slide the view.
    • Turn the wheel to zoom in or out one whole step at a time (100%, 200%, 300%…), towards the pointer. At whole steps every pixel of your game is the same size on screen, so nothing blurs.
  3. Add a 2D camera: with the 2D view in use, Home › Camera. It goes over the middle of the view, on a whole pixel, as a 2D camera. A dashed frame shows what it sees, labelled Game screen for the camera the game looks through (the first camera in the area). To turn an existing camera into one, set its View to 2D in Properties.
  4. Move things on whole pixels: in the 2D view, moves land on whole pixels of your game by themselves, so nothing rests between two pixels and looks smeared. Snap ▾ in the bottom-right corner changes that to whole tiles, or off. Hold Ctrl while dragging to flip it for one move.
  5. Press Play. The Game panel draws the game at its base resolution and scales it up to fill the panel in whole steps, with black bars round the edge if the panel doesn't divide evenly. Move the 2D camera (game code moves it like any entity) and the picture slides smoothly, without shimmering.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Base resolutionThe size the game is drawn at, in pixels, before it's scaled up. 480 × 270 scales to a 1080p screen four times and to 4K eight times exactly; 320 × 180 gives chunkier pixels and shows less of the world; 640 × 360 shows more. The menu offers common sizes, or type your own.
Pixels per unitHow many pixels make one metre of the world. Usually the same as the tile size, so a tile is one metre: physics, sound distances and game code then all count in tiles.
Tile sizeThe 2D view's grid, in pixels, and the size of each cell of a tile map.
Scaling to the screenWhole steps (the standard): every pixel becomes the same whole number of screen pixels, with bars at the edges when the screen doesn't divide evenly: always crisp. Fill the screen: no bars; it scales up as far as whole steps go, then smooths only the last bit at each pixel's edge, so edges stay sharp.
Camera > ViewPerspective (as the eye sees) or 2D (flat, straight down, at the base resolution). A 2D camera follows its entity's place but never turns.
2D view > SnapWhat moves land on: whole pixels, tiles or off.
2D view > ZoomScreen pixels for each pixel of the game, from 25% (to see a big map) to 2400%.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Slide the 2D viewHold right or middle mouse, drag
Zoom the 2D view a stepMouse wheel
Flip snapping for one moveHold Ctrl while dragging

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: black bars round the game. Why: the panel or screen isn't a whole number of times the base resolution, and Whole steps keeps every pixel the same size. Fix: that's expected; choose Fill the screen if you'd rather have no bars, or a base resolution that divides your screen (480 × 270 for 1080p and 4K).
  • Problem: the Game panel looks blurry or the pixels are uneven. Why: the area's first camera is a 3D one. Fix: set its View to 2D, or move the 2D camera first in the Area panel.
  • Problem: something isn't in the game's picture though it's under the camera. Why: a 2D camera sees what's below it, between its Near and Far. Fix: keep the camera above everything (Add camera puts it 100 m up), or raise its Far.
  • The 2D view's frame and the Game panel show the same thing, so you can line up a scene in the editor and know what the player will see.

Related#

  • Settings: Preferences, and Project settings with its 2D tab.
  • Moving around the viewport: the other views.
  • Play mode: cameras and the Game panel.
  • Concepts: base resolution, pixels per unit, pixel-perfect, whole steps.
← Previous · Chapter 37The UI sample: a HUD and a pause menu, start to finishNext → · Chapter 39Sprites from Aseprite

Sprites from Aseprite#

Draw your pixel art in Aseprite, save it into the project, and place it in the world as sprites: Solis reads the file as it is, packs its frames, and shows every save at once.

When to use it#

For the characters, crops, trees, furniture and anything else in a 2D game that's a picture rather than a tile of the ground. A sprite is one frame of a sprite sheet, lying flat on the ground at its entity, standing on its pivot.

Solis reads Aseprite's own .aseprite files: there's nothing to export. Its tags (runs of frames such as walk or swing) and slices (named rectangles such as feet) come with it, so the picture and how it's used stay in one file. Keep the files in the project's assets folder, as you'd keep models and sounds.

Plain pictures work too. A .png or .jpg in the project can be a sprite as it is: drag it from the Library into the viewport, or pick it in a Sprite's Sheet (it's listed as name (picture)). It's a sheet of one frame, the whole picture, standing on its bottom middle. That's handy for a background, a hill or a sign drawn in any paint program; for frames, tags and a feet slice, use Aseprite. A picture is read only once a sprite uses it (so the textures of 3D models aren't read twice), and up to 4096 × 4096 pixels. Saving it again in your paint program updates it in Solis.

Sprites are drawn with the colours you painted, never tone mapped. Whether light falls on them is the area's choice: with Light sprites ticked on its Environment (new areas have it ticked), the day's colour and lamps light them (Sky, fog and exposure). With no lamps and day and night off, a sprite looks exactly as drawn.

For the ground itself, use tile maps. To make sprites move, see Animating sprites: a sprite plays its sheet's tags as clips.

How to use it#

  1. Save your Aseprite file into the project's assets, for example assets/sprites/farmer.aseprite. It appears in the Library with its first frame and how many frames it has. Saving it again in Aseprite updates it in Solis straight away.
  2. Look it over: click it in the Library. Properties shows the frame big, a strip of every frame (click one to see it), and what Solis read from the file: its size, layers, tags (with their direction and repeats), slices and palette. Anything it couldn't use is listed in yellow.
  3. Give it a pivot: in Aseprite, draw a slice called feet (or pivot) round where the character stands, and set the slice's pivot point on the ground between its feet. Without one, a sprite stands on the bottom middle of its frame.
  4. Place it: drag it from the Library into the viewport, double-click it, or right-click it and choose Place. It lands under the pointer (or in the middle of the view) on a whole pixel, standing on its feet or pivot slice, as drawn. The new entity is named after the file and has a Sprite component.
  5. Choose the frame and the rest in Properties: the Sprite component's Sheet offers every sprite sheet in the project, Pivot offers the sheet's slices, and Frame picks which frame it shows.
  6. Front and behind look after themselves: the lower on the screen a sprite stands, the nearer it's drawn, so a farmer walking down past a tree goes in front of it, and walking up goes behind it. Things a whole metre higher (a roof, a bird) are always on top.

Settings#

The Sprite component, in Properties:

SettingWhat it does
SheetThe sprite sheet (an Aseprite file in the project). Empty draws nothing.
Clip, Playing, Speed, Clip timeThe clip it plays, and how: see Animating sprites.
FrameWhich frame it shows when no clip plays, counting from 1 as Aseprite does. A frame past the end shows the first.
PivotThe slice it stands on, such as feet: the slice's pivot point (or its middle, if it has none) sits on the entity's place. Empty: the bottom middle of the frame.
Flip acrossMirrored left to right, round its pivot: one drawing faces both ways.
Flip upMirrored top to bottom.
TintMultiplied into its colours. White leaves it as drawn; a blue tint for night, red for a hurt enemy.
FlashHow white it flashes, 0 to 1. Turn it up for a moment when something's hit.
OutlineA one-pixel outline round it, to show what's selected or can be picked up.
Outline colourThe outline's colour.
See-throughFor glass, smoke, ghosts and shadows painted half see-through. Otherwise each pixel is drawn or not (half see-through pixels are treated as clear), which needs no sorting and is faster.

What Solis takes from the Aseprite file:

In AsepriteIn Solis
Frames and their durationsThe frames, and how long each shows in a clip.
TagsClips: a run of frames with its direction (forward, reverse, ping-pong) and repeats.
SlicesPivots (where a sprite stands), and later 9-slices, hitboxes and attach points.
User data on a celAn event on that frame, such as footstep: it plays the sound event of that name and tells game code (Animating sprites).
Visible layersFlattened into one picture, with each layer's and cel's opacity. Hidden layers and reference layers are left out. Blend modes other than Normal are drawn as Normal (Properties notes it).
PaletteListed in Properties.

Shortcuts#

Sprites add no keys or mouse actions of their own: placing them uses the Library's, and moving them uses the usual move tools.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a sprite looks slightly smeared, or Problems says it rests between pixels. Why: it was moved or typed in at a place that isn't a whole pixel (perhaps with snapping off, or by game code). The game draws it on the nearest pixel, so it may seem to jump a pixel as it moves. Fix: move it with snapping to pixels on (the 2D view's standard), or type a place that's a whole number of pixels (with 16 pixels a metre, a multiple of 0.0625).
  • Problem: the sprite floats above or sinks below where you put it. Why: it stands on its pivot, and the sheet has none, or the slice's pivot point isn't where the feet are. Fix: add a feet slice in Aseprite with its pivot between the feet, then pick it in Pivot.
  • Problem: Properties says the file couldn't be read. Why: it isn't an Aseprite file, it's damaged, or it's bigger than Solis takes (64 MB, 4096 × 4096 pixels, 2048 frames, 256 layers). Fix: save it again from Aseprite. While you're saving, a half-written file keeps the last good picture, so sprites never vanish.
  • Problem: a picture you dragged into the viewport didn't appear, and the Console says Couldn't place the picture as a sprite. Why: it's damaged, isn't really a PNG or JPEG, or is bigger than 4096 × 4096 pixels. Fix: save it again from your paint program, smaller if need be.
  • Problem: Properties says the frames don't fit in a 4096 × 4096 picture. Why: all the frames of one file, packed together, must fit in a 4096 × 4096 atlas. Fix: split the file into several (one per character, say).
  • Problem: Problems says a Sprite has no sprite sheet, or that its sheet isn't in the project. Why: the Sheet field is empty, or the file was deleted or never committed. Fix: choose a sheet in Sheet, or bring the file back.
  • Tip: identical frames (a held pose repeated to last longer) are packed once, so long animations cost little.

Related#

  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view: base resolution, the 2D view, snapping to pixels.
  • Projects and the Library: where asset files live.
  • Entities and components.
  • Concepts: sprite, sprite sheet, tag, slice, pivot, atlas.

Animating sprites#

Make sprites walk, swing and wave: play the clips you tagged in Aseprite, make clips of your own in Solis, and give frames events that play footsteps and tell your game code.

When to use it#

For anything in a 2D game that moves frame by frame: a farmer walking, a hoe swinging, crops swaying, a door opening. A clip is a run of a sprite sheet's frames, each shown for its own time, played forward, backward or there and back (ping-pong), over and over or a number of times.

The quickest way is Aseprite's own: tag runs of frames there (walk, idle, hoe) and every tag is a clip in Solis, with Aseprite's frame times. To change a clip's speed, give frames events (a footstep on the frame a foot lands), or make clips Aseprite doesn't have, Solis keeps a small clips file (.solframes) beside the Aseprite file. A sprite can play either.

To choose clips by what's happening (walking when moving, idle when not, facing the right way), use an animator.

How to use it#

  1. Tag your frames in Aseprite and save. In Solis, click the file in the Library: Properties lists its tags.

  2. Play a clip on a sprite: select a sprite and pick a Clip in its Sprite component. Press Play: it plays at its frame times. To see it move while you edit, open the viewport's ≡ menu and tick Preview animation.

  3. Open the clips: in the Aseprite file's Properties, press Edit clips…. Solis makes walker.solframes beside walker.aseprite (or opens the one there) and opens two tabs:

    • Frames, a tab of the shelf on the Animate tab (the clips file opens there; an × after the Frames or Clip tab closes the file). On its left, Clips: every clip, with how long it is and where it comes from (Aseprite or made here). Click one to choose it. Beside them, the chosen clip's frames in order along a time ruler, each as wide as it lasts, so you see its timing at a glance. A ping-pong's way back is shown faded after them. The line in the accent colour is where it's playing; the lane below shows its events.
    • Clip, the next shelf tab: the chosen clip's Speed, Direction, how many times it Plays, and Plays first. A clip's settings have a tab of their own so the frames keep the shelf's whole width.

    While a clips file is open, Animate's ribbon is the clips file's: Clip (New, Copy, Delete), Frames (Take out), and how the clip plays (Plays, Speed, and a Direction list for a clip of your own). The design's cutscene controls after them (Keys, Step, Linear, Smooth, Tracks) are unfinished parts.

  4. Watch it: press ▶ (or Space over the Frames tab). ⏮ goes back to the start, ■ stops, ⏭ goes to the last frame. − and + zoom the ruler.

  5. Give a frame an event: click the frame, then type a name in event, or pick a sound event from ◆ ▾. When the clip reaches that frame:

    • a sound event of the same name (footstep, or its path, sfx/footstep) plays on the sprite by itself, with no code;
    • game code on the entity hears CueReached, with the event as one of the project's names (Cue.Footstep). Events typed in Aseprite (a cel's user data) work the same way.

  6. Make a clip of your own: the ribbon's New makes an empty one; Copy copies the chosen clip (a tag's copy can then be changed here). In the Frames tab, ＋ Add frames ▾ shows the sheet's frames: click one to add it after the picked frame. Double-click a clip of your own to rename it.

  7. Change frames of your own clips: click a frame to pick it (Ctrl+click or Shift+click for several), then set its time, drag it to a new place, or press Delete to take it out.

  8. Close the file: the × on either tab closes both.

Every change is saved at once and shows at once on every sprite playing the file. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y over either tab undo and redo changes to the file. If the file changes on disk (edited by hand, or by Git), the tabs show it as it is now, as a step Ctrl+Z undoes; if it's deleted or moved, they close. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.

In game code#

Clips and their events are names Lust checks. Solis writes them into solis/project.lst whenever the sheets change: each clip as state Clip, under its sheet's path (sprites/farmer.aseprite's walk is Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Walk), and each frame event as state Cue (Cue.Footstep). A misspelt clip is a mistake before the game runs. Bring in the names and the events at the top of a file:

fetch "solis/project":[Clip, Cue];
fetch "solis/animation":[CueReached, ClipFinished];

component Farmer {
    has {
        int steps = 0;
    }

    -- Count the footsteps as they land.
    on CueReached(Cue cue) {
        is cue == Cue.Footstep? then {
            steps = steps + 1;
        }
    }

    -- Back to standing once the hoe swing is done.
    on ClipFinished(Clip clip) {
        is clip == Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Hoe? then {
            animate(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Idle);
        }
    }
}

pass Farmer;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Farmer {
    steps: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Farmer {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        // The engine's events carry the project's names as text.
        let named = match event.values.first() {
            Some(Value::Text(name)) => name.as_str(),
            _ => "",
        };
        match event.name.as_str() {
            // Count the footsteps as they land.
            "CueReached" if named == "Footstep" => self.steps += 1,
            // Back to standing once the hoe swing is done.
            "ClipFinished" if named == "Sprites.Farmer.Hoe" => {
                let me = cx.me();
                cx.host().play_clip(me, "idle", false);
            }
            _ => return false,
        }
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Farmer = component("Farmer", {
    { "steps", "int", 0 },
})

-- Count the footsteps as they land.
function Farmer:on_CueReached(cue)
    if cue == "Footstep" then
        self.steps = self.steps + 1
    end
end

-- Back to standing once the hoe swing is done.
function Farmer:on_ClipFinished(clip)
    if clip == "Sprites.Farmer.Hoe" then
        solis.entity.animate(self.me, "Sprites.Farmer.Idle")
    end
end

  • animate(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Walk) plays a clip on the component's entity (target:animate(…) on another). If it's already playing that clip, or has finished it, it carries on as it is, so it's safe to call every tick; another clip starts from its beginning.

  • animateFromStart(Clip.Sprites.Farmer.Hoe) plays a clip from its beginning, whatever it was doing: a swing each time a button is pressed.

  • stopAnimation() stops it where it is; animate with the same clip carries on from there.

  • setFlip(across, down) mirrors the sprite (its Flip across and Flip up settings): setFlip(true, false) faces it the other way. So you draw a run facing right only once, and one Run clip does both ways, instead of a RunLeft as well:

    fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":[Action, Clip];

component Runner {
    method update(float dt) {
        -- Face the way the player pushes.
        bool walkingLeft = Input:axis(Action.Move).x < 0;
        setFlip(walkingLeft, false);
        animate(Clip.Sprites.Hero.Run);
    }
}

pass Runner;
end
    use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Runner;

impl RustComponent for Runner {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        // Face the way the player pushes.
        let walking_left = cx.host().action("Move").axis.x < 0.0;
        cx.host().set_flip(me, walking_left, false);
        cx.host().play_clip(me, "run", false);
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
    local Runner = component("Runner", {})

function Runner:update(dt)
    -- Face the way the player pushes.
    local walkingLeft = solis.Input:axis("Move").x < 0
    solis.entity.setFlip(self.me, walkingLeft, false)
    solis.entity.animate(self.me, "Sprites.Hero.Run")
end

    It's safe to call every tick, and like the other calls it lands at the end of the tick.

  • In Lua: solis.entity.animate(e, "Sprites.Farmer.Walk"), solis.entity.animateFromStart(e, …), solis.entity.stopAnimation(e) and solis.entity.setFlip(e, true, false); a function called on_CueReached(cue) or on_ClipFinished(clip) reacts to the events, with the names as text. In Rust: cx.host().play_clip(entity, "walk", false) (true to start it again), stop_clip and set_flip(entity, true, false), and the events arrive in handle named CueReached and ClipFinished.

A clip's place is part of the game: the same inputs give the same frames every time, and a saved game comes back on the same frame.

Settings#

The Sprite component's clip settings:

SettingWhat it does
SheetAn Aseprite file (its tags are its clips) or a clips file (.solframes).
ClipThe clip it plays. Empty: the clips file's clip marked Plays first, or with none, the still Frame.
PlayingWhether the clip moves on while the game runs. Game code's animate and stopAnimation turn it on and off.
Speed1 as drawn, 2 twice as fast, 0 stopped. Multiplies the clip's own speed.
Clip timeHow far into the clip it is, in seconds. Give a crowd of copies different times so they don't all step in step.
FrameThe frame shown when no clip plays.

A clip's settings in the Clip tab:

SettingWhat it does
SpeedHow fast this clip plays for every sprite, 1 as drawn. A tag's speed is kept in the clips file.
DirectionForward, reverse, ping-pong (there and back) or ping-pong reversed. A tag's is Aseprite's.
PlaysOver and over, once, or a number of times; it then stays on its last frame and game code hears ClipFinished. A tag's is Aseprite's (its Repeat field).
Plays firstThe clip a sprite plays when its Clip is empty.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Rename a clip (your own clips)Double-click it in the Frames tab's list of clips (Enter keeps the name, Esc leaves it)
Pick a frameClick it
Pick several framesCtrl + click, or Shift + click for a run
Move picked frames (your own clips)Drag them
Take picked frames out (your own clips)Delete over the Frames tab
Play or stop the clipSpace over the Frames tab
Undo or redo a change to the clips fileCtrl+Z, Ctrl+Y over either tab

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: sprites don't move in the viewport. Why: the editor rests unless something changes. Fix: tick Preview animation in the viewport's ≡ menu, or press Play.
  • Problem: a tag's frames can't be moved, timed or taken out. Why: a tag's frames are Aseprite's, so saving there keeps both in step. Fix: change them in Aseprite, or Copy the clip (on the ribbon) to change the copy here.
  • Problem: an event doesn't play a sound. Why: no sound event has its name. Fix: name it after the sound event (footstep or sfx/footstep), or pick one from ◆ ▾.
  • Problem: a whole field of crops sways in step. Fix: give each a slightly different Clip time.
  • Problem: two footsteps in a ping-pong walk. Why: a ping-pong shows its middle frames twice a pass, there and back. Fix: put the event on the first or last frame, or use Forward for walks.

Related#

  • Sprites from Aseprite: sheets, placing sprites, pivots.
  • Sound events: the sounds an event plays.
  • Game code: components and events.
  • Concepts: clip, clips file, frame event.
