Animators#

Let Solis choose which clip a sprite plays: idle when standing, walking when moving, a swing when a tool is used, each facing the right way.

When to use it#

A farmer has an idle, a walk and a tool swing, each drawn facing up, right, down and left: twelve clips, and rules for when each plays. You could pick every clip yourself (see Animating sprites), but an animator keeps those rules in one place, drawn as a picture you can read at a glance:

  • States are what the sprite can be doing: Idle, Walk, Use tool. Each plays a clip, or a clip for each direction.
  • Transitions are the arrows between them: Idle goes to Walk when moving is on.
  • Parameters are the values transitions look at: moving (a switch), speed (a number), swing (a trigger) and facing (a direction).

Why a picture rather than code? Because animation rules get tangled fast ("swing, unless already swinging, then go back to walking if still moving…"), and a graph shows every way in and out of each state. The animator also runs inside the game's ticks, so the same inputs always give the same animation, on every computer and in every replay and save.

For one-off sprites (a door, a crop swaying) a plain clip on the Sprite is simpler: no animator needed.

How to use it#

  1. Make one: in the Library, open the folder you want it in, then New › Animator (right-click in the Library, or + New). Solis makes animator.solanim with one state, Idle, and opens it. (Rename the file in the Library, as any other.)
  2. The animator opens on the Animate tab of the tab bar, as a document beside the viewport's (a × on its tab closes it), with its Preview as a group of its own on the right. What you pick in its graph shows on the shelf's Properties tab; its parameters are the Parameters shelf tab. While it is open, Animate's ribbon is the animator's: State (Add state, Start here, Delete) and Preview (Start again), then the design's cutscene controls as unfinished parts.
  3. Choose its clips: click empty space in the graph. Properties shows the animator: pick Clips from, the sprite sheet (or clips file) whose clips its states play.
  4. Add states: the ribbon's Add state, or right-click empty space › Add state. Click a state to change it in Properties:
    • Name: what it's called.
    • Plays: one clip, or a clip by facing. With a clip by facing, pick a clip for each direction (↑ up, → right, ↓ down, ← left); + Direction adds the next one, up to eight with the diagonals. Solis makes a direction parameter, facing, the first time.
    • Speed, and Speed by: a number parameter its speed is multiplied by, so a walk speeds up as the character does.
    • Start here: the state the animator starts in, marked Start ▶ in the graph.
  5. Add parameters: on the Parameters shelf tab, the + beside Parameters adds a number, a switch, a trigger or a direction. Click a name to rename it; right-click it to Delete it, or Start at this value.
  6. Join states: drag from the edge of one state to another, or right-click a state › Make transition and click the other. Click the arrow, then in Properties + Condition and choose what must hold: a switch is on or is off, a trigger fired, a number > or < a value, or finished (the state's clip has played all its times). All of a transition's conditions must hold for it to be taken. An arrow from Any state can be taken from every state.
  7. Try it: the preview always plays. Set the parameters on the Parameters tab (tick moving, turn the facing dial, press Fire for a trigger) and watch the state glow in the accent colour as it changes, the clip playing below.
  8. Use it: select an entity with a Sprite, then in Properties + Component › Animator and pick the file in Animator. Press Play: the animator chooses the Sprite's clip and speed every tick. Select the entity while it plays to see its state glow, and its parameters' values on the Parameters tab.

Every change is saved at once and runs at once, in a game that's playing too. Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y over the tab undo and redo changes to the animator. If the file changes on disk (edited by hand, or by Git), the tab shows it as it is now, as a step Ctrl + Z undoes. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.

In game code#

Each animator gets a Lust file of its own, which Solis writes into solis/animators/ whenever the animator changes: farmer.solanim gives solis/animators/farmer.lst. In it are a state of the graph's states (FarmerState) and a class with a method for each thing code can set or ask (FarmerAnimator). Why a file? Because then every name in the graph is something Lust checks: rename the moving switch, and every line still calling setMoving is a mistake in Problems, instead of a setting that silently does nothing.

A component holds the animator as a field with no starting value. Solis fills it in with the entity's own animator before the component's first update:

fetch "solis/animators/farmer":[FarmerAnimator, FarmerState];
fetch "solis/project":Action;
fetch "solis/input":Input;

component Farmer {
    has {
        FarmerAnimator anim;        -- filled in by Solis
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- How is the farmer moving?
        vec3 velocity = velocity();
        float speed = velocity:length();

        -- Tell the animator.
        anim:setMoving(speed > 0.1);
        anim:setSpeed(speed);
        anim:setFacing(velocity);

        -- The use button swings the hoe.
        is Input:pressed(Action.Interact)? then {
            anim:swing();
        }

        -- Stand still while using a tool.
        is anim:current() == FarmerState.UseTool? then {
            setVelocity([0, 0, 0]);
        }
    }
}

pass Farmer;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{AnimatorValue, Context, RustComponent};

// The animator's file is Lust's. Rust reaches the entity's animator
// through its host, by the graph's own names.
pub struct Farmer;

impl RustComponent for Farmer {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();

        // How is the farmer moving?
        let velocity = cx.host().velocity(me).unwrap_or_default();
        let speed = velocity.length();

        // Tell the animator.
        cx.host().animator_set(me, "moving", AnimatorValue::Switch(speed > 0.1));
        cx.host().animator_set(me, "speed", AnimatorValue::Number(speed));
        cx.host().animator_set(me, "facing", AnimatorValue::Direction(velocity));

        // The use button swings the hoe.
        if cx.host().action("Interact").pressed {
            cx.host().animator_set(me, "swing", AnimatorValue::Fire);
        }

        // Stand still while using a tool.
        if cx.host().animator_state(me).as_deref() == Some("Use tool") {
            cx.host().set_velocity(me, Vec3::ZERO);
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The animator's file is Lust's. Lua reaches the entity's animator
-- through solis.Animators, by the graph's own names.
local Farmer = component("Farmer", {})

function Farmer:update(dt)
    -- How is the farmer moving?
    local velocity = solis.entity.velocity(self.me)
    local speed = math.sqrt(velocity.x * velocity.x + velocity.y * velocity.y + velocity.z * velocity.z)

    -- Tell the animator.
    solis.Animators:setSwitch(self.me, "moving", speed > 0.1)
    solis.Animators:setNumber(self.me, "speed", speed)
    solis.Animators:setDirection(self.me, "facing", velocity)

    -- The use button swings the hoe.
    if solis.Input:pressed("Interact") then
        solis.Animators:fire(self.me, "swing")
    end

    -- Stand still while using a tool.
    if solis.Animators:stateOf(self.me) == "Use tool" then
        solis.entity.setVelocity(self.me, vec3(0, 0, 0))
    end
end
A parameter orbecomes
switch movinganim:setMoving(on)
number speedanim:setSpeed(value)
direction facinganim:setFacing(direction) (on the ground: its height is left out)
trigger swinganim:swing()
its states (Idle, Use tool)FarmerState.Idle, FarmerState.UseTool
which state it's inanim:current()
jumping straight to a stateanim:jumpTo(FarmerState.Idle)
how fast it playsanim:setPlaybackSpeed(1.5)

What's set lands at the end of the tick, like a move, and the animator takes it at its next step. current() says the state as the tick started.

  • Names become Lust names: Use tool is UseTool, the file farmer is FarmerAnimator. A name that can't (it starts with a digit, or has a dash), or a parameter whose method would be one the class has already (current, jumpTo, setPlaybackSpeed), is left out, and the Console says which, so you can rename it.
  • The entity needs an Animator component using that file; the field's class says which file.

Settings#

The Animator component:

SettingWhat it does
AnimatorThe animator file (.solanim) it runs.
StateThe state it starts in; empty for the animator's own start. While playing, the state it's in.
SpeedHow fast its states play: 1 as the animator says, 2 twice as fast. It multiplies each state's own speed.

With an Animator, the animator sets the Sprite's Clip and Speed while the game runs; in the editor the sprite shows its own Clip.

Shortcuts#

These work while the pointer is over the Animator tab.

ActionShortcut
Pick a state or an arrow; add to what's pickedClick; Ctrl + click or Shift + click
Pick states with a boxDrag on empty space
Move picked statesDrag one of them
Join two statesDrag from a state's edge to another
Add a state, Make transition, Start here, DeleteRight-click empty space, a state or an arrow (Add state, Start here and Delete are on the ribbon too)
Give up an arrow started with Make transitionEsc
Delete a parameter, or start it at the value shownRight-click its name
Take away what's pickedDelete
PanMiddle-drag
Zoom round the pointerMouse wheel
Fit everything in viewF
Undo or redo a change to the animatorCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: after making an animator, Problems lists mistakes in solis/animators/… ("there's nothing called Animators here"). Why: the animator's own file uses the engine's Animators, which Lust only finds when the game's code fetches solis/animation (or the animator's file) itself. Fix: add fetch "solis/animation":Animators; to main.lst, or fetch the animator's file where you use it.
  • Problem: a transition is taken at once. Why: it has no conditions (its arrow says always). Fix: click the arrow and add one.
  • Problem: the sprite flickers between two states. Why: each one's transition to the other holds at the same time (moving and not moving can't both hold, but speed > 0 and speed < 1 can). Fix: make the conditions exclude each other.
  • Problem: a swing never ends. Why: its clip plays over and over, so it never finishes. Fix: make the clip play once (its Plays in the Clips tab), or leave it on a different condition.
  • Problem: a box says missing beside a clip. Why: the sprite sheet has no clip by that name (renamed in Aseprite?). Fix: pick the clip again.
  • Problem: pressing a trigger twice quickly swings once. Why: a trigger lasts one tick: one fired while already swinging is put out (it doesn't wait). That's on purpose, so presses don't pile up.
  • Problems lists an Animator with no file chosen, or whose file isn't in the project.

Related#

  • Animating sprites: the clips states play.
  • Sprites from Aseprite.
  • Save games: saves keep each animator's state and parameters.
  • Concepts: animator, state, transition, parameter, trigger.

Tile maps#

Lay out a 2D world as a grid of cells (grass, tilled earth, water) in layers under and over your sprites, with values every cell carries, such as what's planted there and whether it's watered.

When to use it#

A farm is a grid. Each square of ground is grass, tilled earth or water, and as you play it changes: the hoe tills it, a seed is planted, the can waters it, the crop grows. A tile map keeps that grid, and the running game changes it cell by cell.

A tile map stores what each cell means, not a picture:

  • Terrains (grass, tilled, water) come from a tileset, a list shared by every map in the project.
  • Layers stack: Ground, then Decoration (fences, flowers), both drawn under sprites, and Above (roofs, treetops), drawn over them so the farmer walks behind a roof.
  • Cell values are things every cell has besides its terrain. crop is a choice (wheat, corn), growth is a number, and watered is a switch.

Why meaning rather than pictures? Because the art can change without touching a single map: Solis works out which picture each cell shows from its neighbours, using the tileset's art (Tilesets and autotiling). And because "every watered crop" is a question about values, not about how things look.

Why values in the map, rather than an entity per plant? A field of a thousand crops as a thousand entities is a lot to run and save. As values, they're a few bytes each, saved with the map. A plant that needs to animate or think can still be an entity standing on its cell.

For a few things that move or think (a scarecrow that turns, a chicken), use sprites instead.

How to use it#

  1. Make a tileset: in the Library, open the folder you want it in, then New › Tileset (right-click in the Library, or + New). Solis makes tileset.tileset.lst with grass, tilled and water, and opens it in Library tools · Tileset, where terrains get their art (see Tilesets and autotiling). Choose a terrain on the Terrains shelf tab to change its name, its code (the one character the map file writes for it) and its colour; the ribbon's Add adds one. Clicking a tileset in the Library shows its terrains in Properties too: change them there, add one with + Terrain, or take one away with ×. Every change to a tileset is an undo step of that tileset's, wherever you make it: Ctrl + Z with the pointer over Properties while it shows the tileset, or over the tileset's own tab, takes it back, so a terrain removed by mistake comes back with its tiles and rules. Dragging a colour is one step, made when you let go. The first terrain fills new maps.
  2. Make a map: New › Tile map. Solis makes map.tilemap.lst, 64 × 64 cells of the project's first tileset's first terrain. Click it in the Library to change its Tileset and its Size (in cells) in Properties.
  3. Place it: double-click the map in the Library (it goes where the viewport looks), or drag it into the viewport. Its top-left corner lands on a whole tile, and each cell is one tile across (the tile size in 2D settings). The 2D view shows it best.
  4. The Map tab of Home's shelf comes to the front while the map's entity is selected (select it in the Area panel), with the Home tools · Tile map tab and its ribbon. It shows four columns:
    • The map (its name, and how many cells across and down), and its Layers, top first. A click on a layer's row paints on that layer. Each has a small picture of its cells, its name (click to rename), under sprites or over sprites, an eye that shows or hides it here in the editor only (the game always shows it), and … to move it up or down or delete it. + in the column's header adds a layer on top.
    • Terrains, the tileset's, each with how many cells use it. They're the tile painter's palette: click one to paint with it.
    • Cell values. + in the column's header adds one (a switch to start). Change its name, its kind (number, switch or choice) and a choice's options (names with commas between).
    • The cell under the pointer in the viewport: each layer's terrain and each value.
  5. See the values on the map: while the map is selected, the Values list in the ribbon's Show group lays chosen values over the cells: a watered cell is tinted blue, and a number or a choice is written on its cell when you're zoomed in enough to read it. Zoomed out so far that more than 256 × 256 cells are in view, values aren't shown at all (each cell would be a speck), which keeps the editor quick over a big map. Chunks outlines the map's 32 × 32 chunks, and Walls shows what's solid.
  6. Play: each placed map is the game's own copy while it runs, so the game can change it and the file stays as it was. Select the map while playing to watch its cells in the Map tab. Save games keep the map as the game left it.

Every change in the Map tab is saved at once. Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y over the tab undo and redo them. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.

Art and painting#

A terrain is drawn in its colour until its tileset gives it art: then each cell's tile is picked from its neighbours, with smooth edges (see Tilesets and autotiling). Seen from far away, a big map is drawn in its colours again, which is much quicker.

Paint a map's cells with the tile painter: while the map is selected, its brush, rectangle, line, fill and eyedropper are on the ribbon of the Home tools · Tile map tab, and the Map tab's terrain swatches are its palette (see Painting tiles). The file is plain text you can also edit by hand: each chunk of a layer is rows of codes (. grass, t tilled, a space for nothing), and cells painted with an exact tile are listed in exact blocks.

The file#

A tile map is an ordinary Lust file, farm.tilemap.lst, and its tileset is another, ground.tileset.lst. Open one in Ledger to read it: a list of the map's layers and values, then its cells in chunks of 32 × 32, each layer's rows of terrain codes (a space for an empty cell). It's safe to change by hand, keeping to the shapes Solis writes (lock values made of numbers, text in quotes, lists in [ ] and new things): Solis checks the file against those and then as Lust when it reads it, and a mistake is shown with its line. Chunks keep a change to one cell to one line, so Git shows exactly what changed. (Older maps, .soltilemap, move to Lust by themselves when the project opens: see Backups and upgrades.)

In game code#

Each tile map gets a Lust file of its own, which Solis writes into solis/maps/ whenever the map or its tileset changes: maps/farm.tilemap.lst gives solis/maps/maps/farm.lst. In it are states of the map's layers (FarmLayer), its tileset's terrains (FarmTerrain, with Empty for nothing painted) and each choice value's options (FarmCrop), and a class with a method for each thing code can ask or change (FarmMap). So watered misspelt is a mistake before the game runs, and renaming it in the Map tab points at every line still using the old name.

A component holds the map as a field with no starting value, which Solis fills in:

fetch "solis/maps/maps/farm":[FarmMap, FarmLayer, FarmTerrain, FarmCrop];

component Sprinkler {
    has {
        FarmMap farm;        -- filled in by Solis
        int x = 3;
        int y = 4;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Water the cell if it's tilled soil and dry.
        bool soil = farm:terrain(FarmLayer.Ground, x, y) == FarmTerrain.Soil;
        is soil && not farm:watered(x, y)? then {
            farm:setWatered(x, y, true);
            farm:setGrowth(x, y, farm:growth(x, y) + 1);
        }

        -- Plant parsnips where nothing grows yet.
        is farm:crop(x, y) == FarmCrop.None? then {
            farm:setCrop(x, y, FarmCrop.Parsnip);
        }
    }
}

pass Sprinkler;
end
// The map's file is Lust's. Rust reads the map through its host by its
// path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map tab's
// lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a choice by
// its place in its list.
use script::{Context, RustComponent};
use tiles::CellValue;

const FARM: &str = "maps/farm";
const GROUND: usize = 0;
const SOIL: u8 = b's';
// The farm's values, in the Map tab's order.
const WATERED: usize = 0;
const GROWTH: usize = 1;
const CROP: usize = 2;
const PARSNIP: u8 = 0;

pub struct Sprinkler {
    x: u32,
    y: u32,
}

impl RustComponent for Sprinkler {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let Some(farm) = cx.host().map(FARM) else {
            return;
        };
        let (x, y) = (self.x, self.y);

        // Water the cell if it's tilled soil and dry.
        let soil = farm.code(GROUND, x, y) == Some(SOIL);
        let dry = farm.value(WATERED, x, y) != Some(CellValue::Switch(true));
        if soil && dry {
            cx.host().set_map_value(FARM, WATERED, [x, y], CellValue::Switch(true));
            let growth = match farm.value(GROWTH, x, y) {
                Some(CellValue::Number(n)) => n,
                _ => 0,
            };
            cx.host().set_map_value(FARM, GROWTH, [x, y], CellValue::Number(growth + 1));
        }

        // Plant parsnips where nothing grows yet.
        if farm.value(CROP, x, y) == Some(CellValue::Choice(None)) {
            cx.host().set_map_value(FARM, CROP, [x, y], CellValue::Choice(Some(PARSNIP)));
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The map's file is Lust's. Lua reaches the map through solis.Maps by
-- its path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map
-- tab's lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a
-- choice by its place in its list (-1 for none).
local FARM = "maps/farm"
local GROUND = 0
local SOIL = string.byte("s")
-- The farm's values, in the Map tab's order.
local WATERED, GROWTH, CROP = 0, 1, 2
local PARSNIP = 0

local Sprinkler = component("Sprinkler", {
    { "x", "int", 3 },
    { "y", "int", 4 },
})

function Sprinkler:update(dt)
    local x, y = self.x, self.y

    -- Water the cell if it's tilled soil and dry.
    local soil = solis.Maps:terrain(FARM, GROUND, x, y) == SOIL
    if soil and not solis.Maps:isOn(FARM, WATERED, x, y) then
        solis.Maps:setSwitch(FARM, WATERED, x, y, true)
        solis.Maps:setNumber(FARM, GROWTH, x, y, solis.Maps:number(FARM, GROWTH, x, y) + 1)
    end

    -- Plant parsnips where nothing grows yet.
    if solis.Maps:choice(FARM, CROP, x, y) == -1 then
        solis.Maps:setChoice(FARM, CROP, x, y, PARSNIP)
    end
end
In the Map tabbecomes
its sizefarm:width(), farm:height() (in cells)
a layer's terrain on a cellfarm:terrain(FarmLayer.Ground, x, y), farm:setTerrain(FarmLayer.Ground, x, y, FarmTerrain.Soil)
a number value growthfarm:growth(x, y), farm:setGrowth(x, y, to)
a switch value wateredfarm:watered(x, y), farm:setWatered(x, y, on)
a choice value cropfarm:crop(x, y) == FarmCrop.Parsnip, farm:setCrop(x, y, FarmCrop.Corn)
the cell at a place in the worldfarm:cellAt(position()): a MapCell with inside (on the map?), x and y
the place at a cell's middlefarm:placeOf(x, y)
the box a map's entity coversground:mapBounds(): a MapBounds with found, low and high corners

Which cell is the player on? Ask the map with the player's place. MapCell comes from solis/tiles:

fetch "solis/maps/maps/farm":[FarmMap, FarmLayer, FarmTerrain];
fetch "solis/tiles":MapCell;

component Hoe {
    has {
        FarmMap farm;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        MapCell here = farm:cellAt(position());
        is here.inside && farm:terrain(FarmLayer.Ground, here.x, here.y) == FarmTerrain.Grass? then {
            farm:setTerrain(FarmLayer.Ground, here.x, here.y, FarmTerrain.Tilled);
        }
    }
}

pass Hoe;
end
// The map's file is Lust's. Rust reads the map through its host by its
// path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map tab's
// lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a choice by
// its place in its list.
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

const FARM: &str = "maps/farm";
const GROUND: usize = 0;
const GRASS: u8 = b'.';
const TILLED: u8 = b't';

pub struct Hoe;

impl RustComponent for Hoe {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let at = cx.host().position(me).unwrap_or_default();
        let (Some(farm), Some(place)) = (cx.host().map(FARM), cx.host().map_place(FARM)) else {
            return;
        };
        let ([x, y], inside) = place.cell_at(at);
        if !inside {
            return;
        }
        let cell = [x as u32, y as u32];
        if farm.code(GROUND, cell[0], cell[1]) == Some(GRASS) {
            cx.host().set_map_tile(FARM, GROUND, cell, TILLED);
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
-- The map's file is Lust's. Lua reaches the map through solis.Maps by
-- its path, with numbers: layers and values by their place in the Map
-- tab's lists (from 0), terrains by their code in the tileset, and a
-- choice by its place in its list (-1 for none).
local FARM = "maps/farm"
local GROUND = 0
local GRASS, TILLED = string.byte("."), string.byte("t")

local Hoe = component("Hoe", {})

function Hoe:update(dt)
    local here = solis.Maps:cellAt(FARM, solis.entity.position(self.me))
    if here.inside and solis.Maps:terrain(FARM, GROUND, here.x, here.y) == GRASS then
        solis.Maps:setTerrain(FARM, GROUND, here.x, here.y, TILLED)
    end
end

It works wherever the map's entity is, even moved or turned. Cells are counted from the map's top left corner, x across and y down, like the Map tab; a place off the map still gets the cell it would be (handy for a tool reaching past the edge), with inside false. A 2D camera that stays inside the map is ready-made: FollowCamera2D (Characters and cameras).

  • Cells count from 0 at the map's first corner, as the Map tab shows them. A cell off the map reads as empty, 0 or off, and changing it does nothing.
  • Changes land at the end of the tick, like moves, and what code reads is the map as the tick started. They're in saves, and a solid terrain painted by code becomes a wall at once.
  • The map is the one placed by the first entity showing that file (most games have one per file).

Settings#

The Tile Map component:

SettingWhat it does
MapThe tile map file (.tilemap.lst) it shows. Its top-left corner is at the entity.

A map file's Properties:

SettingWhat it does
TilesetThe terrains its cells can be. Giving a map with an empty ground its first tileset fills the ground with that tileset's first terrain.
SizeIts width and height in cells, up to 4,096 each. Making it smaller takes away the cells past its new edges. A change that would make the map's file too big to open again isn't made (see the problems below).

A terrain's settings (right-click its swatch in the Map tab):

SettingWhat it does
SolidNothing with a 2D collider walks into its cells: fences, water, walls. A small wall mark shows on its swatch, and the Walls switch on the Tile map ribbon shows the walls it makes. See Walls and walking in 2D.

Value kinds:

KindHoldsStarts at
NumberA whole number, such as days of growth0
SwitchOn or off, such as wateredOff
ChoiceOne of its options, such as wheat or cornNone

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Undo or redo a change in the Map tab, or a painted strokeCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y (pointer over the tab, or a painting tool in use)
Undo or redo a change to a tileset (its terrains, Solid)Ctrl + Z, Ctrl + Y (pointer over Properties while it shows the tileset, or over the tileset's tab)
A terrain's settingsRight-click its swatch in the Map tab
The painting toolsB, U, N, G, I (see Painting tiles)

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: cells are bright pink. Why: their code isn't one of the tileset's terrains (the terrain was taken away, or its code changed), or their terrain's art is missing the tile they need. The Map tab counts unknown codes, and Problems names missing tiles. Fix: add a terrain with that code, change the cells, or fill the slot in the tileset.
  • Problem: clicking the map in the viewport selects what's behind it, or nothing. Why: clicks on a map are kept for the tile painter. Fix: select the map in the Area panel.
  • Problem: the Map tab is gone. Why: it shows only while a map is selected. Fix: select the map's entity.
  • Problem: after making a tile map, Problems lists mistakes in solis/maps/… ("there's nothing called Maps here"). Why: the map's own file uses the engine's Maps, which Lust only finds when the game's code fetches solis/tiles (or the map's file) itself. Fix: add fetch "solis/tiles":Maps; to main.lst, or fetch the map's file where you use it.
  • Problem: numbers don't show on the cells. Why: cells are too small to write on, or too many are in view. Fix: zoom in.
  • Problem: a value's numbers are gone after changing its kind. Why: a value's cells start again when its kind changes. Fix: Ctrl + Z over the Map tab.
  • Problem: on a very big map, + adds no layer or value, or a value's kind won't change to number. Why: a map's layers and values together take at most 512 MB of memory. A layer, a switch or a choice takes a byte for each cell and a number four, so the biggest map (4,096 × 4,096) has room for 32 bytes a cell: 16 layers and 4 numbers, say. Fix: take away a layer or value the map doesn't need, or make the map smaller.
  • Problem: a change to a very big map isn't made, and the Console says … wasn't changed: saved like that, the map couldn't be opened again. Why: a map is kept as text, and reading text takes far more memory than the file's size, so Solis reads a map file of up to 64 MB with up to 12 million numbers, texts and symbols in it (about 2 GB of memory and 10 seconds at worst). The biggest map, 4,096 × 4,096, fits with three layers painted all over; each cell whose value isn't at its start counts too (a number in a million and a half cells is too many), and so does each exact tile. A map saved past that could never be opened again, so Solis checks every change as you make it (painting, filling, a new layer or value, a bigger size) and doesn't make one that would take the map past it. Nothing is lost: the map stays as it was, and undo still goes back through your earlier changes. Fix: split a very big world into several maps, each on its own entity, give values only to the cells that need them, and clear layers the map doesn't use; then make the change again.
  • Problem: a very big map won't open: "the map is too big to read" or "it's too big to read". Why: its file is past what Solis reads (see the problem above). Solis never saves such a file itself, so it was made by hand, by another program, or by a Solis from before this check. Fix: make it smaller in a text editor (take out a layer's Cells, or a value's cells), or go back to an earlier version of it in Git.
  • Problems lists a Tile Map with no map chosen, or whose file isn't in the project.

Related#

  • Painting tiles: the brush, rectangle, line, fill and eyedropper.
  • Tilesets and autotiling: terrains' art.
  • Sprites from Aseprite: what stands on a map.
  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view: the tile size and the 2D view.
  • Save games: saves keep each map as the game changed it.
  • Concepts: tileset, terrain, tile map, layer, cell value, chunk.

Atlas Crop: pictures cut out of a sprite sheet#

Cut named pictures out of a PNG or an Aseprite sheet (a sword, a heart, a button's corner), so one sprite or a few can be used on their own, without changing the picture.

When to use it#

Artists often draw many small pictures on one sheet: every item in a game, every icon of a HUD. Atlas Crop marks each one as a crop with a name, so game code and screens can use just that part of the sheet: Picture.Sprites.Tools.Axe. The picture itself is never changed, so the artist keeps drawing on the same sheet and every crop follows.

For a sprite that plays clips, use sprites and sprite animation instead; for ground made of tiles, a tileset.

How to use it#

  1. In the Library, right-click a picture (a PNG, JPEG or Aseprite file) and choose Atlas Crop…. A Library tools · Picture tab opens after Library in the tab bar (a contextual tab: it is there only while the picture's crops are open), with the picture as its document and its crops on the Crops shelf tab. Solis makes a file beside the picture to keep the crops: sprites/tools.png gets sprites/tools.atlas.lst. ‹ Back to Library, at the right of the document's tab, goes back to the Library and leaves the crops open.
  2. Set the Grid at the top of the Crops tab to the size the pictures are drawn on (16 × 16 for most pixel art); the ribbon's Grid group says it too. Crops snap to it, so a quick drag catches a whole tile.
  3. Drag on the picture to draw a crop. It's named Crop, Crop2… at first: type a better name in Name, in the Crops tab's right-hand column, and press Rename (or Enter). A name starts with a letter and holds only letters, digits and _.
  4. Or press Every tile in the ribbon's Crop group: a crop for every grid cell with something drawn in it, named by its column and row (Tile_3_0).
  5. Click a crop, on the picture or in the Crops list (its size and place beside its name), to pick it: its frame turns the accent colour and thicker, while the others stay a darker grey; the ribbon's Delete, Delete crop or the Delete key over the picture removes it. Zoom in the ribbon's Grid group shows the picture at a chosen size (the wheel zooms too). Every change is saved at once, and Ctrl+Z over the tab undoes it. If a save can't be made, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.
  6. Later, double-click the .atlas.lst file in the Library to open its picture's crops again.

Game code names each crop by its picture's path and its name, from solis/project.lst: fetch "solis/project":Picture; then Picture.Sprites.Tools.Axe for sprites/tools.png's Axe. A screen shows one with image "sprites/tools.png#Axe";: the picture's path, #, and the crop's name.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
GridThe size, in the picture's pixels, crops snap to when drawn and that Every tile cuts by.
ZoomHow big the picture is shown (the ribbon's list, or the wheel).
NameThe picked crop's name, as game code uses it.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Draw a cropDrag with the left button on the picture
Pick a cropClick it
Delete the picked cropDelete, with the pointer over the picture or the Crops tab
ZoomMouse wheel over the picture
Move the pictureDrag with the middle button
Undo, redoCtrl+Z, Ctrl+Y (pointer over the picture or the Crops tab)

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the tab says the picture isn't in the project. Why: an atlas file belongs to the picture beside it, by its file name, and that picture was moved or renamed. Fix: move the .atlas.lst file beside the picture, or rename it to match (tools.png and tools.atlas.lst).
  • Problem: a crop isn't offered to game code. Why: its name, or a folder or picture name in its path, can't be a Lust name (the Console says which). Fix: rename it: start with a letter, and use only letters, digits and _.
  • Problem: Every tile made fewer crops than there are cells. Why: empty cells (every pixel see-through) are left out, and so are cells a crop already covers exactly. That's on purpose.

Related#

  • Sprites, Tilesets, Game screens.
  • Concepts: atlas crop.

Tilesets and autotiling#

Give each terrain its art from a picture of tiles. Solis picks each cell's tile from its neighbours, so the edges between grass and tilled earth, the corners of a pond and the joins of a fence come out right by themselves.

When to use it#

A tile map stores what each cell is: grass, tilled, water. Until a tileset has art, each terrain is drawn as a flat colour. That's enough to lay a farm out, but a game wants pictures, and pictures need their edges. Where tilled earth meets grass, the tile at the edge has to show both, and which tile depends on which neighbours are tilled.

Choosing those by hand, cell by cell, is slow and breaks whenever the map changes. Autotiling does it for you. You draw the tiles once and say which situation each one is for (its slot). Solis then picks the right one for every cell, on every map, as the map changes, even while the game plays.

How many tiles you need depends on the terrain's kind:

KindTilesGood for
Plain1Grass, sand: anything with no edges of its own
16-tile (dual grid)15Most ground: tilled earth, paths, snow. The fewest drawings for smooth edges and corners
47-tile47Ground with the most polished corners, such as water with inner corners
Edges16Fences, walls, roads: things that join their neighbours along their sides
Rulesas many as you useAnything else: your own patterns of the cells around

16-tile works on a dual grid: each tile is drawn half a cell off, where four cells meet, and is chosen by which of those four are the terrain. That's why 15 drawings cover every case. You still paint and the game still thinks in whole cells; only the art is shifted.

How to use it#

  1. Draw your tiles in one picture: a PNG, or an Aseprite file (handy for animated tiles), with every tile the same size in a grid. Not sure what to draw? Open the tileset, choose a terrain's kind, and press Save … template (or the ribbon's Save its template…): Solis saves a picture beside the tileset with every slot laid out at your tile size, ready to draw over.
  2. Open the tileset: double-click it in the Library. A Library tools · Tileset tab joins the tab bar after Library and comes to the front: a contextual tab, there only while the tileset is open. Its document is the tileset itself (the picture on the left, the chosen terrain's slots on the right, Try it under them), its Terrains shelf tab lists the terrains beside the slot picked, and its ribbon has Terrain (Add, Remove), Kind and Picture (the tile size and the Zoom). ‹ Back to Library, at the right of the document's tab, goes back and leaves the tileset open.
  3. Choose the picture on the Terrains shelf tab, under the terrains. Solis cuts it into tiles at the tile size shown. If the art looks cut differently, it offers the size it found: click it.
  4. Choose a terrain on the Terrains shelf tab, and give it a kind (the ribbon's Kind list, or the tab's own). While it has no tiles, the tab guesses its kind from the picture (pick the top-left tile of its block first) and asks you to confirm. Kind at the top right changes it any time.
  5. Fill its slots on the right. Each slot shows the neighbours it's for: the terrain's colour where they're the terrain, dark where they're not.
    • Click a tile in the picture, then the slot it's for, or drag the tile onto the slot.
    • Drawn over the template? Pick the template's top-left tile and press Mark up from the template: every slot is filled from its place in one go.
    • A second tile in the same slot is a variation, so a field doesn't look tiled. Click the slot to see its tiles in Properties, with each one's Weight (how often it's picked).
  6. Try it in the patch below the slots: click cells to turn the terrain on and off and watch the edges. The patch isn't saved.
  7. Look at your map: every map using the tileset draws with the art at once, and while the game plays.

The strip at the top of the picture says where you are: ① picture, ② grid, ③ kind, ④ how many of the terrain's slots are filled.

A terrain of its own rules#

For a kind none of the others fit, choose rules and press + Rule. A rule is a small pattern of the cells around one (3 × 3 to start, up to 9 × 9) and the slot it shows. Click a cell of the pattern to change what it asks for:

MarkMeans
?Anything
=The same terrain
!Not the same terrain
_Nothing on this layer (or past the map's edge)
a terrain's codeThat terrain

The rules are tried in order (↑ and ↓ move one), and the first that matches gives the slot. The slots the rules name appear below them to fill. A cell no rule matches shows pink.

Animated tiles#

Click a slot, then in Properties set a tile's Animation:

  • tiles to the right: that many tiles of the picture, left to right from this one, each shown for so many milliseconds (water, flowers);
  • the picture's frames (an Aseprite picture): the same tile in each of its frames, each for its own time.

Settings#

In the tileset's tab (the Terrains shelf tab and the ribbon):

SettingWhat it does
PictureThe PNG, JPEG or Aseprite file the art comes from.
Tile sizeEach tile's width and height in pixels. Usually the project's tile size (2D settings).
KindHow the chosen terrain's tiles are chosen: plain, 16-tile, 47-tile, edges or rules. Changing it takes its tiles away (Ctrl + Z brings them back).
ZoomHow big the picture is shown (the ribbon's list, or − and + under the steps).

In Properties, for a tile in a slot:

SettingWhat it does
WeightHow often it's picked among the slot's tiles: 2 is twice as often as 1, 0 never. Each cell always gets the same one.
AnimationNone, tiles to the right (with how many and how long each), or the picture's frames.

For the chosen terrain (no slot picked): its Name, Code (the character map files write for it) and Colour (drawn where it has no art), and Remove terrain.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Give a tile to a slotClick the tile in the picture, then the slot; or drag the tile onto the slot
Undo or redo a change to the tilesetCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y (pointer over the tileset or its Terrains tab, or over Properties while it shows the tileset)

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pink cells on a map. Why: a slot those cells need has no tile, or the cells' code isn't a terrain. Fix: the tileset's slots dash the empty ones red; Problems says which map and which slots. Fill them.
  • Problem: the edges look one tile off. Why: the template was marked up from the wrong tile. Fix: pick the template's top-left tile in the picture first; the button says where it will start. Ctrl + Z, then try again.
  • Problem: the grid lines don't match the art. Why: the tile size is different from the picture's. Fix: set it on the left, or click the size Solis found.
  • Problem: a terrain still shows its flat colour. Why: it has no tiles yet (or the tileset has no picture). Fix: fill its slots.
  • Problem: the picture won't open. Why: it isn't a PNG, JPEG or Aseprite file, or it's bigger than 4,096 pixels a side. The tab says why.
  • If a change to the tileset can't be saved, the Console says why and the change is taken back, kept as an undo step: see Undo and redo.
  • PNG and JPEG files get a sidecar (.solmeta) like other assets, so a tileset keeps its picture when the picture is moved or renamed. Commit them with the picture.

Related#

  • Tile maps: the maps tilesets draw.
  • Sprites from Aseprite: Aseprite pictures.
  • Concepts: autotiling, kind, slot, dual grid, variation, template.
← Previous · Chapter 43Atlas Crop: pictures cut out of a sprite sheetNext → · Chapter 45Painting tiles

Painting tiles#

Paint a tile map's cells with a brush, a rectangle, a line or a fill, copy an area to paint with, and place a tile exactly as it is.

When to use it#

A tile map is a grid of terrains: grass, tilled earth, water. The tile painter is how you lay them out: paint a field of tilled earth, a pond, a path, a fence. You paint what each cell means (its terrain); the art is worked out from the neighbours by autotiling, so the edges of a pond come out smooth wherever you paint it.

Painting is for the map file, the world as the game starts. While the game runs, the map is the game's own copy, so painting is off then; game code changes cells as you play.

How to use it#

  1. Select the map's entity (in the Area panel). A Home tools · Tile map tab joins the tab bar after Home and comes to the front, with the Map tab of the shelf. Its ribbon holds everything for painting, so the viewport stays clear: the tools are on the ribbon rather than in the toolbox because there are five of them and they are only there while a map is selected. Bringing another shelf tab to the front (Entity, say) gives Home's own ribbon back; the Tile map tab, or the Map shelf tab, brings the painting ribbon again.
  2. Choose a tool in the ribbon's Paint group or with its key: Brush (B), Rectangle (U), Line (N), Fill (G) or Eyedropper (I). Q, W, R, S or T goes back to the transform tools. While a tool is in use, its keys show in a hint along the foot of the view.
  3. Choose what to paint: click a terrain's swatch in the Map tab's Terrains column. The outlined swatch is the one painted, and the ribbon names it beside the tools. Clicking a swatch takes the brush if no painting tool is in use.
  4. Choose the layer: click its row in the Map tab's first column, or pick it from the ribbon's Layer list (Ground to start). The row painted on is lit. Paint fences and flowers on Decoration so the ground under them stays grass.
  5. Paint in the viewport (the 2D view is easiest):
    • Brush: drag over cells to paint them. Every cell the pointer crosses is painted, however fast you drag.
    • Rectangle: drag from one corner to the other. The cells show while you drag and are painted when you let go.
    • Line: drag from one end to the other; painted when you let go.
    • Fill: click a cell. Every cell joined to it by its sides with the same terrain is painted: one field, stopping at its edges.
    • Eyedropper: drag over cells to copy them (see below). One cell picks its terrain instead.
  6. Empty cells by dragging with the right mouse button: the brush, rectangle, line and fill all take cells away instead.
  7. Undo with Ctrl + Z while a painting tool is in use (or over the Map tab). Each stroke, from pressing the button to letting go, is one step. Esc during a stroke gives it up.

Everything is saved as soon as you let go.

Picking a terrain from the map#

Alt + click a cell to paint with its terrain, like a colour picker. It also picks the cell's exact tile, if it has one.

Copying an area#

Drag over cells with the Eyedropper to copy them: a copy (some programs call it a stamp). The brush takes it, and paints the whole copy round the pointer; dragged, it repeats like a pattern, without seams. Empty cells in the copy leave the map as it is, so a copied fence keeps the grass under it.

While you hold a copy:

  • X flips it left and right, Y top and bottom, Z turns it a quarter clockwise (the ribbon's Copy group does the same: Flip X, Flip Y, Turn, and Put away);
  • the rectangle, line and fill paint with it as a pattern;
  • Esc, or clicking a terrain's swatch, puts it away.

Exact tiles#

Autotiling picks each cell's tile from its neighbours. Sometimes you want one particular tile instead: a cracked stone, a corner that breaks the rule. An exact tile is a cell that shows one tile as it is.

  1. Tick Exact on the ribbon (or hold Ctrl while painting).
  2. The Map tab shows the painted terrain's tiles under the swatches. Click the one to place. To start, it's the tile for the middle of a patch.
  3. Paint. The cell keeps that tile; its neighbours still see its terrain, so their edges still join it.

Painting the cell again without Exact makes it autotiled again. Exact tiles are art only: the game reads the terrain, never the tile.

Art or meaning#

Tab, or the ribbon's Map as list in the Show group, switches the selected map between its art and its meaning: each terrain in its flat colour, which is what the game reads. Meaning is handy for checking that a path of tiles really is all one terrain.

Settings#

The ribbon of Home tools · Tile map, while a map is selected:

GroupSettingWhat it does
PaintBrush, Rectangle, Line, Fill, EyedropperThe painting tools (B, U, N, G, I).
(in hand)The terrain, or Copy W × HWhat is painted now.
(in hand)LayerThe layer painted (a click on a layer's row in the Map tab does the same).
(in hand)ExactPlaces the tile chosen in the Map tab as it is, not the one autotiling picks. Ctrl while painting does the same for one stroke.
ShowMap asWhat the selected map shows: its art, or each terrain in its colour (Tab).
ShowValues, Chunks, WallsWhat is laid over the map: its cell values, its chunks of 32 × 32 cells, and what's solid.
CopyFlip X, Flip Y, Turn, Put awayChange or drop the copy held (X, Y, Z, Esc). Faint until you hold one.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Brush, Rectangle, Line, Fill, EyedropperB, U, N, G, I (a map selected)
PaintLeft-drag (a click for the fill)
Empty cellsRight-drag
Paint with the terrain under the pointerAlt + click
Place exact tiles for one strokeHold Ctrl while painting
Flip the copy left and right, top and bottom; turn itX, Y, Z (holding a copy)
Give up a stroke; put the copy away; leave the painting toolEsc
Art or meaningTab
Undo or redo a strokeCtrl + Z, Ctrl + Y
Slide the view while paintingMiddle-drag

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: on a very big map, what you just painted disappears when you let go, and the Console says the map wasn't changed. Why: with that stroke the map's file would be too big for Solis to open again, so the stroke isn't kept; the map is as it was before it. Fix: see Tile maps for how much a map can hold and what to do.
  • Problem: the painting tools aren't on the ribbon. Why: they are on the Home tools · Tile map tab, there only while a tile map's entity is selected, and faint while the game runs. Fix: select the map in the Area panel and click the Tile map tab (or the Map shelf tab); stop the game.
  • Problem: right-dragging empties cells instead of sliding the view. Why: while a painting tool is in use, the right button empties. Fix: slide with the middle button, or press Q for Select.
  • Problem: the fill painted more than expected. Why: the fill follows every cell of the same terrain joined by its sides, on the layer painted. Fix: Ctrl + Z, then break the field with a line first.
  • Problem: painting does nothing. Why: the map has no tileset (nothing to paint with), or the layer painted is hidden. Fix: choose a tileset in the map file's Properties; check the ribbon's Layer list and the Map tab's eyes.
  • Problem: a flipped copy's exact tiles look the wrong way round. Why: exact tiles move with their cells but aren't mirrored. Fix: pick the mirrored tile from the Map tab, or leave those cells autotiled.
  • Problem: cells show pink. Why: their terrain's art is missing a tile they need (Problems names it). Fix: fill the slot in the tileset.

Related#

  • Tile maps: layers, values and the Map tab.
  • Tilesets and autotiling: how each cell's tile is picked.
  • Undo: what Ctrl + Z undoes where.
  • Concepts: tile map, terrain, layer, copy, exact tile.

Walls and walking in 2D#

Make terrains solid so nothing walks through fences and water, give things a 2D collider, and walk a character around a top-down map in 8 directions or 4.

When to use it#

In any top-down 2D game: a farmer who walks the farm but not through its fences, a shop counter you can't walk through, villagers who stop at walls. Solis gives you the pieces; your game decides what they mean. Solis never decides that water is solid or that NPCs walk in 4 directions: you do.

Three parts work together:

  • Solid terrains: cells nothing with a body can walk into (fences, water, rock). Set per terrain, in its tileset, so every map using the tileset agrees.
  • Collider2D: a shape on the ground for 2D physics, in pixels. Solid and still on its own (a house, a bin); ticked Character, game code walks it.
  • The TopDownController: a ready-made Lust component in the kit that walks a character with the Move action (WASD, the arrow keys, a controller's left stick).

2D physics is its own world, separate from 3D physics, and gives the same result on every PC. For 3D characters, see Characters and cameras.

How to use it#

Make terrains solid

  1. Click your tile map in the Library (or select its Tile Map entity) so the Map tab shows it.
  2. Under Terrains, right-click a terrain's swatch (say, fence) and tick Solid. A small wall mark appears on its swatch. Left-click still picks it for painting.
  3. Do the same for every terrain that should block: water, rock, walls.
  4. Press Walls at the top of the viewport (beside Chunks) to see what's solid: green rectangles over the map. Neighbouring solid cells merge into a few big rectangles, so a character sliding along a fence never catches on the seams between tiles.

Walk a character

  1. Select your player's entity (one with a Sprite, say).

  2. In Properties, choose + Component › Collider2D. Leave its shape a Circle (circles slide round corners best) and set its Radius to about a third of the sprite's width. Set Up to put the circle at its feet. A green outline shows it in the viewport.

  3. Tick Character.

  4. Fetch the kit's walker in your game code (main.lst):

    fetch "solis/kit/topdown":[TopDownController];
end
    // The kit's components are Lust. A game in Rust brings one in from a
// main.lst of two lines beside its Rust:
//
//     fetch "solis/kit/topdown":[TopDownController];
//     end
    -- The kit's components are Lust. A game in Lua brings one in from a
-- main.lst of two lines beside its Lua files:
--
--     fetch "solis/kit/topdown":[TopDownController];
--     end

  5. Save, then in Properties choose + Component › TopDownController.

  6. Press Play and walk with WASD or the arrow keys. It stops at solid tiles and other colliders and slides along them.

Walk an NPC from your own code Add a TopDownController, untick Uses input, set Directions to 4 if you like, and set its wanted field from your code to where it should head ([1, 0, 0] walks right, [0, 0, 0] stops). Or call walk yourself with how far to move this tick:

component Wanderer {
    method update(float dt) {
        walk([1.5 * dt, 0, 0]);
    }
}

pass Wanderer;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Wanderer;

impl RustComponent for Wanderer {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.host().walk(me, Vec3::new(1.5 * dt as f32, 0.0, 0.0));
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Wanderer = component("Wanderer", {})

function Wanderer:update(dt)
    solis.entity.walk(self.me, vec3(1.5 * dt, 0, 0))
end

A 2D character moves on the ground: the move's third number (height) is ignored, and it stays on its layer.

Side-on games (platformers). The second number is up and down, so walk a hero down a little every tick for gravity, and ask how its last move went:

  • grounded() is true when a floor under it stopped it going down: jump only then. A wall, or a slope steeper than about 45°, isn't ground.
  • velocity() is how fast its last tick's move really went, in metres a second: less than you asked for when something stopped it. A head bump shows as velocity().y dropping to 0 while you asked to go up.
fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component Hero {
    has {
        float fall = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        -- Gravity, then a jump from the floor.
        fall = fall - 30 * dt;
        is grounded()? then {
            fall = 0;
            is Input:pressed(Action.Jump)? then {
                fall = 12;
            }
        }
        walk([4 * dt, fall * dt, 0]);
    }
}

pass Hero;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Hero {
    fall: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Hero {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        // Gravity, then a jump from the floor.
        self.fall -= 30.0 * dt;
        if cx.host().grounded(me) {
            self.fall = 0.0;
            if cx.host().action("Jump").pressed {
                self.fall = 12.0;
            }
        }
        let step = Vec3::new((4.0 * dt) as f32, (self.fall * dt) as f32, 0.0);
        cx.host().walk(me, step);
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Hero = component("Hero", {
    { "fall", "float", 0 },
})

function Hero:update(dt)
    -- Gravity, then a jump from the floor.
    self.fall = self.fall - 30 * dt
    if solis.entity.grounded(self.me) then
        self.fall = 0
        if solis.Input:pressed("Jump") then
            self.fall = 12
        end
    end
    solis.entity.walk(self.me, vec3(4 * dt, self.fall * dt, 0))
end

When an entity with a Collider2D is despawned, its collider goes with it at once, so a squashed enemy never leaves an invisible wall.

Settings#

Collider2D

SettingWhat it does
ShapeCircle (best for characters: it slips round corners) or Box (buildings, counters).
RadiusA circle's size, in pixels. A third of a 16-pixel sprite's width (about 5) is a good start.
Width, HeightA box's size, in pixels.
Across, UpWhere the shape's middle is from the entity's place, in pixels. Raise a character's circle to its feet so its head can overlap things above it, as top-down games do.
CharacterTicked: game code walks it (walk, or the TopDownController) and it slides along what's in its way. Unticked: solid and still.

Pixels become metres with the project's 2D settings (File › Project settings, pixels per unit).

TopDownController

SettingWhat it does
SpeedMetres a second at full push. 4 is a brisk walk at 16 pixels a metre.
AccelerationHow quickly it gets up to speed, in metres a second each second. High feels snappy; low feels heavy.
DecelerationHow quickly it stops when let go.
Directions8, or 4 (only the bigger of across and up counts: no diagonals, like older games).
Uses inputTicked: walks with the Move action. Unticked: walks towards wanted, set by your code.
FacingThe way it last walked (read it to choose a sprite's facing).

Terrains (right-click a swatch in the Map tab)

SettingWhat it does
SolidNothing with a Collider2D passes into its cells, on any layer. Saved in the tileset (solid = true;).

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Walk (with the TopDownController)W A S D, the arrow keys, or a controller's left stick

Change them in File › Project settings › Input (the Move action). A project with its own input actions file from before keeps its keys: add the arrows to Move there if you want them.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the character walks through a fence. Why: the fence's terrain isn't solid, or the character has no Collider2D ticked Character. Fix: right-click the fence's swatch and tick Solid; press Walls to check it shows.
  • Problem: nothing moves when I press keys. Why: the entity has no TopDownController, or its Collider2D isn't ticked Character (walk only moves characters). Fix: check both in Properties, and look in the Console for game code mistakes.
  • Problem: the character stops at a doorway it should fit through. Why: its circle is wider than the gap. Fix: make the Radius smaller, or the door wider.
  • Problem: it catches on corners. Why: a Box collider meets corners square on. Fix: use a Circle for characters.
  • Problem: the Console says 2D physics stopped and was started again. Why: 2D physics met something it couldn't work out, usually a Collider2D or a tile map whose size or place is far out of the ordinary. Rather than leave every character standing still, Solis builds 2D physics again from the entities and tile maps as they are, and the game carries on; the message names the character it was moving when it knows. If it keeps happening, it's built again at most once a second (so the game doesn't slow to a crawl), and 2D characters stand still in between. It's said once each time you press Play. Fix: look at the entity named, or at anything very big or very far away, and bring it back into range.
  • Walking into a door or a shop counter to make something happen (a trigger) comes with a later update.

Related#

  • Tile maps, Tilesets and Painting tiles
  • Input actions
  • Game code
  • Physics (3D) and Characters and cameras (3D characters)
  • Concepts: 2D

Parallax layers#

Make a sprite a background or foreground layer that moves with the camera at its own speed, so far hills drift slowly, leaves in front rush past, and a flat 2D level feels deep.

When to use it#

In side-on 2D games (platformers above all) and anywhere the camera travels a long way: a sky that stays put, mountains that crawl, trees that pass a little slower than the ground, and bushes or posts close to the camera that sweep past faster. It's the oldest trick for depth in 2D: things far away seem to move less when you move.

A parallax layer is an ordinary sprite with a Parallax component, so it keeps everything sprites do: clips, tint, flash, lamps and day and night.

Top-down games rarely need it: everything there is about the same distance from the camera.

How to use it#

A background

  1. Draw the layer in Aseprite: a line of hills, say, as wide as you like. For a layer that repeats, make its left and right edges meet.
  2. Drag it from the Library into the viewport, so it's a sprite. Put it where it should be in the game's first picture: around where your game's camera starts.
  3. In Properties, choose + Component › Parallax.
  4. Set Scroll across and Scroll up: 0.2 for faraway mountains, 0.5 for hills, 0.8 for trees just behind the action. Leave Repeat across ticked so the hills never run out.
  5. Press Play and move your character. The hills move slower than the ground.

Layers behind are drawn behind everything, tile maps included: the slowest first, so a 0.2 layer is behind a 0.5 one, whatever their places. The sky is usually a layer of its own with a scroll of 0, so it never moves.

A foreground

  1. Make a sprite of something close to the camera: leaves, a post, fog.
  2. Add a Parallax, tick In front, and give it a scroll above 1, such as 1.5.
  3. Press Play: it sweeps past faster than the world, over everything.

Where it's drawn. A layer is exactly where you put it while the game's camera is where it starts. As the camera moves, the layer moves at its own speed: with 0.5, half as far as the world. So the editor shows your game's first picture, layers and all. A layer can be several sprites (a row of trees with the same scrolls): they stay as far apart as you put them.

Smooth, even when slow. Through a 2D camera, each layer is drawn as a small picture of its own and slides smoothly by less than a pixel at a time, as the camera does, so a far layer crawling slowly never jumps a whole pixel at once. Up to 8 layers are drawn this way; each different set of scrolls, behind or in front, is one layer.

In the editor, layers stay where you put them (the editor's camera isn't the game's), repeated across the view, behind or in front as in the game. Clicking one behind the world selects it only where nothing else is in the way; the Area panel always finds it.

Settings#

Parallax

SettingWhat it does
Scroll acrossHow far it moves sideways with the camera. 0 stays still on the screen (the sky); 0.5 moves half as far (far hills); 1 moves with the world; 2 twice as far (close in front). From 0 to 4.
Scroll upThe same, up and down. Platformers often use the same number as across; a smaller one keeps the horizon steadier when the player jumps.
Repeat acrossDrawn again and again side by side, at its sheet's width, so it never runs out. On to start.
Repeat upDrawn again and again above and below. For skies or walls that should fill the screen whatever the height.
In frontDrawn over everything instead of behind it. Use it with a scroll above 1.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: a repeated layer shows a seam where the copies meet. Why: its left and right edges don't match, or the picture has empty columns at its sides. Fix: draw it so the edges continue into each other, using the whole canvas. Copies are one canvas width apart.
  • Problem: a slow layer moves in little steps during a slow pan. Why: you have more than 8 layers (each different set of scrolls, behind or in front, is one), so they're drawn on the game's whole pixels, and a slow layer reaches the next pixel only now and then. Fix: give layers that are about as far away the same scrolls, so they share one.
  • Problem: a layer far along the level isn't where I put it. Why: layers are where you put them only while the camera is at its start; by the time the camera gets there, a slow layer has gone along with it. Fix: place layers around the camera's start, and use Repeat across for ones that must last the whole level.
  • Problem: the player bumps into nothing in front of a layer. Why: a Parallax only changes how the sprite looks; a Collider2D on the same entity stays where the entity is. Fix: keep layers as pictures only, and put colliders on entities of their own.
  • Tile maps can't be layers yet: draw backgrounds as pictures.

Related#

  • Sprites from Aseprite: making the pictures layers use.
  • 2D: the pixel-perfect view: 2D cameras and the game's pixels.
  • Concepts: parallax, sprite.
← Previous · Chapter 46Walls and walking in 2DNext → · Chapter 48Characters and cameras

Characters and cameras#

A character that walks, sprints, jumps and climbs, and three cameras (third person, first person and RTS), ready-made, so you can walk around a level before writing any code.

When to use it#

Almost every game has someone to move around and a camera to see them with. Getting these right is fiddly: a character has to climb steps, slide along walls instead of sticking to them, not float off the top of a slope, and ride a moving platform; a camera behind it mustn't end up inside a wall. Solis has them ready:

  • CharacterBody (a built-in component) does the hard part: it moves a standing capsule as far as it can go, the way game characters move. It's what moveCharacter moves.
  • CharacterController (a ready-made component in Lust) reads the player's input and tells the CharacterBody where to go.
  • ThirdPersonCamera, FirstPersonCamera and RtsCamera (ready-made, in Lust) put the camera behind the character, in its eyes, or high above a map. FollowCamera2D follows the player in a 2D game.

They're written in Lust and their files are in your project's solis/kit/ folder, so you can read exactly what they do and copy them to make your own. Use them as they are to get going; change a copy when your game needs something different.

For a thing that's pushed around by physics (a ball, a crate) use a RigidBody instead: a character isn't moved by physics, it moves itself and pushes physics things out of its way.

How to use it#

Try the playground first. Make the playground… (press Space and type it, or use File › Learn) makes a new project with a level to walk around in: steps, a gentle ramp and one too steep to climb, crates to push, a moving platform to ride, and a character with the third-person camera. Press Play, click the Game panel, and walk with W A S D, look with the mouse, jump with Space, sprint with Shift. F6 saves the game and F7 loads it. Esc gives the editor the mouse back.

It has sounds too (Sound events): footsteps as the character walks (faster when it runs, made by the playground's Footsteps code), music, a radio on a crate whose chatter makes the music dip as you come near (the Mixer's Voice ducking Music), and a cave with a drip, where every step echoes (a reverb zone). The sounds are Solis's own, free to use for anything.

A character in your own area

  1. Add an entity for the character (Home › Empty, which adds an empty one, or a model of a person) with its feet where it should stand.

  2. In Properties, choose + Component › CharacterBody. A green capsule shows its shape when it's selected. Its feet are at the entity's origin.

  3. Make sure there's ground under it: an entity with a Collider, see Physics.

  4. In main.lst, fetch the ready-made components:

    fetch "solis/kit/character":[CharacterController];
fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[ThirdPersonCamera];
end
    // The kit's components are Lust. A game in Rust brings them in from a
// main.lst of three lines beside its Rust:
//
//     fetch "solis/kit/character":[CharacterController];
//     fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[ThirdPersonCamera];
//     end
    -- The kit's components are Lust. A game in Lua brings them in from a
-- main.lst of three lines beside its Lua files:
--
--     fetch "solis/kit/character":[CharacterController];
--     fetch "solis/kit/cameras":[ThirdPersonCamera];
--     end

    (For a 2D game, fetch FollowCamera2D and the kit's TopDownController instead: see Tile maps.)

  5. Add CharacterController to the character. Set its camera to the camera entity (next step).

  6. On the entity with the Camera component, add ThirdPersonCamera and set its target to the character.

  7. Press Play and click the Game panel.

The other cameras

  • FirstPersonCamera: set its body to the character. It sits at the eyes and turns the character with it, so untick the CharacterController's facesWhereItWalks (it would turn the other way).
  • RtsCamera: needs no character. It looks down on the map from above, as strategy games do.
  • FollowCamera2D, for a 2D game (a camera whose View is 2D: 2D: pixel-perfect): set its target to the player, and its bounds to the entity showing your tile map. It has no keys: it just follows.
    • The player can walk a little way from the middle (the deadZone, in metres across and up) before the camera moves, so small steps don't shake the picture.
    • Then it catches up smoothly in about smoothing seconds, easing in and stopping without going past (0 follows at once). Why: a camera glued to the player jerks with every step; a little slack and easing feels calm, as in farming and adventure games.
    • With bounds set, it never shows past the map's edges: near the edge the player walks towards the side of the screen instead. A map smaller than the view stays in the middle.
    • The picture stays crisp: Solis keeps the camera on whole pixels as it draws, whatever the camera does.
RTS cameraKeyboard and mouseGamepad
Move over the maparrow keysleft stick
Drag the maphold the middle mouse button and move the mouse
TurnAlt + left or right arrowright stick
Zoommouse wheel, Page Up and Page Downright and left triggers

These are the ready-made actions Pan, Drag, Turn and Zoom, so you can rebind them in File › Project settings › Input. A project made before these cameras existed doesn't have them yet: the Input page offers to add them.

Moving a character from your own code

walk(wanted) moves the component's character by wanted metres (target:walk(wanted) moves another), as far as it can: it climbs steps and slopes, slides along walls, pushes crates and rides moving platforms, and stops where it can't go. Two characters standing in one another (spawned on one spot, say) are pushed apart gently as they walk, rather than stuck together. It happens at the end of the tick, after physics has had game code's other changes. Call it once a tick with speed times dt, plus your own falling. Always multiply by dt: it's the tick's length at the game's speed, so the character slows down and stops with World:setGameSpeed like everything else. A walk without dt ignores the game's speed.

fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component Hopper {
    has {
        float fall = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        vec3 move = Input:axis(Action.Move);
        vec3 step = [move.x, move.y, 0];
        is grounded()? then {
            fall = 0;
            is Input:pressed(Action.Jump)? then {
                fall = 5;
            }
        } or {
            fall = fall - 20 * dt;
        }
        walk(step * 4 * dt + [0, 0, fall * dt]);
    }
}

pass Hopper;
end
use glam::Vec3;
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Hopper {
    fall: f32,
}

impl RustComponent for Hopper {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        let me = cx.me();
        let dt = dt as f32;
        let wanted = cx.host().action("Move").axis;
        let step = Vec3::new(wanted.x, wanted.y, 0.0);
        if cx.host().grounded(me) {
            self.fall = 0.0;
            if cx.host().action("Jump").pressed {
                self.fall = 5.0;
            }
        } else {
            self.fall -= 20.0 * dt;
        }
        cx.host().walk(me, step * 4.0 * dt + Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, self.fall * dt));
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Hopper = component("Hopper", {
    { "fall", "float", 0 },
})

function Hopper:update(dt)
    local move = solis.Input:axis("Move")
    local step = vec3(move.x, move.y, 0)
    if solis.entity.grounded(self.me) then
        self.fall = 0
        if solis.Input:pressed("Jump") then
            self.fall = 5
        end
    else
        self.fall = self.fall - 20 * dt
    end
    solis.entity.walk(self.me, step * 4 * dt + vec3(0, 0, self.fall * dt))
end

Why your own falling? Because how a character falls and jumps is part of how a game feels (floaty or snappy), so it's yours to choose. On the ground it stops falling (fall = 0): the CharacterBody keeps it to the ground going down steps and slopes (its Keeps to the ground setting).

In Lua the move is a vec3(x, y, z) (a table works too, but only with its parts named: { x = 1, y = 0, z = 0 }).

Settings#

CharacterBody (built-in)

SettingWhat it does
HeightFeet to head, metres. 1.8 suits a person.
RadiusHalf its width. 0.35 m suits a person; wider characters can't fit through narrow gaps.
Step heightThe tallest step it walks up without jumping. 0.35 m climbs stairs but not a table.
Steepest slopeThe steepest slope it walks up, in degrees; it slides down steeper ones. 45° is usual.
Keeps to the groundHow far down it stays on the ground walking down steps and slopes, instead of flying off them. 0 never.
MassHow hard it pushes crates it walks into.

CharacterController (ready-made)

SettingWhat it does
cameraThe camera following it: forward is the way that camera looks. Nothing: forward is the way the character faces.
walkSpeed, sprintSpeedMetres a second, walking and with Sprint held.
jumpHeightHow high a jump goes, metres.
gravityHow fast it falls. 20 feels snappier than real life's 9.81, as most games do.
facesWhereItWalksIt turns to face where it's walking (third person). Untick for first person.
turnSpeedHow fast it turns to face where it walks, degrees a second.

ThirdPersonCamera (ready-made)

SettingWhat it does
targetThe character it follows.
distanceHow far behind it stays, metres. A wall in between pulls it closer.
heightHow high above the character's feet it looks: about the head.
wheelZoomsTick it to let the mouse wheel (Zoom) change the distance, between closest and farthest. Off, the distance stays fixed.
lowest, highestHow far down and up the player can look, degrees.

FirstPersonCamera (ready-made): body (the character), eyes (how high its eyes are), turnsBody, lowest and highest.

RtsCamera (ready-made): focus (the point on the map it looks at), height, lowest and highest (how far it zooms), tilt (degrees it looks down), panSpeed and turnSpeed.

FollowCamera2D (ready-made): target (who it follows), bounds (an entity with a tile map it stays inside; empty: no edges), deadZone (how far, in metres across and up, the target can move from the middle before it follows; 1 and 0.75 to start), smoothing (about how many seconds it takes to catch up; 0.2 to start, 0 for at once), and speed (how fast it's moving now; you don't need to set it).

The fields at the bottom of each (fall, yaw, pitch) are how it's moving right now: how fast it's falling, and which way it's looking. While playing, Properties shows them changing. They're fields so a save game keeps them; you don't need to set them.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
WalkW A S D (left stick)
LookMouse (right stick)
JumpSpace (A)
SprintShift (left stick click)
Save and load, in the playgroundF6 and F7

All of these are the game's only while it has the mouse and keys (click the Game panel); see Input. The kit's actions (Move, Look, Jump, Sprint, Zoom, Pan, Turn, Drag) are always named in game code, so the kit works in a project that hasn't made them all; one your project hasn't made in File › Project settings › Input is never pressed.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the character doesn't move. Why: the game doesn't have the keys, or there's no ground under it (it fell). Fix: click the Game panel; give the floor a Collider.
  • Problem: W walks the wrong way. Why: the CharacterController's camera isn't set, so forward is the way the character faces. Fix: set it to the camera.
  • Problem: the character can't get up a step. Why: the step is taller than its Step height. Fix: raise Step height, or make the step lower.
  • Problem: it slides down a ramp it should walk up. Why: the ramp is steeper than Steepest slope. Fix: raise it, or make the ramp gentler.
  • Problem: my changes to solis/kit/character.lst disappeared. Why: Solis writes the solis/ folder again whenever the project opens, so it always matches this version of Solis. Fix: copy the file outside solis/ (say, player.lst), rename the component inside (component MyController), and fetch that instead.
  • Problem: the game slows down with a big crowd of characters. Why: each character's move looks around it for walls, steps and slopes, about 10 to 15 microseconds each. Solis works them out on every core at once, so a few hundred cost little, but thousands add up. Fix: for a huge horde, move the far-away ones yourself with moveTo and give a CharacterBody only to those near the player.
  • Problem: the first-person view spins when I walk. Why: both the camera and the controller are turning the character. Fix: untick the CharacterController's facesWhereItWalks.

Related#

  • Physics: colliders, rigid bodies, pushing things
  • Input: the actions, and rebinding them
  • Save games
  • Game code
  • Concepts: character controller, ready-made components
