Save games#

Save the whole game and load it back exactly as it was: every entity, every component's values, the lasers in flight, physics, sprites' clips, animators' states, tile maps as the game changed them, the clock, the time of day and the random numbers.

When to use it#

Whenever a player should be able to stop and carry on later: a quick-save key, a save point, a checkpoint before a boss. Solis saves everything for you, so you don't write any code to list what to keep, and nothing gets forgotten. A loaded game carries on exactly as the saved one would have: the same crate falls the same way, the same random numbers come up.

It's also a debugging tool: save just before something goes wrong, and you can load and watch it again and again.

How to use it#

From game code (in Lust, fetch "solis/world":Saves; then Saves:saveTo("quick"); in Lua, solis.Saves:saveTo("quick"); in Rust, cx.host().save_game("quick", false), with true to load):

fetch "solis/world":Saves;
fetch "solis/input":Input;
fetch "solis/project":Action;

component QuickSave {
    method update(float dt) {
        is Input:pressed(Action.QuickSave)? then {
            Saves:saveTo("quick");
        }
        is Input:pressed(Action.QuickLoad)? then {
            Saves:loadFrom("quick");
        }
    }
}

pass QuickSave;
end
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct QuickSave;

impl RustComponent for QuickSave {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, _dt: f64) {
        // The slot's name, then whether to load it (true) or save it (false).
        if cx.host().action("QuickSave").pressed {
            cx.host().save_game("quick", false);
        }
        if cx.host().action("QuickLoad").pressed {
            cx.host().save_game("quick", true);
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local QuickSave = component("QuickSave", {})

function QuickSave:update(dt)
    if solis.Input:pressed("QuickSave") then
        solis.Saves:saveTo("quick")
    end
    if solis.Input:pressed("QuickLoad") then
        solis.Saves:loadFrom("quick")
    end
end

Add the QuickSave and QuickLoad actions in File › Project settings › Input and bind them to keys of your choice (Input).

  • A slot is a save's name: letters, digits, _ and - (quick, slot_1, before-boss), but not a name Windows keeps for a device (CON, NUL, PRN, AUX, COM1, LPT1 and so on). Saving to a slot that has a save replaces it. A project keeps at most 100 saves, and 2 GB of them together; past that, game code can replace one but not add more (the Console says so).
  • Both happen at the end of the tick, after every component's update, like moves (what game code sees). A load replaces the whole game, so nothing else runs in that frame after it.
  • Asking for the same slot again in one tick saves once (a save is the whole game, so a Saves:saveTo in every unit's update would otherwise make thousands at a time). At most four slots are saved or loaded in one tick.
  • Loading doesn't run the game's starts again (the code outside components, and its fields' starting values): what they did already happened in the saved game.
  • Saves:saveTo, Saves:loadFrom and Input:rebind work from update and events, not while a component starts (the Console says so if you try).
  • A Saves:loadFrom from game code leaves the game the mouse and keys, so the player carries on at once; Debug › Load save gives them back to the editor.
  • Game-wide objects (a clock, the money: Game code) are kept with every field a component's could have, and loading gives them back. An object or field the code no longer has is left out, and the Console says which.
  • Physics is kept as each body's place and motion. Saving starts physics afresh from those, which a loaded game does too, so the loaded game carries on exactly as the saved one does (a stack of crates may settle by a hair as you save).

From the editor: Debug › Load save picks a save from the project's saves folder and plays from it, whether or not the game is running. Stop still puts the area back as it was before you pressed Play: a save is a moment in a game, not a change to your area. If you edit the area after loading, Stop offers to keep those edits as usual, and Keep makes them on your area from before Play, never on the save's (a change to an entity only the save had can't be kept; see Play mode).

Saves survive updates (Backups and upgrades): a save made by an earlier Solis loads in a later one, upgraded as it's read. A save is never refused just for being older, so a game's update never wipes its players' progress. The very first saves (format 1, from before the Phase 6 review) kept physics in a form Solis no longer reads, so things that were moving start at rest where they were, and the Console says so. A save is still refused when it was made by a newer Solis.

Your game's own versions: when your game changes in a way old saves don't fit (a new map, say), that's for your game to decide, not Solis. Keep a version number in a component's has block (int saveVersion = 3;), and check it in code after a load: carry on, put things right, or tell the player.

Where saves live: in the project's saves folder, one .solsave file per slot, beside project.solis. New projects keep this folder out of Git, since saves are your test plays, not part of the game. An exported game keeps players' saves in their own saved-games folder instead (Exporting for playtesting).

Settings#

Save games have no settings: everything is saved.

Shortcuts#

None of its own. A game chooses its own save and load keys through input actions.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the Console says the game wasn't saved because save games are kept in a project. Why: saves are files in a project's folder. Fix: open or make a project (File › New project).
  • Problem: "the saves folder is a link to somewhere else". Why: Solis only writes saves into a real folder in the project, so a project you downloaded can't send them elsewhere on your computer. Fix: delete the saves link (or move the real folder into the project).
  • Problem: "Couldn't load quick: it was saved by the project …". Why: a save belongs to the project that made it. Fix: load it in that project.
  • Problem: "Couldn't load …: it's damaged". Why: the file was cut short or changed (a save carries a checksum, so a damaged one is refused rather than half loaded). Fix: save again.
  • Problem: a value in my component isn't the same after loading. Why: a save keeps every field in a component's has block, but not other variables the code keeps for itself. Fix: put anything that must survive a load in has.
  • Problem: the Console says a component's saved values were left out. Why: the game's code has no component by that name any more (it was renamed or removed since the save). The rest of the save loads. Fix: nothing, if it was removed on purpose; if it was renamed, its values start fresh.
  • Problem: "Couldn't load …: it was made by a newer Solis". Why: someone saved it with a newer build. Fix: update Solis.
  • Problem: "The game wasn't saved: the tile map on … has grown too big to be loaded again". Why: a save keeps each tile map as the game has changed it, and a map is read back within the same limits as a map file: 64 MB and 12 million numbers, texts and symbols, which a number in a million and a half cells is past. A save that couldn't be loaded would be the player's progress lost, so it isn't written; the save in that slot before stays. Fix: keep values only on the cells that need them, or split the world into several maps.
  • Problem: "The game wasn't saved: it would be … MB". Why: a save can be at most 256 MB to load back, and this game is bigger. Fix: fewer entities or physics bodies.
  • Problem: loading ended my recording. Why: a recording plays back from Play, so it can't carry on across a load. What was recorded up to the load is saved in the recordings folder. Fix: record again from Play to record past it.
  • Problem: replaying a recording didn't change my saves. Why: a replay makes the same saves the recorded play did (so it plays out the same), but doesn't write them over your saves.

Related#

  • Game code
  • Input
  • Play mode
  • Concepts: save game, determinism, checksum

Exporting for playtesting#

Makes a folder holding your game, ready to zip and send to a friend, who plays it without the editor.

When to use it#

When you want someone else to try your game: a friend, a tester, or yourself on another computer. They get a folder with a program named after your game. Double-clicking it starts the game straight away, filling its window, with no launcher, no editor and nothing to install.

It's a playtest build, made in seconds, because the game's Lust and Lua code runs as it does when you press Play. A finished release with an installer comes later (the Build tab shows its place: Targets, Build, Installer and Your Rust code are unfinished parts). Until then, a game's own Rust code isn't built into an export.

How to use it#

  1. Open your project, and save the area your game starts in.
  2. Click Build in the tab bar (or Build in the Home ribbon's Project group, or search for Export for playtesting…). The Build tab is Export for playtesting as a page, with the Console on the shelf under it. The same settings are also in File › Project settings › Build.
  3. Check the settings (see the table below). They start from your project's name and the open area, and next time from what you chose last. The name, area and window are remembered with the project. The folder is remembered by Solis on this computer, so a project you got from someone else never decides where its export goes.
  4. Click Export at the end of the Export row (the big Export on the Build tab's ribbon does the same). The card beside the settings and the Console say where it went. Click Open folder on the card, or on the Build tab's ribbon, to see it.
  5. Zip that folder (in Windows Explorer, right-click it, then Send to > Compressed (zipped) folder) and send the zip.

Your friend unzips it (all of it, somewhere they can write, such as their Documents) and double-clicks <Game>.exe inside. Double-clicking it inside the zip doesn't work: Windows takes only the program out, without the game beside it.

What's in the folder, and why:

FileWhat it is
<Game>.exeThe program, named after your game. It's the same program as the editor: finding playtest.txt beside itself, it plays instead.
playtest.txtThe game's name, the area it starts in, and its first window.
game/Your project's files: code, areas, sprites, sounds, screens. The editor's own things stay out: its cache, saves, recordings, backups and Git's history.

Where the player's things go: everything that's the player's goes in their own folder, Saved Games/<Game> on Windows (next to other games' saves):

  • saves/: the game's save games;
  • settings.txt: the player's settings (text size, UI size, fullscreen, window size), kept from one start to the next;
  • log.txt: warnings and mistakes the game reported, like the Console's (past 1 MB it starts again, keeping the one before as log.old.txt);
  • crash log.txt: written if the program stops unexpectedly. It says what happened and the last things the game said. Ask your playtesters to send it to you.

Quitting: give your pause menu a Quit button that calls Window:quit() (see Game code). The game closes at the end of that tick. While you play in the editor, play stops instead, and the Console says the exported game would close. The window's close button always works too.

Settings#

SettingWhat it does
Game's nameThe program's name (Farm.exe), the window's title, and the player's saves folder (Saved Games/Farm). Characters Windows can't use in file names are taken out. Keep it the same between builds, so saves carry over.
Starts inThe area the game opens in.
Into the folderWhere the export goes. Solis suggests a new dated folder each time, beside your last export (in Documents the first time), so older builds stay. A folder that already has files in it isn't used, and nor is one inside your project. If the suggested folder has files in already (a second export the same day), the export goes in a numbered folder beside it, ending (2), then (3); the page and the Console say which. A folder you typed or chose with … is used exactly as given, or refused. Solis doesn't look inside any folder until you click Export.
WindowWindowed or Fullscreen, and the window's size, when the game first starts. After that, the player's own choice (in your game's menu, or with Alt+Enter) is kept.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Switch the exported game between fullscreen and a windowAlt+Enter

In an exported game, every key is the game's, Esc included.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the game says "The game can't start: its code has mistakes." Why: the exported code doesn't compile. Fix: fix the mistakes in the Problems panel, then export again.
  • A game needs no code of its own. A level made only of the editor's own components (sprites, physics, animators, sounds) exports and plays as it does when you press Play. The files Solis writes in assets/solis/, which describe the engine to game code, don't count as your code.
  • Problem: "already has files in it". Why: exports never mix with, or replace, anything, and a folder you chose yourself is never swapped for another. Fix: choose a new folder, or empty that one.
  • Problem: after updating Solis, the page suggests a folder in Documents again, not beside your last export. Why: where a game went used to be written in the project's own folder. A project can come from someone else, so that file could point your export at a folder of their choosing, even one on another computer. Solis now remembers it itself, on this computer, and no longer reads it from the project. Fix: choose your folder once more; it's remembered from then on.
  • Problem: you exported to a folder on another computer (\\server\share\…), and next time the page suggests Documents. Why: only a folder on this computer's own drives is suggested again, so opening the page never reaches for another computer. Fix: type or choose the network folder each time.
  • Problem: the game says "The game's files can't be read", or "The game stopped". Why: the game folder is missing or damaged, or it's somewhere the game can't write (the first start writes a cache into game/). Fix: unzip the whole export again, somewhere like Documents. The message names the log with more.
  • Problem: the export is big. Why: it holds the program and everything in the project's assets, used or not. Fix: move files the game doesn't use out of the assets.
  • Problem: Windows warns about the program when your friend opens it. Why: it isn't signed, as programs from big companies are. Fix: they choose More info › Run anyway. Send builds only to people who trust you.
  • Problem: saves from an older build are gone. Why: the game's name changed, so the saves folder did too. Fix: keep the name the same.
  • Problem: Rust components of your own don't run. Why: building a game's own Rust code comes with the full export (Your Rust code on the Build tab's ribbon, not built yet). Fix: use Lust or Lua for now.

Related#

  • Screens: the player's settings and a pause menu.
  • The UI sample: a pause menu with Quit, ready to export.
  • Save games.
  • Concepts: player setting, playtest.

Your first game: the turret sample#

A small game to read, play and change: a turret shoots at a drone, and the drone's health, armour and sparks react. It's written in all three of Solis's languages, which talk to each other through events.

When to use it#

Right after reading Game code, or instead of it if you learn best from a working example. Everything in it is ordinary game code you can change while it runs.

How to use it#

  1. Choose Make the sample game… (press Space and type it, or use File › Learn) and pick an empty folder. Solis makes a project there called Turret sample, opens it, and opens its area.
  2. Press Play. The sample has no models yet, so its story is told in the Console (later phases give it models). Watch the Console: every half second the turret fires. The drone's armour dents three times ("Sparks fly from Drone: 2 armour plates left"), and after eight hits the drone is destroyed and drops to the ground.
  3. While it plays, click the Game panel and press P (or Start on a controller): the game stops and a pause menu shows (the Pauser component on the Game entity, and ui/pauseMenu.lst). Resume carries on; Quit leaves it stopped with a note. See Game screens.
  4. Press Stop, then open the code from the Library's Code tab.

What's in it#

The turret (Lust, in main.lst) has a target (the drone, set in Properties), ammo, damage and a cooldown. Each tick, update counts the cooldown down. When it reaches zero, it fires: send Hit(this, damage) to target;.

In the sample each component is written in one language: the turret and Health in Lust, Armour in Rust, Sparks in Lua. The switch above each example shows it in all three, so you can read the whole sample in the language you know.

event Hit(entity by, float damage);

component Turret {
    has {
        entity target = nothing;
        int ammo = 12;
        float damage = 2.5;
        float cooldown = 0.5;
        float reload = 0;
    }

    method update(float dt) {
        reload = reload - dt;
        is reload <= 0 && ammo > 0? then {
            send Hit(this, damage) to target;
            ammo = ammo - 1;
            reload = cooldown;
        }
    }
}

pass Turret;
end
use reflect::{EntityId, Value};
use script::{Context, RustComponent};

pub struct Turret {
    target: Option<EntityId>,
    ammo: i64,
    damage: f64,
    cooldown: f64,
    reload: f64,
}

impl RustComponent for Turret {
    fn update(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, dt: f64) {
        self.reload -= dt;
        if self.reload <= 0.0 && self.ammo > 0 {
            let me = cx.me();
            let hit = vec![Value::Entity(Some(me)), Value::Float(self.damage)];
            cx.send(self.target, "Hit", hit);
            self.ammo -= 1;
            self.reload = self.cooldown;
        }
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Turret = component("Turret", {
    { "target", "entity" },
    { "ammo", "int", 12 },
    { "damage", "float", 2.5 },
    { "cooldown", "float", 0.5 },
    { "reload", "float", 0 },
})

function Turret:update(dt)
    self.reload = self.reload - dt
    if self.reload <= 0 and self.ammo > 0 then
        solis.send(self.target, "Hit", self.me, self.damage)
        self.ammo = self.ammo - 1
        self.reload = self.cooldown
    end
end

The drone carries three components, one in each language. Each reacts to the events it cares about:

ComponentLanguageReacts toDoes
HealthLust (main.lst)HitTakes the damage; at 0 it sends Destroyed to the drone.
ArmourRust (armour.rs)HitDents a plate, and sends Dented with the plates left.
SparksLua (sparks.lua)Dented, DestroyedSays so in the Console; when destroyed, drops the drone to the ground.

The drone's armour (in the sample, Rust: armour.rs) dents a plate at each hit and says how many are left:

event Hit(entity by, float damage);
event Dented(int platesLeft);

component Armour {
    has {
        int plates = 3;
    }

    on Hit(entity by, float damage) {
        is plates > 0? then {
            plates = plates - 1;
            send Dented(plates) to this;
        }
    }
}

pass Armour;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Armour {
    plates: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Armour {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Hit" || self.plates == 0 {
            return false;
        }
        self.plates -= 1;
        let me = cx.me();
        cx.send(Some(me), "Dented", vec![Value::Int(self.plates)]);
        true
    }

    // values() and set(), and the RustKind that registers it: see armour.rs.
}
local Armour = component("Armour", {
    { "plates", "int", 3 },
})

function Armour:on_Hit(by, damage)
    if self.plates > 0 then
        self.plates = self.plates - 1
        solis.send(self.me, "Dented", self.plates)
    end
end

And its sparks (in the sample, Lua: sparks.lua) react to each dent:

fetch "solis/world":World;

event Dented(int platesLeft);

component Sparks {
    has {
        int shown = 0;
    }

    on Dented(int platesLeft) {
        shown = shown + 1;
        World:say("Sparks fly from " + name() + ": " + platesLeft.text() + " armour plates left.");
    }
}

pass Sparks;
end
use reflect::Value;
use script::{Context, Event, RustComponent};

pub struct Sparks {
    shown: i64,
}

impl RustComponent for Sparks {
    fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, event: &Event) -> bool {
        if event.name != "Dented" {
            return false;
        }
        self.shown += 1;
        let plates = match event.values.first() {
            Some(Value::Int(left)) => *left,
            _ => 0,
        };
        let me = cx.me();
        let name = cx.host().name(me).unwrap_or_default();
        cx.host().say(&format!("Sparks fly from {name}: {plates} armour plates left."));
        true
    }

    // values() and set(): as Mover's in Game code, under Components.
}
local Sparks = component("Sparks", {
    { "shown", "int", 0 },
})

function Sparks:on_Dented(platesLeft)
    self.shown = self.shown + 1
    solis.World:say("Sparks fly from " .. solis.entity.name(self.me) .. ": " .. platesLeft .. " armour plates left.")
end

The events are declared once, in Lust (event Hit(entity by, float damage);). Lust checks its own sends before the game runs, so a wrongly-sent event in Lust is a mistake in Problems. When Lua or Rust sends one with the wrong values, it isn't sent, and the Console names the component that sent it.

Things to try#

  • While it plays, change the turret's damage to 10 in Properties: the drone goes down in two hits.
  • While it plays, change reload = cooldown; in main.lst to reload = cooldown / 5; and save. The turret fires five times faster at once, keeping the ammo it has left. (Changing a starting value instead, such as cooldown = 0.5, doesn't change a turret that's already running: running components keep their values. Set it in Properties for that.)
  • In sparks.lua, change what it says and save while it plays: the next dent says the new words.
  • Give the drone more armour: select it and set Plates to 10.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: I changed armour.rs and nothing changed. Why: Solis can't build a game's own Rust yet (that comes with the full export, which isn't built yet). Until then, the Armour built into Solis runs, and the Console says your changes don't. Fix: try changes in the Lust and Lua instead.
  • Problem: "Couldn't make the sample game". Why: the folder is already a project, or already has a file where the sample's would go (such as assets/main.lst); Solis never replaces your files. Fix: choose an empty folder.

Related#

  • Game code: components, events and changing code while it runs, in detail
  • Play mode
  • Concepts: component, event, tick
← Previous · Chapter 50Exporting for playtestingNext → · Chapter 52The Console

The Console#

Messages from the editor and the engine, and a command line for doing things by typing.

When to use it#

  • To see what's happening: the Console reports the editor starting, the graphics card in use, models imported and reloaded, files saved, and anything that went wrong. Warnings and errors from the libraries Solis is built on (the graphics layer, for example) show here too, named after the library.
  • To do things by typing: some jobs are quicker typed than clicked, such as selecting every entity called "Lamp", or setting the exact position of ten things at once. Everything a command changes is an ordinary undo step, the same as doing it with the mouse.

How to use it#

Reading messages

  1. Each message shows its time, how serious it is as a word in its colour (INFO, WARN in amber, ERROR in red, with the row faintly tinted), and the text. A long message is cut short: click it to read it in full in a strip below the list (with Copy, to paste it somewhere), and click it again or Close to put the strip away.
  2. The three buttons at the top count the messages of each kind: information (ⓘ), warnings (⚠) and errors (✕). Click one to hide those messages, and again to show them.
  3. Type in Search to show only messages containing that text (capitals don't matter).
  4. Clear empties the Console.

Typing commands

  1. Press ' (on a Norwegian keyboard, the key with ' and * next to Æ) to jump to the command line at the bottom of the Console. You can also click in it.
  2. Type a command, such as select Crate, and press Enter. The Console repeats it after a ›, then answers: what it found, or, if something's wrong, why (in red).
  3. The command line keeps the keyboard, ready for the next command. Press Esc or click elsewhere to leave it.
  4. Up and Down bring back earlier commands. Solis remembers the last 100, even after it's closed.
  5. Tab finishes what you're typing: a command's name, an entity's name after select, or a component's setting after get and set. If several fit, they're listed at the right of the command line, after a Tab key; type a little more and press Tab again.

Names never care about capitals. A name with spaces goes in quotes: select "Point light 1".

Commands#

CommandWhat it does
helpLists every command. help set says how one is used.
clearEmpties the Console.
select Crate LampSelects every entity with those names (or IDs). select all selects everything, select none nothing.
find harLists the entities whose names contain "har", with their IDs.
framePoints the camera at the selection, like F.
new Harbour wallAdds an empty entity where the camera looks, named as you say, and selects it.
deleteDeletes the selection and everything under it.
duplicateDuplicates the selection, like Ctrl + D.
get TransformShows a component's settings on the selected entity. get Light.color shows one. While the game plays, it shows them as the game has them now.
values HeroShows every component of the entity called Hero (or, with no name, the selected one) as it is now. While the game plays, that's as game code has changed it: the score, the hero's health, where things are. Properties shows the same for the selected entity.
set Transform.position 0 0 2Changes a setting on every selected entity that has that component, as one undo step. While the game plays, the running game takes the value as well, whatever it had made of it: set Score.points 0 starts the score again, even though the area held 0 all along (it's get that shows the game's value). Stop then lists it with your other changes.
undo, redoLike Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y.
saveSaves the area, like Ctrl + S.
look unlitChooses the viewport's look: standard, stylized or unlit.
tool rotateChooses a tool: select, move, rotate, scale or transform.
play, pause, step, stopLike the buttons at the top (step runs one tick while paused): see Play mode.
statsCounts the entities, models, lights and triangles, and says how fast the editor is drawing.
seed, seed 42, seed newThe seed the running game started with (where its random numbers come from), and the one in use if game code or a load changed it since. With a number, every Play starts from that seed, so a play can be repeated; seed new gives each Play a new one again.
ui test, ui test keep, ui test whole, ui test offWhile playing, shows a sample HUD over the Game panel (a day box with the date and time, money, an energy bar with its label and a hotbar), laid out by a scale rule: grow with the screen, keep its size, or whole steps for pixel art. Make the panel bigger or smaller to see each part stay pinned to its corner. Game UI you make yourself is a screen.
checksumWhile playing, the game's checksums at this tick: two plays that agree at the same tick are in exactly the same state.

Values for set:

  • Numbers: set Light.strength 250. A unit after the number is fine (2m).
  • Three numbers (positions, scales): 0 0 2 or 0,0,2. Two for a game code's vec2: 3 4.5.
  • Rotations: three angles in degrees, around X, Y and Z, as Properties shows them: set Transform.rotation 0 0 90.
  • Colours: #ff8800 (as in a paint program), or three numbers from 0 to 1. A game code's colour can be see-through: #ff880080, or a fourth number for how solid it is (get shows it the same way).
  • Choices: one of the choices Properties offers, such as set Light.kind spot.
  • On or off: on, off, yes, no, true, false.
  • Models and entities can't be typed yet; choose them in Properties.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Jump to the command line' (not while typing in another field)
Run the commandEnter
Earlier and later commandsUp, Down
Finish a nameTab
Leave the command lineEsc

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: pressing ' types a ' instead of jumping to the command line. Why: another text field (a search box, a name) has the keyboard. Fix: press Esc or click the viewport first.
  • Problem: "nothing is called …". Why: no entity has exactly that name. Fix: find with part of the name lists the real names; Tab finishes them for you.
  • Problem: set says "nothing selected has a Light". Why: set only changes entities that have that component; it never adds one. Fix: select the right entities, or add the component in Properties first.
  • Problem: "No sound: couldn't open the sound card …". Why: Solis found no sound card it could use (none plugged in, or another program holding it). Fix: nothing is broken, and everything else works. Plug in speakers or a headset: Solis tries again every 30 seconds and says "Sound is on." when it finds one.
  • The Console keeps the newest 2,000 messages. Messages from other libraries that repeat every frame are shown once.
  • Mistakes in the area itself (a missing model, say) are listed in the Problems panel, beside the Console.

Related#

  • Undo and redo
  • Entities and components
  • Keyboard shortcuts
  • Interface tour
  • Concepts: command, console

Problems#

A list of the mistakes found in your game's code (with the file and line) and in the open area (naming the entity each is on).

When to use it#

When something in the area doesn't look right, or the Problems tab shows a number beside its name. Problems are things Solis can't fix by itself, usually because files changed outside it: a model deleted in Explorer, an area merged by Git, a component from a newer version of your game's code. The area still opens and saves: nothing is lost, but something needs your attention.

How to use it#

  1. Click the Problems tab (beside the Console). The number on the tab says how many there are; with none, the tab has no number.
  2. Mistakes in the game's code come first, each with its file, line and column: click one to open the file in your code editor. Then come the area's, each naming its entity and what's wrong with it. Point at a line to read it all.
  3. Click an area line to select its entity. The Area panel unfolds to show it, and Properties shows its settings, ready to fix.
  4. Fix it, and the line goes away by itself: Solis looks again whenever the area or the project changes.

What it finds#

ProblemWhy it happensWhat to do
main.lst, line 6:15: …A mistake in the game's code: a misspelt name, text where a number should be, a missing }. The line and column (how far along the line) say where.Click it to open the file, fix it and save.
The game's code starts at main.lst …There are Lust files but no main.lst in assets.Make assets/main.lst and fetch the other files from it.
X's model isn't in the projectThe model's file was deleted, or never committed to Git (with its .solmeta file).Put the file back (or commit it), or choose another model in Properties, or delete the entity.
X's Model has no model chosenA Model component was added but never given a model.Choose one in Properties, or remove the component.
X's sprite sheet isn't in the project / X's Sprite has no sprite sheet chosenThe sprite's Aseprite file was deleted or never committed, or no sheet was chosen.Put the file back, or choose a sheet in Properties.
X rests between pixelsIn a 2D game, a sprite was placed at a spot that isn't a whole pixel (snapping off, or a typed place). The game draws it on the nearest pixel, so it may seem to jump a pixel as it moves.Move it with snapping to pixels on, or type a whole number of pixels.
X has a … component that isn't knownThe area was saved by a newer Solis, or names a component from game code that isn't built yet. The component is kept exactly as it was, so saving loses nothing.Usually nothing: it comes back to life when the code that defines it is there. Remove it if it's left over.
X is a copy of an assembly that isn't in the projectThe assembly's file was deleted or not committed.Put the file back, or unpack the copy to keep it as ordinary entities.
X's parent isn't in the areaUsually a Git merge that kept a child but not its parent.Drag it onto another entity in the Area panel, or onto empty space to make it stand alone.
X is inside itselfEntities are under each other in a loop, so none of them is anywhere in the tree. Area files with such a loop are put right as they open (see the tips below), so this is rare. Until it's fixed, each stands alone, in the editor and the game alike.Drag it onto another entity in the Area panel, or onto empty space to make it stand alone.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: opening an area, the Console says X was inside itself: its parents led back to it. It's now at the top level. Why: the file put entities inside each other in a loop, which no tree can be. It's usually a Git merge that combined two moves: one put A under B while the other put B under A. Solis moves one entity of the loop to the top level and leaves the rest under it; with many loops it names the first five and counts the rest. Fix: drag it to where it belongs in the Area panel and save. The file itself isn't changed until you save.
  • Problem: models show as missing for a moment after opening a project. Why: Solis is still listing the project's files. Fix: nothing; they disappear as soon as the Library is ready.
  • Problem: a code mistake stays after I fixed it. Why: Solis checks again when a file in assets is saved. Fix: make sure you saved the file inside the project's assets folder.

Related#

  • Game code
  • The Console
  • Projects and the Library
  • Saving areas
  • Concepts: entity, component, assembly

The Profiler#

Shows where each frame's time goes, so you can see what makes a game or the editor slow.

When to use it#

A game feels slow, or you want to know how much more it can take: more units, more lights, more code. A frame is one picture on screen; at 60 frames a second each one has about 16.7 milliseconds (ms, thousandths of a second). The Profiler shows how those milliseconds are spent, on the CPU (the computer's processor, which runs game code and the editor) and the GPU (the graphics card, which draws). Fix the biggest part first.

How to use it#

  1. Click Debug in the tab bar: the Profiler fills the middle (the Game is a tab beside it), with the Console and Problems on the shelf.
  2. Press Play, or move around the viewport: the Profiler measures every frame the editor draws. When nothing moves, Solis doesn't draw (the viewport says Idle), so nothing new is measured.
  3. The frame-time graph along the top shows the last 240 frames, a bar each, newest on the right. The dashed lines are 60 and 30 frames a second: a bar above a line is a frame too slow for it, and bars over 60 frames a second's budget are lighter. Click a bar to pick that frame: it turns the accent colour, and the line at the top right says its number and time.
  4. The timeline under it shows the frame picked (or the newest): the CPU's parts laid end to end along a ruler of milliseconds, and under them the GPU's. A part long enough has its name on it. The lanes for threads aren't built yet.
  5. Statistics on the right are averaged over the last 60 frames: the CPU's and the GPU's time a frame (each with a bar, its share of 60 frames a second's 16.7 ms), draw calls, triangles, model copies in view, what was sent to the graphics card, entities and game components running.
  6. CPU and GPU on the ribbon hide or show those lanes and figures.

What the parts mean#

PartWhat it is
Game codeYour Lust, Lua and Rust components: their updates, events, and taking in changes made while playing.
WorldThe game's world: stepping its clock, working out where things are, taking in the area's changes.
Preparing to drawWorking out what each view shows: which models where, the lights.
Drawing (CPU)Handing that to the graphics card.
SoundThe game's sounds: choosing which are heard, placing them, the buses.
EditorEverything else: the panels, the mouse and keys, the interface.
GPU: shadows, models, the last passThe graphics card's own time: the sun's shadows, the models and sky, then exposure and colour. Measured only on cards that offer it; the Profiler says when yours doesn't.
Projectiles drawnHow many lasers and other projectiles the Game tab drew. Shown when there are some.
The countsModel copies in view, copies casting shadows into it, triangles, draw calls (one per model part, however many copies), and how much was sent to the graphics card. Copies out of view aren't drawn at all (culling), and copies that didn't move aren't sent again, so a still scene sends next to nothing.

The CPU and the GPU work at the same time, each on its own frame, so the slower of the two sets the frame rate, not their sum.

Shortcuts#

ActionShortcut
Pick a frame to look atClick its bar in the graph

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: Game code is the biggest part. Why: many components, or one doing a lot each tick. Fix: do less each tick (check things every few ticks, not every one), or move the busiest code to Rust.
  • Problem: the GPU's times say they aren't measured. Why: your graphics card or its driver doesn't offer timestamps. Fix: the CPU's numbers still work; update the graphics driver, which often adds them.
  • Problem: Preparing to draw goes up when I turn the camera towards the crowd. Why: only what's in view is drawn, so looking at more draws more. Fix: nothing to fix; it's the view that counts, not the size of the area.
  • Problem: the numbers jump while nothing changes. Why: other programs share the computer. Fix: read Statistics' averages, not single bars.

Related#

  • Play mode
  • Game code
  • Concepts: frame, CPU, GPU, frames a second
← Previous · Chapter 53ProblemsNext → · Chapter 55The benchmark: how much can this computer play?

The benchmark: how much can this computer play?#

Two fleets of ships flying loops and firing lasers, in three sizes, so you can see what your computer keeps at 60 frames a second.

When to use it#

  • Before you plan a big game: see how many units and projectiles your computer (and your players' computers) can take.
  • After changing your graphics card, driver or settings: compare the numbers.
  • When something feels slow: if the benchmark is fine, the slowness is in your own game, and the Profiler shows where.

How to use it#

  1. Make the benchmark… (press Space and type it, or use File › Learn) and choose an empty folder. Solis makes a new project there and opens it on target.solarea.
  2. Press Play. The ships appear over the first few frames (500 a tick, so no frame stalls), then fly and fire.
  3. Open the Profiler (beside the Console) to see the frame's time, and where it goes.
  4. Press Stop, open another area from the Library, and play that.
AreaShipsLasers in flightWhat it shows
target.solarea2,000about 20,000Solis's target: should hold 60 frames a second.
stress.solarea10,000about 100,000Far past it: should stay playable (30 frames a second or better) without stutter.
ceiling.solarea1,000, then moreten per shipAdds 1,000 ships every few seconds while it holds 60 frames a second, then says in the Console where it ended: "This computer keeps 60 frames a second up to about 14,000 ships and 140,000 lasers."

The ceiling run measures for two seconds after each step settles, so it takes a minute or two. Keep the window in front while it runs; the frame rate of a window in the background says little.

What's in it#

Everything is ordinary Solis, so you can read and change it:

  • ships/fighter.glb: a ship model Solis made (about 2,000 triangles, with levels of detail), and ships/fighter.solassembly, an assembly of it with the Ship component.
  • main.lst: the game code. Ship flies its loop and fires a laser six times a second; Fleets makes the ships with World:spawn; Ceiling is the ceiling run, reading frameTime().
  • The three areas: the sun and sky, a camera, and one entity whose component makes the fleets. Change Ships on it in Properties to try your own number.

Tips and common problems#

  • Problem: the frame rate is stuck at 60 even with few ships. Why: your screen shows 60 pictures a second, and Solis waits for it. Fix: nothing to fix: 60 is the goal. Ships past that are what the ceiling run finds.
  • Problem: the ceiling run's number changes between runs. Why: other programs share the computer. Fix: close what you can and run it twice; the higher number is closer to what the computer can do.
  • Problem: the first frames after Play are slow. Why: the ships are being made, 500 a tick. Fix: watch the numbers once all are made.

Related#

  • The Profiler
  • Game code: World:spawn, World:fire and World:frameTime
  • Levels of detail
  • Concepts: frame, frames a second, CPU and GPU

All but Ctrl + Space don't work while you're typing in a field: there, Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y undo the typing instead. See Undo and redo.

Where the pointer rests decides what a key acts on, so one press never does two things. With the pointer over a tab that edits a file of its own (Clips and Frames, Animator, Tileset, Atlas Crop, the UI editor's Canvas and Elements), the keys are that tab's alone: undo and redo, Delete, Ctrl + D and Esc act on what the tab shows, as its table above says, and never on the area as well. The area's other keys (the tools' and the tile painter's keys, F, F2, Ctrl + A, and X, Y, Z and L) wait until the pointer is back over the viewport or another panel. Over the Map tab, undo and redo are the map's, and every other key is still the area's; the same goes for Properties while it shows a tileset's terrains, where undo and redo are that tileset's. On the UI tab, Properties shows the screen's settings, so over it the keys are the screen's, as over Elements: Delete removes the picked piece, never an entity. On a tab that doesn't show the area (Library, Audio, Debug, Build), the area's keys, undo and redo among them, rest too, since what they would change isn't on screen: a Delete over the Mixer never deletes an entity you can't see. They still work over the Area list and Properties wherever those are, and over the Library, F2 and Delete rename and delete the file picked there. New, open and save, the search and Ctrl + Space work wherever the pointer is.

The search list#

Space, or a click on Search or run a command in the tab bar, opens it (the box shows the key at its right end); see the Interface tour. These keys are the ones Solis has always had: the design the editor's look follows shows other keys in its pictures, and Solis keeps its own (decision 0103↗).

ActionShortcut
Open the search (with nothing being typed)Space
Narrow the listType part of a name
Choose a resultUp, Down
Do what's chosenEnter, or click a result
Close the searchEsc, or click outside it

Over the Frames tab, Space plays and stops the clip instead, so point somewhere else first.

The list shows each thing's shortcut beside it, so it is also the quickest place to look a key up. It finds the things without a button on the ribbon too, such as New area, Open area… and Save area as… (on the area's tab: its + and a right-click), Reset layout (File › Preferences), the examples (File › Learn), and showing or hiding the viewport's corner controls (the Show ▾ pill).
